pages.title: Our Standard for Lesson Plans and Worksheets
pages.metaTitle: Our Standard for ESL Lesson Plans and Worksheets
pages.description: What every ESL lesson plan and worksheet here must have before it is published: CEFR levels, aims as learner outcomes, and answer keys on every sheet.
pages.keywords: ESL lesson plan standard, CEFR lesson plan, what makes a good ESL worksheet, lesson plan components

hero.text: Every plan and worksheet in this section meets these requirements before it is published. They draw on the CEFR, established lesson-planning practice and published readability guidance.

blocks.heading: Levels
text: Everything is set at a level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR): A1, A2, B1, B2, C1 or C2. The level is stated on the page, and the language of every instruction is at or below it, because instructions a learner cannot read defeat the worksheet.

blocks.heading: Every lesson plan has
bullets: **At a glance:** level, learners, length, skills, language focus, materials and preparation time.
**Aims written as learner outcomes:** what learners will be able to do by the end, not what the teacher will cover.
**A language analysis:** meaning with concept-checking questions, form, pronunciation, and the problems learners usually have, each with a solution.
**A staged procedure:** every stage with an aim, a time and an interaction pattern; controlled practice before freer practice; key instructions and instruction-checking questions written out.
**Support and stretch,** and **adaptations** for a large class, a class with no photocopier, an online class and a different age group.
**A way to check learning,** homework, and a matching worksheet.

blocks.heading: Every worksheet has
bullets: Its full content on its own web page, not only a download.
Three to five tasks, graded from recognition to controlled use to freer use, each with a short instruction and an example item.
An answer key and teacher's notes: timing, common mistakes, how to use it and an extension.
A readable layout: a clear sans-serif font, generous line spacing, short lines, left-aligned text, and nothing that depends on colour, so it prints in black and white.

blocks.heading: Material for every classroom
bullets: **Original:** written by RCF English. Nothing is copied from a coursebook, another website or a published test.
**International:** names, places and situations from many countries, and ordinary everyday topics that suit a classroom anywhere, avoiding subjects that are sensitive in many countries.
**British spelling,** with American forms noted where learners often meet them.

blocks.heading: Quality before quantity
text: Each page is written for one real teaching purpose and read through in full before it is published. New material goes up in small, finished batches, and each page shows the date it was last reviewed.

blocks.heading: Free and premium
text: Every free lesson and worksheet is complete enough to teach from. Premium packs, when they are available, add convenience - editable files, slides and whole-unit bundles - never the part of a lesson that makes it work.

blocks.heading: Advertising
text: Where advertising appears, it is labelled, it sits only between sections, and it never appears inside a lesson, inside a worksheet or beside a button. It does not print.

pages.teaches: The first and second conditional in English

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the first and second conditionals for B1: learners meet the two forms through real decisions, discover that the difference is how likely the speaker thinks it is, and finish by arguing their way through dilemmas.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: It deals with the mistake that survives years of study - *if I will go* - and with the question that follows every explanation: how unlikely does something have to be?

items.definition: B1; the zero conditional is revised in the lead-in
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, teach the first conditional only and use the second in a later lesson.
Speaking, reading and writing
First conditional for real future possibilities and second conditional for unreal or unlikely ones, with the form of both and the comma rule
Test-teach-test: learners use both forms first, so you teach the difference they actually need
The dilemma cards or the board, the worksheet
10 minutes

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to talk about future possibilities with the first conditional and about unreal or unlikely situations with the second, choosing between them according to how likely they think the situation is.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to form both conditionals correctly, with no will or would in the if-clause.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to punctuate a conditional sentence written in either order.

blocks.title: The text: "Three decisions"
text: ONE. Dilan has an examination on Monday and his cousin's wedding is on Sunday. He says: "If I go to the wedding, I won't have enough time to revise. But if I stay at home, my aunt will be upset." - TWO. Amina is looking at a job in another city. "If they offer me the job, I'll take it," she says. "It starts next month." - THREE. Her brother is listening. "If I had a job like that," he says, "I would move tomorrow. But nobody is offering me anything!" - Notice: Amina may really get the job. Her brother has no offer at all.
**Gist question:** Which of the three speakers is talking about something that may really happen, and which is imagining?
**Detail questions:** (1) What are Dilan's two choices? (2) When does Amina's job start? (3) Has her brother been offered a job? (4) Why does the brother say "would" and Amina says "will"?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: The first conditional is for a real possibility in the future: the speaker thinks it may well happen. *If they offer me the job, I'll take it* - an offer is expected.
The second conditional is for something unreal now, or unlikely in the future: *If I had a job like that, I would move* - he has no such job.
The difference is not about time. Both can be about the future. It is about what the speaker thinks of the chances, and the same situation can take either form depending on the speaker's view.
The zero conditional is a third, simpler case, for things that are always true: *If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "If they offer me the job, I'll take it." Is an offer possible?
Does she have the job now?
"If I had a job like that, I would move." Does he have the job?
Is he likely to get one?
So which sentence shows more hope?

blocks.heading: Form
rows: If + present simple, + will / won't + verb
**If I go** to the wedding, **I won't have** time to revise.
If + past simple, + would / wouldn't + verb
**If I had** a job like that, **I would move**.
The if-clause may come second, with no comma
I would move **if I had** a job like that.
What will / would you do if ...?
**What would you do if** you lost your phone?

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: One punctuation rule does all of it: when the if-clause comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes second, no comma. Also note *were* in the second conditional: *If I were you* is the form expected in exams, though *if I was* is very common in speech.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **'ll and 'd are easy to miss**: *I'll take it* /aɪlteɪkɪt/ and *I'd move* /aɪdmuːv/. Learners who never hear them never produce them, so drill the contractions, not the full forms.
**would is weak** inside a sentence: /wəd/. It is strong only in a short answer: *Yes, I **would**.*
**The comma is a pause**, and the voice rises before it: *If I had a job like that ↗, I would move ↘.*

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: will in the if-clause: *If I will go to the wedding ...*
The mistake of the lesson, and it survives for years. One rule, boarded and drilled: no will and no would after if. Many first languages allow it, so expect it.
Mixing the two halves: *If I go, I would take it.*
Board the two patterns one above the other and show that each sentence keeps to one line.
Choosing the second conditional to sound polite about a real plan: *If I would have time tomorrow ...*
Ask the CCQ: is it possible? If yes, use the first. Politeness comes from *could* and *might*, not from the second conditional.
Give the single rule and practise it in both orders in Task 4.
"How unlikely does it have to be?"
An honest answer: it is the speaker's choice. *If I win the lottery* takes either form, and the second sounds more realistic about the odds. Let learners hear both and decide.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: First and Second Conditionals, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in: what always happens?
text: **Aim:** To revise the zero conditional and bring if-sentences into the room.
Write a half-sentence on the board: *If you don't water a plant ...* and let the class finish it.
Two or three more: *If you heat ice ... If you mix blue and yellow ...*
In pairs, learners write one of their own and read it to another pair. Keep it quick.

stages.name: Test: your own two sentences
text: **Aim:** To find out what learners already do with both forms.
Two prompts on the board: *Finish these. (a) If it rains tomorrow, ... (b) If I lived in another country, ...*
Learners write both, then compare with a partner.
Walk round and write down what they produce. This is the evidence that shapes the next stage.

stages.name: Teach: three decisions
text: **Aim:** To clarify the difference in meaning, then the form of each.
Learners read the three short situations and answer the gist question in pairs: who may really do it, and who is imagining?
Work through the detail questions, ending on the last: why *would* and not *will*?
Board the two patterns from the text, one above the other. Ring the if-clause in each and show that neither contains will or would.
Ask the CCQs. Then show the same idea both ways - *If I win the lottery, I'll ... / If I won the lottery, I'd ...* - and ask which speaker is more hopeful.
Drill the contractions: I'll, we'll, I'd, they'd.

stages.name: Test again: controlled practice
stages.time: 12 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise both forms accurately and see the progress since the first test.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then check with a partner.
Check as a class, asking each time: real possibility, or imagining?
Put two sentences from the first test on the board, unnamed, and let the class correct them.

stages.name: Chain conditionals
text: **Aim:** To produce the form quickly and repeatedly.
The first learner says a first-conditional sentence: *If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.*
The next takes the result and makes it the condition: *If I stay at home, I'll finish my book.* And so on round the group.
The chain breaks when somebody uses will after if; the group starts again from that learner.
Second round in the second conditional: *If I had a boat, I'd ...*

stages.name: Freer speaking: the dilemma
text: **Aim:** To use both conditionals to argue a real decision.
Give each pair a dilemma, or let them use Dilan's: a wedding or an examination; a good job far away or an ordinary job at home; telling a friend an uncomfortable truth or staying quiet.
Each pair argues both sides, using *if* sentences, and must reach a decision.
Each pair reports the decision and one reason in a conditional sentence.
Write the best two sentences on the board as they are said.

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct the common mistakes and check the main aim.
Four sentences on the board, two correct and two with will after if or mixed halves, for the class to repair.
Exit task: one first conditional about this week and one second conditional about your life. Collect them.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5: give advice on three problems using *If I were you, I'd ...*
blocks.caption: Test-teach-test: learners use both forms first, so you teach the difference they actually need. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners the two patterns on a slip of paper and let them do the chain in the first conditional only.
Stronger learners use *might* and *could* in the result clause - *I might go, I could take it* - and try one mixed sentence: *If I had studied, I would be at university now.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: The chain runs in groups of five at the same time, so forty learners each speak twice in eight minutes. Report from four groups, not forty.
Everything here can go on the board: the three situations, the two patterns and the dilemmas. The chain and the dilemma need no materials at all.
Breakout rooms of four for the chain, with each learner typing their sentence in the chat as they say it, so the whole chain stays visible.
Conditionals appear in B1 sentence-transformation tasks and in the speaking test, where *If I were you, I'd ...* is the standard way of giving advice. Task 5 practises exactly that.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task asks for one of each, so it shows both whether learners can form them and whether they can tell the two meanings apart.

pages.keywords: passive voice lesson plan, passive voice ESL lesson, teaching the passive voice, B1 ESL lesson plan, free ESL lesson plans, EFL lesson plan

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the passive voice for B1: learners compare an active and a passive description of the same thing, work out for themselves why the passive exists, and then use it to write about how something is made.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: The lesson answers the question every class asks - why not just say who did it? - instead of teaching the transformation as a puzzle with no purpose.

items.definition: B1, with a B2 extension in the notes
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, teach the present passive only and leave the past passive for a second lesson.
Reading, speaking and writing
The passive in the present and past simple: form with be + past participle, when to use it, and by + agent
Guided discovery: learners compare two versions of the same information and work out why one uses the passive
The two texts, the worksheet, a board
10 minutes

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to form and use the passive in the present and past simple to describe processes and facts where the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to decide when the passive is the better choice and when the active is.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to add by + agent only when the doer carries real information.

blocks.title: The text: "Two ways to say the same thing"
text: A. Somebody built this bridge in 1908. Workers repaired it after the flood in 1996, and every year the council paints it. People call it the Iron Bridge, and thousands of drivers use it every day. - B. This bridge was built in 1908. It was repaired after the flood in 1996, and it is painted every year. It is called the Iron Bridge, and it is used by thousands of drivers every day. - Text B is the one you would find on the sign beside the bridge.
**Gist question:** Which text is about the bridge, and which is about the people? Which one belongs on a sign?
**Detail questions:** (1) When was the bridge built? (2) How often is it painted? (3) Who uses it? (4) In text B, why is "by thousands of drivers" kept, when "by somebody" is not?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: The passive puts the important thing first. In a text about a bridge, the bridge is the subject of every sentence, and who did the work is secondary - often unknown, obvious, or simply not the point.

So we choose the passive when the doer is unknown (*my bike was stolen*), obvious (*the road is cleaned every night*), or unimportant (*the forms are checked on Monday*), and in writing that describes processes, rules and facts.
We add *by + agent* only when the doer is worth saying: *It is used by thousands of drivers* is information; *it was built by somebody* is not.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "This bridge was built in 1908." Do we know who built it?
No - the bridge is the subject.
"It is painted every year." Once, or regularly?
"My bike was stolen." Do I know who did it?
No - if I did, I would say so.

blocks.heading: Form
rows: is not / was not + past participle
It **is used by** thousands of drivers.

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: Nothing new to spell: the passive uses the past participle, the same third form learners already need for the present perfect. Regular verbs repeat the past form (repair → repaired); irregular verbs use their own (build → built, take → taken, write → written, make → made).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **is and was are weak** inside the sentence: /ɪz/ and /wəz/. *It was built* runs together as /ɪtwəzˈbɪlt/.
**were** is very weak indeed: /wə/. Learners who expect /wɜː/ often miss it entirely when listening.
**The stress falls on the participle**, not on be: it was **BUILT**, they are **CHECKED**. This is what makes a passive sentence sound natural.

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: The verb be is dropped: *The bridge built in 1908.*
This is the mistake of the lesson. Board the pattern with a box round *be*, and drill short pairs until the box is never empty.
Past participle confused with past simple: *It was build. / It was wrote.*
Return to the three forms. Test the third column only, since that is the one the passive needs.
by + agent added everywhere: *The window was broken by somebody.*
Give the test: does the doer tell the reader anything? If not, leave it out.
The passive used where the active is natural: *The ball was kicked by me.*
Show two versions and ask which sounds like a report and which like a person talking. The passive is a choice, not a better form.
Intransitive verbs made passive: *The accident was happened.*
Some verbs take no object, so they cannot be passive: happen, arrive, come, go, die. Give the five and move on.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Passive Voice, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in: what is it made of?
text: **Aim:** To create interest and let the target language appear naturally.
Hold up or name three ordinary objects: a pencil, a plastic bottle, a shirt.
Ask what each is made of and where it was made. Accept any answer, in any form.
In pairs, learners choose one object in the room and say three things about it. Do not correct yet.

stages.name: Two ways to say the same thing
text: **Aim:** To let learners discover why the passive exists before it is named.
Learners read texts A and B and answer the gist question in pairs: which is about the bridge, and which is about the people?
Take the answers, then work through the four detail questions. The last one - why keep *by thousands of drivers* - is the heart of the lesson.
Elicit the three reasons onto the board: the doer is unknown, obvious, or not important.
Only now name it: this is the passive.

stages.name: Clarify the form
text: **Aim:** To make the form clear in both tenses and to fix the stress.
Board the pattern with a box around be: *be + past participle*. Fill the box with is, are, was, were from sentences in text B.
Elicit the negative and the question from the same text.
Drill four sentences, with the stress on the participle: *it was BUILT, they are CHECKED.*
Ask the CCQs to check that a regular action and a finished one are told apart.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 13 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately in both tenses.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then compare with a partner.
Check as a class. For every answer, ask which tense and why.
Put two sentences with a missing *be* on the board - your own - and let the class repair them.

stages.name: Choose: active or passive?
text: **Aim:** To practise the decision, not only the form.
Read out six short situations: *You are writing a notice about the library. You are telling a friend what you did yesterday.*
Pairs decide active or passive for each, and say why in one sentence.
Take the answers quickly. Disagreement is useful here: some are genuinely either.

stages.name: Freer writing: how it is made
stages.time: 10 min · Pairs, then groups of four
text: **Aim:** To use the passive for its real purpose: describing a process.
Pairs choose something they know how it is made or done: tea, a school timetable, a cricket pitch, a dish from home.
They write four or five sentences describing the process, in the passive where it fits.
Two pairs join and read their processes to each other, who ask one question each.
Collect two good sentences for the board.

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct the common mistakes and check the main aim.
Write four sentences from the freer stage on the board - two correct, two with a missing be or a past simple instead of a participle - for the class to repair.
Exit task: two sentences about your town, one present passive and one past passive. Collect them.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5: describe a process from your own life in six sentences.
blocks.caption: Guided discovery: learners compare two versions of the same information and work out why one uses the passive. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners the three forms of ten verbs on a slip, and let them write their process sentences in the present passive only.
Stronger learners use the passive with modals - *it must be checked, it can be repaired* - and try one sentence with the present perfect passive: *it has been painted*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: The choose-active-or-passive stage works as a whole-class vote by hands, which is fast and shows you immediately who is guessing. Collect exit tasks from two rows.
Write texts A and B on the board before the lesson, one above the other - the comparison is easier to see that way than on paper.
Put texts A and B on screen side by side. The process-writing stage works well in a shared document, one pair per line.
Point out that the passive appears in nearly every B1 writing task about rules, processes or reports, and that Task 3 is the exact transformation exercise those exams use.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task requires one sentence in each tense, so a learner who can only manage one of them is visible at once.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson for teaching the past simple to A2 learners: a short story to meet the verbs in context, a clear focus on form and on the three sounds of -ed, controlled practice, a speaking mingle, and a freer task where learners tell a partner about a day they remember.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: It works with teenagers and adults, and every stage has notes for large classes, classes without a photocopier, and online lessons.

items.definition: A2, adaptable for A1+ and B1
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, drop the "Find someone who" mingle and set Worksheet Task 5 as homework.
Speaking, reading and writing
Past simple: regular and irregular verbs; negatives with didn't; questions with did; -ed pronunciation
PPP (presentation, practice, production), with the language met first in a short text
The reading text (on the board or the worksheet), the worksheet, a board
10 minutes

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to talk about finished events in the past using the past simple of regular and common irregular verbs, in positive sentences, negatives and questions.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to pronounce regular past endings correctly as /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to read a short narrative for the main idea and for detail.

blocks.title: The text: "Lina's Saturday"
text: Last Saturday, Lina visited her grandmother in the countryside. She got up early and caught the eight o'clock bus. The journey took two hours, so she listened to music and read a book. When she arrived, her grandmother cooked a big lunch. After lunch, they walked to the river and watched the birds. Lina wanted to take some photos, but she didn't have her phone. She left it on the bus! Luckily, the driver found it and called her grandmother's number. Lina went back to the bus station and got her phone before she went home. It was a long day, but she enjoyed it.
**Gist question:** Was Lina's day good or bad? Why?
**Detail questions:** (1) How did Lina travel? (2) What did they do after lunch? (3) What problem did Lina have? (4) Who found the phone?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: We use the past simple for actions and states that are finished, at a time in the past that we know or that is clear: *Lina visited her grandmother last Saturday.*
Time words that go with it: yesterday, last week, last Saturday, two days ago, in 2019, when I was a child.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "Lina visited her grandmother." Is she visiting her now?

blocks.heading: Form
rows: Yes, + subject + did. / No, + subject + didn't.
Yes, she did. / No, she didn't.

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: Regular verbs add -ed (walk → walked). Verbs ending in -e add -d (arrive → arrived). Consonant + y becomes -ied (study → studied). One vowel + one consonant, stressed, doubles the consonant (stop → stopped). Irregular verbs have their own past forms (go → went, get → got, take → took) and are learned as vocabulary.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **/t/** after voiceless sounds such as /k/, /p/, /s/, /tʃ/: worked, stopped, watched.
**/d/** after voiced sounds and vowels: played, called, listened.
**/ɪd/**, an extra syllable, only after /t/ and /d/: wanted, visited, needed.
In "didn't" and "did you", the vowel is short and "did you" often sounds like /dɪdʒu/ in fast speech.

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: Learners use the past form after didn't: *I didn't went.*
Show that did already carries the past, so the verb goes back to the base form: *didn't go*. Board it as a rule: did + base verb.
Learners use was with a main verb: *I was go to the market.*
Contrast *I was tired* (was + adjective) with *I went* (past verb). Many first languages use a past marker this way, so expect it and correct gently.
Treat irregular verbs as vocabulary: a short list each lesson, practised aloud.
Adding an extra syllable to every -ed: *walk-ed* /wɔːkɪd/.
Drill the three sounds with gestures; only /t/ and /d/ endings add a syllable.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Simple, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To create interest and find out what learners already know.
Tell the class three things you did last weekend, one of them false: *I cooked for eight people. I went swimming. I watched a film.* Learners guess the false one.
In pairs, learners do the same: three sentences, one false. Listen, but do not correct yet. Note who already uses the past simple, and which mistakes come up.

stages.name: Reading for meaning
text: **Aim:** To meet the past simple in a context and understand the story.
Write the gist question on the board: *Was Lina's day good or bad? Why?* Learners read the text quickly and answer. Check in pairs, then as a class.
Learners read again and answer the four detail questions. Check answers.
ICQ before they read: *Do you need to understand every word?* (No.) *How long do you have?* (Two minutes.)

stages.name: Focus on form and sound
text: **Aim:** To make the meaning, form and pronunciation of the past simple clear.
Learners underline every past verb in the text. Elicit them onto the board in two columns: regular (visited, listened) and irregular (got, took).
Use the CCQs to check the meaning. Build the positive, negative and question forms on the board from sentences in the text.
Drill the three -ed sounds with a gesture for each: worked /t/, played /d/, wanted /ɪd/.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 12 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then compare answers with a partner.
Check answers as a class. Ask learners to say the full sentence, not just the verb, so you hear the pronunciation.

stages.name: Find someone who
text: **Aim:** To practise past simple questions and short answers in speech.

Learners each get or copy six prompts: *Find someone who ... cooked a meal yesterday / watched a film last weekend / got up before six today / visited a relative last month / didn't sleep well last night / went somewhere new this year.*
Model the question first: *Did you cook a meal yesterday?* - *Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.* When someone says yes, they ask one more question: *What did you cook?*
ICQ: *Do you write your own name or your classmate's name?* (My classmate's.) *What do you ask when someone says yes?* (One more question.)

stages.name: Freer speaking: a day I remember
text: **Aim:** To use the past simple fluently to tell a short personal story.
Learners think of a good day from last year and make short notes: where, who with, what happened. Give two minutes; no full sentences.
In pairs, each learner tells their story. The listener asks at least three questions with *did*.
While they talk, write down good sentences and common mistakes, without interrupting. Two or three learners share their partner's story with the class.

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct the most common mistakes and check the main aim.
Write four sentences you heard on the board, two correct and two with mistakes, and let the class find and fix the mistakes.
Exit task: each learner writes three sentences about yesterday: one positive, one negative, one question. Collect them to check who met the aim.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5, if not done in class: five sentences about yesterday and two questions for a partner.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production), with the language met first in a short text. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners a list of the irregular verbs from the text with their past forms, and let them do the Lead-in with a partner who helps. In the freer task, they may use their notes.
Stronger learners add time expressions and linking words to their story (first, then, after that, in the end), and in the mingle ask two follow-up questions instead of one.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Run the mingle in rows: learners ask the people on their left, right, in front and behind, then change seats with the next row once. Collect exit tasks from one row each lesson.
Write the text and Tasks 2 and 3 on the board or a large sheet before the lesson. Learners write answers in their notebooks. The mingle prompts can be dictated.

Share the text on screen. Put learners in breakout rooms of two or three for the Lead-in and the freer task. Replace the mingle with a shared document: each learner writes a Did you ... question and answers two others'.
Use a picture story instead of the text, and keep the mingle to four prompts about school and home.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task shows who can form positive, negative and question sentences correctly. Anyone who wrote *didn't* + past form needs the Lead-in rule again next lesson.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the present perfect for talking about life experience: Have you ever ...? and I have never ... . Learners meet it in a short interview, work out the rule themselves, and finish by interviewing each other.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: The lesson deals head-on with the mistake every class makes - putting a finished time with the present perfect - and with the difference between been and gone.

items.definition: B1, usable with a strong A2 class
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, drop the mingle and set Worksheet Task 5 as homework.
Speaking, reading and writing
Present perfect for life experience: ever and never, questions and short answers, and the contrast with the past simple
Test-teach-test: learners try the language first, so you teach what they actually need
The interview text, the worksheet, a board
10 minutes

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to ask about and describe life experiences using the present perfect with ever and never, and answer with short answers.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to choose the present perfect or the past simple according to whether a finished time is mentioned.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to say have and has in their weak forms inside a question.

blocks.title: The text: "Two minutes with a new volunteer"
text: INTERVIEWER: You start on Monday. Have you ever worked with children before? - MAYA: Yes, I have. I've taught reading at a community centre for two summers. INTERVIEWER: And have you been abroad for work? - MAYA: No, I haven't. I've never left my country, actually. I went to the coast last year, and that was my longest journey! INTERVIEWER: Have you done any first-aid training? - MAYA: Yes, I've done a short course. I did it in March, at the hospital near my house. INTERVIEWER: Good. One more: have you ever managed a team? - MAYA: Not yet. But I've helped my aunt in her shop since I was fifteen, so I'm not afraid of hard work.
**Gist question:** Is Maya a good person for the job? Find two reasons.
**Detail questions:** (1) Has Maya worked with children? (2) Has she worked in another country? (3) When did she do the first-aid course? (4) What has she done since she was fifteen?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: We use the present perfect for an experience in someone's life, when the time is not stated and does not matter: *I have taught reading. She has never left her country.* The period - her life - is not finished, so the experience can still be added to.
As soon as we say when, we change to the past simple: *I went to the coast last year. I did it in March.* This is the point the whole lesson turns on.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "I've taught reading at a community centre." Do we know when?
"I went to the coast last year." Do we know when?
So which tense goes with a finished time?
"She has never left her country." Can that change tomorrow?
Yes - her life is not finished.

blocks.heading: Form
rows: I **have taught**. She **has done** a course.
I **haven't** worked abroad. She **has never** left.
Yes, + subject + have/has. / No, + subject + haven't/hasn't.
Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: The past participle of regular verbs is the same as the past simple: work → worked, study → studied, stop → stopped. Irregular verbs have a third form to learn beside the past: go → went → gone, do → did → done, see → saw → seen, be → was → been. Note the pair *been* and *gone*: *She has been to Italy* means she went and came back; *She has gone to Italy* means she is there now.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **Have and has are weak** inside a sentence: /həv/ and /həz/, not /hæv/ and /hæz/. *Have you ever ...?* runs together as one piece: /həvjuːˈevə/.
**Contractions are normal in speech**: I've /aɪv/, you've /juːv/, she's /ʃiːz/, we've /wiːv/. Learners who say every word in full sound formal and slow.
**In the short answer, have is strong**: *Yes, I **have**.* The stress lands there, and "Yes, I've" is not possible.
**She's** can be *she is* or *she has*. The word after it tells you which: *she's tired* (is), *she's finished* (has).

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: The commonest mistake of all: a finished time with the present perfect - *I have been to Paris last year.*
Give the rule as a test, not a grammar label: if the sentence says when, use the past simple. Drill pairs: *I've been to Paris. / I went to Paris in June.*
Using the past simple where English prefers the experience meaning: *Did you ever eat sushi?*
Accept it as natural American usage, and teach *Have you ever eaten ...?* as the form expected in international exams and in British English. Learners meet both.
Wrong participle: *I have went, I have ate.*
Teach the three forms together from the start - go, went, gone - and test the third column, not only the second.
Two board pictures: a person back home with a suitcase (*has been to*), and an empty chair (*has gone to*).
Learners put ever in the answer: *Yes, I have ever.*
Show that ever belongs to the question only; the answer takes *once, twice, a few times*, or *never*.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Perfect, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in: three things about me
text: **Aim:** To create interest and put the target language in the air before it is taught.
Write three sentences about yourself on the board: *I have never eaten raw fish. I have ridden a horse. I have been to five countries.*
Learners ask you two questions about any of them. Answer briefly.
Do not explain the grammar yet. Just let them hear it.

stages.name: Test: what can they already do?
text: **Aim:** To find out what learners know, so that the teaching fits them.
Dictate four prompts: *eat / octopus*, *visit / another country*, *break / your arm*, *lose / your keys*.
In pairs, learners make a question from each prompt and ask their partner.
Walk round and write down exactly what they say. You are collecting evidence: *Did you ever ...?*, *Have you ever broke ...?*, silence - all of it is useful.

stages.name: Teach: the interview and the rule
text: **Aim:** To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present perfect for experience.
Learners read the interview and answer the gist question, then the four detail questions. Check in pairs, then as a class.

Put two sentences from the text side by side on the board: *I've taught reading at a community centre.* and *I went to the coast last year.* Ask the CCQs and elicit the rule: a stated time means the past simple.
Build the question and short-answer forms from the text. Drill *Have you ever ...?* with the weak /həv/, and the short answers with the stress on *have*.
Board the three forms of the five irregular verbs in the text: be, do, go, teach, leave.

stages.name: Test again: controlled practice
stages.time: 12 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately, and to show learners their own progress since the first test.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then compare with a partner.
Check as a class. For Task 3, always ask *why* - the answer is either "it says when" or "it doesn't".
Put two of the mistakes you collected earlier on the board, unnamed, and let the class correct them.

stages.name: Find someone who has
text: **Aim:** To ask the question form many times with different partners.
Six prompts: *Find someone who has ... slept in a tent / cooked for ten people / forgotten an important birthday / swum in the sea / ridden a motorbike / never drunk coffee.*
Model: *Have you ever slept in a tent?* - *Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.* After a yes, one follow-up question in the past simple: *When was that? Where?*
ICQ: *After yes, what tense is your next question?* (Past simple.)

stages.name: Freer speaking: interview for the job
text: **Aim:** To use the present perfect freely in a short, purposeful conversation.
Pairs choose a job or a role together: a volunteer, a guide, a camp helper.
Each pair writes four *Have you ever ...?* questions that matter for that job.
They interview each other, answering with short answers and one extra detail in the past simple.
Each interviewer tells the class one thing about their partner: *Sara has organised a school trip.*

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct what you heard and check the main aim.
Write four sentences from the freer stage on the board, two right and two wrong, and let the class fix them.
Exit task: each learner writes two true sentences - one with *never*, one with a time expression in the past simple - and hands them in.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5: five sentences about your own experiences, two of them with never.
blocks.caption: Test-teach-test: learners try the language first, so you teach what they actually need. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners the three forms of ten common irregular verbs on a slip of paper to keep on the desk, and let them write their four interview questions before speaking.
Stronger learners add *How many times ...?* and answer with *once, twice, a few times*, and use *been* and *gone* correctly in the report stage.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Replace the mingle with rows: each learner asks the four people nearest them. Collect exit tasks from two rows each lesson rather than all of them.
Write the interview and Tasks 2 and 3 on the board before the lesson; learners answer in their notebooks. The mingle prompts can be dictated.

Share the interview on screen; use breakout rooms of three for the interview stage. Replace the mingle with a shared document where each learner writes one Have you ever question and answers two others'.
Monolingual class with a similar tense

Ask early whether their language has a form like this and what it does. Where the first language allows a stated time with it, that is exactly where the mistakes will come, so spend longer on the contrast.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task shows whether learners can keep the two tenses apart. Anyone who wrote a time expression with the present perfect needs the contrast again at the start of the next lesson.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the present simple for daily routines: learners meet it in a short text about two very different mornings, work out the third-person -s themselves, practise the question and negative forms, and finish by finding out who in the class has the earliest start.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: The lesson gives proper time to the two things beginners always drop - the -s on he, she and it, and do or does in the question - and every stage has a note for large classes.

items.definition: A1, adaptable for A2
Teenagers and adults; works with young learners too
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, drop the survey and set Worksheet Task 5 as homework.
Speaking, reading and writing
Present simple for routines and habits: the third-person -s, negatives with don't and doesn't, questions with do and does, and adverbs of frequency
PPP (presentation, practice, production), with the language met first in a short text
The reading text, the worksheet, a board
10 minutes

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe daily routines and habits using the present simple in positive sentences, negatives and questions, with the third-person -s.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to place adverbs of frequency - always, usually, often, sometimes, never - correctly in a sentence.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to hear and say the three sounds of the third-person -s: /s/, /z/ and /ɪz/.

blocks.title: The text: "Two mornings"
text: Ndidi wakes up at half past four. She works in a bakery, so she starts at five. She doesn't eat breakfast at home; she eats at work, after the first bread comes out of the oven. She usually finishes at one o'clock, and she sleeps for an hour in the afternoon. Her brother Emeka never gets up early. He studies at night, from nine until two in the morning, because the house is quiet then. He gets up at eleven, makes coffee and reads for an hour before his classes. "We live in the same house," says Ndidi, "but we don't often meet!"
**Gist question:** Why do Ndidi and Emeka almost never see each other?
**Detail questions:** (1) What time does Ndidi start work? (2) Where does she eat breakfast? (3) When does Emeka study? (4) What does he do before his classes?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: We use the present simple for things that are generally true, and for routines and habits - what somebody does again and again: *She works in a bakery. He studies at night.*
It does not mean now. For something happening at this moment we use the present continuous: *She is working now* is a different idea from *She works in a bakery.*
Frequency words say how often: always, usually, often, sometimes, never. They go before the main verb - *He never gets up early* - but after *be*: *She is always tired.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "She works in a bakery." Is she working at this moment?
We don't know - and it doesn't matter.
Is it her job every day?
Is it a habit or one time?
"He never gets up early." How often does he get up early?

blocks.heading: Form
rows: I / you / we / they + verb; he / she / it + verb + -s
They **live** here. She **works** in a bakery.
don't + verb; doesn't + verb (no -s on the verb)
We **don't** meet. She **doesn't eat** at home.
Do / Does + subject + verb (no -s on the verb)
Yes, I do. / No, I don't. Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.
*Does she finish at one?* - *Yes, she does.*

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: Most verbs add -s (work → works). Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -ss, -x or -o add -es (watch → watches, go → goes). Consonant + y becomes -ies (study → studies), but vowel + y just adds -s (play → plays). Two verbs are irregular: have → has, be → is.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **/s/** after voiceless sounds: works, starts, eats.
**/z/** after voiced sounds and vowels: lives, reads, goes.
**/ɪz/**, an extra syllable, after /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/: finishes, watches, uses.
**Does he** and **does she** run together in speech: /dəziː/, /dəʃiː/. Learners who expect two clear words often miss the question altogether when they hear it.

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: The -s disappears: *She work in a bakery.*
This is the mistake of the lesson. Drill he/she/it sentences alone, and make a class signal - a raised finger - that you use silently every time it is dropped, instead of correcting aloud.
The -s is added twice: *She doesn't works.* or *Does she works?*
Show that do and does already carry the person: after do, does, don't or doesn't, the verb has no ending. Board it beside the positive so the pair is visible.
Frequency words in the wrong place: *She goes always early.*
Give one rule: before the main verb, after *be*. Practise with three sentences on the board and let learners place the word themselves.
Present simple used for now: *Look! She works.*
Contrast two pictures - a woman at work today, and the same woman's weekly timetable - and elicit which sentence fits which.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults; works with young learners too
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Simple, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in: my morning in five verbs
text: **Aim:** To create interest and bring out what learners already know.
Write five verbs about your own morning on the board, nothing else: *wake up, drink, walk, teach, eat.*
Learners guess your routine: *You wake up at six?* Answer briefly and let them try again.
In pairs, learners write five verbs for their own morning and their partner guesses the times.

stages.name: Reading: two mornings
text: **Aim:** To meet the present simple in a context and read for meaning.
Write the gist question on the board and give two minutes: *Why do Ndidi and Emeka almost never see each other?*
Learners read, answer, and check in pairs. Take the answer from the class.
Learners read again for the four detail questions, then check together.
ICQ before reading: *Do you need every word?* (No.)

stages.name: Focus on form: where does the -s go?
text: **Aim:** To clarify the third-person -s, the negative and the question, and the sound of the ending.
Learners find every verb in the text about Ndidi or Emeka and call them out. Write them in one column: *wakes, works, starts, eats, finishes, sleeps, gets up, studies, makes, reads.*
Ask what all of them have in common, and elicit the -s. Then write *We live in the same house* beside them and ask why that one has no -s.
Build the negative and the question from the text: *She doesn't eat at home. Does he study at night?* Point out that the -s has moved to does.
Drill the three endings with a gesture each: works /s/, lives /z/, finishes /ɪz/.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 12 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then compare with a partner.
Check as a class, asking for the whole sentence aloud so you hear the ending.
Put two sentences with a dropped -s on the board - your own, not a learner's - and let the class repair them.

stages.name: Class survey: who starts earliest?
text: **Aim:** To ask and answer present simple questions many times.
Each learner writes three questions: *What time do you get up? How do you come here? What do you eat for breakfast?*
They ask five classmates and note the answers in three words each.
Find out as a class: who gets up earliest, who travels furthest, what most people eat.
ICQ: *Do you write full sentences?* (No, three words.)

stages.name: Freer speaking: a day I would like
text: **Aim:** To use the present simple freely for a routine of their own invention.
Learners invent a perfect daily routine - any job, any country - and make short notes.
In pairs, each describes their day. The partner asks three questions with do or does.
Two or three learners describe their partner's day to the class, which is where the third-person -s gets its real test.

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct the common mistakes and check the main aim.
Write four sentences you heard, two correct and two with a missing or extra -s, and let the class find them.
Exit task: three sentences about a family member - one positive, one negative, one question - all in the third person. Collect them.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5: eight sentences about a person in your family, with at least two negatives.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production), with the language met first in a short text. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners a strip of paper with the three forms modelled - *I work / She works / She doesn't work / Does she work?* - to keep on the desk during the speaking stages.
Stronger learners add frequency adverbs to every sentence in the freer stage, and use *hardly ever* and *once a week* as well as the five basic adverbs.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: The survey becomes rows: ask the five people nearest you. Take the class results from five volunteers rather than everyone.
Write the text and Tasks 2 and 3 on the board before the lesson; learners answer in their notebooks. The survey needs no materials at all.
Share the text on screen; use breakout rooms of three for the survey, with one learner asking and two answering, then rotate.
Replace the freer stage with a drawing: learners draw their perfect day in four pictures and say one sentence about each.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task is written in the third person on purpose: it shows immediately who has taken on the -s and who has not.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on reported speech for B1: learners carry real messages around the room, then work out for themselves what changes when we report what somebody said.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: It covers statements and questions, the difference between said and told, and the changes to pronouns and time words that most textbooks rush - and it ends with a task where reporting is genuinely necessary, not an exercise.

items.definition: B1, with a B2 extension in the notes
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For a 45-minute lesson, teach statements only and leave reported questions for a second lesson.
Speaking, listening and writing
Reported speech: statements with said and told, reported questions with asked, and the changes to tense, pronouns and time words
Guided discovery: learners find the changes in an example themselves before the rule is named, then practise and use it
The worksheet, a board; slips of paper for the message game
10 minutes, including cutting slips

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to report statements and questions that other people made, changing the tense, the pronouns and the time words correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to choose between said and told according to whether the listener is named.
**Subsidiary aim.** Learners will be able to form a reported question without do, does or did, and without question word order.

blocks.title: The text: "Three messages"
text: At break, three people spoke to the teacher. Sara said, "I can't come to the trip on Friday." Karim said, "I finished the project yesterday, and I gave it to my sister to check." Then Lucia asked, "Where does the bus leave from?" and, a moment later, "Have you seen my bag?" - The teacher wrote it all down for the class teacher, like this: Sara said that she couldn't come to the trip on Friday. Karim told me that he had finished the project the day before, and that he had given it to his sister to check. Lucia asked where the bus left from, and whether I had seen her bag.
**Gist question:** Which words changed when the teacher wrote the messages down? Find three kinds of change.
**Detail questions:** (1) Who could not come on Friday? (2) When did Karim finish the project? (3) What did Lucia want to know first? (4) Why is it "her bag" and not "my bag"?

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Meaning
text: Reported speech tells somebody what another person said, at a later moment and often in another place. Because the moment has moved, the words that point to a time, a person or a place move with it.
The tense usually steps back one: present becomes past, past becomes past perfect, will becomes would, can becomes could. This is called backshift, and it happens because the speaking is now over.
If the thing said is still true - *She said she lives in Kandy* - fluent speakers often keep the present. Teach the backshift as the safe form, and accept the unshifted one when the fact still holds.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
rows: "Sara said she couldn't come." Are these Sara's exact words?
Did Sara speak before or after this sentence?
"I finished it yesterday" becomes "the day before". Why not "yesterday"?
Because we are reporting it on a different day.
"Lucia asked where the bus left from." Is that a question?
No - it is a sentence about a question, so there is no question mark.

blocks.heading: Form
rows: She **said that** she couldn't come. He **told me that** he had finished.
She **asked where the bus left from**. (Not *where did the bus leave*.)
She **asked whether I had seen** her bag.
present → past; past → past perfect; will → would; can → could
*I am tired* → he said he **was** tired.

blocks.heading: Spelling
text: Nothing unusual to spell, but two pairs of words decide the sentence: *said* takes no person after it (*said that ...*), *told* must have one (*told me that ...*); and in a reported question there is no *do*, *does* or *did*, and no inversion.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: **that is nearly always weak** and is often dropped altogether: *She said (that) she couldn't come* - /ðət/, never /ðæt/.
**told me** links into one piece: /ˈtoʊldmi/.
**The reported clause keeps normal statement intonation**, falling at the end, even when it reports a question. Learners who keep the rising question tune give themselves away.

blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions
rows: Question word order kept in the report: *She asked where did the bus leave.*
This is the mistake of the lesson. Show the two sentences one above the other and cross out the *did*: a reported question is a statement inside a sentence.
said and told swapped: *He said me that ...* / *He told that ...*
One line on the board: *tell* needs a person, *say* does not. Drill four quick pairs.
Time words left alone: *He said he finished it yesterday* reported a week later.
Make it real: report something a classmate actually said last lesson, and ask whether *yesterday* is still true.
Backshift applied where it is not needed: *She said the earth went round the sun.*
Teach the safe rule first, then show this exception once. It rewards the strong learners without confusing the rest.
Pronouns not changed: *He said I was tired* meaning the speaker was tired.
Ask *who is tired?* every time until the class hears the ambiguity themselves.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Reported Speech, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in: the message chain
text: **Aim:** To create a real need to report what somebody said.
Two lines. Whisper a sentence to the first learner in each: *My cousin is moving to Dubai next month and she has sold her car.*
Each learner whispers it to the next. The last one says it aloud.
Compare the two endings with the original. The class will laugh; that is the point.
Ask: when you tell somebody what another person said, what has to change?

stages.name: Three messages: noticing the changes
text: **Aim:** To let learners discover the changes for themselves before any rule is given.
Learners read the text and answer the gist question in pairs: which words changed, and what kind of change was it?
Take the three kinds from the class and put them on the board as headings: tense, pronouns, time words.
Work through the four detail questions, especially the last one - why *her bag* and not *my bag*.
Only now give the name: this is reported speech.

stages.name: Clarify: said, told, and reported questions
text: **Aim:** To make the form clear, including the question without do and without inversion.
Board the two statement patterns side by side: *said (that)* and *told + person + (that)*. Drill four short pairs.
Write Lucia's two questions in direct speech, then the reports underneath, and cross out *does* and the inversion in front of the class.
Elicit the tense ladder onto the board: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
Ask the CCQs to check that a report is a statement, not a question.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 14 min · Individual, then pairs to check
text: **Aim:** To practise both patterns accurately.
Learners do Worksheet Tasks 1 to 3 alone, then compare with a partner.
Check as a class, asking each time which word changed and why.
Any sentence with *asked* should be read aloud, so the falling intonation is heard.

stages.name: Freer task: the interview relay
text: **Aim:** To use reported speech where it is genuinely needed.
In each group of three, A interviews B with four questions of A's own while C sits with their back to them and cannot hear.
A then reports the whole exchange to C: *I asked her where she was born, and she said that ...*
C writes down what they are told, then checks the facts with B: *Is it true that ...?*
Rotate roles once if time allows. Two groups report one interesting fact to the class.

stages.name: Feedback and exit task
text: **Aim:** To correct the common mistakes and check the main aim.
Write four sentences you heard, two right and two with question word order or the wrong verb, and let the class repair them.
Exit task: report one statement and one question that you actually heard in this lesson. Collect them.

blocks.homework: Worksheet Task 5: report five things somebody said to you today.
blocks.caption: Guided discovery: learners find the changes in an example themselves before the rule is named, then practise and use it. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker learners the tense ladder and the two patterns on a slip of paper for the freer stage, and let them report statements only.
Stronger learners use a wider range of reporting verbs - explained, admitted, complained, promised - and notice that some take a person and some do not.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: The message chain runs in four lines at once. In the freer stage, groups of three work simultaneously; hear two groups, not twenty.
Write the three messages on the board before the lesson. The interview relay needs nothing but the learners themselves.
Use breakout rooms of three for the relay, with C turning their camera and sound off during the interview. It works better online than in a noisy classroom.
Point out that reported speech appears in most B1 exams as a sentence-transformation task, and that the marks go for the tense and the word order, exactly what Task 3 drills.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The exit task asks learners to report real speech from the lesson, so it cannot be answered from memory of a rule. Look for question word order, which is the thing that fails first.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Present Simple, built round the theme "My Day: Daily Routines".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who know the verb be, numbers, telling the time (o'clock, half past) and basic daily verbs. They may have met the present simple but cannot yet use the third person -s accurately.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Change partners" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and listening
Grammar: Present Simple
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (Nimal's Day text and activity table), Handout 2 (controlled practice), Handout 3 (interview grid), board, markers in two colours, optional clock face.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the present simple (affirmative, negative and questions) for daily routines, with a focus on the third person -s.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can ask and answer questions about daily routines and describe another person's day in 5–6 accurate sentences.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise speaking (asking and answering about routines) and listening for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To review times and daily routine vocabulary.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: Spelling rules for he / she / it:
bullets: Most verbs add *-s*: work → works, play → plays, get → gets.
Verbs ending in *-ch, -sh, -s, -x, -o* add *-es*: watch → watches, wash → washes, go → goes, do → does.
Consonant + *y* → *-ies*: study → studies. (Vowel + *y* just adds *-s*: play → plays.)
Irregular: have → has.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
text: We use the present simple for habits and routines (things we do regularly) and for facts. Time expressions: *every day, on Mondays, at 7 o'clock, in the morning, in the evening, at night*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
text: The *-s* ending has three sounds:
In questions, *do you* is often weak and joined: /dəjə/. Short answers are stressed: *Yes, I DO.*
bullets: /s/ after voiceless sounds: works, gets, eats, walks
/z/ after voiced sounds: plays, goes, comes, reads, has /hæz/
/ɪz/ after /s, z, ʃ, tʃ, dʒ/: watches, washes, finishes, relaxes

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Nimal gets up at 6.30.*** Is this today only? (No.) · Is it every day? (Yes.) · Is it a habit? (Yes.) · Who gets up? Nimal: is he *I, you* or *he*? (He.) So what do we add? (-s.)

rows: Students forget the -s with he / she (He work in a bank).
Highlight -s in a second colour on the board. Use a gesture (a finger drawing an "s" in the air) to prompt self-correction throughout the lesson.
Students add -s after doesn't (She doesn't works).
Show that the -s "moves" to does: draw an arrow from works to does on the board.
Students use be with the main verb (I am go to school).
Contrast I am a student (be) with I go to school (action verb, no am).
Draw a clock on the board in the lead-in and review o'clock, half past, quarter past / to.
Mixed-level class: stronger students finish early.
Fast finishers write three extra sentences using usually, always, never (see Differentiation).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: get up · have breakfast · go to school / work · have lunch · come home · do homework · watch TV · go to bed
I get up at 6.30. / Nimal gets up at 6.30. / He doesn't eat breakfast. / Do you walk? Yes, I do. / Does he walk? No, he doesn't.
/s/ works, gets · /z/ plays, goes · /ɪz/ watches, washes
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Simple, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students, introduce the topic of daily routines and activate vocabulary.
Draw a large clock on the board showing 6.30. Say: *"This is my morning. Look!"* Mime waking up and stretching. Ask: *"What am I doing?"* Elicit or teach **get up**.
Mime four more actions in order: **have breakfast, go to work, have lunch, go to bed**. After each mime, students call out the phrase. Write each phrase on the left of the board.
Ask two or three students: *"What time do you get up?"* Accept short answers (*Six o'clock*). Do not correct grammar at this stage.
**Transition:** *"Now let's meet Nimal. He is a student in Kandy."*

stages.name: Presentation
stages.time: 20 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in a meaningful context and check general understanding. To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present simple, focusing on the third person *-s*.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Point to the table. Say: *"These are six things Nimal does every day. They are not in order."*
**Task 1 (gist):** *"Read the text. Number the activities 1 to 6. You have three minutes. Work alone."*
ICQs: *"Do you work alone or with a partner?"* (Alone.) *"How many activities?"* (Six.) *"How many minutes?"* (Three.)
Students read and number the activities. Monitor and help with vocabulary if needed.
Students compare answers with a partner (1 minute). Then check as a class: read each activity and ask *"What number?"*

**Task 2 (detail):** *"Read again. Write the times."* Students complete the time column on Handout 1. Check answers by asking: *"What time does Nimal get up?"* Model the full answer: *"He gets up at six thirty."*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Write on the board: *Nimal gets up at 6.30.* Ask the CCQs from the language analysis (Is this today only? Is it every day? Is it a habit?).

**Form (positive).** Write *I get up at 6.30.* above Nimal's sentence. Ask: *"What's different?"* Elicit the **-s**. Underline *-s* in a second colour. Elicit more examples from the text: *goes, has, watches, studies*. Ask: *"Why goes, not gos?"* Write the spelling rules on the board (see Language analysis).

**Form (negative).** Point to the text: *He doesn't eat breakfast at home.* Ask: *"Is there an -s on eat?"* (No.) *"Where is it?"* (In doesn't / does.) Draw an arrow from *eats* to *does*. Contrast with *I don't eat breakfast.*
**Form (questions).** Write *Does Nimal walk to school?* and *Do you walk to school?* Elicit the short answers. Highlight the word order: Do/Does + subject + verb.

**Pronunciation.** Say *works, plays, watches* clearly. Ask students to listen: *"Are the endings the same?"* Write the three columns /s/, /z/, /ɪz/ on the right of the board. Drill chorally, then individually:
*works – he works – he works in a bank*
*plays – she plays – she plays cricket*
*watches – he watches – he watches TV*
Drill the question and short answer: T: *"Does Nimal walk to school?"* Ss: *"Yes, he does."* (Back-chain if needed.)
**Transition:** *"Now let's practise. Take Handout 2."*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To give students accurate written practice of the form.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the sentences with the verb in brackets. Look at the person: I or he/she? Five minutes. Work alone."*
ICQs: *"Alone or with a partner?"* (Alone.) *"Do you need to add -s for I?"* (No.)
Monitor. Note common errors on a piece of paper for later.
Students check with a partner (1 minute). Nominate students to read sentences aloud. Write answers on the board. Ask the class to correct any errors.
**Exercise B (spelling and sound):** students write the *he/she* form and tick the sound (/s/, /z/ or /ɪz/). Check quickly as a class and drill the trickier ones (*finishes, goes, studies*).

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then new pairs, then individual writing
text: **Aim:** To give students freer, personalised speaking practice using the target language.

Give out Handout 3. **Model first:** ask a strong student the first question: *"What time do you get up?"* Write the answer in the grid on the board. Then show how to report it: *"Ayesha gets up at 5.45."*
Say: *"Ask your partner all the questions. Write the answers in the grid. You have six minutes. Then change: your partner asks you."*
ICQs: *"Do you write your answers or your partner's answers?"* (My partner's.) *"Do you show your partner the paper?"* (No, ask and listen.)
Students interview each other. Monitor actively: listen for errors with *do/does*, word order and times. Write errors and good examples on your notes.

**Change partners.** Say: *"Stand up. Find a new partner. Tell your new partner about your first partner."* Model: *"Ayesha gets up at 5.45. She doesn't have breakfast. She goes to school by bus."* (5 minutes.)
**Writing (4 minutes):** students write 5–6 sentences about their first partner at the bottom of Handout 3. Fast finishers add *always, usually, sometimes, never*.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback on language used in the production stage and consolidate learning.
Ask two or three students to read their sentences aloud. Praise accurate *-s* endings.

**Error correction:** write four sentences from your notes on the board, two correct and two incorrect (e.g. *She work in a shop. / Does he plays football?*). Ask pairs: *"Which are correct? Correct the wrong ones."* Check as a class.
**Good language:** board one or two good sentences you heard and praise them.
Set the homework (see below). Ask a final question round the class: *"What time does your mother/father get up?"* as students leave.

blocks.homework: Write 6–8 sentences about a family member's day. Use at least two negatives and one question you would like to ask them. *Example: My brother gets up at 7 o'clock. He doesn't eat breakfast. He goes to work by train ...*
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give a verb bank with the *he/she* forms already written. Let them use the sentence frames on Handout 3: *He/She ___ at ___.* Pair them with a supportive partner for the interview.

Add frequency adverbs: *She usually gets up at 6. He never eats breakfast.* (Adverb before the main verb.) Ask two follow-up questions with *Why?* or *How?* (*How do you go to school?*). Write a paragraph comparing their routine with their partner's.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Change partners" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Change partners" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students are successful if they can: produce the *he/she* form with *-s* correctly in at least 4 out of 5 sentences; form *Do/Does* questions with correct word order; use short answers (*Yes, I do / No, she doesn't*). Check through monitoring in Stage 5 and the written sentences collected at the end.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students achieve the learning outcome? How do I know? Which stage worked best? Which needed more or less time? Which errors were most common? What will I review next lesson?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Nimal's Day
text: **Read about Nimal. Number the activities 1–6 in the order Nimal does them. Then write the time for each one.**

Nimal is 15 years old. He lives in Kandy with his family. He gets up at half past six every day. He doesn't eat breakfast at home. He has a cup of tea and goes to school by bus. School starts at 7.30.
Nimal has lunch at school at 12 o'clock. He usually eats rice and curry. School finishes at 1.30, and he comes home at 2 o'clock. In the afternoon, he plays cricket with his friends.
In the evening, Nimal studies and does his homework. He watches TV at 8 o'clock. His favourite programme is a cricket show. He goes to bed at 10 o'clock.
**Answer these questions.**
bullets: Does Nimal eat breakfast at home? ______________________________
What does he do in the afternoon? ______________________________

rows: Nimal goes to school by bus.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete the sentences with the correct form of the verb in brackets.**
**B. Write the he/she form. Then tick the sound of the ending.**
**C. Make questions and write short answers.**
bullets: Nimal ___________ (get) up at 6.30.
I ___________ (not / drink) coffee.
She ___________ (watch) TV after dinner.
My father ___________ (not / work) on Sundays.
We ___________ (have) lunch at 12 o'clock.
___________ your sister ___________ (play) cricket?
He ___________ (study) English every evening.
They ___________ (not / go) to school on Saturday.
My mother ___________ (finish) work at 5 o'clock.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Interview Your Partner
text: **Ask your partner the questions. Write the answers.**
**Now write 5–6 sentences about your partner.**
*Example: Ayesha gets up at 5.45. She doesn't have breakfast.*

rows: What time do you get up?
Do you have breakfast? What do you have?
How do you go to school / work?
What time do you have lunch?
What do you do in the afternoon?
Do you watch TV in the evening?
What time do you go to bed?

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1**
**Handout 2, Exercise A**
**Handout 2, Exercise B**
**Handout 2, Exercise C**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Questions: 1. No, he doesn't. 2. He goes by bus. 3. He plays cricket with his friends.
gets · 2. don't drink · 3. watches · 4. Do ... walk · 5. doesn't work · 6. have · 7. Does ... play · 8. studies · 9. don't go · 10. finishes

Does she like tea? No, she doesn't.
