hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Present Continuous vs Present Simple, built round the theme "What Are They Doing Now?".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who can use the present simple for routines and know common action verbs. Most have met the present continuous but confuse it with the present simple and often leave out be.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Information gap" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Reading
Grammar: Present Continuous vs Present Simple
PPP (presentation, practice, production)

Handout 1 (text messages), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3A and 3B (café scene cards for the information gap), a busy photo for the warm-up (any market or street photo projected or printed, or a board sketch).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise the present continuous for actions happening now, contrasted with the present simple for routines.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe what people are doing at the moment and contrast it with what they usually do, e.g. He usually walks to work, but today he's taking a taxi.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in describing scenes.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise reading for specific information (text messages).
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise -ing spelling rules.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: Spelling of *-ing*:
bullets: Most verbs add *-ing*: read → reading, play → playing.
Verbs ending in *-e* drop the *e*: make → making, write → writing.
One vowel + one consonant (stressed) doubles the consonant: sit → sitting, run → running, swim → swimming.
*-ie* → *-ying*: lie → lying, die → dying.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: **Present continuous:** actions happening at the moment of speaking or around now: *Look! It's raining. I'm reading a good book this week.*
**Present simple:** routines, habits and permanent facts: *I take the bus every day.*
**Contrast:** *He usually walks to work, but today he's taking a taxi.*
Time words: *now, right now, at the moment, today, this week, Look! Listen!* vs *every day, usually, always, often, on Mondays*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contractions are normal in speech: *I'm /aɪm/, she's /ʃiːz/, they're /ðeə/*.
*-ing* is pronounced /ɪŋ/ with no hard /g/ at the end.
In questions, *are* is weak: *What are you doing?* /wɒt ə jə ˈduːɪŋ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: For *Ravi is taking a taxi today.* · Is Ravi in the taxi now? (Yes.) · Does he take a taxi every day? (No.) · Is this a habit? (No, it's just today / now.) · For *Ravi usually walks to work.* · Does he walk most days? (Yes.) · Is he walking now? (We don't know / not necessarily.)

rows: Board the three parts in separate boxes: subject + be + verb-ing. Use a finger-counting gesture: three fingers for He – is – reading.
Using the continuous for routines (I am going to school every day).
Use the timeline contrast and highlight time words. Students sort time words into two columns.
Quick spelling race on the board in the presentation; add the spelling rules box to Handout 2.
Students run out of ideas in the café task.
Provide the prompt questions on the board: Who? What are they doing? Where?
Info-gap students look at each other's cards.
Seat pairs back to back or ask them to hold the card up close and not show it.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: NOW: now, at the moment, today, this week, Look!, Listen! · EVERY DAY: usually, always, often, every day, on Mondays
Timeline: routine (x x x x) vs NOW (~~~). He usually walks to work. Today he's taking a taxi. subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. Negative: isn't / aren't. Question: Is he ...? Are they ...?
make → making · sit → sitting · lie → lying · play → playing
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Continuous vs Present Simple, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest in the topic and get students talking about actions in a scene.
Show a busy market or street photo (or sketch a simple scene on the board: a man on a phone, a girl running, a woman buying fruit). Say: *"Look at this photo for 30 seconds."*
Hide the photo. Ask: *"How many people can you remember? What are they doing?"* Accept any answers; do not correct grammar yet.
Ask: *"What do you usually do on Saturday morning?"* Students tell a partner in one minute.
**Transition:** *"Let's read some messages. What are these people doing right now?"*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the present continuous in context and clarify its meaning, form and pronunciation, contrasted with the present simple.
Give out Handout 1. **Reading for gist:** *"Read the four messages. Where is each person? Write the place. Two minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many messages?"* (Four.) *"What do you write?"* (The place.)
Students check in pairs, then check as a class.
**Reading for detail:** students answer the three *Find and write* questions. Check answers.
**Noticing:** *"Underline the verbs that end in -ing."* Elicit: *I'm sitting, It's raining, We're having, They're cleaning ...*
**Meaning.** Write on the board: *Dilini usually walks to school. Today she's sitting on the bus.* Draw a timeline: crosses for every day, a wavy line at NOW. Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.

**Form.** Elicit the three parts: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing. Elicit the negative (*aren't, isn't*) and the question (*Is she ...? Are they ...?*) from the messages. Write the form table on the board.
**Spelling.** Write *make, sit, lie, play* on the board. Students come to the board and write the *-ing* forms. Elicit the rules.
**Pronunciation.** Drill chorally and individually with contractions: *I'm sitting on the bus. She's taking a taxi. What are you doing?* Model the weak form of *are*.
**Transition:** *"Now let's practise."*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To give accurate written practice of the form and the contrast with the present simple.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: put the time words in the right column. Exercise B: circle the correct form. Exercise C: write the -ing form. Seven minutes. Work alone."*
ICQs: *"In B, do you write or circle?"* (Circle.) *"Alone or with a partner?"* (Alone, then check.)
Monitor and help weaker students by pointing to the time words.
Pairs compare. Nominate students to read answers aloud and explain choices: *"Every day, so present simple."*

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups of three
text: **Aim:** To use the target language fluently in a communicative information-gap task and personalised speaking.

**Information gap (10 minutes).** Give out Handout 3A to Student A and Handout 3B to Student B. Say: *"This is a café. You have eight people on your card. Your partner has a different card. Don't show your partner! Tell your partner what the people are doing. Find six differences."*
ICQs: *"Can you show your card?"* (No.) *"How many differences?"* (Six.)
Monitor and note errors (missing *be*, wrong tense) and good sentences.
Check the differences as a class.

**Personalised speaking (8 minutes).** Write on the board: *What are you doing this week that is different from usual?* Model: *"I usually drink coffee, but this week I'm drinking green tea."* In groups of three, students tell each other two things they usually do and one thing they're doing differently this week. Each group reports one sentence about a member to the class.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback on language from the freer practice and consolidate learning.
Board four sentences heard during Stage 4: two correct, two with errors. Pairs decide which are correct and fix the others.
Board one or two good sentences and praise them.
Quick review: say a time word; students say *present simple* or *present continuous*.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Take or find a photo of a busy place. Write 6 sentences about what is happening, and 2 sentences about what usually happens there. *Example: A man is selling mangoes. Two boys are playing. On Sundays, this market is usually very busy.*
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a verb list for the café task: *carry, drink, read, talk, eat, write, sleep, wait, pay, laugh*. Let them write two sentences before speaking in the personalised task.

Stronger students add a reason or a contrast: *She's drinking tea because she usually doesn't sleep well after coffee.* They write a short message describing what they are doing right now, including one contrast with their routine.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Information gap" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Information gap" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students are successful if they: use *be + verb-ing* with the correct form of *be* in most sentences in the café task; choose the present simple for routines and the continuous for now in Handout 2 (8 out of 10 or better); find all six differences using accurate sentences.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use *be* consistently by the end of the lesson? Which stage took longer than planned? What will I review next lesson?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Messages

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on State Verbs, built round the theme "Temporary and Permanent: Lifestyles".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who know the basic forms of both present tenses but are unsure about temporary vs permanent situations, changing trends and stative verbs.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Reading
Grammar: Present Simple vs Present Continuous: State Verbs
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (three profiles), Handout 2 (language focus), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (trend discussion cards, cut up).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students understand and practise the present simple for permanent situations and the present continuous for temporary situations and changing trends, and to recognise stative verbs.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe permanent and temporary situations in their lives, talk about trends in their town and avoid stative verbs in the continuous.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise reading for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussing trends and expressing opinions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I live in Colombo. She works for a bank.
I'm staying with my aunt this month.
More people are working from home. Prices are rising.
I know the answer. This bag belongs to me.
blocks.heading: Form and use
Stative verbs
bullets: **Mind / opinion:** know, believe, understand, think (= have an opinion), remember, mean, agree
**Feelings:** like, love, hate, want, prefer, need
**Possession:** have (= own), own, belong
**Senses / appearance:** seem, look (= appear), taste, smell, sound

blocks.heading: Verbs with two meanings
bullets: *I think it's a good idea.* (opinion: stative) vs *I'm thinking about moving.* (mental process: dynamic)
*She has a car.* (possession) vs *She's having lunch.* (activity)
*I see what you mean.* (understand) vs *I'm seeing the doctor tomorrow.* (meeting)

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contractions in speech: *I'm staying, they're working*.
Stress on the contrast words: *I USUALLY live in Kandy, but THIS month I'm staying in Colombo.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I'm staying with my aunt this month.*** Is this my permanent home? (No.) · Is it true now? (Yes.) · Will it change? (Yes, probably soon.)
***I know the answer.*** Is knowing an action you can see? (No, it's a state.) · Can we say *I'm knowing*? (No.)

rows: Stative verbs in the continuous (I'm knowing, I'm wanting).
Card sort in the language focus task; keep a stative verb list on the board for the whole lesson.
Show the meaning pairs side by side; CCQ: Is it an opinion or an activity?
Students find the guiding questions hard.
Monitor and give the first answer for one example; allow pairs to compare with another pair.
Give the sentence starters on Handout 4.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, belong, own, seem, mean

PERMANENT → present simple: I live in Colombo. · TEMPORARY → present continuous: I'm staying with my aunt this month. · CHANGING TRENDS → continuous: More people are working from home. · STATES → simple only: I know. (not I'm knowing)
think: opinion vs process · have: own vs activity · see: understand vs meet
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: State Verbs, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To generate interest and personalise the topic.
Write on the board: *Always true about me* and *Different at the moment*. Model: *"I always drink tea in the morning. At the moment, I'm learning to swim."*
Students tell a partner one thing for each column (2 minutes).
Take two or three examples from the class. Write one of each on the board without comment; you will return to them in Stage 2.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context and help students work out and understand the rules for permanent, temporary and changing situations and stative verbs.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about three people. Whose life is changing the most? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Take a quick class vote and ask for reasons.
Students answer the three questions under the profiles. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the profiles. Answer the questions with your partner. Think about the meaning."*
ICQs: *"Alone or with a partner?"* (With a partner.) *"Do you need a grammar book?"* (No, look at the sentences.)
Pairs complete Parts A, B and C. Monitor. If pairs are stuck, ask: *"Is Tharindu's life in Melbourne forever?"*
Pairs compare with another pair (1 minute).
**Part C: Clarification (6 minutes)**
Elicit the answers to Part A. Build the rules in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Elicit the stative verbs from Part B and board them on the left. Ask: *"Why is I'm knowing wrong?"*
Show the verb pairs (*think, have, see*). Ask: *"Which one is an opinion? Which is an activity?"*
Return to the students' warm-up sentences on the board. Ask: *"Are these correct? Why?"*
Drill the contrast sentence with stress: *I USUALLY live in Kandy, but THIS month I'm staying in Colombo.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct form accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: present simple or present continuous? Six minutes. Work alone."*
Pairs compare and justify each answer using the rules: *"Temporary, so continuous."*
Check as a class. For each stative verb, ask: *"Why not the continuous?"*
Fast finishers do Exercise B (error correction); check it quickly with the class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three or four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the target language fluently in a discussion about trends and opinions.

Give each group a set of trend cards (Handout 4). Model with one card: *"Online shopping. In my town, more people are shopping online. My mother still goes to the market every day. I believe online shopping is convenient, but I don't think it's good for small shops."*
Say: *"Take a card. Talk for one minute: what is changing in your town? What do you think about it? Use the sentence starters."* Each student takes at least two cards (12 minutes).
ICQs: *"How long do you talk for?"* (One minute.) *"What two things do you talk about?"* (What is changing, and my opinion.)
Monitor and note good examples and errors, especially stative verbs in the continuous.
Each group chooses the most interesting trend and reports it to the class in two or three sentences.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback on language from the freer practice and consolidate the rules.
Board three errors and two good sentences from your notes. Pairs correct the errors.
Students close their handouts and tell a partner the four rules from today.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 120-word paragraph: *My life at the moment.* Include two permanent facts, three temporary situations, one trend in your town and two opinions using stative verbs.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Highlight the key time words (*this year, at the moment, these days*) on Handout 1 before reading. Let weaker students do Part A of the language focus only, then copy Part B from the board.

Ask stronger students to find two verbs on Handout 3 that change meaning in the continuous, and write a pair of sentences for each. In the discussion, they must use *these days, nowadays, more and more*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Trend Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students can explain in their own words when to use each tense. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. In the discussion, students avoid stative verbs in the continuous.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Were the guiding questions clear enough for students to find the rules? Did any pairs reach the wrong rule? How did I handle it? How well did students use stative verbs in the discussion?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Changing Lives
text: **Read the three profiles. Whose life is changing the most?**

**Tharindu, 22, student** Tharindu comes from Galle, but this year he's studying engineering in Melbourne. He's sharing a flat with two other students from India. "I love the city, but I miss my mother's cooking," he says. "I'm learning to cook, slowly! Life here is expensive, and prices are going up every month, so I'm working part-time in a café at the weekends."

**Nadeesha, 35, marketing manager** Nadeesha works for a big company in Colombo. Before, she spent two hours a day in traffic. Now, like many people, she's working from home three days a week. "My company is changing the way it works," she explains. "More and more meetings are happening online. I don't know if it's better, but I have more time for my children."

**Mr Fernando, 68, retired teacher** Mr Fernando lives in a village near Kurunegala. He taught English for forty years. These days, he's teaching his grandchildren to read, and he's writing a book about the history of his village. "Young people are leaving the village for the cities," he says. "I understand why, but it makes me sad."
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Where does Tharindu come from? Where is he living now? ______________________________
What is changing about Nadeesha's company? ______________________________
What trend does Mr Fernando talk about? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Part A. Look at these sentences from the profiles.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
**Part B. Look at these verbs from the profiles. Can we use them in the -ing form here? Sort them.**
*love · miss · learn · know · understand · work · have (= own) · cook · teach · write*
**Part C. Think!**
bullets: Tharindu **comes** from Galle.
This year he**'s studying** engineering in Melbourne.
Nadeesha **works** for a big company in Colombo.
She**'s working** from home three days a week.
Prices **are going up** every month.
Young people **are leaving** the village.
Mr Fernando **lives** in a village near Kurunegala.
Which sentences describe situations that are permanent (true for a long time)? ______________
Which describe situations that are temporary (true now, but will change)? ______________
Which describe something that is changing gradually (a trend)? ______________
Which tense do we use for permanent situations? ______________________________
Which tense do we use for temporary situations and trends? ______________________________
Find the time words in the profiles that go with the temporary situations: ______________________________
Nadeesha says *I don't know*. Why not *I'm not knowing*? ______________________________
Look: *I think it's a good idea.* / *I'm thinking about moving.* What is the difference in meaning? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Put the verb into the present simple or the present continuous.**
**B. Correct the mistakes. One sentence is correct.**
bullets: My brother ______________ (study) in Melbourne this year.

This soup ______________ (taste) delicious.
She lives with her cousin until July. ______________________________
Are you understand the rules? ______________________________
These days, more people are working from home. ______________________________

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Present Continuous with Always, built round the theme "Habits, Annoyances and Changing States".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who are confident with basic present tenses. They have rarely used always + continuous for complaints, and they are inconsistent with verbs that have both stative and dynamic meanings.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Present Continuous with Always; State and Action Verbs
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (blog: Things My Flatmate Does), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (role-play cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of present forms for (a) annoying habits (always + continuous), (b) gradual change (getting + comparative), (c) stative/dynamic verb meanings and (d) the present simple for timetables.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can make a polite but honest complaint about someone's habits, using always + continuous and appropriate softening language.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency and appropriate intonation in a polite complaint role-play.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a blog for writer's attitude.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: She always borrows books from the library.
I see what you mean. She has a car. This tastes good.
I'm seeing the doctor at 4. She's having a hard time. The chef is tasting the sauce.
blocks.heading: Form, meaning and use
Pronunciation
bullets: *always* + continuous: the main stress falls on *always*, often with a fall-rise to show irritation: *He's ALways leaving the lights on!*
Softening language is stressed less and spoken more quickly: *It's just that ..., I don't know if you've noticed, but ...*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***He's always leaving dirty dishes in the sink.*** Does it happen often? (Yes, very often, maybe too often.) · How does the speaker feel? (Annoyed.) · Does it really happen every single time? (Probably not; the speaker is exaggerating.)
***You're being very quiet today.*** Are you usually quiet? (No.) · Is it just your behaviour today? (Yes.)

rows: Word order: He always is losing his keys.
Show the position on the board: be + always + verb-ing.
Overuse of always + continuous making complaints sound rude.
Teach softening language (I've noticed that ..., It's just that ...) before the role-play.
Give pairs of sentences and ask: Can you own it? Is it an activity?
Too many uses in one lesson.
Prioritise always + continuous and stative/dynamic verbs; treat timetables briefly.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: borrow · leave the lights on · interrupt · sing in the shower · flatmate · patient · fair

always + continuous = annoyance: She's always borrowing ... · getting + comparative = change: It's getting hotter. · being + adjective = temporary behaviour · stative vs dynamic: have, see, think, taste · timetable: The bus leaves at 8.
I've noticed that ... · It's just that ... · I don't mean to complain, but ... · Would you mind ...? · Could you try to ...?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Continuous with Always, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of annoying habits and engage students personally.
Say: *"Think about people on buses, in class, at home or online. What habits annoy you?"* Give one example: *"People who talk loudly on the phone on the bus."*
Students list three annoying habits with a partner (2 minutes).
Take ideas from the class and board key words only (*phone, late, borrow, noise*).

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the blog. How does the writer feel about her flatmate? Is she being fair? Three minutes."*
Pairs discuss. Elicit that she is annoyed but also funny and kind.
Students answer the three questions under the blog. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**

Say: *"Underline every present form in the blog."* Pairs compare. Elicit examples and write them in groups on the board: *always + -ing*; *getting + comparative*; *being + adjective*; verbs like *have, see, taste*.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**

**always + continuous.** Write *She's always borrowing my charger!* and *She always leaves the lights on.* Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis. Elicit that the first shows annoyance. Board the word order: be + always + verb-ing.
**Gradual change.** Write *Our bill is getting higher and higher.* Ask: *"Is it changing? Is it finished?"*

**Stative / dynamic.** Board pairs: *I see what you mean / I'm seeing the doctor*; *She has a cat / She's having a difficult time*; *This curry tastes strange / The chef is tasting the curry.* Students explain the difference to a partner.
**being + adjective.** *I'm being patient. You're being very quiet today.* CCQ: *"Are you usually quiet?"* (No.)
**Timetables.** Board *The concert starts at 7.30.* Ask: *"Present or future? Why present simple?"* (A fixed timetable.)
**Pronunciation.** Model the irritated intonation: *He's ALways leaving the lights on!* Students repeat chorally, then say it with different feelings (annoyed, amused).

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Then do Exercise A: choose the best form. Four minutes."*
Pairs check. Then students do Exercise B (rewrite neutral sentences as complaints).
Check both exercises as a class.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it as part of the homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the language fluently and appropriately in a polite complaint role-play.
Give out Handout 4. Teach the complaint language on the right of the board and drill two phrases.

Say: *"You are flatmates. Student A has a problem with Student B's habits. Make a polite but honest complaint. Student B, respond, explain and suggest a change. Use at least three phrases from the board."*
ICQs: *"Are you angry or polite?"* (Polite but honest.) *"Who suggests a change?"* (Student B.)
Students read their cards and prepare for 2 minutes.
**Role-play 1** (4 minutes). Monitor and note language use.
Students swap roles and use Scenario 2 (4 minutes).
Two or three pairs perform for the class. The class listens and notes: *How many examples of always + continuous? Was the complaint polite?*

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard during the role-plays. Students identify and correct errors.
Board one or two very natural complaints and praise them.
Ask: *"Which phrase from today will you use outside class?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write a humorous blog post (150 words) about someone's annoying habits. Use *always* + continuous at least three times, *getting* + comparative once and one stative/dynamic pair.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide sentence frames for the role-play: *I've noticed that you're always ... . Could you try to ...?* Allow weaker students to do the role-play in a group of three, with one student as an observer.
Stronger students add sarcastic stress patterns and hedging (*a bit, kind of, sort of*). Ask them to use *forever* and *constantly* as alternatives to *always*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Role-play 1" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Role-play Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Role-play 1" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use *always* + continuous accurately and appropriately in the role-play. Students choose the correct stative or dynamic form in 7 of 8 items on Handout 2. Complaints include at least one softening phrase.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which use of the present caused the most difficulty? Were the complaints polite as well as accurate? What will I recycle next lesson?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Blog
text: **Read the blog. How does the writer feel about her flatmate? Underline all the present forms.**
**Things My Flatmate Does That Drive Me Crazy**
I love my flatmate, Shanika. Really, I do. She's funny, kind and she has the best cat in Colombo. But living with her is getting more difficult every week.
First, she's always borrowing my phone charger. I buy a new one, it disappears. I buy another one, it disappears too. Where do they go? Nobody knows.
Second, she's constantly singing in the shower at 6 am. She has a lovely voice, but not at 6 am!
Third, she always leaves the lights on. Our electricity bill is getting higher and higher. When I mention it, she says, "I see what you mean," and then she does it again.
At the moment she's having a difficult time at work, so I'm being patient. And tonight she's cooking dinner for me, which is very sweet. The problem is, this curry tastes a little strange ...
Am I being unfair? Tell me in the comments!
**Questions**
bullets: What does the writer like about Shanika? ______________________________
Why is the writer being patient at the moment? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice
text: **Language reference**
**A. Choose the best form.**
**B. Rewrite these neutral sentences as complaints.**
bullets: He **always loses / is always losing** his keys! It's so frustrating.
My father **always reads / is always reading** the newspaper at breakfast. It's his routine.
Look, the sky **gets / is getting** darker. It's going to rain.
I **have / am having** two sisters and a brother.
We **have / are having** a party on Saturday. Can you come?
You **are / are being** silly. Stop it!
This fish **smells / is smelling** bad.
I **think / am thinking** about changing jobs.
My neighbour plays loud music. → ______________________________

rows: It's getting more difficult every week.
I see what you mean. She has a cat. This tastes strange.
She's having a difficult time. I'm seeing the doctor.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Further Practice
text: **Complete the sentences with an appropriate present form of the verb in brackets.**
bullets: My brother is so annoying! He ______________________ (always / leave) dirty dishes in the sink!
The planet ______________________ (get) warmer and warmer.
I ______________________ (see) what you mean, but I don't agree.
You ______________________ (be) very quiet today. Is anything wrong?
The concert ______________________ (start) at 7.30 tonight, according to the ticket.
My grandmother ______________________ (always / go) to the temple on poya days. It's her tradition.
Sorry, I can't talk now. I ______________________ (have) dinner.
This coffee ______________________ (taste) strange. Is the milk old?
I ______________________ (see) my dentist on Friday. It's my check-up.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Role-play Cards
text: **Scenario 1: Student A**

You share a flat with Student B. You are unhappy because B: leaves dishes in the sink, borrows your clothes without asking, and plays games late at night. Make a polite but honest complaint. Use *always* + continuous and softening language.
**Scenario 1: Student B**
You share a flat with Student A. Listen to A's complaint. Explain your side (you are having a busy time at work, you are getting tired, etc.). Suggest one change and ask for one change from A.
**Scenario 2: Student A**
You work in an office with Student B. B is a nice colleague, but B: talks loudly on the phone, takes your stapler and arrives late to meetings. Make a polite complaint.
**Scenario 2: Student B**
You work with Student A. Listen to A's complaint. Explain (you are being given more work, your bus is always late, etc.). Agree to one change. Mention one habit of A's that also annoys you!
**Useful language**
bullets: *I've noticed that you're always ...*
*It's just that ...*
*I don't mean to complain, but ...*
*Would you mind not ...-ing?*
*Could you try to ...?*
*I'm sorry, I didn't realise. I'm having a really busy time at the moment.*

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Historic Present, built round the theme "Telling It Live: The Present for Stories, Commentary and Headlines".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students with a strong command of tenses. They tell stories in the past tense only and are not aware of how and why present forms are used for dramatic effect, live commentary, headlines and summaries.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Part B, commentary" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Present Simple and Present Continuous for Past Events (Historic Present)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)

Handout 1 (headlines), Handout 2 (texts for language analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (story prompts and commentary task), phones for recording (optional), a short silent video clip (sport or cooking, 60–90 seconds) or a set of sequenced images.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' ability to recognise and use present forms for dramatic narrative (the historic present), live commentary, newspaper headlines and plot summaries.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell a short anecdote in the historic present, deliver a 60-second live commentary and write headlines and a plot summary using appropriate present forms.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency and vividness in spoken anecdotes.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of genre conventions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Present continuous for background; present simple for main events
So I'm walking home and this man comes up to me and says ...
Present simple for quick completed actions; continuous for longer ones
He passes to Kumar, Kumar shoots ... and it's in! The crowd is going wild.
Present simple for past events; to + infinitive for future; past participle for passive
Minister resigns over scandal · President to visit Jaffna · Three injured in crash
Plot summaries, reviews and reporting what writers argue
In the novel, the hero returns home ... · Smith argues that ...
A man walks into a bar ...
blocks.heading: Uses of present forms with past or general reference
Why use the present?
bullets: It creates **immediacy and drama**: the listener feels the action is happening now.
Speakers often **switch** from past to present at the most exciting moment of a story.
Headlines use the present to save space and to make news feel current.
Summaries use the present because the story "exists" in the text permanently.

blocks.heading: Discourse features of anecdotes
bullets: Fillers and markers: *So ..., Anyway ..., And then ..., Next thing I know ..., Suddenly ...*
Reporting with *says* / *goes* (informal): *And he goes, "Excuse me, is this your bag?"*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Commentary: fast pace, rising pitch at climaxes, stress on names and key verbs.
Anecdotes: pausing before the key moment for effect.

rows: Students mix tenses randomly rather than for effect.
In analysis, highlight where switches happen and why. Rule of thumb: start in the past, switch to the present for the drama, and stay there.
Students don't see the historic present as "correct" English.
Show authentic-style examples from speech, journalism and literature. Discuss register: very common in speech, less common in formal written narrative.
Over-use of goes for says in formal contexts.
Point out it is informal speech only.
Weak students struggle to produce commentary in real time.
Let them watch the clip once first and note verbs; allow pairs to share the commentary.
Use a sequence of six images (e.g. a cricket shot or a cooking process) displayed one by one.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: Anecdote · Commentary · Headline · Plot summary · Joke
Background: present continuous (I'm walking home) · Events: present simple (this man comes up) · Headlines: resigns / to visit / injured · Summary: the hero returns home
So ... · Anyway ... · And then ... · Next thing I know ... · Suddenly ... · He goes, "..."
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Historic Present, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage interest and raise the question of why present forms are used for past events.
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Here are six newspaper headlines. With a partner, guess the full story behind each one."* (3 minutes.)
Take some guesses. Ask: *"Did these events happen in the past or are they happening now?"* (Past.) *"So why are the verbs in the present?"* Don't explain yet: *"Let's find out."*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present present forms used for past and general reference in four genres, and to clarify their form, function and effect.
**Part A: Teacher's anecdote (3 minutes)**

Tell a short anecdote yourself (about 1 minute), switching into the historic present at the dramatic moment: *"Last week I was at the market. It was busy. So I'm standing at the fish stall, and this man comes up behind me and grabs my bag ..."*
Ask: *"Did you notice anything about how I told the story? When did I change tense?"*
**Part B: Text analysis (9 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2 (four extracts: anecdote, commentary, headlines, film synopsis). Say: *"In groups, read the four extracts and answer the questions."* (7 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many extracts?"* (Four.) *"Alone or in groups?"* (Groups.)
Monitor and help with the questions about effect.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback on the questions. Build the centre of the board: which forms appear in each genre and why.

Highlight: the switch from past to present at the climax of an anecdote; present continuous for background, present simple for events; what headlines leave out (articles, auxiliaries) and the meaning of *to* + infinitive (future) and past participle (passive) in headlines; the present simple convention for plot summaries.
Highlight the anecdote language on the right of the board and its informal register (*goes* = *says*).
Model the pace of commentary: fast, rising at the climax. Students repeat one line from Extract 2.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite the story in the historic present from the word So. Exercise B: rewrite each sentence in the style given. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check answers as a class.
**Exercise C:** pairs write three headlines about recent school or local events and read them out. The class guesses the full story.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use present forms fluently and for effect in spoken anecdotes and live commentary.

Give out Handout 4. **Part A, anecdote (8 minutes).** Each student chooses a prompt (a lost item, a surprise, an embarrassing moment, a near miss), thinks for one minute and tells the story to a partner in about two minutes, switching to the present at the dramatic moment. The partner asks two questions.
ICQs: *"When do you switch to the present?"* (At the exciting moment.) *"What does your partner do?"* (Listens and asks two questions.)

**Part B, commentary (6 minutes).** Play the silent video (or show the images). In groups of four, students take turns to give a 60-second live commentary while it plays again. Record it on a phone if possible.
**Share (4 minutes).** Each group plays or performs one commentary or story for the class. The class votes for the most dramatic.
Monitor throughout and note good examples and errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board two or three sentences you heard that used present forms effectively, and one that switched tense confusingly. Discuss the effect.
Ask: *"Where would you use these forms? Where would you avoid them?"* (Speech, journalism, summaries: yes. Formal written narrative: less often.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 200-word synopsis of a film or book using the present tense, and three headlines about real events from this week.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide the anecdote language as a written list during the freer practice. Let weaker students tell their story first in the past, then retell it in the present with a partner's help.
Stronger students compare the historic present with free indirect speech in a short literary extract. They write a plot summary using the present simple and at least two participle clauses.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Part B, commentary" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Part B, commentary" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students switch to the present deliberately at the climax of their story. The commentary uses the present simple for quick actions and the continuous for longer ones. Students can explain why headlines and summaries use the present. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the analysis make the uses clear before the speaking task? Did students use the present for effect, or randomly? What would I change about the commentary activity?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Headlines
text: **With a partner, guess the full story behind each headline.**
**Think:** Did these events happen in the past, or will they happen in the future? Why do you think the headlines use these verb forms?
bullets: MINISTER RESIGNS OVER SCANDAL
LOCAL GIRL WINS NATIONAL SPELLING BEE
PRESIDENT TO VISIT FLOOD AREA
THREE INJURED IN BUS CRASH NEAR KANDY
ELEPHANT BLOCKS HIGHWAY FOR TWO HOURS
PRICES SET TO RISE AGAIN

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Analysis
text: **Extract 1: A spoken anecdote**

It was last December, and I was flying home from Dubai. Everything was normal. So I'm sitting there, I'm reading my book, and suddenly the plane drops, like, a hundred metres. People are screaming, drinks are flying everywhere. And the man next to me turns to me, totally calm, and goes, "Is this your first time on a plane?"
**Extract 2: Cricket commentary**

And he runs in, he bowls ... it's a short ball, and Perera pulls it ... it's high, it's long, and it's going all the way! That's six! The crowd are on their feet, they're singing, they're dancing in the stands!
**Extract 3: Headlines**
STORM HITS COAST: THOUSANDS WITHOUT POWER NEW BRIDGE TO OPEN IN MAY PAINTING STOLEN FROM NATIONAL MUSEUM
**Extract 4: Film synopsis**

In the film, a young teacher moves from Colombo to a remote village school. At first, the children ignore her, and the villagers don't trust her. However, when a flood threatens the village, she organises the rescue, and slowly she wins their respect.
**Questions**
bullets: In Extract 1, which verbs are in the past? Where does the speaker switch to the present? Why at that moment? ______________________________
Find a present continuous verb in Extract 1. What does it describe: background or main events? ______________________________
In Extract 2, why does the commentator use the present simple for *runs, bowls, pulls*? ______________________________
In Extract 3, what words are missing? What does *to open* mean? Is *stolen* active or passive? ______________________________
Why is Extract 4 in the present simple when the story is fiction and "finished"? ______________________________
Which of these texts is the most informal? Which words show this? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite the story in the historic present, from the word "So".**

Yesterday I was standing at the bus stop. **So** a car stopped in front of me. The driver opened the window and asked me for directions. I pointed to the left, and he smiled and drove away. Then I realised he had my bag!
**B. Rewrite each sentence in the style given.**
**C. Write three headlines about recent events at your school or in your town.**
bullets: (Headline) The president has visited the flood area. → ______________________________
(Headline) The government will build a new airport. → ______________________________
(Headline) Two people were hurt in a fire. → ______________________________
(Synopsis) In the film, a young girl found a lost dog and looked for its owner. → ______________________________
(Commentary) He hit the ball and it went for six! → ______________________________
(Anecdote) I was walking home when this woman stopped me. → So ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Speaking Task
text: **Part A: Tell a story**
Choose one prompt. Take one minute to think. Then tell your partner your story in about two minutes. Make it dramatic! Your partner listens and asks two questions at the end.
**Part B: Live commentary**
Watch the video once. Then, in your group, take turns to give a 60-second live commentary while the video plays again. Imagine you are on the radio: the listeners cannot see anything!
**Notes**

rows: A time you lost something important (a passport, a phone, a ticket).
A time someone surprised you, or you surprised someone.
A time something embarrassing happened to you in public.
A time something almost went very wrong.

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1:** The headlines use the present simple for past events (1, 2, 4, 5), *to* + infinitive for a future plan (3) and *set to* for a likely future (6). The present makes the news feel current and saves space.
**Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A (model)**
So a car stops in front of me. The driver opens the window and asks me for directions. I point to the left, and he smiles and drives away. Then I realise he has my bag!
**Handout 3, Exercise B**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Past: was, was flying, was. The switch happens at *So I'm sitting there*, just before the dramatic event, to make it feel immediate.
*I'm sitting, I'm reading, are screaming, are flying*: background and ongoing actions.
They are quick, completed actions happening as the commentator speaks.
Articles and auxiliaries are missing (*A storm has hit the coast; The new bridge is to open; A painting has been stolen*). *To open* = will open (future plan). *Stolen* = passive.
Plot summaries conventionally use the present because the story exists permanently in the text.
Extract 1: *So, like, totally, goes*.

President visits flood area · 2. Government to build new airport · 3. Two hurt in fire · 4. In the film, a young girl finds a lost dog and looks for its owner. · 5. He hits the ball and it goes for six! · 6. So I'm walking home and this woman stops me.

rows: (Plot summary) At the end, Hamlet died.
Mixing tenses randomly within one scene.
Switch tense once, at the dramatic moment, and stay in the present.
Prime Minister resigns / Prime Minister to resign.
Using goes for says in a formal essay.
Use says or a reporting verb in formal writing.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Past Simple, built round the theme "Last Weekend".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who can use the present simple for routines and know common activity verbs. They have heard was/were and some past forms but cannot yet form past simple sentences, negatives or questions.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Past Simple
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (Sunil's diary), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (Find someone who ...), irregular verb flashcards (go/went, have/had, see/saw, eat/ate, get/got, buy/bought, make/made, do/did).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the past simple of be and of regular and common irregular verbs to talk about last weekend.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say and write 6 sentences about their last weekend and ask a classmate Did you ...? questions.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise the pronunciation of -ed endings.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking (asking and answering about past activities).

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Was he happy? Yes, he was. / No, he wasn't.
Were you at school? Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
blocks.heading: Form: be

rows: I played cricket. She visited her aunt.
We went to Galle. He had lunch. They saw a film.
I didn't (did not) go out. He didn't watch TV.
Did you go out? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
Where did you go? What did you do?
blocks.heading: Form: other verbs (the same for all persons)
Form: other verbs (the same for all persons): notes
text: Spelling of regular verbs:
bullets: Most verbs add *-ed*: play → played, watch → watched.
Verbs ending in *-e* add *-d*: like → liked, dance → danced.
Consonant + *y* → *-ied*: study → studied (but play → played).
One vowel + one consonant: double it: stop → stopped, plan → planned.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
text: We use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time in the past: *last weekend, yesterday, on Saturday, last night, two days ago*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation of -ed
bullets: /t/ after voiceless sounds: walked, watched, cooked, danced
/d/ after voiced sounds: played, cleaned, listened, stayed
/ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/: visited, wanted, needed, started

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: For *I played cricket on Saturday.* · Is Saturday now or in the past? (In the past.) · Is it finished? (Yes.) · For *I didn't go out.* · Did I go out? (No.) · After *didn't*, is the verb *go* or *went*? (Go.)

rows: Flashcard drill in the presentation; irregular verb list on Handout 2.
Past form after didn't or did (Did you went?).
Board: did + base verb. Gesture: hold up one finger for "only one past".
Three-column sound sort; drill minimal examples.
Using was with other verbs (I was go).
Contrast I was at home (place/feeling) with I went home (action).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: yesterday · last night · last weekend · on Saturday · two days ago
I was at home. They were tired. · I played / went / had. · I didn't go. · Did you go? Yes, I did.
/t/ walked, watched · /d/ played, cleaned · /ɪd/ visited, wanted
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Simple, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and set the context of last weekend.
Write *Saturday* and *Sunday* on the board and draw an arrow pointing backwards. Say: *"Last weekend. Not this weekend. Last weekend."*
Tell the class three things you did, with mime: *"On Saturday, I cleaned my house. I went to the market. On Sunday, I watched a film."*
Ask: *"Did I watch a film?"* (Yes.) *"Did I go to the beach?"* (No.) Students just answer *yes* or *no*.
**Transition:** *"Now read about Sunil's weekend."*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Sunil's diary. Tick the things he did. Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you tick things he did or didn't do?"* (Did.)
Students read and tick. Pairs compare. Check answers by asking *"Did Sunil go to the beach?"* and modelling *"Yes, he did."*
Students answer the three comprehension questions.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**was/were.** Board from the text: *I was very tired. The beach was beautiful. My cousins were there.* Elicit: was for I/he/she/it; were for you/we/they.
**Regular verbs.** Students underline verbs ending in *-ed* in the diary. Board: *visited, played, walked, cooked, watched, stayed*. Elicit the rule: add *-ed*. Show the spelling rules.
**Irregular verbs.** Ask: *"Is there an -ed on went?"* (No.) Board *go → went*. Use flashcards: show the base form; students call out the past form. Repeat quickly three times.
**Negatives.** Board *I didn't go to the cinema.* CCQ: *"Did he go?"* (No.) *"Is it went or go after didn't?"* (Go.)
**Questions.** Board *Did you have a good weekend? Yes, I did.* and *Where did you go?* Highlight did + subject + base verb.
**Pronunciation.** Say *walked, played, visited*. Ask: *"Are the endings the same?"* Draw three columns. Students sort the six verbs from the text. Drill chorally and individually.

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercise A (gap fill) and Exercise B (irregular verbs) alone (6 minutes).
Pairs check. Nominate students to read sentences aloud; correct pronunciation of *-ed* as you go.
**Oral drill:** say a sentence; students make it negative. T: *"I went to the beach."* Ss: *"I didn't go to the beach."* Then: T: *"You / go out?"* Ss: *"Did you go out?"*

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Mingle, then whole class, then individual
text: **Aim:** To use the language in a personalised speaking task.
Give out Handout 3. Model the first item with a strong student: *"Did you watch a film last weekend?" "Yes, I did." "What did you watch?"* Write the name in the box.
Say: *"Stand up. Ask your classmates. Find one name for each box. Ask one more question. You have eight minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you ask one person or many people?"* (Many.) *"What do you write?"* (Names.)
Students mingle. Monitor and note errors with *Did you ...?* and past forms.
Students sit down. Ask several students to report: *"Kasun watched a film. He watched an action film."* (4 minutes.)
**Writing:** students write 6 sentences about their own weekend at the bottom of Handout 3 (4 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences from your notes, two correct and two incorrect. Students correct them in pairs.
Quick irregular verb review with the flashcards.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences about your last weekend. Include one sentence with *was/were*, two irregular verbs and one negative.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the verb list with past forms during the mingle. Allow them to answer *Yes, I did / No, I didn't* without follow-up questions.
Stronger students add time phrases (*in the morning, after lunch, at night*). They ask two follow-up questions with *Where? / Who with? / What?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Writing" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Writing" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use correct past forms in 5 of 6 written sentences. Students form *Did you ...?* questions correctly during the mingle. Students pronounce at least the /ɪd/ endings correctly.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which irregular verbs caused the most problems? Did the mingle give enough speaking practice for everyone?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Sunil's Diary
text: **Read Sunil's diary. Tick (✓) the things he did last weekend.**

**Saturday** In the morning, I visited my grandmother in Galle. We had lunch together: she cooked my favourite fish curry. In the afternoon, my cousins and I went to the beach. The beach was beautiful, and the water was warm. We played volleyball and walked along the beach. I was very tired in the evening, so I stayed at home and watched TV.

**Sunday** I got up late, at 10 o'clock! I didn't have breakfast. I studied English for two hours, and then I helped my father in the garden. In the evening, my friends wanted to go to the cinema, but I didn't go. I finished my homework and went to bed at 9.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Where did Sunil go on Saturday morning? ______________________________
What did he and his cousins do at the beach? ______________________________
What time did he get up on Sunday? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete the sentences with the past simple of the verb in brackets.**
**B. Write the past simple form.**
**C. Put the verbs in the correct sound column: walked · played · visited · cooked · cleaned · wanted · watched · stayed · needed**
bullets: I ______________ (visit) my grandmother on Saturday.
We ______________ (go) to the beach.
She ______________ (not / watch) TV.
They ______________ (be) very happy.
My brother ______________ (study) for his exam.
I ______________ (be) tired on Sunday.
We ______________ (not / go) to the cinema.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Find Someone Who ...
text: **Ask your classmates: "Did you ... last weekend?" Write a name. Ask one more question.**
**Now write 6 sentences about your weekend.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Past Continuous, built round the theme "What Were You Doing When ...?".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who use the past simple with reasonable accuracy and know the present continuous. They have not yet learned the past continuous and use the past simple for all past actions.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Set up" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Past Continuous
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (news story), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (alibi role cards and detective question sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise the past continuous for actions in progress at a past time and for actions interrupted by a past simple event (when / while).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say what they were doing at a specific past time and describe an interrupted action, e.g. I was cooking when the lights went out.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a game-like speaking task (an alibi game).
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a short news story for specific information.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Was she working? Yes, she was. / No, she wasn't.
Were you studying? Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: An action **in progress at a specific time** in the past: *At 8 pm last night, I was watching TV.*
A **longer action interrupted** by a shorter one: *I was walking home when it started to rain.* (past continuous = long action; past simple = short action)
**when** usually goes before the short action; **while** usually goes before the long action: *While she was sleeping, the phone rang.*
Two actions in progress at the same time: *While I was cooking, my brother was doing his homework.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *was* and *were* are usually weak in positive sentences: /wəz/, /wə/. *I was cooking* /aɪ wəz ˈkʊkɪŋ/.
They are strong in short answers and negatives: *Yes, I was* /wɒz/. *wasn't* /ˈwɒznt/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I was cooking when the lights went out.*** Which action started first? (Cooking.) · Which action was short? (The lights went out.) · Did the lights going out interrupt the cooking? (Yes.) · Which is in the past continuous? (Cooking.)

rows: Board formula with three boxes. Finger gesture: three fingers for was – watch – ing.
Using the continuous for both actions (When I was arriving, they were eating).
Timeline: one long wavy line, one cross. CCQ: Which is short?
Highlight the general pattern on the board; accept when with both in speech.
Alibi game: students forget their story.
Give each pair time to write a short alibi plan on the card.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: the lights went out · the phone rang · it started to rain · power cut · alibi · suspect
Timeline: ~~~~~ (long action) interrupted by X (short action). I was cooking when the lights went out. While she was sleeping, the phone rang. was/were + verb-ing. Q: What were you doing at 8?
I was cooking /wəz/ · They were watching /wə/ · Yes, I was /wɒz/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To generate interest and get students thinking about a moment in the past.
Turn off the classroom lights (or mime it). Say: *"Imagine: last night at 8 o'clock, all the lights in the city went out! A power cut!"*
Ask: *"Do you remember a power cut? Where were you? How did you feel?"* Take two or three answers.
Students tell a partner where they were at 8 o'clock last night (1 minute). Don't correct.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the past continuous in context and clarify its meaning, form and pronunciation, including when and while.
**Part A: Reading (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the news story. Match each person to what they were doing when the lights went out. Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many people?"* (Four.) *"Do you write or match?"* (Match.)
Pairs check, then check as a class. Students do the True / False questions.
**Part B: Noticing (3 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline was/were + -ing in one colour and the past simple verbs in another."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Mr Perera was cooking when the lights went out.* Draw a timeline: a long wavy line (cooking) and a cross (the lights went out). Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Form.** Elicit was/were + verb-ing; the negative (*wasn't, weren't*); the question: *What were you doing at 8 pm?* Write the form table on the board.
**when / while.** Board two sentences from the text. Ask: *"Which word comes before the long action?"* (while) *"Which comes before the short action?"* (when)
**Pronunciation.** Drill with weak forms: *I was cooking. They were watching TV.* Then strong short answers: *Yes, I was. No, I wasn't.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form and the contrast with the past simple.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: past simple or past continuous. Exercise B: when or while. Six minutes. Work alone."*
Pairs compare and justify: *"It's the long action, so past continuous."*
Check as a class. Drill two or three sentences.
Students answer Exercise C about themselves and read one answer to a partner.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four (two suspects, two detectives)
text: **Aim:** To use the past continuous fluently and accurately in a communicative game.

**Set up (2 minutes).** Read the situation on Handout 3: *"Yesterday between 10.00 and 11.00, a birthday cake disappeared from the staff room. Two students are suspects."* Divide each group: two suspects and two detectives.
**Preparation (4 minutes).** Suspects agree on a detailed alibi: where they were and what they were doing at 10.00, 10.15, 10.30 and 10.45. Detectives prepare questions with the question sheet.
ICQs: *"Suspects, must your answers be the same?"* (Yes.) *"Detectives, do you interview them together?"* (No, separately.)
**Interviews (8 minutes).** Detectives interview each suspect separately; the other suspect waits out of earshot. Detectives note answers.

**Decision (2 minutes).** Detectives compare notes and decide: innocent or guilty, with reasons: *"Suspect A said they were reading in the library at 10.30, but Suspect B said they were eating in the canteen."*
Each group announces its verdict to the class (2 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences from the game: two correct, two with errors. Students correct them.
Ask a final question round the class: *"What were you doing at 7 o'clock this morning?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a paragraph (80–100 words) about where you were and what you were doing during a memorable event (a big match, a storm, a celebration).
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give suspects a time-plan template to complete before the interviews. Weaker detectives can read questions directly from the sheet.

Detectives must ask at least two follow-up questions (*Exactly what time? Who were you with? What were they wearing?*). Stronger suspects add a *while* sentence: *While I was reading, Kamal was sitting next to me.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Set up" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 1: Power Cut! works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Set up" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the alibi game, students form past continuous questions and answers accurately most of the time. Students choose past continuous vs past simple correctly in 7 of 8 items on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students use *when* and *while* in at least one sentence each.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the timeline make the long action / short action clear? Was the alibi game well organised? How could I set it up faster?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Power Cut!
text: **Read the news story. Match each person to what they were doing when the lights went out.**
**CITY IN THE DARK**
At exactly 8 pm last night, all the lights in the city went out. The power cut lasted for two hours. We asked some people what they were doing.
"I was cooking dinner for my family," said Mr Perera, 45. "The rice was nearly ready. We ate by candlelight!"
Nimali, 16, was doing her homework when the lights went out. "I was writing an essay on my computer. I didn't save it, so I lost everything!"

Mrs Fernando, 70, wasn't worried. "I was sleeping in my chair. I didn't notice anything!"
**True or false?**

Nimali saved her essay. ______
Mrs Fernando was worried. ______
