blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use the past simple and past continuous but rarely use the past perfect, so their stories are hard to follow when events are not told in order.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Past Perfect (Narrative Tenses)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (story strips, cut up), Handout 2 (language focus), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (story prompt cards and listener sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students understand and use the past simple, past continuous and past perfect together to tell a clear personal story.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell a two-minute personal story using all three narrative tenses and at least four sequencers.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise sequencing words.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in storytelling.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise contracted 'd.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I arrived at the airport at 6.
It was raining and everyone was rushing.
An action before another past action
I realised I had left my passport at home.
blocks.heading: Form and use
Form and use: notes
text: Sequencers: *at first, then, after that, suddenly, as soon as, by the time, eventually, in the end*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *had* is usually contracted in speech: *I'd left* /aɪd left/, *she'd gone*. Students often don't hear the *'d*.
Weak *had* in full form: /əd/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***When I got to the gate, the plane had left.*** Which happened first: I got to the gate, or the plane left? (The plane left.) · Did I see the plane leave? (No.) · Which tense shows the earlier action? (Past perfect.)
***It was raining when I left home.*** Did the rain start before I left? (Yes.) · Is it a main event in the story or the background? (Background.)

rows: Not using the past perfect (When I arrived, the plane left = it left as I arrived).
Contrast the two meanings with timelines; CCQs.
Emphasise: only for the earlier event, when the order is not clear.
Give prompt questions on the story cards; listeners must ask two follow-up questions.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: at first · then · after that · suddenly · as soon as · by the time · eventually · in the end
Timeline: [had left passport] → [was raining / arrived at airport] → [realised]. Background = past continuous · Main events = past simple · Earlier = past perfect (had + pp)

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Perfect, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage interest and personalise the topic.
Ask: *"Have you ever had a problem on a journey? Missed a bus, lost a ticket?"* Give your own one-sentence example.
Students share with a partner in one or two sentences (2 minutes).
Take two examples from the class.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present narrative tenses in a story and help students work out when to use the past simple, past continuous and past perfect.
**Part A: Story strips (6 minutes)**
Give each pair the cut-up story strips (Handout 1). Say: *"This story is called The Day I Missed My Flight. Put the strips in order. Look for clues in the verbs and the sequencing words."*
ICQs: *"How many strips?"* (Eight.) *"What clues help you?"* (Verbs and sequencing words.)
Pairs compare with another pair. Read the story aloud in the correct order for students to check. Ask: *"Did the story have a happy ending?"*
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the four sentences from the story. Answer the questions with your partner."*
Monitor. Help struggling pairs by asking: *"Which happened first? Draw it."* Pairs draw timelines for sentences 3 and 4.
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit the answers. Build the timeline and rules on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Meaning contrast:** board *When I got to the gate, the plane left* vs *When I got to the gate, the plane had left.* Ask: *"In which sentence did I see the plane leave?"* (The first.)
**Form:** had + past participle; contraction *'d*. Elicit three irregular participles (*left, forgotten, gone*).
**Pronunciation:** drill *I'd left my passport at home*, slowly and then at natural speed.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing and forming the tenses accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the story. Exercise B: join the sentences with the past perfect. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check as a class and ask for timeline explanations for two items.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use narrative tenses fluently in personal stories.
Give each group a set of story cards (Handout 4). Each student chooses one card and plans a story for 2 minutes, making notes (not full sentences).
Model briefly: tell the first two sentences of your own story using all three tenses.
Students take turns to tell their stories (about 2 minutes each). Listeners complete the listener sheet: tick each tense they hear and write one follow-up question.
ICQs: *"What do listeners tick?"* (The tenses they hear.) *"What do they write?"* (A follow-up question.)
After each story, listeners ask their questions.
Each group nominates the best story; one or two are retold briefly to the class.
Monitor and note errors and good examples.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors and good sentences from your notes for students to correct and notice.
Ask students to explain the past perfect to a partner in one sentence.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 150-word story that begins: *It was a perfectly normal day until ...*
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a story skeleton: *It was ... (background). I was ... when ... . I realised I had ... . In the end, ...* Allow them to write their story notes in more detail.
Stronger students add feelings with adjectives and adverbs (*terrified, luckily, unfortunately*). They try the past perfect continuous: *I had been waiting for an hour.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 1: Story Strips (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use the past perfect correctly at least once in their story. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. Listeners can identify all three tenses in a partner's story.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the story strips work as a context? Could students explain the past perfect in their own words?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Story Strips (cut up)
text: **The Day I Missed My Flight**

rows: A. I ran to the check-in desk. People were queuing everywhere and everyone was rushing.
B. Last December, I was flying to Dubai for my cousin's wedding. I was very excited.
C. I called my brother. He jumped in a tuk-tuk and brought it to me, but when I got to the gate, the plane had left.
D. By the time I arrived at the airport, it was already 6.30. My flight was at 7.
E. In the end, I arrived in Dubai six hours late, but I didn't miss the wedding!
F. On the morning of the flight, it was raining heavily and the roads were full of traffic.
G. When I got to the desk, I opened my bag and realised that I had left my passport at home!
H. I was so upset. But then a kind airline worker found me a seat on the next flight.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these sentences from the story.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: It **was raining** heavily and the roads **were** full of traffic.
I **ran** to the check-in desk.
I **realised** that I **had left** my passport at home.
When I **got** to the gate, the plane **had left**.
In sentence 1, is the rain a main event in the story, or is it the background (the scene)? ______________________________
In sentence 2, is running a main event? ______________________________
In sentence 3, which happened first: *realised* or *left my passport*? ______________________________
Draw a timeline for sentence 3.
In sentence 4, did the writer see the plane leave? ______________________________
What is the form of the verb for the earlier action? ______ + ______________________________
Complete the rules:
We use the ______________________ for the main events of a story.
We use the ______________________ for the background.
We use the ______________________ for an action that happened before another past action.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Complete the story with the correct narrative tense.**

When I (1) ______________ (arrive) at the station, the train (2) ______________ (already / leave). It (3) ______________ (rain) and everyone (4) ______________ (run) for shelter. I (5) ______________ (realise) that I (6) ______________ (forget) my umbrella. While I (7) ______________ (wait) for the next train, I (8) ______________ (meet) an old school friend. In the end, we (9) ______________ (catch) the next train together and (10) ______________ (talk) all the way home.
**B. Join the sentences using the word in brackets. Use the past perfect for the earlier action.**
bullets: The film started. Then we arrived at the cinema. (When) → ______________________________
I finished my homework. Then I went out. (after) → ______________________________
She lost her keys. She couldn't get into the house. (because) → ______________________________
They didn't eat all day. They were very hungry. (because) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Story Cards and Listener Sheet
text: **Listener sheet:** tick the tenses you hear and write a follow-up question.

rows: A lost item: When was it? Where were you? What were you doing? When did you realise? What had happened?
A big surprise: Who surprised you? What were you doing? What had they planned?
An embarrassing moment: Where were you? Who was there? What happened? Had you prepared for it?
A journey that went wrong: Where were you going? What was the weather like? What had you forgotten?

**Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Background · 2. Yes, a main event · 3. Left my passport happened first · 5. No · 6. had + past participle · 7. past simple; past continuous; past perfect
arrived · 2. had already left · 3. was raining · 4. was running · 5. realised · 6. had forgotten · 7. was waiting · 8. met · 9. caught · 10. talked

When we arrived at the cinema, the film had started. · 2. I went out after I had finished my homework. · 3. She couldn't get into the house because she had lost her keys. · 4. They were very hungry because they hadn't eaten all day.

When I arrived, the film had already started.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Past Perfect Continuous, built round the theme "What Had Happened? The Detective's Notebook".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who know the past perfect simple but rarely use the past perfect continuous, and confuse the two when talking about causes and duration.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Past Perfect Continuous
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (detective's notebook), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (scene cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of the past perfect simple and continuous to explain causes, visible results and duration before a past moment.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can explain a past scene logically, e.g. The floor was wet because it had been raining and someone had left the window open.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in speculating and explaining.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise weak forms of had been.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: She had been working all night.
How long had you been waiting?
blocks.heading: Form

rows: Completed action before a past moment (result, number)
By 10 pm, he had written three emails.
Activity continuing up to a past moment (duration)
She had been working there for ten years when she resigned.
Visible result of a recent activity
His eyes were red because he had been crying.
I had known him for years. (not had been knowing)
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Meaning and use: notes
text: Time markers: *by the time, by (10 pm), for, since, already, just, when, before*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *had been* is weak and contracted: *She'd been working* /ʃid bɪn ˈwɜːkɪŋ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The ground was wet. It had been raining.*** Was it raining at the moment I looked? (Not necessarily; maybe it had stopped.) · Was the rain before the moment I saw the ground? (Yes.) · Can we see a result? (Yes, the wet ground.)
***By the time I arrived, they had finished the meeting.*** Was the meeting finished when I arrived? (Yes.) · Is the focus on the activity or the completion? (Completion.)

rows: State verbs in the continuous (had been knowing).
Mini state verb list on the board.
Continuous with a number of things (had been writing three emails).
Using past simple instead (He was tired because he ran).
Accept as possible in some cases; show that the past perfect makes the order clear.
Groups produce weak explanations in the deduction task.
Provide clue prompts on the scene cards.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: suspect · force a lock · breathe heavily · clue · evidence · explanation
Simple: had + pp → completed result / number: had written three emails · Continuous: had been + -ing → duration / activity / visible evidence: had been raining · State verbs → simple only: had known
She'd been working /ʃid bɪn/ · had been /əd bɪn/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Perfect Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage interest with a visual puzzle.
Describe or show a photo: *A man arrives at the office. He's soaking wet, exhausted, his shoes are muddy and he's holding a broken umbrella.*
Ask: *"Why? What had happened to him before he arrived?"* Students speculate with a partner (2 minutes). Don't correct.
Take a few ideas and board one or two.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the past perfect simple and continuous in context and clarify the difference in meaning and form.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the detective's notes. What had the suspect been doing before 10 pm? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline all the past perfect forms. Put them in two groups: had + past participle and had been + -ing."* Pairs compare. Board the two lists.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
Draw a timeline for *He had been running* (a wavy line ending just before 10 pm) and *Someone had forced the lock* (a cross before 10 pm). Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Elicit the rules: completed result or number → simple; duration, activity or visible evidence → continuous; state verbs → simple only.
Contrast: *By the end of the interview, he had changed his story three times* (number → simple) vs *She had been living next door for five years* (duration → continuous).
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak forms: *She'd been working. They'd been waiting for hours.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing and forming the two tenses accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Do Exercise A: choose the correct form. Then Exercise B: write explanations. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check as a class, asking for the reason each time.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use both forms fluently in a deduction task.

Give each group a scene card (Handout 4). Say: *"You are detectives. Look at the clues. Explain exactly what had happened and what people had been doing before the police arrived. Write at least six sentences using both past perfect forms."* (10 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many sentences?"* (At least six.) *"Which forms?"* (Both past perfect forms.)
Monitor and help with logic and language.
Groups present their explanation (1 minute each). Other groups challenge: *"But if he had been sleeping, why was the coffee hot?"*
The class votes for the most convincing explanation.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences heard during the presentations: correct and incorrect. Students correct them.
Ask: *"How do you decide between had done and had been doing?"* Elicit the rules.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write the detective's final report (180 words) explaining what had happened in your group's scene.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker groups the timeline images on their scene cards. Provide sentence starters: *The window was open because someone had ... . The floor was wet because ... had been ...*
Stronger groups include passive forms: *The window had been forced.* They use modal deductions: *He must have been sleeping.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Scene Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the deduction task, students choose simple vs continuous correctly most of the time. Correct use of state verbs in the simple form. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Was the difference between the two forms clear after the clarification? Was the deduction task motivating?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Detective's Notebook
text: **Detective Jayasinghe, 11 March, 10.15 pm**

When we arrived at the flat at 10 pm, the door was open. Someone had forced the lock. The suspect, Mr Dias, was sitting on the sofa. He was breathing heavily, and his shirt was wet: he had obviously been running.

The kitchen was a mess. Someone had been cooking: there was rice on the floor, and the cooker was still warm. Two glasses were on the table. Mr Dias said he had been watching a film all evening, but the TV was cold. He hadn't been watching anything.
His neighbour told us she had heard shouting at about 9.30. She had been living next door for five years and had never heard anything like it before.
By the end of the interview, Mr Dias had changed his story three times.
**Questions**
bullets: What had the suspect been doing before 10 pm? How do we know? ______________________________
What had someone done to the lock? ______________________________
Why don't the detectives believe his story about the film? ______________________________

**A. Choose the correct form.**
**B. Write an explanation for each situation using the past perfect continuous.**

Her eyes were red. She **had cried / had been crying**.
We **had walked / had been walking** for hours when we found the village.
By 2015, he **had visited / had been visiting** twelve countries.
I **had known / had been knowing** her since primary school.
The children were dirty because they **had played / had been playing** in the garden.
She **had read / had been reading** the book twice before the film came out.
How long **had you waited / had you been waiting** when the doctor arrived?
The teacher's voice was very tired. → ______________________________
The streets were full of water. → ______________________________

Police arrive at 11 am. The front door is locked. A back window is open. The swimming pool area is wet. There are two towels on chairs. A cake is half eaten. The guest's car is gone. A phone on the table shows 14 missed calls.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Inversion and Participle Clauses, built round the theme "Crafting Suspense: Writing a Story Opening".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who write accurate but "flat" narratives in which every sentence has the same structure. They have met negative inversion but rarely use it.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Past Perfect in Inversion and Participle Clauses (No sooner had ... / Having + past participle)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (two story openings), Handout 2 (analysis), Handout 3 (practice and style checklist), Handout 4 (writing task: the flat paragraph).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' ability to create suspense in written narrative using delaying structures, negative inversion, was about to / was going to, and participle clauses.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can rewrite a flat paragraph into a suspenseful one using at least four techniques, and explain the effect of each.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop collaborative writing and peer-editing skills.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of sentence rhythm.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I was just reaching for the door when the light went out.
No sooner had + S + pp ... than; Hardly / Scarcely / Barely had + S + pp ... when
No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang. Hardly had she left when the storm began.
Inversion with Never / Not until / Only then
Never had I felt so alone. Only then did I realise the truth.
was about to / was going to + infinitive
I was about to scream when a hand covered my mouth.
Having locked the door, she turned off the lights. Hearing a noise, he froze.
long sentence followed by a very short one
... and I walked slowly down the corridor, counting the doors, listening for any sound. Silence.
blocks.heading: Techniques
Accuracy points
bullets: *No sooner* ... **than** (not *when*); *Hardly / Scarcely* ... **when** (not *than*).
The participle clause must share the subject of the main clause (avoid dangling participles: *Having locked the door, the lights went out* ✗).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation (when reading aloud)
bullets: Pause before the key event; lower volume for tension; stress the inverted auxiliary: *No sooner HAD I ...*

rows: Wrong word order after inversion (No sooner I had arrived).
Show the "question order" pattern; quick transformation drill.
Board the pairs clearly and include in practice.
Include one deliberate example in the analysis for students to spot.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: delaying · inversion · about to · participle clauses · short sentences
No sooner had I + pp than ... · Hardly had she + pp when ... · Never had I felt ... · I was about to ... when ... · Having + pp, S + V
No sooner ... than (not when) · Hardly / Scarcely ... when (not than) · participle subject = main subject
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Inversion and Participle Clauses, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of suspense and engage students.
Give out Handout 1. Read aloud Version A (flat) and Version B (suspenseful). Ask: *"Which one would you continue reading? Why?"*
Pairs discuss what makes Version B more exciting (2 minutes). Take ideas but don't name the grammar yet.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the structures writers use to create suspense and clarify their form, meaning and accuracy points.
**Part A: Analysis (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Compare Version A and Version B. For each technique, find an example in Version B and describe its effect on the reader."*
ICQs: *"Which version do you take examples from?"* (B.) *"What else do you write?"* (The effect.)
Groups complete the table. Monitor and help.
**Part B: Clarification (12 minutes)**
Feedback on the table. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.

**Negative inversion.** Board *I had never felt so alone → Never had I felt so alone.* Ask: *"What happens to the subject and the auxiliary?"* (They swap, like a question.) Show *No sooner had I ... than* and *Hardly / Scarcely had she ... when*.
**Interrupted plans.** *I was about to call out when I heard it.* CCQ: *"Did I call out?"* (No.)

**Participle clauses.** *Having fumbled for my keys, I pushed the door open.* Ask: *"Who fumbled? Who pushed?"* (The same person.) Answer the accuracy questions on Handout 2, including the dangling participle (*Having locked the door, the lights went out*).
**Rhythm.** Point out the one-word sentences (*Nothing. Empty.*) after long sentences.
**Pronunciation.** Read a line aloud with a pause before the key event and stress on the inverted auxiliary: *No sooner HAD I ...* Students repeat.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite the sentences using the word in brackets. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class, focusing on word order after inversion and *than / when*.
**Exercise B:** pairs improve the two flat sentences using a technique of their choice. Two pairs read theirs aloud.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the techniques creatively in a piece of suspense writing.

Give out Handout 4. Say: *"Rewrite this flat paragraph so that it is full of suspense. Keep the same basic events. Use at least four techniques from today and tick them on the style checklist (Handout 3)."* (10 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Can you change the events?"* (No, keep them.) *"How many techniques?"* (At least four.)
Pairs swap with another pair and underline the most effective line (3 minutes).
Three or four pairs read their versions aloud. The class votes for the most gripping version (5 minutes).
Monitor throughout and note accuracy problems.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board two or three of the most effective lines and one or two sentences with errors. Students correct the errors.
Discuss balance: *"What happens if every sentence uses inversion?"* (The writing becomes heavy.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 250-word suspense story opening. Use the style checklist and highlight each technique you use.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give model sentences for each technique on a reference card. Pair weaker students with stronger writers for the writing task.
Students vary the point of view or use free indirect speech. They write the next paragraph of the story for homework, using a technique not yet practised.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice and Style Checklist on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The final text uses at least four techniques accurately. Students can name and explain each technique. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the analysis make the structures noticeable? Were students accurate with word order after inversion?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Openings
text: **Version A**

I got home at 11 pm. I opened the door. The house was dark. I turned on the light, but it didn't work. I heard a noise upstairs. I went up the stairs. A door was open. I looked inside. There was nobody there. Then the phone rang.
**Version B**

It was almost midnight by the time I reached the house. Having fumbled for my keys in the dark, I pushed the door open and reached for the light switch. Nothing. I was about to call out when I heard it: a slow, heavy footstep, directly above my head. Never had the staircase seemed so long. I was halfway up, counting each step, holding my breath, when I noticed that my bedroom door, the door I always close, was wide open. I stepped inside. Empty. No sooner had I let out a breath than the phone began to ring.
**Discuss:** Which version do you want to continue reading? Why?

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Analysis
text: **Compare Version A and Version B. Find an example of each technique and describe its effect.**
**Think about accuracy.**
bullets: What is the word order after *No sooner*? ______________________________
Which word follows *No sooner*: *than* or *when*? ______________________________
Which word follows *Hardly*: *than* or *when*? ______________________________
What is wrong with this sentence? *Having locked the door, the lights went out.* ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice and Style Checklist
text: **A. Rewrite using the word in brackets.**
**B. Improve these two flat sentences using a technique from today.** *I opened the box. There was a letter inside.* / *She heard a noise and looked out of the window.*
**Style checklist**
bullets: As soon as I closed my eyes, the alarm went off. (No sooner) → ______________________________
She had only just left when the parcel arrived. (Hardly) → ______________________________
I was going to call him, but the line went dead. (about) → ______________________________
After he had checked the windows, he went upstairs. (Having) → ______________________________
I had never felt so alone before. (Never) → ______________________________
I didn't understand what had happened until I saw the letter. (Only when) → ______________________________
He heard the scream and ran outside. (Hearing) → ______________________________
We had just started eating when the power went off. (Scarcely) → ______________________________
I didn't realise he was lying until much later. (Not until) → ______________________________
The moment she opened the box, she screamed. (No sooner) → ______________________________

rows: was about to / was going to
A very short sentence after a long one

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **Rewrite this paragraph so that it is full of suspense. Keep the same basic events.**

Maya was walking home from the station. It was late and the street was empty. She heard footsteps behind her. She walked faster. The footsteps got faster too. She turned the corner and saw her house. She ran to the door. She couldn't find her key. A hand touched her shoulder. It was her brother.
**Your version:**

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 2 (examples)**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Participle clause: *Having fumbled for my keys in the dark* (adds detail and tension, speeds up the action)
One-word sentence: *Nothing.* / *Empty.* (creates a shock and a pause)
*was about to ... when*: *I was about to call out when I heard it* (interrupts the action)
Negative inversion: *Never had the staircase seemed so long* (emphasises fear)
Delaying: *I was halfway up ... when I noticed* (builds tension)
*No sooner ... than*: *No sooner had I let out a breath than the phone began to ring* (a sudden twist)
Auxiliary + subject (*had I*) · 2. than · 3. when · 4. Dangling participle: the lights didn't lock the door. Correct: *Having locked the door, she turned off the lights.*
No sooner had I closed my eyes than the alarm went off.
Hardly had she left when the parcel arrived.
I was about to call him when the line went dead.
Having checked the windows, he went upstairs.
Never (before) had I felt so alone.
Only when I saw the letter did I understand what had happened.
Hearing the scream, he ran outside.
Scarcely had we started eating when the power went off.
Not until much later did I realise he was lying.
No sooner had she opened the box than she screamed.

rows: No sooner I had arrived than ...
No sooner had I arrived than ...
Hardly had she left than he came.
Hardly had she left when he came.
Having locked the door, the lights went out.
Having locked the door, she turned off the lights.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Present Perfect for Experiences, built round the theme "Our Experiences".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners (high A1) who can use the present simple and the past simple of common verbs. They have not studied the present perfect and cannot ask about life experiences.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Present Perfect for Experiences (Have you ever ...?)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (speech bubbles), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (class survey), picture cards: a plane, snow, an elephant, the sea, a mountain, a famous building.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the present perfect with ever and never to talk about life experiences.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can ask Have you ever ...?, answer with short answers and say 5 sentences about their own experiences.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To learn ten common past participles.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise short answers.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a class survey.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I haven't been to India. / I've never been to India.
Have you ever been to India?
Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
He hasn't eaten sushi. / He's never eaten sushi.
Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: **have / has + past participle.** Common participles:

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use the present perfect for **experiences in our life up to now**. The exact time is not important and is not said.
*ever* = at any time in your life (in questions). *never* = at no time (in positive sentences with negative meaning).
If we say **when**, we change to the past simple: *I've been to Galle. I went there last year.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contractions: *I've* /aɪv/, *she's* /ʃiːz/, *haven't* /ˈhævnt/.
*Have you ever* is joined: /həv juː ˈevə/.
Short answers are stressed: *Yes, I HAVE.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I have been to Kandy.*** Did I go to Kandy? (Yes.) · Do we know when? (No.) · Is the time important? (No, it's about my life.)
***I've never seen snow.*** Have I seen snow in my life? (No.)

rows: Using the past simple form after have (Have you ever went?).
Board the participle table; drill go – went – been.
Using a time word with the present perfect (I have been to Galle last year).
Show the rule: time = past simple.
Board: never = not ever; one negative only.
At A1, teach been for experiences only; note gone later.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: be → been · eat → eaten · see → seen · fly → flown · ride → ridden · swim → swum · meet → met
I have been to Kandy. She has eaten durian. Have you ever seen snow? I've never flown in a plane. · Time? → past simple: I went last year.
Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. · Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Perfect for Experiences, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and introduce the idea of life experiences.
Hold up the picture cards one by one: a plane, snow, an elephant, the sea, a mountain, a famous building.
For each, ask: *"Who has seen this? Raise your hand!"* Students raise hands. Count them: *"Ten students have seen the sea!"*
Say: *"Interesting! Let's read about some teenagers' experiences."*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context. To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present perfect for experiences.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the speech bubbles. Match each person to an experience."* (3 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you write or match?"* (Match.) *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Alone.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
Ask detail questions: *"Has Nadia been to India?"* Model the answer: *"Yes, she has."*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *I have been to Kandy.* Ask the CCQs. Draw a timeline from birth to NOW with a cross somewhere in between and a question mark under it: *"When? Not important."*
**Form.** Elicit: *have / has + past participle*. Highlight *has* for he/she. Elicit participles from Handout 1 and complete the participle table on the left of the board.
**Negative and never.** Board *I've never flown in a plane* and *I haven't flown in a plane*. Ask: *"Same meaning?"* (Yes.) Point out: never = no *n't*.
**Questions.** Board *Have you ever seen snow?* Elicit short answers.
**The time rule.** Board *I've been to Galle. I went there last year.* Ask: *"Which sentence has a time?"* (The second.) *"Which tense?"* (Past simple.)
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *Have you ever been to Jaffna? Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.* Use back-chaining: *Jaffna – been to Jaffna – ever been to Jaffna – Have you ever been to Jaffna?*

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise form accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
ICQs: *"In Exercise A, do you write have or has?"* (Both; look at the person.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers. Drill any difficult participles.
**Quick-fire drill:** say a base verb; students say the participle (*eat → eaten, see → seen*).

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Mingle, then groups, then individual
text: **Aim:** To use the language in a personalised speaking task.
Give out Handout 3. Model with a strong student: *"Have you ever ridden an elephant?" "No, I haven't." "Have you ever eaten durian?" "Yes, I have."* Write the name in the box.
Say: *"Stand up. Ask your classmates. Find a name for each question. When someone says yes, ask: When? Use the past simple!"* (8 minutes.)
ICQs: *"What do you ask when they say yes?"* (When?)
Monitor and note errors.
Groups of four compare results and make a class poster: *Five students have been to Jaffna. Nobody has flown in a helicopter.* (5 minutes.)
Students write five sentences about their own experiences at the bottom of Handout 3 (4 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Groups read their posters.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Pairs correct.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences about things you have and haven't done. Write one past simple sentence giving more information about one experience.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a participle list during the survey. Allow them to ask the questions on the sheet without follow-up questions.
Stronger students ask two follow-up questions in the past simple (*When did you go? Who did you go with?*). They write a short paragraph: *Three things I've never done but want to do.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students form *Have you ever ...?* questions correctly during the survey. Students use the correct participle in 8 of 10 items on Handout 2. Students switch to the past simple when they give a time.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which participles caused problems? Did students switch to the past simple for details?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Our Experiences
text: **Read the speech bubbles. Match each person to one experience: India, an elephant, a mountain, the sea, a plane.**
**Nadia (14):** I have been to India three times! But I have never seen snow.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Present Perfect vs Past Simple, built round the theme "Sharing News".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know the present perfect for experiences and the past simple. They mix the two tenses and use time words like yesterday with the present perfect.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Pairs" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Present Perfect vs Past Simple (just, already, yet)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (social media posts), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (news cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise the difference between the present perfect (news, no time, recent with just / already / yet) and the past simple (finished time, details).

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can share a piece of news in the present perfect and give or ask for details in the past simple, e.g. I've bought a new phone! I bought it yesterday.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in sharing news and asking follow-up questions.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read social media posts for specific information.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: News, no time given: I've lost my keys!
Finished time given: I lost my keys yesterday.
Recent actions with just: I've just finished.
Details and questions about the news: Where did you lose them?
already (sooner than expected): She's already left.
Time words: yesterday, last week, in 2022, ago, when
yet (questions and negatives): Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.
Unfinished time: this week, today, this year
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Word position
bullets: *just* and *already* go between *have* and the participle: *I've* ***just*** *eaten. She's* ***already*** *gone.*
*yet* goes at the end: *Have you done it* ***yet? I haven't done it*** ***yet.***

blocks.heading: been vs gone
bullets: *She's* ***been*** *to Paris.* (She went and came back.)
*She's* ***gone*** *to Paris.* (She is there now.)

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *I've just* /aɪv dʒʌst/ – the *'ve* is short but must be heard.
*yet* at the end often has rising intonation in questions: *Have you finished yet?* ↗

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I've lost my keys!*** Do I have my keys now? (No.) · Do we know when I lost them? (No.) · Is it news? (Yes.)
***I lost my keys yesterday.*** Do we know when? (Yes, yesterday.) · Is yesterday finished? (Yes.) So which tense? (Past simple.)

rows: Present perfect with finished time (I have seen him yesterday).
Time-word sort; rule on the board: finished time = past simple.
Show yet belongs with the present perfect (in British English).
Colour-code the position in board examples.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: PRESENT PERFECT: just, already, yet, ever, never, this week, today · PAST SIMPLE: yesterday, last week, in 2022, two days ago, when
NEWS (no time): I've lost my keys! → DETAILS (time): I lost them yesterday. Where did you lose them?
have just + pp · have already + pp · haven't + pp ... yet · Have ... + pp ... yet?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Perfect vs Past Simple, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To generate interest in sharing news.

Act excited. Say: *"Guess what! I've bought a new bicycle!"* Let students react. Ask: *"What questions can you ask me?"* Answer naturally in the past simple: *"I bought it on Saturday. It cost 40,000 rupees."*
Ask: *"Do you have any news this week?"* Students tell a partner (1 minute).

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the present perfect and past simple in context and clarify the difference, including *just, already, yet* and *been / gone*.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the posts. What is each person's news? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many people?"* (Four.) *"What do you find?"* (Their news.)
Pairs check; then students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (3 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline present perfect verbs with a straight line and past simple verbs with a wavy line."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (11 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board Priya's post: *I've passed my driving test! I took it this morning.* Ask the CCQs. Elicit the rule: news with no time → present perfect; details and finished time → past simple.
**Time words.** Pairs sort the time words in Handout 2, Exercise A. Check and build the left of the board.
**just / already / yet.** Board examples from the posts. Ask: *"Where does just go? Where does yet go? Do we use yet in positive sentences?"* (No: questions and negatives.)
**been vs gone.** Board *Kamal has gone to Jaffna* and *Kamal has been to Jaffna.* Ask: *"Where is Kamal now?"*
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *I've just passed my test! Have you finished yet? She's already left.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct tense and placing *just, already, yet*.
Say: *"Now do Exercises B and C on Handout 2. Six minutes."*
Pairs compare and explain: *"Yesterday is finished time, so past simple."*
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the present perfect for news and the past simple for details in fluent conversation.
Give each student two news cards (Handout 3) or let them use real news. Model with a strong student: *"I've adopted a puppy!" "Really? When did you get it?" "I got it on Sunday."*
**Pairs (7 minutes):** students share their news in the present perfect; the partner asks at least three past simple questions. Swap.
ICQs: *"Which tense for the news?"* (Present perfect.) *"Which tense for the questions?"* (Past simple.)
**Mingle (7 minutes):** students share one real piece of news from this week with three different people. Each listener asks one question.
Ask: *"Who had the best news?"* Students report: *"Ravi has adopted a puppy! He got it on Sunday."*
Monitor throughout and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Quick test: say a time expression; students say *present perfect* or *past simple*.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a social media post (80 words) with a piece of news. Add three comments from friends asking questions, and your replies.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide question starters: *When did you ...? Where did you ...? How much did it ...? Who did you ...?* Allow weaker students to read the news cards directly.
Stronger students use *just, already, yet* at least once each in the freer practice. They write a short social media post with three comments and replies.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Pairs" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: News Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Pairs" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students introduce news with the present perfect and give details in the past simple. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise B. Correct position of *just, already, yet* in written practice.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand the news / details distinction? Did they understand *yet* in questions and negatives?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Social Media Posts
text: **Read the posts. What is each person's news?**

**Priya:** I've passed my driving test! I took it this morning and I was SO nervous. Now I need a car! *Comment from Kasun:* Congratulations! Did you pass first time? *Priya:* No, I failed last year, but I've practised a lot since then.
**Malik:** Has anyone seen my black cat? She went out on Monday and she hasn't come home yet. Please call me!
**Shalini:** We've just moved into our new flat! We moved on Saturday. I haven't unpacked my boxes yet, but I've already put my plants on the balcony.
**Ravi:** Bad news: I've broken my phone. I dropped it in the canteen yesterday. I've already ordered a new one.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: When did Priya take her test? ______________________________
What hasn't Shalini done yet? ______________________________
When did Ravi break his phone? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Sort the time words.**
*yesterday · just · last week · already · in 2022 · yet · two days ago · this week · ever · when I was a child*
**B. Choose the present perfect or the past simple.**
**C. Put the word in the correct place.**
bullets: I ______________ (lose) my keys! Can you help me look?
We ______________ (go) to Nuwara Eliya last month.
______________ you ______________ (finish) your homework yet?
She ______________ (start) her new job two weeks ago.
I ______________ (just / see) your message.
______________ you ______________ (see) the match last night?
They ______________ (already / eat). They aren't hungry.

My grandparents ______________ (get) married in 1975.
I ______________ (never / be) to Japan.
I have finished my lunch. (just) → ______________________________

She has left the office. (already) → ______________________________

text: **Useful questions:** *When did you ...? Where did you ...? How did you ...? Who did you ... with? How much did it cost? How did you feel?*

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Present Perfect Continuous, built round the theme "Clubs and Hobbies".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use the present perfect simple for experiences and news, but say I am learning English since six years and don't use the present perfect continuous.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Present Perfect Continuous (for and since)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (club interviews), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (interview sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover and use the present perfect continuous for duration (with for / since) and recent activity, and to contrast it with the present perfect simple for results and quantities.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can interview a partner about hobbies, work and studies and write a short profile using both perfect forms and for / since.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read interviews for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in interviewing and writing a profile.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I've been running for five years.
How long have you been learning English?
How many books have you read?
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: **have / has + been + verb-ing**

rows: Duration of an activity up to now: I've been learning English for six years.
Result or quantity: I've learned 500 words.
Recent activity with visible evidence: I've been painting (that's why I'm dirty).
Completed action: I've painted the room (it's finished).
Not with state verbs: I've known her for years (not been knowing).
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
for and since
bullets: **for** + a period of time: *for three years, for two hours, for ages*.
**since** + a point in time: *since 2019, since Monday, since I was ten*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *been*: /bɪn/. *I've been running* /aɪv bɪn ˈrʌnɪŋ/.
*How long have you been ...?* is said as one unit, stress on *long* and the main verb.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I've been learning English for six years.*** Did I start in the past? (Yes, six years ago.) · Am I still learning? (Yes.) · Are we talking about how long or how many? (How long.)
***I've run three marathons.*** Are the marathons finished? (Yes.) · Is the focus on how long or how many? (How many.)

rows: Present simple / continuous for duration (I am living here since 2018).
Contrast with the timeline from past to now; CCQs.
Card sort; rule: period vs point.
Continuous with quantities (I've been writing five emails).
How long vs how many contrast.
State verbs in the continuous (I've been knowing her).
Remind of state verbs from earlier lessons.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: FOR: five years · two hours · ages · a long time · SINCE: 2019 · Monday · I was ten · last summer

Timeline: started in the past → continuing now. How long? → have been + -ing: I've been running for five years. · How many? → have + pp: I've run three marathons. · Evidence: I've been painting (dirty hands). · States: I've known her for years.
I've been /aɪv bɪn/ · How LONG have you been RUNning?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Perfect Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic and create interest.
Say: *"Tell your partner about a hobby or sport you do. When did you start?"* Model: *"I play badminton. I started when I was twelve."*
Students talk for 2 minutes. Take two examples without correcting.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the present perfect continuous in context and help students work out its form and use, contrasted with the present perfect simple.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about three club members. Who has been a member the longest? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the interviews. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Pairs.) *"Where are the sentences from?"* (The interviews.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Is Amal still running? Did he start in the past?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit the answers. Draw the timeline: a line from a point in the past to NOW, with an arrow. Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Contrast: *How long have you been running?* vs *How many marathons have you run?*
**for / since:** students call out time expressions; the class decides *for* or *since*. Board them on the left.
**Pronunciation:** drill *How long have you been learning English? I've been learning it for six years.* Focus on weak *been*.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form and the contrast accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: for or since. Exercise B: simple or continuous. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare and justify: *"How long, so continuous."*
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then individual, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use both forms fluently in a personalised interview and writing task.
Give out Handout 4. Model one question with a strong student: *"How long have you been living in your house?" "Since 2015." "How many times have you moved?"*
Pairs interview each other and take notes (9 minutes).
ICQs: *"Do you write full sentences or notes?"* (Notes.)
Students write a short profile of their partner (5 sentences) using both forms (6 minutes).
Two or three students read their profiles aloud (3 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors and good sentences from monitoring. Students correct them.
Quick check: say a time expression; students say *for* or *since*.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 120-word profile of someone you admire, including how long they have been doing their job or hobby and what they have achieved.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide question starters on the board. Let weaker students write profile sentences using a frame: *___ has been ___ing for / since ___. He/She has ___ (number) ___.*

Stronger students include both forms in one answer: *I've been training for a year and I've run two races.* They add a sentence with visible evidence: *You look tired. Have you been studying all night?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students choose *for / since* correctly in 7 of 8 items. In the profiles, students use both forms appropriately. Students avoid the present simple for duration up to now.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students find the rules from the examples? Were *for / since* still a problem in the interviews?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Club Members
text: **Read about three club members. Who has been a member the longest?**

**The Running Club: Amal, 34** "I've been running for five years. I started because my doctor told me to lose weight! I've run three marathons and I've lost 15 kilos. Recently I've been training for the Colombo Marathon. That's why I look so tired!"

**The Chess Club: Sanduni, 17** "I've been playing chess since I was eight. My grandfather taught me. I've been a member of this club for four years and I've won two national competitions. I've been practising online every evening this month."

**The Choir: Mrs Perera, 61** "I've been singing in this choir since 1995, so that's a long time! We've performed in Kandy, Galle and even in Chennai. I've known some of the members for thirty years. They're like my family."
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: How long has Amal been running? ______________________________
How many competitions has Sanduni won? ______________________________
How long has Mrs Perera known some of the members? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these sentences from the interviews.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: I've **been running** for five years.
I've **run** three marathons.
I've **been playing** chess since I was eight.
I've **won** two national competitions.
I've **been training** for the marathon. That's why I look so tired!
I've **known** some of the members for thirty years.
In sentence 1, did Amal start running in the past? Is he still running? ______________
Which sentences tell us **how long**? ______________
Which sentences tell us **how many**? ______________
What is the form of the verb in sentences 1, 3 and 5? have / has + ______ + ______
In sentence 5, what can we see now that shows the activity? ______________
Why is sentence 6 not *I've been knowing*? ______________________________
Look at *for five years* and *since I was eight*. Which word goes with a **period** of time? Which goes with a **point** in time? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Write for or since.**
**B. Use the present perfect simple or continuous.**
bullets: ______ three weeks · 2. ______ 2019 · 3. ______ Monday · 4. ______ two hours · 5. ______ I was a child · 6. ______ ages · 7. ______ last summer · 8. ______ a long time
I ______________________ (wait) here for 40 minutes!
She ______________________ (read) four books this month.
How long ______ you ______________________ (live) in Colombo?
They ______________________ (play) football since 3 o'clock.
Your hands are dirty. What ______ you ______________________ (do)?
I ______________________ (know) my best friend since primary school.
How many cups of tea ______ you ______________________ (drink) today?
He ______________________ (study) for his exams all week. He's exhausted.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Interview Your Partner
text: **Ask the questions. Write short notes.**
**Write a profile of your partner (5 sentences).**

rows: How long have you been living in your house / town?
How many times have you moved house?
How long have you been learning English?
