hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Future Perfect and Future Continuous, built round the theme "My Life in Five Years".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who use will and going to confidently but rarely use the future perfect or future continuous, and say By 2030 I will graduate.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Interviews" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Future Perfect and Future Continuous
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (university brochure), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (life timeline and interview questions).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of the future perfect (simple and continuous) and the future continuous to talk about achievements and activities at future points in time.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe their life at points 1, 5 and 10 years from now, e.g. By 2030, I'll have graduated. This time next year, I'll be living in Melbourne.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in talking about plans and predictions.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise contracted will have /ˈwɪləv/.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: An action completed before a future point
Duration up to a future point
By June, I'll have been working here for five years.
An action in progress at a future moment
This time next year, I'll be living abroad.
blocks.heading: Form and meaning
Form and meaning: notes
text: Time expressions: *by (2030), by the time + present simple, this time next week / year, in five years' time, at 9 pm tomorrow*.

blocks.heading: Accuracy points
bullets: *By the time you* ***arrive,*** (present simple after time conjunctions, not *will arrive*).
*by* = not later than; *until* = continuing up to.
The future continuous is also used for polite questions about plans: *Will you be using the car tonight?*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *I'll have* /aɪl əv/; *will have been* /wɪl əv bɪn/. Students should hear the contracted forms.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***By 2030, I will have graduated.*** Will I graduate before 2030 or after? (Before, or by 2030.) · In 2030, will graduation be finished? (Yes.)
***This time next year, I'll be living in Melbourne.*** Will I be in Melbourne next year at this time? (Yes.) · Is the living finished? (No, it's in progress.)

rows: Using will + base verb instead of the future perfect (By 2030 I will graduate).
will after time conjunctions (By the time you will arrive).
Board the rule; include several items in the practice.
Not hearing have in fast speech.
Listening and drilling of contracted forms.
Give an example timeline; encourage both personal and world predictions.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: by 2030 · by the time + present · this time next year · in five years' time · at 9 pm tomorrow

NOW ———— [X graduated] ——— 2030: By 2030, I'll have graduated (finished). · NOW ———— [~~~living~~~] next year: This time next year, I'll be living ... (in progress). · 2021 =========> June: By June, I'll have been working here for five years (duration). · By the time you arrive (present)
I'll have /aɪl əv/ · will have been /wɪl əv bɪn/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Future Perfect and Future Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and introduce the theme.
Ask: *"Imagine it's five years from now. Where are you? What's your life like?"*
Students tell a partner (2 minutes). Don't correct.
Take two or three ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the three future forms in context and clarify their meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about the course. What will graduates have done by the end? What will they be doing in their final year? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Draw three timelines on the board (see Board plan) without labels. Say: *"Underline the future forms in the brochure. Match each one to a timeline."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
Label each timeline with its form and an example from the brochure. Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Highlight *by* (= not later than) and *by the time* + present simple. Board *By the time you will arrive* and ask what's wrong.
Show the future continuous for polite questions: *Will you be using the car tonight?*
**Pronunciation.** Drill contracted forms: *By 2030, I'll have graduated. This time next year, I'll be living abroad. By June, I'll have been working here for five years.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing and forming the three forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Do Exercise A: choose the best form. Then complete Exercise B about you. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check Exercise A as a class; two students read their Exercise B sentences.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the forms freely in personalised and group speaking.
Give out Handout 4. Students complete their personal timeline for 1, 5 and 10 years from now (4 minutes).
**Interviews (7 minutes).** Pairs interview each other with the questions: *"By the time you're 30, what will you have achieved? What will you be doing this time next year?"*
ICQs: *"Do you talk about your own timeline or your partner's?"* (Both: we ask and answer.)
**World predictions (7 minutes).** Groups make three predictions about technology and the world in 2050 using all three forms, and present the boldest one to the class.
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which form was most useful today?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write a letter to your future self (180 words) to be opened in ten years, using all three forms.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide the three timelines on a card during the freer practice. Give sentence frames: *By ___, I'll have ___. This time next ___, I'll be ___ing.*
Stronger students add hedging: *I'll probably have ..., I doubt I'll have ..., I might be ...* They use the future continuous for polite enquiries: *Will you be coming to the meeting?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Interviews" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Interviews" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use the future perfect with *by* correctly in the interviews. They use the present simple after *by the time / when* in future clauses. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which form did students find hardest? Did the timelines help students understand the difference?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: University Brochure
text: **BSc in Environmental Science: Your Future Starts Here**

In three years' time, your life will look very different. By the end of the course, you will have studied ecology, climate science and data analysis. You will have completed two research projects and you will have spent six months on a work placement with a real company.
In your final year, you will be working on your own research project, and you will be presenting your findings at our international student conference.
By graduation day, you will have been studying with experts from around the world for three years, and you will have made friends for life.
And five years from now? Our graduates tell us they will be working in conservation, government and business, and many of them will be living and working abroad.
**Questions**
bullets: What will students have done by the end of the course? ______________________________
What will they be doing in their final year? ______________________________
How long will they have been studying by graduation day? ______________________________

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Perfect Infinitives and Perfect Gerunds, built round the theme "The Missing Painting".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who are accurate with perfect tenses but rarely use perfect infinitives (seems to have left, is said to have been stolen) or perfect gerunds (denied having taken), so their reporting sounds simple and repetitive.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Press conference" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Perfect Infinitives and Perfect Gerunds (to have done / having done)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (the scene), Handout 2 (model news article for analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (case file and role cards for the press conference).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of perfect infinitives and perfect gerunds to speculate, report and refer to earlier events, especially in news-style reporting.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and present a short news report about a mystery using at least six perfect infinitive or gerund forms.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop collaborative speaking (a press conference role-play) and formal written reporting.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Perfect infinitive after seem / appear / happen / claim / pretend
The thief seems to have entered through the roof.
Refers to an action earlier than the main verb
Passive perfect infinitive after reporting passives
be said / thought / believed / reported + to have been + pp
The painting is believed to have been stolen at night.
Objective, distanced reporting of past events
Perfect gerund after deny / admit / regret / remember / forgive and prepositions
The guard denied having seen anything. He was praised for having raised the alarm.
Emphasises that the action is earlier and completed
She was proud of having been chosen.
Perfect infinitive after would like / would love / would rather
I would like to have seen his face!
Past wish that did not happen
blocks.heading: Form and use
Accuracy points
bullets: After *deny, admit, regret*, the simple gerund is often possible too (*He denied taking it*); the perfect gerund makes the time order explicit and sounds more formal.
Not: *He is said to steal the painting yesterday.* → *He is said to have stolen the painting yesterday.*
Not: *It is said him to have ...* → *He is said to have ...* / *It is said that he has ...*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *to have* is weak: /tə həv/ or /tu‿əv/: *seems to have left* /siːmz tə həv left/.
*having been* /ˈhævɪŋ bɪn/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The thief seems to have entered through the roof.*** Did the thief enter before now? (Yes.) · Are we sure? (No; it seems so.)
***The guard denied having seen anything.*** What did the guard say? (I didn't see anything.) · Did the seeing (or not seeing) happen before the denial? (Yes.)

rows: Using the simple infinitive for a past action (He seems to leave).
Timeline: main verb now, perfect infinitive earlier.
Wrong form after reporting passives (is said to steal).
Board the two patterns and transformation practice.
Discuss clarity in feedback; one or two per paragraph is enough.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: seem · appear · claim · pretend · happen · be said / thought / believed / reported · deny · admit · regret · remember
S + seem + to have + pp · S + is said + to have been + pp · deny / admit + having + pp · prep + having (been) + pp · would like + to have + pp
earlier action than the main verb · distance / not proven (news) · past wish that didn't happen
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Perfect Infinitives and Perfect Gerunds, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic and engage students.
Give out Handout 1. Read the description of the scene and the headline.
Ask: *"What happened? What do you think the guard did, or didn't do?"* Pairs speculate for 2 minutes. Take ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present perfect infinitives and perfect gerunds in a news article and clarify their form, meaning and use.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the news article. Was your guess right? What do the police think happened?"*
Pairs compare their ideas with the article.
**Part B: Analysis (7 minutes)**
Say: *"In groups, answer the analysis questions under the article."*
ICQs: *"How many structures do you look for?"* (Three types.) *"Do you also explain why?"* (Yes, question 4.)
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.
Draw a timeline for *The thief seems to have entered through the roof*: *seems* = now; *to have entered* = earlier. Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.

Discuss: *"Why does the writer say is believed to have been stolen and not was stolen?"* (Distance; not yet proven.) *"What's the difference between He denied taking it and He denied having taken it?"* (Very little; the second is more formal and stresses the earlier time.)
Highlight *would like to have seen* (a past wish that didn't happen).
**Pronunciation:** drill weak forms: *seems to have left* /siːmz tə həv left/; *having been* /ˈhævɪŋ bɪn/.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite the sentences using the words given. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class.
**Exercise B:** pairs rewrite the two sentences in news style. Two pairs share.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four or five
text: **Aim:** To use the structures fluently in a press conference role-play and a short news report.
Give each group the case file and role cards (Handout 4): Museum Director, Head of Security, Police Inspector, and one or two Journalists. Students read their cards (3 minutes).

**Press conference (8 minutes).** Journalists ask questions; officials answer using their cards and their own speculation. Encourage today's structures: *"The thieves appear to have used a van." "Mr Silva denies having seen anything."*
ICQs: *"Who asks the questions?"* (The journalists.) *"Can officials invent details?"* (Yes, if they fit the case file.)
**News report (7 minutes).** Each group writes a 100-word news report about the press conference using at least four structures from today. One group reads its report aloud.
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board the most effective sentences from the reports and one or two with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Where would you see these structures?"* (News, reports, formal writing.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 220-word news report on an unsolved mystery (real or invented) using at least six of today's structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give a pattern card with the five structures and an example of each. Assign weaker students the Journalist role, with question cards to read.

Stronger students use the continuous perfect infinitive: *The thieves appear to have been planning this for months.* They write the follow-up article a week later, using *would like to have* and *regret having*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Press conference" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Case File and Role Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Press conference" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The group report includes at least four perfect infinitive or gerund forms used accurately. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. Students can explain why reporters use distancing structures.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the article make the structures noticeable? Did students use the structures naturally in the press conference?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Scene
text: **Look at the scene. What happened?**

The National Art Gallery, 7 am. In Room 4, an empty golden frame hangs on the wall. Above it, a skylight in the roof is broken. Glass is on the floor. There is a ladder against the wall that does not belong to the gallery. The alarm is silent. A security guard stands in the doorway, holding a cup of tea, looking shocked.
**Headline:** PRICELESS PAINTING VANISHES OVERNIGHT
**Discuss:** What do you think happened? What might the guard have done (or not done)?

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Model News Article
text: **MASTERPIECE STOLEN IN DARING ROOFTOP RAID**

A painting worth $3 million is believed to have been stolen from the National Art Gallery in the early hours of Monday morning. The thieves appear to have entered through a skylight in the roof, and they are thought to have used a ladder to climb down into Room 4.

The gallery's alarm system seems to have been switched off at 1.12 am. Police say whoever did this is likely to have known the security code. The night guard, Mr Silva, has denied having seen anything unusual and admitted having fallen asleep at around midnight. He has not been accused of any crime.
A delivery van is reported to have been seen near the gallery at 1 am. The thieves appear to have been planning the raid for months.
The gallery director said she regretted not having upgraded the alarm last year. "I would like to have seen this coming," she told reporters.
**Analysis questions**
bullets: Find four examples of *be + said / thought / believed / reported + to have (been) + pp*. ______________________________
Find two examples of *seem / appear + to have + pp*. ______________________________
Find three examples of *having + pp*. Which verbs come before them? ______________________________
Why does the writer avoid saying *Mr Silva didn't see anything* or *Thieves stole the painting*? ______________________________
What does *I would like to have seen this coming* mean? Did she see it coming? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite the sentences using the words given.**
**B. Rewrite these two sentences in a more distanced, news-report style.** *People say the mayor took the money.* / *We think the fire started in the kitchen.*
bullets: People believe that the thief worked alone. (is believed) → ______________________________
It seems that he has left the country. (seems) → ______________________________
He said he hadn't taken the money. (denied) → ______________________________
It is reported that the bridge was damaged in the storm. (is reported) → ______________________________
She admitted that she had lied. (having) → ______________________________
It appears that the company has lost millions. (appears) → ______________________________
I wish I had been there to see it. (would like) → ______________________________
They were happy that they had been chosen. (having been) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Case File and Role Cards
text: **Case file**
**Museum Director**
You are embarrassed. You want to protect the museum's reputation. You believe the thieves were professionals and had help from inside. You regret not upgrading the alarm last year.
**Head of Security**
You defend your team. You say Mr Silva has worked for you for 15 years and is honest. You think the alarm was switched off by someone who knew the code.
**Police Inspector**

You are careful and do not want to say too much. You can say: two people probably entered through the roof; they probably used the van; they may have been planning this for months. A cleaner is being questioned.
**Journalists**
Ask difficult questions. Find out: How did the thieves get in? Who switched off the alarm? Did the guard really fall asleep? Has anyone been arrested? Does the museum regret anything?
bullets: Painting: *Woman at the Window* (1890), valued at $3 million.
Last seen: 10 pm on Sunday by the night guard, Mr Silva.
Discovered missing: 7 am on Monday.
Clues: broken skylight; ladder; alarm switched off at 1.12 am; muddy footprints of two different sizes; a delivery van seen nearby at 1 am; Mr Silva says he fell asleep at about midnight.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who use the present simple and am/is/are confidently. They talk about the future with the present simple (Tomorrow I visit my aunt).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Pairs" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Be Going To for Plans
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (Hasini's holiday diary), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (my week planner), teacher's weekend calendar drawn on the board.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise be going to + base verb for future plans and intentions.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say 6 sentences about their plans and ask a partner Are you going to ...? questions.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise future time expressions.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking by arranging a time to meet.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I'm going to visit my aunt.
Am I going to see you?
Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.
Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: **am / is / are + going to + base verb**

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Plans and intentions: something we have **already decided** to do.
Time expressions: *tonight, tomorrow, this weekend, next week, next month, next year, on Saturday, in the holidays*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: In fast speech, *going to* often sounds like /ˈɡənə/ (*gonna*). Students should understand it but write *going to*.
Weak *to*: /tə/. *I'm going to visit* /aɪm ˈɡəʊɪŋ tə ˈvɪzɪt/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I'm going to visit my aunt on Saturday.*** Is Saturday in the past or the future? (Future.) · Did I decide before now? (Yes, it's my plan.) · Is it a plan or a guess? (A plan.)

rows: Three-box board model: I'm + going to + swim.
Adding -s or -ing to the base verb (going to plays).
Present simple for plans (Tomorrow I visit).
Contrast routine vs plan on a calendar.
Pronouncing going to very carefully and slowly.
Model natural speed; allow gonna in speech.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: tonight · tomorrow · this weekend · next week · next month · next year · on Saturday · in the holidays
I'm going to visit my aunt. · She isn't going to work. · Are you going to swim? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. · am / is / are + going to + base verb
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Be Going To for Plans, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and introduce plans.
Draw a calendar for this weekend on the board with three pictures: a bus, a cake, a football.
Say: *"This weekend is busy! Guess my plans!"* Students guess freely. Confirm with the target language: *"Yes! I'm going to visit my sister. I'm going to make a cake."*
Ask: *"Are you busy this weekend?"* Take a few yes/no answers.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Hasini's diary. Match the days and the plans."* (3 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you match or write?"* (Match.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
Students answer the true/false questions. Check: *"Is Hasini going to go to the beach on Monday?"* Model: *"No, she isn't. She's going to visit her grandmother."*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Hasini is going to visit her grandmother on Monday.* Ask the CCQs. Draw a timeline with NOW and an arrow to Monday.
**Form.** Elicit the three parts: *am / is / are + going to + base verb*. Write the form table on the board with all persons.
**Negative and questions.** Elicit from the diary: *She isn't going to work. Are you going to come?* Elicit short answers.
**Time words.** Students find time words in the diary; build the list on the left of the board.
**Pronunciation.** Model full and natural speed. Drill chorally and individually: *I'm going to swim. Are you going to come? Yes, I am.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers.
**Picture drill:** point to the weekend pictures on the board and a student's name; students make sentences: *"Dinesh is going to play football."*

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the language in a personalised, communicative task.
Give out Handout 3. Students write their real or imagined plans for next week in the planner, leaving **one** afternoon free (4 minutes).
Model with a strong student: *"Are you going to do anything on Monday afternoon?" "Yes, I'm going to play cricket." "What about Tuesday?"*
**Pairs (6 minutes):** students ask each other to find a free afternoon to meet. When they find one, they decide what they are going to do together.
**Report (4 minutes):** pairs tell the class: *"We're going to meet on Thursday. We're going to go to the cinema."*
**Writing (4 minutes):** students write 6 sentences about their plans at the bottom of Handout 3.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Students correct them.
Quick round: each student says one plan for tonight.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences about your plans for the next school holidays.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide picture prompts in the planner. Give the question frame: *Are you going to ___ on ___?*
Stronger students add reasons with *because*: *I'm going to study because I have an exam.* They ask *What are you going to do ...? / Where are you going to go?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Pairs" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Pairs" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students form *going to* sentences with the correct *be* in 5 of 6 written sentences. Students ask and answer *Are you going to ...?* correctly in the meeting task.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use the correct form of *be*? Did the meeting task work? Did every pair find a time?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Hasini's Holiday Diary
text: **Read Hasini's diary for next week. Match the day and the plan.**
**Monday:** I'm going to visit my grandmother in Matara. We're going to cook string hoppers together.
**Tuesday:** My friends and I are going to go to the beach. We aren't going to swim because the sea is rough, but we're going to play volleyball.
**Wednesday:** I'm not going to do anything! I'm going to stay in bed and read.
**Thursday:** My brother is going to take me to the zoo.
**Friday:** I'm going to start a new hobby: I'm going to learn the guitar!
**True (T) or False (F)?**
bullets: Hasini is going to swim on Tuesday. ______
Her brother is going to take her to the zoo. ______
She is going to learn the piano. ______

rows: a. stay in bed and read

text: **A. Complete with the correct form of be going to.**
**B. Make questions and answer them about you.**
bullets: I ______________________ (watch) a film tonight.
She ______________________ (not / go) to school tomorrow.
______ they ______________________ (visit) their grandparents?

My parents ______________________ (not / work) this weekend.
your friends / go / to the beach / tomorrow? → ______________________________

Are you going to play sport this weekend? · 2. Are you going to visit your family next week? · 3. Are your friends going to go to the beach tomorrow?

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Will vs Going To, built round the theme "At the Café and Looking at the Sky".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know going to for plans and have met will, but use them interchangeably, e.g. I will go to the cinema tonight, I bought tickets.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Café role-play" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Will vs Going To (Decisions, Offers and Predictions)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (three dialogues), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (café menu and role cards), Handout 4 (picture situations described in words).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise will for instant decisions, offers and opinion-based predictions, and going to for plans and evidence-based predictions.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can order and make offers with I'll ..., and make predictions using will (opinion) and going to (evidence).
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a café role-play.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise I'll and won't.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Form
bullets: **will / won't + base verb:** *I'll help you. It won't rain.* (Same form for all persons.)
**be going to + base verb:** *I'm going to paint my room. It's going to rain.*

rows: Instant decision (decided at the moment of speaking): The phone's ringing. I'll answer it.
Plan (decided before speaking): I've bought paint. I'm going to paint my room.
Offer: That bag looks heavy. I'll carry it.
Prediction with present evidence: Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.
Ordering: I'll have the rice, please.
Prediction based on opinion: I think Sri Lanka will win.
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Meaning and use: notes
text: Useful with *will*: *I think ..., I don't think ... will, probably, definitely, I'm sure ...*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *I'll* /aɪl/, *you'll* /juːl/, *it'll* /ˈɪtl/; *won't* /wəʊnt/ (different from *want* /wɒnt/).

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***A: The phone's ringing. B: I'll answer it.*** Did B plan to answer the phone before? (No.) · When did B decide? (Now, at the moment of speaking.)
***Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.*** Can we see something now? (Yes, clouds.) · Is it a guess based on evidence? (Yes.)

rows: Ask: "Did you decide before?" Board the decision flowchart.
Minimal-pair drill: I won't go / I want to go.
Students only use will in the café role-play.
Role cards include a plan question (What are you going to do after lunch?).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: Did you decide BEFORE? → yes → going to · no, NOW → will · Prediction: evidence you can see → going to · opinion (I think) → will
I'll answer it! (decision now) · I'll carry it. (offer) · I'll have the curry. (order) · I'm going to paint my room. (plan) · It's going to rain. (evidence) · I think Sri Lanka will win. (opinion)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Will vs Going To, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest and introduce decisions and predictions.
Describe a scene in words or with a quick sketch: *a man on a ladder leaning too far to one side.* Ask: *"What's going to happen?"* Accept any answers.
Pretend to drop a pile of books. Ask: *"Can anyone help me?"* A student helps; elicit or say for them: *"I'll help you!"*
Ask two students: *"What are you doing after class? Do you have plans?"*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present *will* and *going to* in context and clarify the difference in meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the three dialogues. For each underlined sentence, write P (plan), D (decision now), O (offer) or PR (prediction). Four minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many dialogues?"* (Three.) *"What do you write?"* (P, D, O or PR.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
**Part B: Clarification (14 minutes)**

**Decisions and plans.** Board *The phone's ringing. I'll answer it.* and *I've bought paint. I'm going to paint my room.* Ask the CCQs. Build the decision flowchart on the left of the board: *"Did you decide before? → going to. Now? → will."*
**Offers and orders.** Board *I'll carry them. I'll have the rice, please.* Elicit: *will* for offers and ordering.
**Predictions.** Contrast *Look at those clouds! It's going to rain* (evidence) with *I think it'll look great* (opinion). Ask: *"Which one has evidence you can see?"*
**Form.** Elicit *will / won't + base verb* (same for all persons) and *be going to + base verb*.
**Pronunciation.** Drill *I'll get it! I'll have the rice. It won't hurt.* Minimal pair: *I won't go / I want to go.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct form.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: choose will or going to. Exercise B: complete the sentences. Six minutes."*
Pairs compare and justify using the flowchart.
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use *will* and *going to* fluently in a role-play and in making predictions.

**Café role-play (9 minutes).** Give out Handout 3. Student A is a waiter; Student B is a customer. Customers must order a drink, food and a dessert; waiters must make two offers; both must ask about each other's plans for the afternoon. Model one exchange. Swap roles after four minutes.
ICQs: *"How many offers does the waiter make?"* (Two.) *"What do you ask about at the end?"* (Plans.)

**Predictions (6 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Groups decide what is going to happen in each situation (evidence), then make three opinion predictions about their classmates' futures: *I think Ravi will become a famous chef!*
Groups share their funniest prediction (3 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Ask: *"How do you decide between will and going to?"* Elicit the flowchart.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a short dialogue (8–10 lines) in which one person offers help, one person orders something and both talk about their plans.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a phrase card: *I'll have ..., I'll get you ..., Shall I ...?, I'm going to ...* Let them play the customer (the simpler role) first.
Stronger students add *probably / definitely* in the correct position (*I'll probably ..., I probably won't ...*). They use *Shall I ...?* for offers.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Café role-play" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Café Menu and Role Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Café role-play" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the role-play, students use *I'll* for ordering and offers and *going to* for plans. 10 out of 13 or better on Handout 2. Students distinguish evidence and opinion predictions in the group task.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use the decision test (before / now) on their own? Was the café role-play realistic and useful?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Three Dialogues
text: **Read the dialogues. Is each underlined sentence a plan (P), a decision now (D), an offer (O) or a prediction (PR)?**
**Dialogue 1: At home** Mum: The phone's ringing! Nimal: **I'll answer it.** (1) Mum: Thanks. And can you help me with the shopping bags? Nimal: Sure, **I'll carry them.** (2)

**Dialogue 2: At school** Sara: Why have you got paint and brushes? Kumar: **I'm going to paint my bedroom this weekend.** (3) I bought the paint yesterday. Sara: Nice! What colour? Kumar: Blue. **I think it'll look great.** (4)
**Dialogue 3: At the park** Ruwan: Look at those black clouds! Dilini: Oh no, **it's going to rain.** (5) Let's go home. Ruwan: Wait, **I'll call my brother.** (6) He has a car.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Choose will or going to.**
**B. Complete with will ('ll), won't or the correct form of going to.**
bullets: The phone's ringing. I (will / am going to) answer it.
I've bought paint. I (will / am going to) paint my room.
Watch out! You (will / are going to) fall!
I think Sri Lanka (will / is going to) win the match.
This bag is heavy. I (will / am going to) carry it for you.
We've booked a hotel. We (will / are going to) stay in Ella for three days.
I'm thirsty. I think I (will / am going to) have a lime juice.
Don't worry, I (won't / am not going to) tell anyone. I promise.
A: I don't have any money. B: Don't worry, I ______________ lend you some.
Look at that boy on the wall! He ______________ fall!
We ______________ visit Kandy next month. We booked the train last week.
I'm sure you ______________ pass the exam. You studied hard.
A: Would you like tea or coffee? B: I ______________ have coffee, please.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Café Menu and Role Cards
text: **Waiter:** Welcome customers. Take the order. Make two offers (*I'll bring you some water. I'll get you a menu.*). Ask about their plans after lunch.
**Customer:** Order a drink, food and a dessert. Ask for something extra. Talk about your plans for the rest of the day.
**Useful language:** *I'll have ..., please. · Can I have ...? · I'll bring you ... · Shall I ...? · What are you going to do after lunch? · I'm going to ...*

blocks.heading: Handout 4: What's Going to Happen?
text: **Read the situations. What's going to happen? Use going to.**
**Now make three opinion predictions about people in your class. Use I think ... will ...**
bullets: A man is running for the bus. The bus doors are closing.
A little girl is holding a big ice cream. It's very hot and the ice cream is melting.
The sky is dark and there is thunder.
A boy is standing on a chair to reach a high shelf. The chair is moving.
A woman is putting on her running shoes and stretching.
The football is flying towards the goal and the goalkeeper is on the ground.

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1**
**Handout 2, Exercise A**
**Handout 2, Exercise B**
**Handout 4 (examples)**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: D · 2. O · 3. P · 4. PR (opinion: *will*) · 5. PR (evidence: *going to*) · 6. D
will · 2. am going to · 3. are going to · 4. will · 5. will · 6. are going to · 7. will · 8. won't
'll · 2. 's going to · 3. 're going to · 4. 'll · 5. 'll
He's going to miss the bus. · 2. The ice cream is going to fall / melt. · 3. It's going to rain. · 4. He's going to fall. · 5. She's going to go running. · 6. It's going to be a goal.

rows: I will go to the cinema tonight. I bought the tickets last week.
I'm going to go to the cinema tonight. I bought the tickets last week.
It will rain. Look at the clouds!

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Present Forms for the Future, built round the theme "The School Trip to Sigiriya".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use will and going to but don't use the present continuous for arrangements or the present simple for timetables, and say I'll call you when I will arrive.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Present Continuous and Present Simple for the Future; Future Time Clauses
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (trip itinerary and diary), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4A and 4B (busy-week diaries).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 5, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover and use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, the present simple for timetables, and the present simple after when, as soon as, before, after, until in future time clauses.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can arrange a meeting using the present continuous and write an email with at least two future time clauses.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read an itinerary for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in arranging to meet.
**Subsidiary aim.** To write a confirmation email.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I'm meeting Dilshan at 6 on Friday.
The bus leaves at 7.15. The exam starts on Monday.
I'm going to take lots of photos.
when / as soon as / before / after / until / by the time + present simple, main clause with will
I'll call you when I arrive. (not when I will arrive)
blocks.heading: Form and use
Pronunciation
bullets: Arrangement questions: *What are you doing on Saturday?* /wɒt ə jə ˈduːɪŋ/ (weak *are you*).
*as soon as* /əz ˈsuːn əz/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I'm meeting Dilshan at 6 on Friday.*** Is this now or in the future? (Future.) · Have we agreed the time and place? (Yes, it's arranged.)
***The bus leaves at 7.15.*** Is it a personal plan or a timetable? (Timetable.)
***I'll call you when I arrive.*** Is arriving in the future? (Yes.) · Which tense follows *when*? (Present simple.)

rows: will after when / as soon as (when I will arrive).
Highlight the rule clearly; include several items in practice.
Present simple for personal arrangements (I meet my friend tomorrow).
Thinking the present continuous is only for now.
Students choose going to every time.
Explain that going to is often possible; continuous emphasises the arrangement.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: when · as soon as · before · after · until · by the time → + present simple
ARRANGEMENT (diary): I'm meeting Dilshan at 6. · TIMETABLE: The bus leaves at 7.15. · PLAN / INTENTION: I'm going to take photos. · TIME CLAUSE: I'll call you when I arrive. (not will arrive)
Are you doing anything on ...? · Sorry, I'm ...ing. · How about ...? · That works for me.

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Forms for the Future, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Ask: *"What are you doing this weekend? Is anything already arranged, with a time and a place?"* Model: *"I'm having lunch with my cousins on Sunday at 1."*
Pairs share (2 minutes). Take two examples.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present present tenses for the future and time clauses in context, and help students work out the rules.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the trip itinerary and Nethmi's diary. What time does the bus leave on Saturday? What is Nethmi doing on Monday?"*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Are the sentences about the past or the future?"* (Future.) *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Pairs.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Is this from a timetable or a personal diary?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit the answers. Build the four rules in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Board *I'll call you when I will arrive.* Ask: *"What's wrong?"* Elicit the rule and list the time conjunctions on the left.
Drill: *What are you doing on Saturday? I'm meeting my cousins. I'll text you as soon as I get there.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct future form.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: choose the best form. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare and justify. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the forms fluently in a realistic task and in writing.
Give Student A Handout 4A and Student B Handout 4B (busy diaries). Teach the arranging phrases on the right of the board.
Say: *"You want to meet to plan a class party. Find a free two-hour slot. Don't show your diary!"* Model one exchange (8 minutes).
ICQs: *"Can you show your diary?"* (No.) *"How long do you need?"* (Two hours.)

When they find a time, each student writes a short confirmation email to their partner, including two time clauses: *I'll bring the list when I come. As soon as I hear from the teacher, I'll message you.* (7 minutes.)
Partners swap emails and check the time clauses (3 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Pairs report their meeting time.
Board errors from the role-play and emails; students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write an email (100 words) to a friend confirming a weekend arrangement. Include one timetable fact and two time clauses.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Mark the free slots in Handouts 4A/4B with a pencil dot so weaker pairs succeed. Give an email frame.
Stronger students negotiate with alternatives: *How about Thursday instead? I could ... if ...* They add *by the time* and *until* to their emails.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 5 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the role-play, students use the present continuous for diary arrangements. In the email, students use the present simple after time conjunctions. 10 out of 12 or better on Handout 3.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students find the difference between arrangement and timetable? How many still used *will* after *when*?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The School Trip
text: **Grade 10 Trip to Sigiriya: Itinerary** **Saturday** 6.30 am: Meet at the school gate. 7.15 am: The bus leaves. 11.00 am: The bus arrives at Sigiriya. The guided tour starts at 11.30. 1.00 pm: Lunch at the Lion Rock Restaurant. 4.00 pm: The bus leaves for the hotel in Dambulla. **Sunday** 9.00 am: Visit to the Dambulla Cave Temple. 3.00 pm: The bus leaves for Colombo. It gets back at about 8 pm.

**Nethmi's diary** Saturday: *I'm sitting next to Ishara on the bus. I'm going to take lots of photos!* Sunday: *Dad's picking me up at the school at 8.15 pm. I'll call him as soon as we get to the expressway.* Monday: *I'm seeing the dentist at 4.*
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What time does the bus leave on Saturday? ______________________________
Who is Nethmi sitting next to? ______________________________
When is Nethmi going to call her dad? ______________________________
What is Nethmi doing on Monday at 4? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these sentences.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: The bus **leaves** at 7.15 am.
The guided tour **starts** at 11.30.
I**'m sitting** next to Ishara on the bus.
Dad**'s picking** me **up** at 8.15 pm.
I**'m going to take** lots of photos!
I**'ll call** him as soon as we **get** to the expressway.
Are all these sentences about the future? ______________
Which sentences come from a timetable or programme? What tense are they? ______________________________
Which sentences describe arrangements with other people (a time and maybe a place are agreed)? What tense are they? ______________________________
Which sentence is an intention (Nethmi's own plan, not arranged with others)? ______________________________
In sentence 6, *get* is in the future. Why isn't it *will get*? Find the word before it. ______________________________
Complete the rule: after *when, as soon as, before, after, until* we use the ______________________ to talk about the future.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Choose the best future form.**
**B. Correct the mistakes.**
bullets: The train ______________ (leave) at 9.45 tomorrow.
I ______________ (see) the dentist at 3 tomorrow. It's all booked.
I'll text you as soon as I ______________ (get) home.
We ______________ (have) dinner with my uncle on Friday.
Don't go until I ______________ (come) back.
______________ you ______________ (do) anything on Saturday evening?
Before you ______________ (leave), please close the windows.
I will call you when I will arrive. ______________________________
I meet my friend tomorrow at 5. (arranged) ______________________________
The plane is leaving at 6 according to the timetable. ______________________________
As soon as she will finish, we'll go. ______________________________

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Future Probability, built round the theme "Life in 2050".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who make predictions only with will and might. They make errors such as It is likely to it will rain and He will bound to win.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Future Probability (likely to, bound to, could well, I doubt)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (news report), Handout 2 (certainty scale and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (scenario cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To expand students' range of structures for expressing degrees of future probability and improve their accuracy.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can discuss future scenarios, expressing different degrees of certainty accurately, e.g. Cash is bound to disappear eventually, but I doubt it'll happen before 2040.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussion and justification.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a news report for specific information.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: will definitely / certainly; be bound to / be sure to + infinitive
will probably; be likely to + infinitive; It's likely that + clause; There's a good chance that ...; could well / may well
Storms are likely to increase. We could well see more flooding.
probably won't; be unlikely to; I doubt (whether / if) ...; There's little chance that ...
Cash is unlikely to disappear soon. I doubt robots will replace teachers.
definitely won't; There's no chance that ...
Humans definitely won't live on the sun.
blocks.heading: Form and degree of certainty
Accuracy points
bullets: Adverb position: *will* **probably** *go* but **probably** *won't go*.
*likely* is an adjective: *He is likely to win* / *It is likely that he will win* (not *He will likely to win* in British English).
*bound to* needs *be*: *He's bound to win.*
*I doubt* + clause (no negative): *I doubt he'll come* (= I think he won't come).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Stress on the probability word: *It's BOUND to happen. It could WELL rain.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Prices are bound to rise.*** Is the speaker sure? (Yes, very sure.)
***I doubt he'll come.*** Does the speaker think he'll come? (No, probably not.)

rows: It is likely to it will rain (mixed patterns).
Board the two separate patterns with colour.
Missing be with bound / likely / unlikely.
Show will probably / probably won't side by side.
Keep to I doubt at this level; mention I have no doubt for stronger students.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: population · metro · flood defences · cashless · economist · prediction

100%: bound to · sure to · definitely · 80%: likely to · could well · probably · good chance · 50%: may · might · could · 20%: unlikely to · probably won't · I doubt · 0%: definitely won't · no chance
be + bound/likely/unlikely + to + infinitive · It's likely that + clause · will probably / probably won't · I doubt + clause
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Future Probability, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic.
Write five predictions on the board: *flying cars, a cashless world, a four-day school week, robots as teachers, holidays on the moon.*
Pairs rank them from most likely to least likely by 2050 (2 minutes). Take brief feedback.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present expressions of future probability in context and clarify their degree of certainty and form.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the report. Which prediction is the most certain? Which is the least? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Put the bold expressions from the report on the certainty scale."*
ICQs: *"Where do you put bound to: 100% or 50%?"* (100%.)
Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**
Build the certainty scale on the board.
Focus on form: *be likely to* + infinitive vs *It's likely that* + clause; *be bound to*; adverb position (*will probably / probably won't*); *I doubt* + positive clause.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Pronunciation.** Drill with stress on the probability word: *It's BOUND to happen. It could WELL rain.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Say: *"Now do Exercise A on Handout 2: correct the mistakes. Then Exercise B: three predictions about your town."* (7 minutes.)
Pairs check. Check Exercise A as a class; two students read their predictions.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use a range of probability structures fluently and accurately in discussion.

Give each group a set of scenario cards (Handout 4). Say: *"Discuss each scenario. Agree a group prediction and a certainty level. Use at least five different structures from the scale."* (12 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you need to agree?"* (Yes, a group prediction.) *"How many different structures?"* (At least five.)
Each group presents its most controversial prediction with a reason (1 minute each). Other groups agree or disagree using the structures.
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which new structure will you use most?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write a 180-word article: *Life in 2050*. Use at least six different probability structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Keep the certainty scale visible during the discussion. Give weaker groups sentence starters on the scenario cards.
Stronger students hedge academically: *It seems likely that ..., There is a strong possibility that ...* They challenge other groups: *I'm not convinced that ... is bound to happen, because ...*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Certainty Scale and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Scenario Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the discussion, students use at least five different probability structures accurately. 5 out of 6 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which structures were new to most students? Did students use the structures naturally in the discussion?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: News Report
text: **COLOMBO 2050: WHAT WILL OUR CITY LOOK LIKE?**

Experts agree that the population of Colombo **is bound to** grow, and traffic **is likely to** become an even bigger problem unless public transport improves. **There's a good chance that** the city will have a metro system by 2040, and electric buses **could well** replace most diesel buses within twenty years.
Climate scientists warn that sea levels **are likely to** rise, and coastal areas **may** need new flood defences. Temperatures **will probably** increase by one or two degrees.

But not everything will change. **I doubt** people will stop eating rice and curry! And cash **is unlikely to** disappear completely, says economist Dr Wijesinghe: "Many small traders still prefer it. Online payments **will definitely** grow, but **there's little chance that** cash will vanish before 2050."
**Questions**
bullets: Which predictions are the most certain? ______________________________
What might coastal areas need? ______________________________
What does Dr Wijesinghe think about cash? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Certainty Scale and Practice
text: **Put the highlighted expressions from the report on the scale.**
**A. Correct the mistakes. One sentence is correct.**
**B. Write three predictions about your town in 2050, each with a different degree of certainty.**
bullets: It is likely to it will rain. ______________________________
She probably will not come. ______________________________
I don't doubt he won't come. (meaning I think he won't) ______________________________
Prices could well rise next year. ______________________________
They are unlikely winning. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Further Practice
text: **Rewrite each sentence using the word in brackets. Keep the meaning the same.**
bullets: It will almost certainly rain this afternoon. (bound) → ______________________________
It's probable that prices will rise. (likely) → ______________________________
Maybe they'll cancel the match. (might) → ______________________________
There's a strong possibility we'll move abroad. (well) → ______________________________
It's improbable that cash will disappear soon. (unlikely) → ______________________________
She probably won't pass. (likely) → ______________________________
I'm sure he'll be late. He always is. (sure) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Scenario Cards
text: **Useful language**
bullets: *I think it's bound to happen because ...*
*There's a good chance that ...*
*It could well happen, but ...*
*I doubt it'll happen before ...*
*It's unlikely to happen in our lifetime.*
*I'm not so sure. I think ...*

rows: AI teachers: Will robots or AI replace teachers in schools?
A four-day week: Will most people work only four days a week?
Space tourism: Will ordinary people go on holiday in space?
Cashless world: Will cash disappear completely?
Electric vehicles: Will petrol cars be banned in Sri Lanka?
Online-only shopping: Will physical shops close?
Climate: Will summers in your country be much hotter?
Languages: Will everyone speak English as a second language?
