hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Formal Future Forms, built round the theme "Writing a Press Release".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who use will and going to well but whose formal writing sounds conversational. They don't know be to, be due to, be set to or the future in the past (was to, would).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Formal Future Forms (be to, be due to, be set to, Future in the Past)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (two notices), Handout 2 (texts for analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (writing task: a press release).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of formal future forms in official announcements, news and biography.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a press release announcing an event using at least five formal future forms, and a short biography paragraph using the future in the past.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop collaborative writing.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of register.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Official arrangement or plan; instructions; formal
The President is to visit Jaffna next month. Students are to report to the hall at 8.
The new bridge is due to open in May.
The company is set to announce job cuts.
be on the point / verge of + -ing
The talks are on the verge of collapsing.
The ceremony is about to begin.
Future in the past: was / were going to, would, was to
A future seen from a past viewpoint; was to often = destiny
Nobody knew then that she was to become a famous scientist. He said he would call.
Should you require assistance, please contact reception.
blocks.heading: Form and use
Register
bullets: These forms are typical of news, official notices, formal letters and biographies. In conversation they sound stiff: *I'm to have pizza tonight* ✗ → *I'm having pizza tonight.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *to*: *is to visit* /ɪz tə ˈvɪzɪt/; *was to become* /wəz tə bɪˈkʌm/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The President is to visit Jaffna next month.*** Is this an official plan? (Yes.) · Would you hear this in a casual chat? (Not usually; in the news.)
***Nobody knew then that she was to become famous.*** Did she become famous? (Yes.) · Is the writer looking at the future from a point in the past? (Yes.)

rows: Using formal forms in casual contexts.
Confusing due to (because of) and be due to (scheduled).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: FORMAL: news, notices, press releases, biographies · INFORMAL: conversation, messages
be to + inf · be due to + inf · be set to + inf · be on the verge of + -ing · be about to + inf · was to + inf · Should + S + inf
official plan / instruction · scheduled · likely (news) · very soon · very near future · destiny (biography) · formal if
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Formal Future Forms, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of register.
Give out Handout 1. Read the two notices about the same event (a casual message and an official notice).
Ask: *"Where would you see each one? Which words make the second one sound official?"* Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Take ideas; don't name the grammar yet.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present formal future forms in authentic-style texts and clarify their meaning, form and register.
**Part A: Analysis (9 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2 (a government press release and a biography extract). Say: *"In groups, find all the future forms and answer the questions."*
ICQs: *"How many texts?"* (Two.) *"What do you look for?"* (Future forms.)
Monitor and help.
**Part B: Clarification (11 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns and meanings on the board.

Contrast: *be to* (official arrangement or instruction), *be due to* (scheduled), *be set to* (likely, news style), *be on the verge of* (very soon), *was to* (future seen from the past; often destiny in biographies).
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Highlight *Should you require ...* = *If you require ...* and its word order.
Return to Notice B on Handout 1 and identify each form.
Point out register: *"Would you say 'I'm to have pizza tonight' to a friend?"* (No.)

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite in a more formal style using the word given. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class.
Students start Exercise B (biography paragraph); they finish it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use formal future forms in an authentic writing task.
Give out Handout 4. Say: *"Your school is holding a major event. Write an official press release (120–150 words) announcing it. Use at least five formal future forms."*
ICQs: *"Formal or informal?"* (Formal.) *"How many formal future forms?"* (At least five.)
Groups choose an event, decide the details and write (12 minutes).
Groups read their press releases aloud. The class votes for the most professional one (6 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board the most effective lines and one or two sentences with errors. Students correct them.
Ask: *"Which forms would you use in an email to a friend? Which would you avoid?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Finish the biography paragraph (Handout 3, Exercise B). Then write a 200-word press release for a real or invented event.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide a press release template with gaps. Give a pattern card.
Stronger students include *be on the verge of*, *Should you ...* and a passive (*is to be opened by*). They rewrite a casual email as an official notice.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The press release uses at least five formal future forms accurately. The register is consistent throughout. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students notice the difference in register? Which forms appeared most in the press releases?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Notices
text: **Notice A (a message in the class WhatsApp group)**
Hey everyone! The new library's opening next Friday at 10. The minister's coming to cut the ribbon, apparently! Be there by 9.30, OK? If you need anything, just ask me.
**Notice B (an official notice)**

The new school library is to be officially opened on Friday 14 March at 10.00 am. The Minister of Education is due to attend the ceremony and is set to announce a new national reading programme. All students are to assemble in the main hall by 9.30 am. Should you require any further information, please contact the school office.
**Discuss:** Where would you see each notice? Which words and phrases make Notice B sound official?

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Texts for Analysis
text: **Text 1: Government press release**

**NEW EXPRESSWAY TO OPEN IN JUNE** The Southern Link Expressway is due to open to the public on 1 June. The President is to perform the opening ceremony, and the Minister of Transport is set to announce plans for a second phase. Construction is on the verge of being completed, ahead of schedule. Drivers are to use the new toll system from the first day. Should you have any questions, please call the Road Development Authority.
**Text 2: Biography extract**

In 1960, a young woman from Colombo became the world's first female prime minister. At the time, few people imagined that she was to lead the country for three separate terms. She would later say that she had never planned a life in politics. Her daughter, too, was to become a national leader.
**Questions**
bullets: Find four formal future forms in Text 1. What does each one mean? ______________________________
Which form in Text 1 gives an instruction? ______________________________
What is the meaning of *Should you have any questions*? ______________________________
In Text 2, when is the writer "standing" in time? What does *was to lead* mean? ______________________________
Find an example of *would* used for the future in the past. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite in a more formal style using the word given.**
**B. Write a short biography paragraph (60 words) about a famous person. Use was to, would and was going to.**
bullets: The Minister plans to visit the school next week. (is) → ______________________________
The new library will probably open in June. (due) → ______________________________
The company will soon announce job cuts. (set) → ______________________________
If you need any help, please contact us. (Should) → ______________________________
Nobody knew then that he would later become president. (was) → ______________________________
The two sides have almost reached an agreement. (verge) → ______________________________
All visitors must sign in at reception. (are) → ______________________________
The ceremony will begin in a moment. (about) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **Write an official press release (120–150 words) announcing a major event at your school.**
Choose one event:
Include:
**Your draft:**
bullets: a national science fair
the opening of a new sports complex
a visit by a famous author
a charity run for flood victims
what, when and where the event is
who is expected to attend
the programme
instructions for visitors
a contact line at the end

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: *is due to open* (scheduled); *is to perform* (official arrangement); *is set to announce* (likely, news style); *is on the verge of being completed* (very soon); *are to use* (instruction)
*Drivers are to use the new toll system.*
If you have any questions.
In 1960, looking forward. *was to lead* = would later lead (it really happened).
*She would later say ...*

The Minister is to visit the school next week. · 2. The new library is due to open in June. · 3. The company is set to announce job cuts. · 4. Should you need any help, please contact us. · 5. Nobody knew then that he was to become president. · 6. The two sides are on the verge of reaching an agreement. · 7. All visitors are to sign in at reception. · 8. The ceremony is about to begin.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Indefinite Articles A and An, built round the theme "What's in My Bag? Jobs and Things".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who know some classroom objects and jobs but often leave out the article (She is teacher) or choose a / an by spelling, not sound.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "What's in my bag?" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: A and An
PPP (presentation, practice, production)

A bag of real objects (a pen, an apple, an umbrella, a book, an orange, an eraser, a phone, an ID card), Handout 1 (What's in my bag? script), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (jobs guessing game cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise a and an with singular countable nouns, for objects and jobs.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe 8 objects in their bag and say people's jobs using a / an correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review classroom and personal objects.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise vowel and consonant sounds at the start of words.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a guessing game.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: a book, a pen, a car, a doctor, a uniform, a university, a one-day trip
an apple, an egg, an orange, an engineer, an hour, an honest man, an MP3
I've got two pens. They're doctors.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: Note: It's the **sound** that matters, not the letter: *a uniform* /ə ˈjuːnɪfɔːm/ (starts with a /j/ sound); *an hour* /ən ˈaʊə/ (the *h* is silent).

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: *a / an* = one, any one (not a specific one): *I've got a pen.*
Jobs always need *a / an*: *She's a nurse. He's an engineer.* (not *She's nurse*)

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *a* is weak: /ə/. *an* is weak: /ən/. They link to the next word: *an apple* /ə‿ˈnæpl/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***an apple*** Is *apple* one thing or many? (One.) · What sound does *apple* start with? (A vowel sound, /æ/.)
***a uniform*** Does *uniform* start with the letter u? (Yes.) What sound? (/j/, like *you*.) So *a* or *an*? (A.)

rows: Missing article with jobs (She is teacher).
Board: She is a teacher. Use a finger gesture for the missing word.
Say the words aloud; ask "What sound?"
a + plural (a two books, a books).
Contrast one vs many with real objects.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: pen · book · phone · apple · orange · umbrella · eraser · ID card · doctor · engineer · teacher · artist
a + consonant sound: a pen, a doctor, a uniform · an + vowel sound: an apple, an engineer, an hour · plural: no a/an: two pens · Jobs: She's a nurse.
a /ə/ · an /ən/ · an‿apple · a uniform /j/ · an hour (silent h)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Indefinite Articles A and An, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and activate vocabulary.
Show the bag. Say: *"What's in my bag? Guess!"* Take a few guesses.
Pull objects out one at a time. Students name them. Board the nouns without articles first.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about Ishara's bag. Tick the things in her bag."* (3 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you tick or write?"* (Tick.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
Students answer two questions: *What is Ishara's mother's job? What is her father's job?*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
Point to the nouns on the board. Ask students to tell you *a* or *an* for each from the text. Write *a* or *an* in front.
Sort into two columns: *a* and *an*. Ask: *"What's the same about the an words?"* Elicit: they start with a vowel sound.
**The sound rule.** Write *university* and *umbrella*. Say them slowly. Ask: *"Same first sound?"* (No.) Write *a university, an umbrella.* Do the same with *hour* and *house*.
**Jobs.** Board *She's a doctor. He's an engineer.* Ask: *"Can I say She's doctor?"* (No.)
**Plurals.** Hold up two pens: *"Two pens. A two pens?"* (No.)
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak forms and linking: *a pen, an apple, an engineer, an hour.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the rule accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers aloud, linking *an* + vowel.
**Quick-fire game:** say a noun; students shout *"A!"* or *"An!"*. Include tricky ones: *hour, uniform, egg, umbrella, one-day trip*.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use *a / an* in personalised speaking.

**What's in my bag? (6 minutes):** students draw five things from their own bag in a box on Handout 2 (without words), then describe them to a partner, who draws them: *"I've got a phone, an eraser and a red pen."*
**Jobs guessing game (8 minutes):** in groups, students take a card from Handout 3 and mime the job. Others ask: *"Are you a doctor?" "No, I'm not." "Are you an artist?" "Yes, I am!"*
**Writing (4 minutes):** students write 6 sentences about their bag and their family's jobs.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard (two incorrect). Students correct them.
Final quick-fire round with tricky words.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write 8 sentences about your bag and your family's jobs.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Highlight vowel letters on the noun cards in a colour. Give weaker students a list of jobs with *a / an* already written.
Add adjectives: *an old book, a big apple, an expensive phone*. Ask: *"Does the article change?"* Introduce tricky sounds: *an MP3, a European city, an honest boy*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "What's in my bag?" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Jobs Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "What's in my bag?" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use *a / an* correctly in 8 of 10 items on Handout 2. Students use *a / an* with jobs in the guessing game.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand the sound rule, not the letter rule? Did they remember the article with jobs?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: What's in My Bag?
text: **Read about Ishara's bag. Tick (✓) the things in her bag.**

Hi, I'm Ishara. I'm 14 and I'm a student. This is my school bag. What's in it? I've got a book, an English dictionary and a pencil case. In my pencil case, I've got a pen, a pencil and an eraser. I've also got a phone, an umbrella (it rains a lot in Kandy!) and an apple for lunch. Oh, and I've got an ID card. My mother is a doctor and my father is an engineer, so they're very busy. I take a bus to school every day.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What is Ishara's mother's job? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Write a or an.**
**B. Write the job. Use a or an.**
**C. My bag: draw five things (no words!). Then tell your partner.**
bullets: ______ orange · 2. ______ notebook · 3. ______ hour · 4. ______ university · 5. ______ egg · 6. ______ uniform · 7. ______ apple · 8. ______ elephant · 9. ______ house · 10. ______ umbrella
She works in a hospital. She's ______________________________

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on A, An or The?, built round the theme "The Dog in the Market".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who use a / an correctly but don't use the, or use the everywhere. Their stories are confusing: I saw dog. Dog took fish.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Story" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: A, An or The? (First and Second Mention, Unique Things)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (story: The Dog in the Market), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (town map and directions task), story picture prompts (drawn on the board or described).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise a / an for first mention and the for second mention, unique things and things both speakers know.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell a short story and give directions using a / an and the correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in telling a short picture story.
**Subsidiary aim.** To give and follow directions in a town.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: First mention (the listener doesn't know which one)
I saw a dog in the market.
Second mention (now the listener knows which one)
the sun, the moon, the sea, the sky, the internet
Shared knowledge (both speakers know which one)
Can you close the door? (the door in this room) Let's meet at the station. (our town's station)
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Pronunciation
bullets: *the* /ðə/ before consonant sounds: *the dog*; /ði/ before vowel sounds: *the apple, the end*.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I saw a dog. The dog was huge.*** In the first sentence, does the listener know which dog? (No.) · In the second sentence, do we know which dog? (Yes, the dog I just talked about.)
***The sun is hot.*** How many suns are there? (One.) So *a* or *the*? (The.)

rows: No article at all (Sun is hot).
Board the "only one" rule with pictures.
the for first mention (I bought the new phone = any phone).
Ask: "Does your friend know which phone?"
Drill the apple, the old man.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: 1. a market · 2. a dog · 3. a fish stall · 4. the dog takes a fish · 5. the man chases the dog · 6. the fish lands in a basket
FIRST time → a / an: I saw a dog. · SECOND time → the: The dog took a fish. · ONLY ONE → the: the sun, the sea, the internet · WE BOTH KNOW → the: Close the door. Meet me at the station.
the /ðə/ + consonant: the dog · the /ði/ + vowel: the apple
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: A, An or The?, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest with a funny picture story.
Draw or describe six simple pictures on the board: a market; a dog; a fish stall; the dog taking a fish; a man chasing the dog; the fish landing in a woman's basket.
Ask: *"What's happening? Is it funny?"* Take ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present *a / an* and *the* in a story and clarify first and second mention, unique things and shared knowledge.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the story. Is it the same as the pictures? Three minutes."*
Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Circle every a / an. Underline every the."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**First and second mention.** Board: *I saw a dog. The dog was huge.* Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis. Build the rule.
**Unique things.** Elicit *the sun* from the text. Ask: *"How many suns are there?"* Add *the moon, the sea, the sky, the internet.*
**Shared knowledge.** Ask: *"The market: which market? Do the people in the story know?"* (Yes, their local market.) Add *Close the door. Meet me at the station.*
**Superlatives.** Elicit *the best day* from the text.
**Pronunciation.** Drill *the dog, the apple, the end, the old man.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise article choice.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: a, an or the. Exercise B: find and correct seven mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs explain each choice: *"First time, so a."*
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use articles accurately in storytelling and giving directions.
**Story (6 minutes).** Pairs retell the dog story without looking, then invent a new ending.

**Directions (9 minutes).** Give out Handout 3. Student A chooses a place on the map and gives directions from the bus station: *"Go past the bank. There's a café next to the park."* Student B follows and guesses the place. Swap.
ICQs: *"Where do you start?"* (The bus station.) *"Do you say the name of the place?"* (No, your partner guesses.)
**Writing (3 minutes).** Students write a 4-sentence mini-story at the bottom of Handout 3 using first and second mention.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two students read their mini-stories. The class checks each article.
Board errors from Stage 4; students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a funny 6-sentence story about an animal, using first and second mention correctly.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give a decision flowchart: *Is it the first time? → a / an. Do we know which one? → the.* Provide the first sentence of each story.
Stronger students explain each article choice to their partner. Add superlatives to the directions: *the biggest temple, the oldest shop*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Story" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Story" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students change from *a* to *the* on second mention in their stories. 12 out of 16 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Correct *the* with unique and shared-knowledge nouns.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Were unique and shared-knowledge uses clear? Did the directions task produce accurate article use?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Dog in the Market
text: **Read the story. Circle a / an. Underline the.**
Last Saturday, I went to the market with my grandmother. The sun was very hot and the market was busy. There was a man with a bicycle, a woman with a big basket and an old man selling fruit.

Suddenly, I saw a dog. The dog was huge and very hungry. It walked to a fish stall and took a big fish! The man with the bicycle shouted, "Stop!" and chased the dog. The dog ran under a table and the fish flew into the air. Where did it land? In the woman's basket!
The woman laughed and gave the fish back to the fish seller. The dog didn't get a fish, but my grandmother bought it a bun. It was the best day at the market ever!
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Who did the writer go to the market with? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete with a, an or the.**
**B. Find and correct seven mistakes.**
Yesterday I saw a film at cinema. Film was about a girl and a horse. Girl lived on farm near sea. One day, a horse ran away. It was a saddest day of her life.
bullets: I bought ______ new phone. ______ phone is black.
______ moon is very bright tonight.
There's ______ old man at the door.
Can you close ______ window, please? It's cold.
We had ______ amazing holiday. ______ hotel was next to ______ sea.
I read ______ interesting article on ______ internet.
She has ______ cat and ______ dog. ______ cat is called Kitty.
______ Mount Everest is ______ highest mountain in ______ world. (Careful!)

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Town Map and Directions
text: **Look at the map. Choose a place. Give your partner directions. Your partner guesses the place.**
You are at the bus station.
**Useful language:** *Go straight on. Turn left / right at the ... Go past the ... It's next to / opposite / between the ... and the ... There's a ... on the corner.*
**Write a 4-sentence mini-story. Use a / an the first time and the the second time.**

text: **Handout 1**
**Handout 2, Exercise A**
**Handout 2, Exercise B**

Yesterday I saw a film at **the** cinema. **The** film was about a girl and a horse. **The** girl lived on **a** farm near **the** sea. One day, **the** horse ran away. It was **the** saddest day of her life.
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Her / his grandmother · 2. A big fish · 3. In the woman's basket
a ... The · 2. The · 3. an · 4. the · 5. an ... The ... the · 6. an ... the · 7. a ... a ... The · 8. – (no article) ... the ... the

rows: I saw a film. A film was great.
I saw a film. The film was great.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use a / an / the for first and second mention but say The life is beautiful, I like the football and He speaks the English.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: The Zero Article (General vs Specific)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (magazine article), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (opinion cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover when to use no article (general plural and uncountable nouns; meals, sports, languages; institutions for their purpose) and when to use the (specific).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can give opinions about general topics without using the incorrectly, e.g. Children love sweets. Money can't buy happiness.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read a magazine article for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in giving opinions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: General plural nouns: Ø Dogs are loyal.
Specific plural: The dogs next door bark all night.
General uncountable nouns: Ø Rice is cheap here. Ø Life is beautiful.
Specific uncountable: The rice in this shop is old.
Abstract nouns in general: Ø Happiness is important.
Specific: the happiness of my children
Meals: have Ø breakfast / lunch / dinner
Specific: The lunch we had was delicious.
Sports and games: play Ø cricket / chess
Languages and school subjects: speak Ø Tamil; study Ø maths
Institutions for their main purpose: go to Ø school / hospital / prison / university / church / bed
Visit the building for another reason: My mother went to the school to meet my teacher.
blocks.heading: Use
Pronunciation
bullets: No special issue; contrast stress on *the* when emphasising specificity: *THE rice in THIS shop*.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Dogs are loyal.*** Are we talking about particular dogs? (No, dogs in general.) · Do we use *the*? (No.)
***The dogs next door bark all night.*** Do we know which dogs? (Yes, next door.)
***He's in hospital.*** Is he a patient or a visitor? (A patient.)

rows: L1 transfer: the with general nouns (The life is hard).
Repeated contrast pairs; opinion task forces general statements.
Overcorrection: dropping the for specific nouns.
Keep pairs side by side on the board.
Picture contrast: a child going to school vs a parent visiting the school.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: Dogs are loyal. · Rice is cheap. · Life is beautiful. · I play cricket. · I speak Tamil. · I have lunch at 1. · He's in hospital (patient).
GENERAL → no article · SPECIFIC (we know which) → the · Meals, sports, languages → no article · Institution for its purpose → no article
The dogs next door ... · The rice in this shop ... · The lunch we had ... · She went to the hospital to visit him.

blocks.heading: Procedure: The Zero Article, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Write three questions on the board: *Is coffee healthy? Are cats better than dogs? Is rice better than bread?*
Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Take a few opinions; don't correct.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present general and specific noun use in context and help students work out when to use no article.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the article. Which country's food habits surprise you most? Three minutes."*
Pairs discuss. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the pairs of sentences. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"How many pairs?"* (Five.) *"Alone or with a partner?"* (With a partner.)
Monitor. Help with: *"Which dogs? All dogs, or particular dogs?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit answers. Build the two columns and the rules on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Draw a quick picture: a child with a school bag (*goes to school*) and a parent at the school gate (*goes to the school*). Ask: *"Who is studying? Who is visiting?"*
Elicit meals, sports and languages without articles: *have lunch, play cricket, speak Sinhala.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise article choice.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: the or no article. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs justify: *"General, so no article."* Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To make general statements fluently and accurately in discussion.
Give each group the opinion cards (Handout 4). Model: *"Money can't buy happiness. I agree, because ... But the money my parents saved helped my education."*
Students take turns to read a card, agree or disagree, and give a reason (13 minutes).
ICQs: *"What do you do after you read the card?"* (Agree or disagree and give a reason.)
Monitor and note article errors.
Each group reports the card they disagreed about most.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors and good sentences; students correct the errors.
Ask students to give one general and one specific sentence about food.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 120-word paragraph about food habits in your country, using at least five general statements and two specific ones.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give a general / specific checklist: *All of them in general? → no article. Do we know which? → the.* Let weaker students write their opinion before speaking.
Stronger students write their own pairs of contrasting sentences. They use abstract nouns in discussion: *freedom, education, success*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Opinion Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the discussion, students make general statements without *the*. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students stop saying *the life / the people* in general statements? Was the institution rule clear?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Eating Around the World
text: **What Does the World Eat?**

Rice is the most important food for more than half of the world's population. In Sri Lanka, people often have rice for breakfast, lunch and dinner! In many European countries, however, bread is more common, and people rarely eat rice every day.
Tea is popular everywhere, but the tea grown in the hills of Sri Lanka is famous around the world. Coffee is the favourite drink in Brazil and Ethiopia.

Children love sweets in every country. However, doctors say that sugar is one of the biggest health problems today. The children in a recent study in the UK ate three times more sugar than they should.
In Japan, people eat a lot of fish, and life expectancy is one of the highest in the world. The fish served in Tokyo's famous market is very fresh, and visitors queue for hours for breakfast there.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What do many Sri Lankans eat three times a day? ______________________________
Why is Sri Lankan tea special? ______________________________
What did the study in the UK find? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these pairs of sentences from the article and other examples.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: In column A, are we talking about things **in general** or **particular** things? ______________
In column B, do we know **which** rice / children / tea / fish? How? ______________________________
Complete the rule: For general plural and uncountable nouns, we use ______________ article.
In pair 5, who is a patient? Who is a visitor? ______________________________
Look at the article again. Find a meal, a sport or a language. Is there an article? ______________________________

The rice in this shop is old.
The children in the study ate too much sugar.
The tea grown in Sri Lanka is famous.
The fish in Tokyo's market is fresh.
5. He's in hospital. He broke his leg.
I went to the hospital to visit him.

text: **A. Write the or – (no article).**
**B. Correct the mistakes. Two sentences are correct.**

______ children in my class are very noisy.
My grandmother is in ______ hospital. She's having an operation.
I love ______ music, especially jazz.
______ music in that café was terrible.
We have ______ dinner at 8.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Articles with Place Names, built round the theme "Geography and Inventions Quiz".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who are generally accurate with articles but make errors with geographical names (the Sri Lanka, Himalayas) and don't know the generic singular the (The tiger is endangered).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Articles with Place Names, Organisations and Generic Nouns
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (encyclopedia extracts), Handout 2 (reference chart and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (quiz-writing sheet), a world map (optional).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To improve students' use of articles with place names, organisations and generic singular nouns.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and answer quiz questions about geography and inventions using articles correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in team quiz games.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read encyclopedia-style texts.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Oceans, seas, rivers, canals: the Indian Ocean, the Nile, the Suez Canal
Most countries: Sri Lanka, India, Japan
Mountain ranges and island groups: the Alps, the Himalayas, the Maldives
Single mountains: Mount Everest, Adam's Peak
Countries with Republic / Kingdom / States / plural names: the USA, the UK, the Netherlands, the Philippines
Regions with of: the north of India, the Middle East
Cities, towns, streets: Colombo, Galle Road
Many buildings and organisations: the British Museum, the United Nations, the Taj Mahal
Buildings with a person's or place name + building type: Colombo Airport, Kandy Station, Buckingham Palace
blocks.heading: Place names
Generic reference
bullets: *The* + singular noun for a whole species or invention (formal / encyclopedic): **The tiger** is endangered. **The smartphone** changed our lives.
Plural without article (general, neutral): **Tigers** are endangered.
*A* + singular (any one example): **A tiger** can swim well.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *the* /ði/ before vowels: *the Indian Ocean, the Alps, the USA* /ði ˌjuː es ˈeɪ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The tiger is endangered.*** Are we talking about one particular tiger? (No, tigers as a species.) · Is this formal or informal style? (Quite formal, like an encyclopedia.)

rows: the Sri Lanka, the Mount Everest
Two-column chart kept on the board.
Point out plurals and water usually take the.
Generic the sounds wrong to students.
Show encyclopedia examples; compare with plural generic.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: the Nile · the Indian Ocean · the Himalayas · the Maldives · the USA · Sri Lanka · Asia · Mount Everest · Lake Victoria · Colombo
THE: oceans, seas, rivers · ranges · island groups · deserts · the USA / UK · the north of ... · the United Nations · NO ARTICLE: countries · continents · single mountains · lakes · cities · streets
The tiger is endangered. (species, formal) · Tigers are endangered. (general) · A tiger can swim. (any one)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Articles with Place Names, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students with a quick quiz.
Ask three quick questions: *"What's the longest river in Africa? What's the highest mountain in the world? Which ocean is around Sri Lanka?"* Teams write answers.
Check the facts without focusing on articles yet.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present article use with place names and generic nouns in encyclopedia texts and clarify the rules.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the encyclopedia extracts. What surprised you?"*
Pairs share one surprising fact.
**Part B: Noticing (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Find all the place names in the extracts. Put them in the table: the or no article."*
ICQs: *"Where do you find the names?"* (In Handout 1.) *"How many columns?"* (Two.)
Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**

Build the chart on the board category by category: oceans and rivers; ranges and island groups; deserts; plural or *Republic / Kingdom / States* countries; organisations; versus countries, continents, single mountains, lakes, cities.

Present the generic *the* from the extracts (*The Asian elephant ..., The printing press ...*) and contrast with the plural generic (*Elephants are ...*) and *a* (*An elephant can ...*). Ask the CCQs.
Mention exceptions briefly: *the Netherlands, The Hague.*
**Pronunciation.** Drill *the* /ði/ before vowels: *the Indian Ocean, the Alps, the USA.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise accurately.
Say: *"Do Exercise A on Handout 2: correct the mistakes. Then Handout 3: write the or no article."* (7 minutes.)
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use articles accurately in a motivating team quiz.
Give out Handout 4. Teams write a 10-question quiz about geography and inventions. Each question must include at least one place name or generic noun (8 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many questions?"* (Ten.) *"What must each question include?"* (A place name or generic noun.)
Teams exchange quizzes and answer them (6 minutes).
Teams mark each other: 1 point for the correct fact and 1 point for correct articles (4 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Announce the winning team.
Review the trickiest items from the quizzes on the board.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 150-word travel guide entry for a region you know, including at least eight place names.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker teams the chart during the quiz. Provide question frames: *Which river flows through ...? Who invented ...?*
Stronger teams research three exceptions and explain them. They write questions with generic *the*: *When was the telephone invented?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Controlled practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Reference Chart and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Controlled practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Teams' quiz questions and answers use place-name articles accurately. Correct generic *the* in at least two quiz questions. 6 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which categories were most problematic? Did the quiz motivate accurate article use?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Encyclopedia Extracts
text: **The Asian Elephant** The Asian elephant is found in India, Sri Lanka and parts of South-East Asia. Smaller than the African elephant, it lives in forests and grasslands. Many elephants live in Minneriya National Park, where hundreds gather around Minneriya Lake in the dry season.
**The Nile** The Nile is often called the longest river in the world. It flows north through eleven countries, including Egypt and Sudan, and ends in the Mediterranean Sea.
**The Printing Press** The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg in Germany around 1440, changed the world. Books became cheaper, and ideas spread quickly across Europe.
**The Himalayas** The Himalayas stretch across five countries. Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and China, is the highest mountain on Earth.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Reference Chart and Practice
text: **Sort the place names from Handout 1.**
**A. Correct the mistakes. Three are correct.**

I visited the Lake Victoria. ______________________________
The smartphone has changed how we communicate. ______________________________
They climbed the Mount Kilimanjaro. ______________________________
She studies at Oxford University. ______________________________
Pacific is the largest ocean. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Further Practice
text: **Write the or – (no article).**
bullets: ______ Indian Ocean surrounds ______ Sri Lanka.
______ Mount Fuji is in ______ Japan.
______ Sahara is the largest hot desert.
______ computer has transformed education.
She works for ______ United Nations in ______ New York.
We crossed ______ Himalayas on our way to ______ Nepal.
______ Lake Victoria is in ______ Africa.
My cousin lives in ______ USA, near ______ Mississippi.
They went on holiday to ______ Maldives.
______ elephant is an intelligent animal.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Write Your Quiz
text: **Write 10 questions about geography and inventions. Check your articles!**
**Scoring:** 1 point for the correct fact + 1 point for correct articles in the answer.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Articles in Academic Writing, built round the theme "Urbanisation in Asia".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students preparing for university or IELTS. Their academic writing is fluent but contains frequent article errors with abstract nouns and of-phrases (The globalisation has changed ..., Impact of technology is ...).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Articles in Academic Writing and Fixed Expressions
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (fixed expressions warm-up), Handout 2 (two paragraphs for analysis), Handout 3 (practice and editing checklist), Handout 4 (writing task: data and paragraph brief).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To improve accuracy with articles in academic writing: abstract nouns in general vs specific use, nouns followed by of-phrases, pre-modified nouns, and fixed expressions.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and self-edit a 150-word academic paragraph with accurate article use.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop collaborative academic writing and peer editing.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Abstract or uncountable noun in general: no article
Ø Education is essential. Ø Technology is changing fast.
Abstract noun made specific (by of-phrase, relative clause or context): the
the education of girls · the technology that we use
the role of women · the impact of tourism · the growth of cities
Ø rapid urban growth · Ø online learning
Countable singular noun always needs an article
a / the study, a / the survey (not Study shows ...)
Ø Studies show that ... Ø Young people ...
in the long run · on the whole · at first · by chance · in hospital · at sea · in the meantime · on the other hand · for the time being
That's THE best curry in Colombo. /ðiː/
blocks.heading: Key patterns
Pronunciation
bullets: Emphatic *the*: /ðiː/ with stress.

rows: General vs specific contrast pairs in analysis.
Highlight of-phrases in the model text.
Students think both options are always possible.
Discuss genuine cases where both are possible with a change of meaning.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: in the long run · on the whole · at first · by chance · in the meantime · on the other hand · for the time being

GENERAL abstract / plural → Ø: Education matters. Studies show ... · SPECIFIC (of / that / context) → the: the education of girls · NOUN + OF → the: the impact of ... · SINGULAR COUNTABLE → never bare: a study / the study
general? specific? countable singular? followed by of? fixed phrase?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Articles in Academic Writing, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To activate awareness of articles in fixed expressions.
Give out Handout 1. Pairs complete the five fixed expressions with *a, an, the* or no article (2 minutes).
Check quickly. Board the expressions on the left.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To analyse article use in academic writing and clarify the key patterns.
**Part A: Analysis (9 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Paragraph A has article errors. Paragraph B is corrected. Find at least ten differences and explain each one."*
ICQs: *"Which paragraph has errors?"* (A.) *"Do you just find the differences?"* (No, explain them too.)
Pairs work. Monitor and help with explanations.
**Part B: Clarification (11 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board:
general abstract or uncountable nouns → no article (*Urbanisation, economic growth, housing*);
nouns followed by *of* → usually *the* (*the proportion of, the rapid growth of*);
singular countable nouns always need an article (*a recent study*);
organisations and superlatives (*the United Nations, the most important*);
fixed expressions (*in the long run*).
Contrast pairs: *Education is essential / the education of girls*; *Technology changes fast / the technology that we use*.
Discuss cases where both are possible with a change of meaning: *Research shows ... / The research shows ...* (general research vs a specific study already mentioned).

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise accurate article use.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: correct the article errors. Some sentences are correct. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class, asking for the rule each time.
Read through the editing checklist (Exercise B) together.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To write an academic paragraph with accurate article use and self-edit it.
Give out Handout 4. Say: *"Write an academic paragraph (about 150 words) describing the data and discussing one effect of rapid urban growth."* (11 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many words?"* (About 150.) *"Formal or informal?"* (Formal, academic.)
Pairs use the editing checklist (Handout 3, Exercise B) to edit their own paragraph and mark every change (4 minutes).
Pairs swap with another pair and check each other's articles (3 minutes).
Monitor and note common errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two pairs read their paragraphs. Board two or three sentences with interesting article choices; the class decides if they are correct.
Ask: *"Which pattern do you most need to check in your writing?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 250-word discursive paragraph on a social issue and self-edit for articles using the checklist.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide an article decision checklist card. Give a paragraph frame for the writing task.
Analyse article choices in a real journal abstract. Explore further cases where both options are possible with a change of meaning.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice and Editing Checklist on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The final paragraph has no more than one article error. Students can explain each correction using the patterns. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which pattern caused the most errors in the writing? Did self-editing improve the paragraphs?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Fixed Expressions
text: **Complete with a, an, the or – (no article).**
bullets: In ______ long run, renewable energy will be cheaper.
On ______ whole, the results were positive.
At ______ first, nobody believed the study.
We met by ______ chance at a conference.
He's been in ______ hospital since Monday.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Two Paragraphs
text: **Paragraph A (contains article errors)**

The urbanisation is one of most important trends in the Asia today. According to the recent study by United Nations, proportion of people living in cities will rise significantly by 2050. Main reason for this is the economic growth. In China, for example, the urban population more than doubled between 1990 and 2020. However, the rapid growth of cities creates the serious problems. Traffic congestion and the air pollution are major concerns, and the housing is becoming unaffordable for young people. In long run, governments will need to invest in the public transport.
**Paragraph B (corrected)**

Urbanisation is one of the most important trends in Asia today. According to a recent study by the United Nations, the proportion of people living in cities will rise significantly by 2050. The main reason for this is economic growth. In China, for example, the urban population more than doubled between 1990 and 2020. However, the rapid growth of cities creates serious problems. Traffic congestion and air pollution are major concerns, and housing is becoming unaffordable for young people. In the long run, governments will need to invest in public transport.
**Find at least ten differences and explain each one.**

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice and Editing Checklist
text: **A. Correct the article errors. Some sentences may be correct.**
**B. Editing checklist (use it for your paragraph on Handout 4)**
bullets: The globalisation has changed the way we live. ______________________________
Impact of social media on teenagers is significant. ______________________________
In long run, the policy will fail. ______________________________
Research shows that the unemployment is falling. ______________________________
The history of the Sri Lanka is fascinating. ______________________________
Study by Harvard found that sleep improves memory. ______________________________
The role of the government is to protect citizens. ______________________________
On the whole, students preferred online learning. ______________________________
The education of girls has improved since 1990. ______________________________
Young people are leaving the villages for the cities. (in general) ______________________________

rows: General abstract / uncountable nouns have no article
Nouns followed by of usually have the
No bare singular countable nouns (a study / the study)
Country names have no article (except the USA, the UK, etc.)
Fixed expressions are correct (in the long run, on the whole)

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **Data: Urban population (% of total population)**
**Write an academic paragraph (about 150 words):**
**Your paragraph:**
bullets: describe the main trends in the data
discuss one effect of rapid urban growth (e.g. housing, transport, pollution, employment)
use a formal academic style

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1**
**Handout 2 (differences)**

The urbanisation → Urbanisation (general) · most important → the most important (superlative) · the Asia → Asia (continent) · the recent study → a recent study (first mention) · United Nations → the United Nations (organisation) · proportion of → the proportion of (of-phrase) · Main reason → The main reason (specific) · the economic growth → economic growth (general) · the serious problems → serious problems (general plural) · the air pollution → air pollution (general) · the housing → housing (general) · In long run → In the long run (fixed expression) · the public transport → public transport (general)
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Globalisation has changed the way we live. · 2. The impact of social media ... · 3. In the long run, ... · 4. ... unemployment is falling. · 5. The history of Sri Lanka ... · 6. A study by Harvard found ... · 7. Correct. · 8. Correct. · 9. Correct. · 10. Young people are leaving villages for cities.

rows: The role of the government is ...
A study shows that ... / Studies show that ...

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Prepositions of Place, built round the theme "Where Is It? My Bedroom".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who know There is / There are and common furniture and classroom words, but confuse in and on and leave out to in next to.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Hide and find" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and listening
Grammar: Prepositions of Place (in, on, under, next to, behind, in front of, between)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
A box and a ball (or a cup and a pen), Handout 1 (Kamal's bedroom description), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (picture dictation grid), classroom objects.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise seven prepositions of place to describe where things are.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe where 8 things are in a room and draw a room from a partner's description.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review furniture vocabulary.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise Where is / Where are ...? questions.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop listening and speaking in a picture dictation.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: The ball is in the box.
on top of, touching a surface
The book is on the table.
The cat is under the bed.
The lamp is next to the bed.
The bag is behind the door.
The chair is in front of the desk.
in the middle of two things
The desk is between the bed and the window.
blocks.heading: Form and meaning
Form and meaning: notes
text: Structures: *Where is the ...? It's on the ... · Where are the ...? They're under the ... · There's a ... next to the ...*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *of*: *in front of* /ɪn ˈfrʌnt əv/. Weak *the*: /ðə/.
*next to* – the /t/ sounds often join: /ˈneks tə/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: *The ball is in the box.* — Can I see all of the ball? (No, it's inside.) *The ball is on the box.* — Is it inside? (No.) Is it touching the top? (Yes.) *The desk is between the bed and the window.* — How many things are on the sides? (Two.)

rows: Real objects; repeat with the box many times.
Contrast is / are with singular / plural.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: bed · desk · chair · wardrobe · shelf · lamp · window · door · rug
in · on · under · next to · behind · in front of · between ... and ...
Where is the lamp? It's next to the bed. · Where are the shoes? They're under the bed.
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Prepositions of Place, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic with real objects.
Hold up a box and a ball. Put the ball in the box. Ask: *"Where's the ball?"* Students point. Say: *"It's in the box."*
Move the ball: on, under, next to, behind, in front of the box. Let students guess the words.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about Kamal's bedroom. Where are his things? Answer the questions."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you draw or write?"* (Write.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
Draw seven box-and-ball pictures on the board. Elicit each preposition from the text and write it under the picture.
Ask the CCQs.
Highlight *next* ***to***, *in front* ***of***, *between ...* ***and*** *...*
Questions: board *Where is the lamp? Where are the shoes?* Contrast *is / are*.
Drill: *Where's the cat? It's under the bed. Where are the books? They're on the shelf.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
Pairs check. Feedback.
**Classroom drill:** ask about real objects in the classroom: *"Where's my bag?" "It's on the desk."*

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the prepositions in communicative tasks.
**Hide and find (6 minutes):** Student A hides a small object (an eraser) while B closes their eyes. B asks: *"Is it under the chair?" "No, it isn't." "Is it in your bag?" "Yes, it is!"* Swap.
**Picture dictation (10 minutes):** give out Handout 3. Student A draws their dream bedroom in their grid (8 things) without showing B. A describes it; B draws it. Then compare drawings and swap.
Students write 4 sentences about their partner's drawing.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To consolidate.
Compare a few drawings. Which pairs have the most similar pictures?
Correct errors heard (*in the table, next the window*).
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Draw your bedroom and write 6 sentences about where things are.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Label the box-and-ball pictures and leave them on the board. Weaker students describe 5 things instead of 8.
Add *opposite, above, near, on the left / right of*. Students describe the classroom from memory with eyes closed.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Hide and find" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Picture Dictation works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Hide and find" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use the correct preposition in 8 of 10 items on Handout 2. In the picture dictation, the partner's drawing matches in at least 6 of 8 positions.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which prepositions caused most confusion? Did the picture dictation work well?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Kamal's Bedroom
text: **Read about Kamal's bedroom. Answer the questions.**

My bedroom is small but I love it. My bed is next to the window. There's a lamp on a small table next to my bed. My desk is between the bed and the wardrobe, and my chair is in front of the desk. My books are on a shelf above the desk. My school bag is behind the door. My cat, Tiger, is always under the bed. And my shoes? They're in the wardrobe, of course!
**Where is / are ...?**

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete with in, on, under, next to, behind, in front of or between.**
**B. Look at your classroom. Write 4 sentences.**
bullets: The cat is ______________ the bed. (below it)
The books are ______________ the shelf.
The ball is ______________ the box. (inside it)
The lamp is ______________ the bed and the desk.
The bag is ______________ the door. (at the back of it)
The car is ______________ the house. (facing it)
The phone is ______________ my bag. (inside it)
The chair is ______________ the window. (at the side of it)

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Picture Dictation
text: **Student A: Draw your dream bedroom (8 things). Don't show your partner. Describe it. Student B: Listen and draw.**
**Useful words:** bed · desk · chair · lamp · wardrobe · shelf · rug · TV · plant · window · door · guitar · computer
**Write 4 sentences about your partner's room.**
