blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know days, months and times but mix in, on, at (in Monday, at June, on next week).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Part B" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Prepositions of Time (in, on, at)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (school calendar), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (Find someone who ...), time expression cards.
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise in, on, at with times, days, dates, months, years and parts of the day, and expressions with no preposition.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can ask and answer questions about birthdays, routines and events using in, on, at correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a mingle activity.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a school calendar for specific information.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *at* /ət/: *at seven* /ət ˈsevn/. Linking: *on‿Monday*, *in‿April*.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: *in the morning / at night* — Which one uses *at*? (night) Is *night* an exception? (Yes, learn it.) *on Monday morning* — Why *on*, not *in*? (Because it's a specific day.) *next week* — Is there a preposition? (No.)

rows: on next week, in last year
in the night vs at night
Teach at night as a fixed phrase.
on Monday morning vs in the morning
Rule: a day makes it on.
Point to the calendar: a date is a day → on.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: IN (big): months, years, seasons, parts of the day · ON (medium): days, dates · AT (small): times, night, the weekend, festivals
at 7 o'clock · on Monday · on 4 February · in June · in 2025 · in the morning · at night · on Monday morning
next week · last year · tomorrow · this morning · every day
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Prepositions of Time, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create personal interest.
Write your birthday on the board: *4 February*. Tell students it's your birthday.
Ask: *"When's your birthday? When do you get up? When do you have lunch?"* Students ask a partner (2 minutes).

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present *in, on, at* in context and clarify their use with times, days, dates, months, years and parts of the day.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the school calendar. When is sports day? When do classes finish on Fridays? Answer the four questions."*
ICQs: *"How many questions?"* (Four.)
Pairs check. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Look at the words in bold: in, on, at. What comes after each one?"* Pairs list the time expressions under *in, on, at*.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
Draw the triangle on the board: *in* (big) at the top, *on* (medium), *at* (small). Pairs sort the time expression cards into the triangle. Check and build the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Highlight the "no preposition" column: *next week, last year, tomorrow, this morning, every day.*
Highlight special cases: *at night* (but *in the morning*), *on Monday morning*.
Drill: *at seven, on Monday, in June, at night, next week.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: in, on, at or nothing. Exercise B: sort the expressions. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use prepositions of time accurately in personalised speaking.
Give out Handout 3. **Part A (6 minutes):** students mingle and ask the questions. They write a name for each question.
**Part B (6 minutes):** students mingle again with the new questions and must answer in full sentences: *"My birthday is on 12 August."*
ICQs: *"In Part B, do you answer with one word or a full sentence?"* (A full sentence.)
**Holidays quiz (6 minutes):** pairs write five questions about festivals and holidays (*When is Vesak? When do people celebrate Avurudu?*) and swap with another pair.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors heard in Stage 4; students correct them.
Quick test: say a time expression; students shout *in, on, at* or *nothing*.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write your weekly timetable in 8 sentences using *in, on, at* and two expressions with no preposition.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Keep the triangle visible; give a card version. Weaker students answer with short phrases in Part A.
Add *in the 1990s, at the end of, in the middle of*. Write a weekly timetable with 10 time expressions.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Part B" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Part B" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students answer accurately in full sentences in Part B.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which expressions were hardest? Did students answer more accurately in Part B than in Part A?

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Prepositions of Movement and Transport, built round the theme "A Walking Tour of Kandy".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who know prepositions of place but confuse across / through, into / in, and transport phrases (by foot, get out the bus).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Prepositions of Movement and Transport
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (walking tour text and map), Handout 2 (discovery task with arrow diagrams), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (information gap maps).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover and use prepositions of movement (across, along, through, over, past, into, out of, up, down, towards, around) and transport phrases (by bus, on foot, get on / off, get into / out of).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can give clear directions on a map and describe their journey to school using at least six prepositions of movement.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To follow a route on a map.
**Subsidiary aim.** To give and follow directions.
**Subsidiary aim.** To describe a journey.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: from one side to the other (on a surface)
Walk across the bridge / the road / the field.
from one end to the other, inside something
Go through the park / the tunnel / the forest.
Walk along the lake / the river / the road.
Climb over the wall. Fly over the city.
Walk into the museum. Come out of the shop.
Go up the hill. Come down the steps.
in a circle / on the other side
Walk around the lake. Turn around the corner.
blocks.heading: Meaning

rows: by bus, by train, by car, by tuk-tuk
I go to school on foot.
blocks.heading: Transport
Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *to* and *of*: *towards* /təˈwɔːdz/; *out of* /ˈaʊt əv/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: *We walked through the park.* — Were we inside the park? (Yes.) *We walked across the road.* — Were we on the surface, from one side to the other? (Yes.) *I get off the bus.* — Big vehicle or small car? (Big, you can stand in it.)

rows: get out the bus / get off the car
No article after by for transport.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: → across (surface) · → through (inside) · → along (line) · ↷ over · → past · ↘ into / ↗ out of · ↑ up / ↓ down · ↻ around · → towards
Surface: across · Inside: through · Line: along · Entering: into · Leaving: out of
by bus / train / car (no article) · on foot · get on / off (bus, train, plane) · get into / out of (car, taxi)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Prepositions of Movement and Transport, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage interest.
Mime movements: walking through a door, across the room, around a desk, past a student. Students guess the movement.
Ask: *"How do you come to school? What do you go past?"*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present prepositions of movement and transport phrases in context and help students work out their meanings.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the walking tour. Draw the route on the map."*
ICQs: *"Where do you start?"* (The Clock Tower.) *"Do you write or draw?"* (Draw the route.)
Pairs compare their routes. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the meanings (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Pairs match each preposition to its meaning (Part A) and answer the questions about transport (Part B).
Monitor and prompt: *"Were they inside the park, or on the surface of the road?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit matches and draw the arrows on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis. Focus on *across / through*.
Elicit the transport rules. Ask: *"Do we say by the bus?"* (No.) *"By foot?"* (No, on foot.)
Drill: *Go across the bridge. Walk along the lake. Go past the temple. I go to school on foot.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: complete with the correct preposition. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs justify. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the language fluently in giving directions and describing journeys.
Give out Handout 4. Student A is a tourist; Student B is a local. Tourists ask for directions to three places; locals guide them using the map (10 minutes, swap after 5).
ICQs: *"Who has the map?"* (The local.) *"How many places?"* (Three.)
Students describe their own journey to school to a partner, using six prepositions and a transport phrase, then write it on Handout 4 (6 minutes).
Two students share with the class (2 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors and good sentences; students correct the errors.
Mime three movements; students say the preposition.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write directions from your school to your home (120 words), using at least eight prepositions of movement.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Keep arrow diagrams on the board; give a direction phrase card. Weaker students give directions to one place only.
Add distances and landmarks: *about 200 metres, on your left, opposite the bank*. Describe an exciting journey using past tenses and movement prepositions.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Information Gap works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Partners reach the correct places using the directions. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Was the *across / through* distinction clear? Did the information gap produce accurate directions?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: A Walking Tour of Kandy
text: **Start at the Clock Tower.** Walk **along** Dalada Veediya **towards** the lake. Go **past** the Queen's Hotel on your right. Then walk **across** the road (carefully!) to Kandy Lake.
Walk **around** the lake until you reach the Temple of the Tooth. Go **into** the temple and spend some time inside. When you come **out of** the temple, walk **through** the Royal Palace Park.
Climb **up** the steps to the viewpoint and enjoy the view of the city. Then come **down** the hill and walk **over** the small bridge to the market. Finish your tour with a cup of tea!
**Map (draw the route):**

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **A. Match the prepositions from the tour to the meanings.**
**B. Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: We walked *through* the park. Were we inside the park or on the edge? ______________
We walked *across* the road. Why not *through* the road? ______________________________
Look: *by bus, by train, by car*. Is there an article (*the*) after *by*? ______________
Do we say *by foot* or *on foot*? ______________
Look: *get on the bus / get into the car*. Can you stand up inside a bus? A car? Which verb goes with which? ______________________________

rows: a. following a line (a road, a river)
b. from one side to the other, on a surface
c. from one end to the other, inside something
d. going by something without stopping

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Complete with the correct preposition.**
**B. Correct the mistakes.**
bullets: We walked ______________ the park to get to the station.
Go ______________ the bridge and turn left.
The cat jumped ______________ the window.
I usually go to school ______________ bus.
Walk ______________ the river until you see the temple.
My grandmother goes to the market ______________ foot.
Get ______________ the bus at the second stop.
The children ran ______________ the hill to the top.
A plane flew ______________ our house.
She got ______________ the taxi and paid the driver.
We walked across the forest. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Information Gap
text: **Tourist (Student A):** You are at the bus station. Ask how to get to: (1) the museum, (2) the beach, (3) the old fort.
**Local (Student B):** Use this map to give directions.
**Useful language:** *Go along ... · Walk across / over the bridge · Go past the ... · Walk through the park · Go up the hill · It's on your left / right · You can't miss it!*
**Now describe your journey to school.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Dependent Prepositions, built round the theme "A Workplace Complaint".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students with good general accuracy whose writing contains errors such as interested about, depends of, succeeded to pass.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Dependent Prepositions (Verbs, Adjectives and Nouns + Preposition)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (complaint email), Handout 2 (reference table and dominoes, cut up), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (discussion questions and email task).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To improve students' use of common verb, adjective and noun + preposition combinations, including preposition + -ing.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can use at least 15 dependent prepositions accurately in speaking and in a formal email.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussion.
**Subsidiary aim.** To write a reply to a formal email.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Preposition + -ing
bullets: After prepositions we use the **-ing** form: *She's good* ***at*** ***managing*** *people. He apologised* ***for*** ***being*** *late. She succeeded* ***in*** ***passing*** *the exam.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Prepositions are usually weak and link to the next word: *depend on it* /dɪˈpend‿ɒn‿ɪt/; *interested in* /ˈɪntrəstɪd‿ɪn/.

rows: Learn as chunks; dominoes game for memory.
Focus on the most common; students make a personal learning list.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: complain · delay · demand · excuse · discount · customer service

ON: depend, rely, insist, keen · OF: afraid, aware, accuse sb, consist, lack · IN: interested, succeed, increase · FOR: apologise, responsible, reason, demand · AT: good, bad · TO: solution, damage · ABOUT: complain, worried · WITH: satisfied, disappointed
preposition + -ing: good at managing · apologise for being late
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Dependent Prepositions, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Ask: *"Tell your partner one thing you are good at, afraid of and interested in."*
Take two examples. Board the three adjectives with their prepositions.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present dependent prepositions in context and clarify the most common combinations and the preposition + *-ing* rule.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the email. What is the customer complaining about? What does she want? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check the two questions as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (5 minutes)**
Say: *"The prepositions in bold go with a word before them. Underline the word: complain about, insisted on ..."* Pairs list all the combinations.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**
Group the combinations by preposition on the board (centre). Elicit more examples for each group.
Point out that these are learned as chunks; there is often no logical rule.
Show the preposition + *-ing* rule: *She apologised for being late. He succeeded in passing.*
Contrast *angry with* (a person) and *angry about* (a thing).
**Pronunciation.** Drill linking: *depend on it, interested in it, good at it.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Pairs, then individual, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise and memorise the combinations.
**Dominoes (4 minutes).** Give each pair the dominoes from Handout 2. Pairs build the chain as fast as possible.
**Gap fill (5 minutes).** Give out Handout 3. Students write the missing prepositions alone, then check with a partner.
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups, then individual, then pairs
text: **Aim:** To use the combinations fluently in discussion and accurately in writing.
Give out Handout 4. **Discussion (8 minutes):** groups discuss the questions (*What do you rely on most? What are you worried about at the moment? What's the best solution to traffic in your town?*).
ICQs: *"Do you answer all the questions?"* (As many as possible.)
**Email (8 minutes):** students write a reply to the complaint email as the company manager, using at least eight combinations.
Partners check each other's emails for prepositions (2 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board errors from the discussion and emails; students correct them.
Each student writes a personal list of five combinations to learn.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Learn 15 combinations and write a sentence about yourself for each.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the reference table during the freer practice. Provide an email frame.
Add less common combinations: *object to, cope with, take advantage of*. Students write discussion questions for other groups.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Email" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 2: Reference Table and Dominoes works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Email" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the discussion, students use correct prepositions in most combinations. The email contains at least eight correct combinations. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which combinations were most problematic? Did the dominoes help memory?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Complaint Email
text: **Subject:** Delay to my kitchen order
Dear Mr Fernando,

I am writing to complain **about** the delay to my kitchen order. When I placed the order in May, your sales manager insisted **on** a delivery date of 1 July. I relied **on** this date and arranged for workers to install the kitchen.

It is now 20 July and the kitchen has still not arrived. Nobody has apologised **for** the delay or explained the reason **for** it. I am aware **of** the high demand **for** your products, but I am very disappointed **with** your customer service.

I am not interested **in** excuses. I would like to know who is responsible **for** my order and what the solution **to** this problem is. I also expect a discount because of the lack **of** communication.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours sincerely, Ms N. Perera
**Questions**
bullets: What is Ms Perera complaining about? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Reference Table and Dominoes
text: **Reference**
**Dominoes (cut up along the lines)**

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **Write the missing preposition.**
bullets: She apologised ______ being late.
It depends ______ the weather.
Are you aware ______ the risks?
There has been an increase ______ prices.
He insisted ______ paying for dinner.
I'm not very good ______ maths.
What's the solution ______ this problem?
She was accused ______ stealing the money.
Who is responsible ______ this mess?
They succeeded ______ climbing the mountain.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Discussion and Email
text: **Discussion questions**
**Email task:** You are Mr Fernando. Write a reply to Ms Perera (120–150 words). Apologise, explain, and offer a solution. Use at least eight word + preposition combinations.
bullets: What do you rely on most in your daily life?
What are you worried about at the moment?
What are you really interested in? How did you become interested in it?
What's the best solution to traffic problems in your town?
Who should be responsible for keeping streets clean?
Have you ever complained about a product or service? What happened?

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1**
**Handout 2, dominoes (correct order)**
START: depend → on / interested → in / good → at / afraid → of / reason → for / solution → to / complain → about / rely → on / aware → of / succeed → in / apologise → for / END
**Handout 3**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: The delay to her kitchen order and the lack of communication. · 2. To know who is responsible, a solution, and a discount.
for · 2. on · 3. of · 4. in · 5. on · 6. at · 7. to · 8. of · 9. for · 10. in

rows: She succeeded to pass the exam.
She succeeded in passing the exam.
He apologised for to be late.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Complex Prepositions, built round the theme "A Report to the Principal".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students whose formal reports rely on because of, about and but. They misuse due to + clause and in spite of + clause.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Complex Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases in Formal Writing
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (informal and formal sentences), Handout 2 (model report for analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (writing task: survey results and report brief).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop accurate use of complex prepositions (with regard to, in accordance with, on behalf of, owing to, in spite of, regardless of, by means of) and formal prepositional phrases (under review, at stake, on the grounds that), and preposition placement in formal relative clauses.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a 200-word formal report using at least eight complex prepositions accurately.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To write a formal report collaboratively.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop awareness of register.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: with regard to, regarding, with respect to, as regards, in terms of
owing to, due to, on account of, as a result of, in view of, in the light of
Owing to the strike, trains were cancelled.
in spite of, despite, regardless of, notwithstanding, as opposed to, in contrast to
In spite of the cost, they bought it.
by means of, on behalf of, in accordance with, with the aid of
I'm writing on behalf of the class.
in addition to, as well as, instead of, apart from
blocks.heading: Complex prepositions (+ noun / -ing, not a clause)
Clauses vs phrases
bullets: Clause after *because / although*: *because it was raining; although it was late*.
Noun / -ing after complex prepositions: *due to the rain; in spite of being late; in spite of the fact that it was late*.

blocks.heading: Formal phrases
text: *under review, under consideration, in jeopardy, at stake, on the grounds that, in the event of, with a view to + -ing*.

blocks.heading: Prepositions in relative clauses
bullets: Informal: *the person I spoke* ***to***. Formal: *the person* ***to whom*** *I spoke*.

rows: Board: phrase + noun; clause needs because or due to the fact that.
Correct form: with regard to / regarding.
Discuss balance; limit to one phrase per sentence.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: REFERENCE: with regard to, regarding · CAUSE: owing to, due to, on account of, in the light of · CONTRAST: in spite of, regardless of · MEANS: on behalf of, in accordance with, by means of · ADDITION: in addition to
complex preposition + noun / -ing: owing to the strike · in spite of being late · in spite of the fact that + clause · because / although + clause · the person to whom I spoke
under review · at stake · on the grounds that · with a view to + -ing · in the event of
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Complex Prepositions, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of formal language.
Give out Handout 1. Pairs match the informal sentences to the formal versions (3 minutes).
Check. Ask: *"What makes the formal versions formal?"* Accept ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present complex prepositions and formal prepositional phrases in a model report and clarify their meaning and grammar.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the report. What are the main problems with the canteen? What does the council recommend?"*
Pairs compare answers.
**Part B: Analysis (7 minutes)**
Say: *"Find the complex prepositions and put them in the table by function."*
ICQs: *"How many functions?"* (Five columns.) *"Alone or in groups?"* (Groups.)
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the functions on the left of the board.
**Phrase vs clause.** Board *Due to it was raining* ✗. Ask: *"What's wrong?"* Elicit: complex prepositions take a noun or *-ing*; clauses need *because / although* or *the fact that*.
Show formal relative clauses: *the man I wrote to → the man to whom I wrote.*
Highlight formal phrases from the report: *under review, at stake, with a view to + -ing.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite using the phrase in brackets. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class.
**Exercise B:** pairs rewrite the informal paragraph formally. One pair reads theirs aloud.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To write a formal report using complex prepositions accurately.

Give out Handout 4. Say: *"You are the student council. Write a formal report (about 200 words) to the principal about the canteen survey and your recommendations. Use at least eight complex prepositions."*
ICQs: *"Who is the report for?"* (The principal.) *"How many complex prepositions?"* (At least eight.)
Groups plan (3 minutes) and write (10 minutes).
Two groups read their reports aloud. The class identifies the most formal-sounding phrases (5 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board strong phrases and two or three errors from the reports. Students correct the errors.
Discuss balance: *"Is it possible to be too formal?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a formal letter of complaint (220 words) using eight complex prepositions.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide a phrase bank grouped by function. Give a report template with headings.
Use *on the grounds that, with a view to + -ing, in the event of*. Compare phrases in a real policy document.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The final report uses at least eight complex prepositions accurately. No *due to / in spite of* + clause errors. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students over- or under-use formal phrases? Was the phrase vs clause distinction clear?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Informal and Formal
text: **Match each informal sentence (1–5) to a formal version (a–e).**

rows: 1. About your email, I can confirm the date.
a. Owing to the strike, all trains were cancelled.
2. Because of the strike, the trains were cancelled.
b. I am writing on behalf of the whole class.
3. I'm writing for the whole class.
c. In spite of the cost, the school approved the plan.
4. It was expensive, but the school said yes.
d. With regard to your email, I can confirm the date.
5. The man I wrote to has replied.
e. The gentleman to whom I wrote has replied.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Model Report
text: **Report on the School Canteen**
**Purpose:** This report has been prepared on behalf of the student council with regard to the school canteen. It is based on a survey of 300 students conducted in accordance with school guidelines.

**Findings:** In spite of recent improvements, only 35% of students are satisfied with the quality of food. Owing to rising costs, 72% feel that prices are too high. In addition to price, healthy eating is a major concern: 81% want more healthy options. Queues are also a problem on account of the short lunch break.

**Recommendations:** In the light of these findings, we recommend that the menu be placed under review. Regardless of the cost, fresh fruit should be available daily. With a view to reducing queues, a pre-order system could be introduced by means of a simple mobile app. The success of the canteen is at stake, and we would be grateful for the principal's support.
**Find and categorise the complex prepositions.**

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite using the phrase in brackets.**

**B. Rewrite this informal paragraph in a formal style.** *About the school trip, lots of parents complained because it was too expensive. But even though it cost a lot, most students enjoyed it. I'm writing for the parents' committee.*
bullets: About your request, we can offer a discount. (with regard to) → ______________________________
Because of the rain, the match was postponed. (owing to) → ______________________________
I'm writing for my parents. (on behalf of) → ______________________________
Although it was expensive, they bought it. (in spite of) → ______________________________
The man who I wrote to has replied. (to whom) → ______________________________
We'll follow the school rules. (in accordance with) → ______________________________
The decision is being reviewed. (under) → ______________________________
It doesn't matter how old you are; you can apply. (regardless of) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **You are the student council. Write a formal report (about 200 words) to the principal about the school canteen.**
**Survey results (300 students)**
**Your report should include:**
bullets: the purpose of the report
the main findings
at least three recommendations

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Can and Can't for Ability, built round the theme "The Class Talent Show".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Beginners who know common action verbs (swim, dance, sing, cook, drive) and the verb be. They add -s or to after can (He cans swim, I can to cook).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Survey" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Can and Can't for Ability
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (talent show entries), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (class survey), action picture cards (swim, dance, sing, cook, drive, play the guitar, ride a bike, speak Tamil).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise can / can't + base verb to talk about abilities.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can ask and answer Can you ...? questions and describe 6 abilities of their own and their classmates.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise the pronunciation of weak can /kən/ and strong can't /kɑːnt/.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a class survey.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **can / can't + base verb** (no *-s*, no *to*): *She can swim.* (not *She cans swim / She can to swim*)
The same form for all persons.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Ability: something a person is able to do. *Fish can swim. Babies can't walk.*
Modifiers: *very well, quite well, a little, not at all*: *I can sing quite well. I can't cook at all.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Positive *can* is weak: /kən/ – *I can SWIM*. The main verb is stressed.
Negative *can't* is strong: /kɑːnt/ – *I CAN'T swim.*
Short answers are strong: *Yes, I CAN* /kæn/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***She can swim.*** Is she swimming now? (Not necessarily.) · Is she able to swim? (Yes.)
***He can't drive.*** Does he know how to drive? (No.)

rows: Board: can = same for all persons; cross out -s.
Highlight: can + base verb, no to.
Question: Can goes first. Word cards to reorder.
Students can't hear can vs can't.
Listening game: teacher says sentences; students hold up ✓ or ✗ cards.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: swim · dance · sing · cook · drive · play the guitar · ride a bike · speak Tamil · draw · run fast
I / You / He / She / We / They can swim. · He can't drive. · Can you cook? Yes, I can. / No, I can't. · can + base verb (no -s, no to)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Can and Can't for Ability, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and introduce abilities.
Show the action picture cards one by one. Students say the verb (*swim, dance, sing ...*). Stick them on the left of the board.
Mime swimming well and singing badly. Ask: *"Am I good at swimming? Am I good at singing?"* Students laugh and answer *yes / no*.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present *can / can't* in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Our school has a talent show. Read the entries. What can each person do? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many people?"* (Five.) *"What do you find?"* (What they can do.)
Students complete the table with ✓ and ✗. Pairs compare.
Check as a class: *"Can Nethmi sing?" "Yes, she can."*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Kavindu can play the guitar.* Ask the CCQs.
**Form.** Board the form table. Ask: *"He cans or he can?"* (He can.) *"Can to play or can play?"* (Can play.) Cross out wrong forms.
**Negative and questions.** Elicit *can't* and the question *Can you ...?* with short answers.
**Pronunciation.** Say *I can swim* (weak) and *I can't swim* (strong). Students listen and hold up ✓ for *can* and ✗ for *can't*. Play six rounds.
Drill: *I can swim. She can't drive. Can you cook? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete with can or can't and the verb. Exercise B: put the words in order. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers; correct pronunciation of *can / can't*.
**Picture drill:** point to a picture card and a student: *"Ravi, swim?"* Student asks a partner: *"Can you swim?"*

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use *can / can't* in a personalised survey and a class talent show plan.
Give out Handout 3. Model with a strong student: *"Can you dance?" "Yes, I can." "How well?" "Quite well!"*
**Survey (8 minutes):** students mingle and ask about the abilities on the sheet. They write names and how well.
ICQs: *"What do you write?"* (Names and how well.)
**Talent show plan (6 minutes):** in groups of four, students use their survey results to plan a class talent show: *"Ruwan can sing very well. Maya can dance. Nobody can play the piano."*
**Writing (4 minutes):** students write 6 sentences about their own abilities at the bottom of Handout 3.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Groups announce their talent show line-up.
Board four sentences heard (two with errors such as *He cans swim*). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write 8 sentences about what your family members can and can't do. Use *very well, quite well* or *not at all* in three sentences.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students picture prompts on the survey sheet. Allow short answers only (*Yes, I can / No, I can't*).
Stronger students add *how well* in every answer. They ask *Could you ... when you were five?* (past ability).

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Survey" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Survey" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use *can / can't* + base verb correctly in 8 of 10 items on Handout 2. Students ask and answer *Can you ...?* correctly during the survey. Students hear the difference between *can* and *can't* in the listening game.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Could students hear and say the difference between *can* and *can't*? Did the survey give everyone enough speaking practice?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Class Talent Show
text: **Read the talent show entries. Write ✓ (can) or ✗ (can't) in the table.**
**Nethmi (14):** I can sing and I can play the piano. I can't dance, so I'm going to sing!
**Kavindu (15):** I can play the guitar very well. I can sing a little, but I can't play the piano.
**Ayesha (13):** I can dance! I can do traditional Kandyan dancing. I can't sing at all.
**Ravi (16):** I can do magic tricks. I can also juggle with three balls! I can't play an instrument.
**Shalini (14):** I can draw very fast. I can draw your face in two minutes! I can sing a little, too.
**Answer the questions.**

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete with can or can't and the verb.**
**B. Put the words in order.**
bullets: My baby brother ______________ (walk) yet. He's only six months old.
She ______________ (speak) three languages: Sinhala, Tamil and English.
I ______________ (ride) a bike. I learned last year.
Elephants ______________ (jump).

can / my / sister / dance / well / very → ______________________________

*very well · quite well · a little · not at all*
**Write 6 sentences about your abilities.**
*Example: I can swim quite well. I can't play the guitar.*

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Must, Have To, Don't Have To and Can't, built round the theme "Rules in Public Places".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know can for ability and permission. They confuse mustn't (prohibition) with don't have to (no obligation) and say I must to go.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Must, Have To, Don't Have To and Can't (Rules and Obligation)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (rules from three places), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (club rules planning sheet), pictures of common signs (no smoking, wear a helmet, free entry, no swimming).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise must / have to (obligation), mustn't / can't (prohibition) and don't have to (no obligation), and had to for the past.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can explain the rules of places they know and write 8 rules for a new club using the four structures correctly.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read signs and rules for gist and detail.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking by designing rules for a club.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: must + base verb · have to / has to + base verb
You must wear a seat belt. I have to wear a uniform. She has to work on Saturdays.
mustn't + base verb · can't + base verb
You mustn't smoke here. You can't use phones in the exam.
don't / doesn't have to + base verb
You don't have to come on Sunday. He doesn't have to pay.
I had to stay late yesterday. (No past form of must.)
Do I have to ...? Does she have to ...?
Do we have to wear a uniform?
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: *must* often shows the speaker's own feeling or written rules (*Visitors must sign in*); *have to* often shows external rules (*I have to wear a uniform at school*). At A2, treat them as very similar.
**Key contrast:** *You mustn't go* (= don't go!) vs *You don't have to go* (= it's not necessary, you can choose).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *have to* /ˈhæftə/; *has to* /ˈhæstə/; *had to* /ˈhættə/.
*mustn't* /ˈmʌsnt/ – the first *t* is silent.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***You mustn't swim here.*** Can I swim here? (No.) Is it allowed? (No.)
***You don't have to come on Sunday.*** Is it necessary to come? (No.) · Can I come if I want? (Yes.)

rows: mustn't and don't have to confused.
Traffic-light chart: red = mustn't; green = don't have to; CCQs.
Board: must + base verb (no to); have to has its own to.
Highlight has to for he / she / it.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: No smoking · Wear a helmet · Free entry · No swimming · Silence · Show your ticket
NECESSARY (✓ do it): must / have to / has to · NOT ALLOWED (✗ don't do it): mustn't / can't · NOT NECESSARY (choose): don't / doesn't have to · PAST: had to

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Must, Have To, Don't Have To and Can't, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of rules.
Show pictures of four signs (or draw them). Ask pairs: *"Where can you see this sign? What does it mean?"* (2 minutes.)
Take answers in simple language; don't correct.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the three sets of rules. Where are they from: a library, a swimming pool or a school? Two minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many sets of rules?"* (Three.) *"What do you decide?"* (Where they are from.)
Pairs check. Then students answer the True / False questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Language clarification (13 minutes)**
Board three sentences from the text: *You must show your library card. You mustn't eat in the library. You don't have to pay to borrow books.*
Draw a three-column chart: *Necessary ✓ / Not allowed ✗ / Not necessary (you choose)*. Students tell you where each sentence goes.
Ask the CCQs. Focus on the key contrast: *mustn't* vs *don't have to*.
**Form.** Elicit: *must + base verb* (no *to*); *have to / has to*; questions with *Do / Does ... have to ...?*; past *had to*.
**Pronunciation.** Drill *I have to go* /ˈhæftə/, *She has to work* /ˈhæstə/, *You mustn't run* /ˈmʌsnt/.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct form.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: choose the correct answer. Exercise B: write about your school. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check and explain using the chart. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the structures to create and discuss rules.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Your group is starting a new club. Choose a club and write 8 rules: necessary things, things not allowed and things that are not necessary."* (10 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many rules?"* (Eight.) *"Do you only write things that are not allowed?"* (No, all three types.)
Groups present their club and rules. Other groups ask questions: *"Do we have to pay? Can we bring friends?"* (8 minutes.)
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
The class votes for the best club.
Board errors heard, especially *mustn't / don't have to* confusion. Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write the rules for your home (8 sentences). Include two things you had to do when you were younger.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide the meaning chart with icons (✓, ✗, ?) on a card. Weaker groups write 5 rules instead of 8.
Stronger students compare rules in two countries: *In Sri Lanka you have to ..., but in the UK you don't have to ...* They use *had to* to talk about past rules at primary school.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. The club rules use all three meanings correctly. Students no longer confuse *mustn't* and *don't have to* in the presentations.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Was the *mustn't / don't have to* contrast clear? Did the club task produce accurate rules?

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use should but say You should to call him and How about go ...? They don't know had better or the difference in strength between advice forms.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Problem cards" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Should, Ought To, Had Better and Suggestions (Advice)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (advice column), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (problem cards), Handout 4 (agony aunt reply sheet).

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise forms for giving advice and making suggestions: should, ought to, had better, could, Why don't you ...?, How about + -ing?, If I were you, I'd ...
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and speak advice using at least five different structures with correct form.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read problem letters and replies.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in giving and responding to advice.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise polite intonation.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Why don't you + base verb? · How about / What about + -ing?
Why don't you join a club? How about asking your teacher?
should / shouldn't + base verb · ought to + base verb
You should see a doctor. You ought to apologise.
If I were you, I'd + base verb
If I were you, I'd talk to her.
had better ('d better) / had better not + base verb
You'd better hurry or you'll miss the bus.
blocks.heading: Form and strength
Accuracy points
bullets: No *to* after *should, could, had better*: *You should call* (not *should to call*).
*ought* takes *to*: *You ought to call.*
*How about* + **-ing**: *How about going ...?*
*had better* refers to now / the future (not the past), and often implies a bad result if you don't.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *You'd better* /jʊd ˈbetə/ – the *'d* is often hard to hear.
Polite suggestion intonation: rising-falling, friendly: *Why don't you join a CLUB?*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***You'd better hurry.*** Is it a gentle suggestion or strong advice? (Strong.) · What will happen if I don't hurry? (Something bad: I'll be late.) · *How about asking your teacher?* · Is it an order? (No, a suggestion.)

rows: Board the patterns with a crossed-out to.
Advice reply must use five different forms.
had better thought to be past.
CCQ: Is it about the past or now?
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: stressed · can't sleep · lonely · argue · homesick · nervous · waste time
GENTLE: You could ... · Why don't you ...? · How about + -ing? · ADVICE: You should / ought to ... · If I were you, I'd ... · STRONG: You'd better (not) ...
You'd better /jʊd ˈbetə/ · Why don't you ...? ↗↘

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Should, Ought To, Had Better and Suggestions, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic and personalise it.
Say: *"Tell your partner about a small problem you have, for example: I can't sleep. I'm always late."*
The partner gives any advice. Students swap (2 minutes). Take two examples.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present advice and suggestion forms in context and clarify their strength, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the three problem letters and the replies. Do you agree with the advice? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many letters?"* (Three.)
Pairs discuss. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every phrase the writer uses to give advice."* Pairs compare. Elicit and board the phrases.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**
Pairs rank the phrases from gentle to strong. Build the strength scale on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Form.** Highlight: no *to* after *should, could, 'd better*; *ought to*; *How about* + *-ing*; *If I were you, I'd* + base verb.
**Pronunciation.** Drill with polite intonation: *Why don't you join a club? How about asking your teacher? You'd better hurry!*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the advice. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To give advice fluently in speaking and writing.
**Problem cards (8 minutes).** Give each pair a set of problem cards (Handout 3). Student A reads a problem as if it's theirs; Student B gives advice using two different structures. Swap.
ICQs: *"How many different structures?"* (Two each time.)

**Agony aunt (10 minutes).** Groups write a short problem letter, pass it to the next group, and that group writes a reply on Handout 4 using at least five different structures. Groups read the best replies aloud.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Discuss which advice was most helpful.
Board errors (*should to, How about go*); students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a reply to an advice letter (130 words) using at least five different structures from today.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide the strength scale on a card. Weaker students use three structures in the reply instead of five.
Stronger students add reasons with *otherwise* and *so that*: *You'd better leave now, otherwise you'll miss the bus.* They use *shouldn't have* for past mistakes (preview).

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Problem cards" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Problem Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Problem cards" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. The agony aunt reply uses at least five different structures accurately.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand the difference in strength? Were *How about + -ing* and *had better* used accurately?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Advice Column
text: **Problem 1:** *I'm 15 and I can't sleep before exams. I lie in bed and worry. What can I do? – Dinuka* **Reply:** You should try to relax before bed. Why don't you read a book instead of looking at your phone? You'd better not drink tea or coffee in the evening. If I were you, I'd make a study plan, so you don't feel so worried.

**Problem 2:** *My best friend is angry with me because I forgot her birthday. – Malsha* **Reply:** You ought to apologise as soon as possible. How about making her a card or a small present? You could also invite her for an ice cream. Don't wait too long!

**Problem 3:** *I've just moved to a new school and I don't have any friends. – Arun* **Reply:** That's hard, but it will get better. You should join a club, like football or drama. Why don't you sit with different people at lunch? You could also ask your teacher to introduce you.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What shouldn't Dinuka drink in the evening? ______________________________
What should Malsha do first? ______________________________
Where could Arun meet new people? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete with should, ought, 'd better, could, Why don't or How about.**
**B. Correct the mistakes.**
bullets: You look tired. You ______________ go to bed early.
You ______________ to apologise to her.
______________ asking your teacher for help?
You ______________ leave now or you'll miss the bus.
You ______________ try studying in the library.
______________ you call your grandmother? She'd be happy.
You ______________ not eat that. It smells bad!
If I were you, I ______________ buy the cheaper phone.
______________ joining a gym?
You ______________ to drink more water.
How about go to the cinema? ______________________________
If I was you, I will apologise. ______________________________

I want to get fit but I hate running.
My neighbour plays loud music at night.
I want to learn a new language.
I'm nervous about speaking in class.
My little brother always uses my things.
I don't have enough money for a birthday present.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Modals of Deduction, built round the theme "The Missing Student".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who use must and might for present deduction but say He mustn't be at home (meaning can't) and She must have went.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Modals of Deduction (must, might, can't – present and past)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (the mystery scenario), Handout 2 (certainty scale and practice), Handout 3 (clue cards), close-up photos of everyday objects (or descriptions).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise modals of deduction for present and past situations: must, might / may / could, can't / couldn't + base verb / be + -ing / have + past participle.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can solve a mystery by making and justifying deductions about present and past events.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in speculating and reasoning.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise connected speech in must have /ˈmʌstəv/.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: It might / may / could be him.
She might / may / could have forgotten.
He can't / couldn't have seen us.
blocks.heading: Form and certainty
Accuracy points
bullets: Negative deduction is *can't*, not *mustn't*: *He can't be at home* (not *He mustn't be at home*).
Past: modal + *have* + **past participle**: *must have gone* (not *must have went*).
*couldn't have* and *can't have* are both used for the past.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *have*: *must have* /ˈmʌstəv/, *might have* /ˈmaɪtəv/, *can't have* /ˈkɑːntəv/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The lights are off. They must be out.*** Am I sure? (Almost sure.) Why? (The lights are off: evidence.)
***He can't have seen us. He didn't say hello.*** Am I sure he didn't see us? (Almost sure.) · Is it about the past or now? (The past.)

rows: Board the certainty scale: must ↔ can't.
Drill past participles; error correction in practice.
Hearing of instead of have (must of).
Require because + evidence in the freer task.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: evidence · clue · theory · suspect · disappear · alibi
100% YES: must + be / be -ing / have + pp · 50%: might / may / could + ... · 100% NO: can't / couldn't + ... · Past = modal + have + past participle
must have /ˈmʌstəv/ · might have /ˈmaɪtəv/ · can't have /ˈkɑːntəv/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Modals of Deduction, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students in speculating.
Show (or describe) three close-up photos of everyday objects (the bristles of a toothbrush, the inside of a mango, a coconut shell).
Pairs guess: *"It might be ... It can't be ..."* (2 minutes). Reveal the answers.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present modals of deduction in context and clarify certainty, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about Tharushi. Where do you think she is? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"Who is missing?"* (Tharushi.)
Pairs share their theories in any language they have.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Read the friends' comments at the bottom. How sure is each speaker? Write 100%, 50% or 0% next to each."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
Build the certainty scale on the board using the friends' comments.
Ask the CCQs. Point out *can't* (not *mustn't*) for negative certainty.
**Form.** Show present (*must be*), continuous (*might be studying*) and past (*must have gone*). Elicit the past participle in each past example.
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak *have*: *She must have gone to the library. He can't have seen her.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete with must, might or can't in the correct form. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check and explain their certainty. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use deductions fluently and logically in a group mystery.
Say: *"New information about Tharushi arrives. Each time you get a clue card, discuss and update your theory. Use must, might and can't, and always give a reason."*
ICQs: *"What must you always give?"* (A reason / the evidence.)
Give each group clue card 1 (Handout 3). After 2 minutes, give clue 2, and so on, until all five clues are out (10 minutes).
Groups write their final theory in three sentences and present it (6 minutes).
Reveal the solution (on the last clue card, which you keep). Groups get a point for each correct deduction (2 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences heard during the mystery: correct and incorrect. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"How do you say you're sure something didn't happen?"* (*can't have* + pp.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Find a strange or mysterious photo online or in a newspaper. Write 150 words explaining what might have happened, using at least six modals of deduction.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Keep the certainty scale on the board and give a sentence-frame card: *She must / might / can't have ... because ...* Give weaker groups the clues with key words highlighted.
Stronger students add *could have* and *couldn't have*, and *may well have*. They challenge other groups' theories: *But if she had gone to the library, her friend would have seen her.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Certainty Scale and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Clue Cards (cut up; give one at a time) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use *can't* (not *mustn't*) for negative deduction. Past deductions use *have + past participle* correctly. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students give evidence for their deductions? Were past forms accurate?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Missing Student
text: It's 4.30 pm. Tharushi, 16, didn't come home after school. Her mother is worried. Here's what we know:
**What her friends say:**

**Kasun:** "She must be with Nimesha. They're always together." **Dilan:** "She might be at the pool. She took her swimming bag." **Ishara:** "She can't be at home. Her mother would know!" **Ravi:** "Her phone must have run out of battery. She always forgets to charge it." **Amaya:** "She can't have forgotten about her mother. She's very responsible."
**How sure is each speaker? Write 100%, 50% or 0%.**
bullets: Tharushi left school at 1.30 pm.
Her phone is switched off.
She took her swimming bag this morning, but it's Tuesday and she usually swims on Thursdays.
Her best friend, Nimesha, is also not answering her phone.
There is a big school swimming competition next Saturday.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Certainty Scale and Practice
text: **A. Complete with must, might or can't and the correct form of the verb.**
**B. Correct the mistakes.**
bullets: The lights are off. They ______________________ (be) out.
He didn't say hello. He ______________________ (see) us.
I'm not sure where she is. She ______________________ (be) in the library.
The ground is wet. It ______________________ (rain) last night.
She ______________________ (forget) the meeting. I reminded her this morning.
Don't call him now. He ______________________ (sleep). He works nights.
That ______________________ (be) Ravi's bag. His is red, and this one is blue.
They ______________________ (take) the bus. It's possible, but they usually walk.
You ______________________ (be) hungry. You haven't eaten all day!
He ______________________ (lose) his keys. He's looking everywhere.
He mustn't be at home. The car isn't there. ______________________________
It can't be rain. The sky is blue. ______________________________

rows: might / may / could + be / be -ing / have + pp
can't / couldn't + be / be -ing / have + pp

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Clue Cards (cut up; give one at a time)
text: **Our final theory:**

rows: Clue 1 (4.45 pm): Nimesha's mother says Nimesha is at home, sick in bed, and hasn't seen Tharushi today.
Clue 2 (5.00 pm): The swimming pool receptionist says a girl in a school uniform came in at 2.30 pm with a swimming coach.
Clue 3 (5.15 pm): Tharushi's swimming coach posted on social media at 3 pm: "Extra training today for the team. Big competition on Saturday!"
Clue 4 (5.30 pm): A charger is found on Tharushi's desk at home.
Clue 5 (5.45 pm): Tharushi's younger brother says she told him at breakfast, "I'll be late today," but he forgot to tell their mother.

Solution (teacher only): Tharushi went to extra swimming training for Saturday's competition. She told her brother, but he forgot to pass on the message. Her phone ran out of battery because she left her charger at home.
