hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Past Modals and Nuances of Modality, built round the theme "The Project Review Meeting".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who use core modals accurately but miss attitude and nuance: they don't distinguish needn't have / didn't need to, use should have for all criticism, and don't know might have for annoyance or wouldn't for refusal.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Past Modals and Nuances of Modality (needn't have, might have, would, wouldn't, might as well)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (workplace transcripts), Handout 2 (meaning chart and practice), Handout 3 (role cards for the project review meeting).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise modal structures that express unnecessary past actions, criticism and annoyance, willingness and refusal, and resignation.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can review a failed project diplomatically, expressing criticism, regret, refusal and resignation with appropriate modals and tone.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop awareness of tone and intonation.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a diplomatic workplace role-play.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: You did it, but it wasn't necessary.
I needn't have cooked; they'd already eaten.
It wasn't necessary (so usually you didn't do it).
I didn't need to cook; we went out.
should have / ought to have + pp
Criticism or regret: it was the right thing but it didn't happen.
Annoyance: you didn't do something polite or helpful.
Refusal (people or things) in the past.
The door wouldn't open. She wouldn't listen.
He WOULD say that, wouldn't he?
We might as well go home.
Expectation or rule that is often not followed.
We were supposed to finish in May.
blocks.heading: Form and meaning
Pronunciation
bullets: Annoyance: strong stress and fall-rise on *might*: *You MIGHT have told me!*
Weak *have*: *needn't have* /ˈniːdntəv/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I needn't have brought a coat.*** Did I bring a coat? (Yes.) · Was it necessary? (No.)
***I didn't need to bring a coat.*** Was it necessary? (No.) Did I bring one? (Probably not; we don't know.)
***You might have told me!*** Did you tell me? (No.) · How does the speaker feel? (Annoyed.)

rows: needn't have / didn't need to confused.
Timelines and the CCQs above; sorting task.
might have heard only as possibility.
Contrast intonation: neutral possibility vs annoyed stress.
Teach softeners: To be fair ..., I appreciate that ..., With respect ...
Leave dare for the stretch task.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: unnecessary · critical · annoyed · refusing · resigned · expected

needn't have + pp (did it, not necessary) · didn't need to + inf (not necessary) · should have + pp (criticism) · MIGHT have + pp (annoyance) · wouldn't + inf (refusal) · might as well + inf (resignation) · was supposed to + inf (expectation)
To be fair ... · I appreciate that ... · With respect ... · I take your point, but ...
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Modals and Nuances of Modality, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of attitude in modals.
Write on the board: *You should have told me.* / *You might have told me!* Say both with appropriate intonation.
Pairs discuss the difference in meaning and feeling (2 minutes). Take ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the structures in context and clarify meaning, attitude, form and intonation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1 (three short transcripts from a company after a failed product launch). Say: *"Read. What went wrong with the project? How does each speaker feel?"*
ICQs: *"How many transcripts?"* (Three.) *"What two things do you find?"* (What went wrong; how speakers feel.)
Pairs discuss. Check the questions as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (5 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every modal structure. Next to each, write the speaker's attitude: annoyed, regretful, resigned, refusing, or 'not necessary'."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the structures and attitudes on the board.
Contrast *needn't have* and *didn't need to* with timelines. Ask the CCQs.
Contrast *should have* (criticism / regret) with stressed *might have* (annoyance).
Show *wouldn't* for past refusal by people and things (*The system wouldn't load*), and *might as well* for resignation.
**Intonation.** Drill: *You MIGHT have told me! The door WOULDn't open. We might as well give up.* Students say each sentence with the right feeling.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite using the word given. Exercise B: match the sentence to the attitude. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the structures fluently and diplomatically in a role-play.
Give out Handout 3. Teach the softeners on the right of the board.

Say: *"You are in a project review meeting about the failed product launch. Read your role card. Discuss what went wrong and agree on three lessons for next time. Use at least five of today's structures and two softeners."* (12 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many lessons do you agree on?"* (Three.) *"Should the meeting be rude?"* (No, diplomatic.)
One group performs the last two minutes of its meeting; others report their three lessons (6 minutes).
Monitor and note language and tone.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board examples of effective and less effective language from the meetings. Discuss how tone changes meaning.
Correct any form errors.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write an email (200 words) to a colleague reviewing a problem diplomatically. Use at least six of today's structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give an attitude chart with one example per structure. Give weaker students the Project Manager role, which has the most prompts on the card.
Stronger students use *dare* (*How dare you ...? I daren't tell her*) and *be supposed to have* + pp. They analyse modals in a political interview transcript.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Meaning Chart and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Role Cards: Project Review Meeting works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the meeting, students use at least five structures appropriately and with suitable tone. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students can explain the difference between *needn't have* and *didn't need to*.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students hear and produce the attitude through intonation? Did the role-play stay diplomatic?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: After the Launch
text: **A company launched a new mobile app, but it failed. Read three short conversations.**

**Conversation 1: Manager and team leader** **Manager:** We were supposed to launch in May, but we launched in August. And the app wouldn't load on older phones! **Team leader:** I know. We should have tested it on more devices. To be fair, the designers wouldn't change the design when we asked.

**Conversation 2: Two developers** **Dev 1:** I worked all weekend on the payment system, and then they cancelled it. I needn't have bothered. **Dev 2:** You might have told me you were working! I'd have helped. Anyway, I didn't need to work on Saturday because my part was finished.

**Conversation 3: The director** **Director:** Our competitor's app is already number one. Costs may well rise next year. Honestly, we might as well start again with a new idea. And of course Marketing say it wasn't their fault. Well, they would say that, wouldn't they?
**Questions**
bullets: When was the app supposed to launch? ______________________________
What problem did the app have? ______________________________
Did Dev 1 work at the weekend? Was it necessary? ______________________________
What does the director suggest? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Meaning Chart and Practice
text: **A. Rewrite using the word given.**
**B. Match each sentence to an attitude: annoyed / regretful / resigned / refusing / not necessary.**
bullets: It wasn't necessary for me to bring food, but I did. (needn't) → ______________________________
It was annoying that you didn't call me. (might) → ______________________________
The car refused to start. (wouldn't) → ______________________________
There's nothing else to do, so let's go home. (might as well) → ______________________________
It's very likely that prices will go up. (may well) → ______________________________
The plan was to finish by May, but we didn't. (supposed) → ______________________________
It was a mistake not to check the figures. (should) → ______________________________
It wasn't necessary to take a taxi, so I walked. (need) → ______________________________
She wouldn't answer my questions. ______________
You could have asked before borrowing my laptop! ______________
We might as well cancel the trip. ______________
I shouldn't have said that. ______________
You needn't have waited for me. ______________

rows: did it, but it wasn't necessary

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Role Cards: Project Review Meeting
text: **Project Manager**
You led the project. You admit some mistakes (*we should have tested more*). You feel the designers *wouldn't* listen. You want to agree three clear lessons for next time.
**Lead Designer**
You think the managers changed the plan too often. The design team *needn't have* redesigned the app three times. You feel nobody told you about the older phones (*you might have told us!*).
**Finance Director**
The project cost twice the budget. You are frustrated: *We were supposed to spend half this amount.* You think the company *might as well* stop the app, but you will listen to good ideas.
**Useful softeners:** *To be fair ... · I appreciate that ... · With respect ... · I take your point, but ... · Let's focus on what we can learn.*
**Our three lessons for next time:**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Zero Conditional, built round the theme "Facts About Our World".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** High beginners who use the present simple for facts and routines (Water boils at 100 degrees. I drink tea in the morning.) but cannot yet join two ideas with if. They say If I tired, I sleep.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Find your partner" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Zero Conditional (If + present, present)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
A glass of water, an ice cube and a plant (or pictures), Handout 1 (science facts), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (half-sentence cards), Handout 4 (my routines).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the zero conditional (If + present simple, present simple) for facts and routines.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say and write 6 true sentences with If ..., ... about science facts and their own routines.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review the present simple, including he/she/it -s.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a matching game and a partner interview.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Form: notes
bullets: The two clauses can change places: *Ice melts* ***if*** *you heat it.* We use a comma only when *If* comes first.
*If* can be replaced by *When* with the same meaning: *When I'm hungry, I eat fruit.*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Facts that are always true: *If you mix red and yellow, you get orange.*
Routines and habits: *If I'm late, my mother drives me to school.*
Both clauses are about **general time** (always), not one future moment.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Intonation rises a little at the end of the *if* clause and falls at the end of the sentence: *If you heat ice ↗, it melts ↘.*
*-s* endings: *melts* /s/, *boils* /z/, *dies* /z/, *freezes* /ɪz/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***If you heat ice, it melts.*** Is this true only today? (No, always.) · Do we heat the ice first? (Yes.) Then what happens? (It melts.)
***If I'm tired, I go to bed early.*** Is this about one night or every time I'm tired? (Every time.)

rows: Board If I am tired and drill.
Missing third-person -s (If water get cold, it freeze).
Highlight -s in a different colour; quick drill.
Using will (If you heat ice, it will melt).
Accept as understandable but teach the zero conditional for "always true" facts.
Show both orders on the board.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: heat · melt · boil · freeze · mix · water (v.) · grow · die · tired · hungry · thirsty
If + present, present · If you heat ice, it melts. · Ice melts if you heat it. (no comma) · If I'm tired, I go to bed. · If = When (always true)
If you heat ice ↗, it melts ↘. · melts /s/ · boils /z/ · freezes /ɪz/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Zero Conditional, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students with simple real-life "experiments".
Show a glass of water and an ice cube (or a picture). Ask: *"What happens if I put the ice in the sun?"* Students answer freely (*It melts / water*).
Show the plant. Ask: *"What happens if I don't give it water?"* (*It dies.*)
Say: *"Today we talk about things that always happen."*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the science facts. Match the beginnings and the endings."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you write sentences or match?"* (Match.) *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Alone first.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class. Students read the full sentences aloud.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *If you heat ice, it melts.* Ask the CCQs. Draw two boxes with an arrow: *heat ice → melts*. Say: *"Always. Every time."*
**Form.** Underline both verbs. Ask: *"Past, present or future?"* (Present, both.) Write *If + present, present* in the centre of the board.
**Order.** Board *Ice melts if you heat it.* Ask: *"Same meaning?"* (Yes.) *"Where is the comma?"* (No comma.)
**-s and be.** Board *If water* ***gets*** *cold, it* ***freezes.*** and *If I* ***am*** *tired, I go to bed.* Highlight -s and *am*.
**Routines.** Give a personal example: *"If I'm hungry at school, I eat a banana."* Ask two students: *"What do you do if you're hungry?"*
**Pronunciation.** Model the intonation and drill chorally and individually: *If you heat ice ↗, it melts ↘. If I'm tired ↗, I go to bed ↘.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: write the verbs. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"Present or past?"* (Present.) *"Remember -s for he, she, it?"* (Yes.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read their answers.
**Quick chain drill:** say the start of a sentence (*If you don't sleep, ...*); students finish it.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Mingle, then pairs, then individual
text: **Aim:** To use the zero conditional in speaking and writing about facts and routines.

**Find your partner (6 minutes).** Give each student one card from Handout 3 (a beginning or an ending). Students stand up, read their card and find the person with the matching half. Pairs read their full sentence to the class.
ICQs: *"Do you show your card or read it?"* (Read it.)

**My routines (8 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Students complete the sentences about themselves, then ask a partner: *"What do you do if you're bored?"* They write the partner's answers in the "My partner" column.
**Writing (4 minutes).** Students write 3 sentences about their partner: *If Kasun is bored, he plays cricket.*
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two or three students read their sentences about their partner.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences with *if*: 3 science facts and 3 sentences about your family's routines (*If my father is tired, he watches TV.*).
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the verbs for Handout 4 in a box (*eat, sleep, drink, call, play, read*). Allow them to write only the main clause in Handout 4.
Stronger students use *When* and *unless* (preview): *Plants die unless you water them.* They write a two-step fact: *If you heat water, it boils, and if it boils, it makes steam.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Find your partner" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Find Your Partner (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Find your partner" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students use the present simple in both clauses in their written sentences. Students match and read sentences correctly in the card game.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students remember the -s in the main clause? Was the difference between facts and routines clear?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Science Facts
text: **Match the beginnings (1–6) and the endings (a–f).**
**Read about Kasun. Answer the questions.**

Hi, I'm Kasun. I'm 12. If I'm hungry after school, I eat a banana. If it rains, I don't play cricket. I play games on my phone. If I'm tired, I go to bed at 8 o'clock. My little sister is funny. If she is happy, she sings!
bullets: What does Kasun eat if he's hungry? ______________________________
What does he do if it rains? ______________________________
What does his sister do if she's happy? ______________________________

rows: 2. If you don't water a plant,
3. If you mix blue and yellow,
6. If you put oil in water,

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know the zero conditional and will for predictions. They put will in both clauses (If it will rain, we will stay home) and confuse the first conditional with the zero conditional.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Chain story" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: First Conditional (If + present, will)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (class WhatsApp chat), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (chain story cards), Handout 4 (trip planning sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the first conditional (If + present simple, will / won't + base verb) for real possibilities in the future.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can discuss a plan and its possible problems, e.g. If it rains, we'll go to the museum. If we leave late, we might miss the train.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise might for less certain results.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a planning discussion.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise contracted 'll and won't.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: we won't get stuck in traffic.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: Question: *What will we do if it rains?*
*might* for a less certain result: *If we're late, we* ***might*** *miss the train.*
The clauses can change places: *We'll go to the museum if it rains.*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: A **real** possibility in the future: it is possible and quite likely.
Compare: zero conditional = always true (*If it rains, the roads get wet*); first conditional = one future situation (*If it rains on Saturday, we'll stay inside*).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contracted *'ll*: *we'll* /wiːl/, *you'll* /juːl/, *it'll* /ˈɪtl/. *won't* /wəʊnt/.
Intonation: rise at the end of the *if* clause, fall at the end: *If it rains ↗, we'll go to the museum ↘.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***If it rains on Saturday, we'll go to the museum.*** Do we know if it will rain? (No.) · Is it possible? (Yes.) · Is it about the past, now or the future? (The future, Saturday.) · What's the plan if it rains? (The museum.)

rows: will in the if clause (If it will rain).
Board the rule with will crossed out in the if clause.
Missing will in the main clause (If it rains, we go).
Contrast with the zero conditional: one future day vs always.
Drill contracted forms; minimal pairs We go / We'll go.
Drill I won't /wəʊnt/ vs I want /wɒnt/.

rows: trip · leave · arrive · traffic · miss the train · sunburnt · picnic · museum · cancel · packed lunch
If + present, will / won't + verb · If it rains, we'll go to the museum. · not: If it will rain ✗ · less sure: might · Zero: always · First: one future situation

blocks.heading: Procedure: First Conditional, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the context and generate interest.
Say: *"Our class is going on a trip to Nuwara Eliya on Saturday!"* Ask: *"What can go wrong?"* Pairs list three problems (2 minutes).
Take ideas and board key words: *rain, late, traffic, sick, forget*.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the first conditional in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the class chat. What will the class do if it rains? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you read the whole chat?"* (Yes.)
Pairs check. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every sentence with if. Circle the verbs."* Pairs compare.
Ask: *"Which tense comes after if? What comes in the other part?"*
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *If it rains on Saturday, we'll go to the museum.* Ask the CCQs. Draw a timeline: NOW → Saturday with a question mark over a rain cloud.
**Form.** Elicit *If + present simple, will / won't + base verb*. Cross out *will* in *If it will rain*.
**might.** Board *If we leave late, we might miss the train.* Ask: *"Are we sure we'll miss it?"* (No, maybe.)
**Zero vs first.** Board *If it rains, the roads get wet* (always) and *If it rains on Saturday, we'll stay inside* (one future situation).
**Pronunciation.** Drill contractions and intonation: *If it rains ↗, we'll go to the museum ↘. If you're late ↗, you'll miss the bus ↘.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the sentences. Exercise B: match and write. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class; ask students to say the sentences with contractions.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the first conditional fluently in a game and a planning task.

**Chain story (6 minutes).** Give each group a starter card from Handout 3. Student 1 reads it (*If I don't go to school tomorrow, ...*) and finishes it (*I'll stay in bed*). Student 2 uses the result to start a new sentence (*If I stay in bed, I'll watch TV*). Continue around the group as long as possible.
ICQs: *"Where does your sentence start?"* (With the end of the last sentence.)

**Plan the trip (10 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Groups choose a destination and plan the day. For each problem on the sheet, they write a solution with *If ..., we'll ...* Then they present their plan to the class (1 minute each).
The class votes for the best-prepared group.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Quick round: each student finishes *If I have time this weekend, ...*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a message (80 words) to a friend about your plans for the weekend. Include at least four first conditional sentences, one with *might*.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a list of base verbs for the chain story. Provide the frame *If ..., we'll ...* on the planning sheet.
Stronger students use *unless* and *as soon as* (preview): *We'll leave as soon as the bus arrives.* They add a second result: *If it rains, we'll go to the museum and then we'll have tea.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Chain story" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Chain Story Starters (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Chain story" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. In the planning task, students use the present simple after *if* and *will* in the main clause. Students use contracted *'ll* in speech.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: How many students still used *will* after *if*? Did the chain story keep going? Was it fun?

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use the first conditional well. They talk about imaginary situations with will (If I win the lottery, I will buy a house) and use would in both clauses (If I would have money, I would travel).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Second Conditional (If + past, would)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (magazine quiz), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (dilemma cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students work out and use the second conditional (If + past simple, would / could + base verb) for imaginary or unlikely present and future situations, and to contrast it with the first conditional.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can discuss imaginary situations and dilemmas, e.g. If I found a wallet in the street, I'd take it to the police.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise If I were you for advice.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussing moral dilemmas.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise contracted 'd.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I'd buy a house for my parents.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: Question: *What would you do if you found a wallet?*
*were* is used for all persons in formal English and in *If I were you*: *If she were here, she'd help.* (*was* is common in informal speech.)
*'d* = *would*: *I'd* /aɪd/, *she'd* /ʃiːd/.

rows: Real, possible: If I pass the exam, I'll celebrate.
Imaginary or unlikely: If I won a million rupees, I'd travel the world.
Speaker thinks it's unlikely or impossible.
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Meaning and use: notes
bullets: Imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. The past form does **not** mean past time.
*If I were you, I'd ...* = advice.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contracted *'d* is short and easy to miss: *I'd go* /aɪd ɡəʊ/. Drill so students hear it.
*wouldn't* /ˈwʊdnt/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house.*** Have I won the lottery? (No.) · Do I think I will win? (No, probably not.) · Is *won* about the past? (No, it's about an imaginary present or future.)
***If I were you, I'd talk to the teacher.*** Am I you? (No, it's impossible.) · What am I doing? (Giving advice.)

blocks.heading: Procedure: Second Conditional, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce imaginary situations and engage students.
Write on the board: *a million rupees · invisible for a day · any job in the world*.
Say: *"Imagine! Tell your partner what you'd do."* Students talk for 2 minutes. Don't correct.
Take two or three answers and board one sentence exactly as a student says it.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the second conditional in context and help students work out its form and meaning.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Do the magazine quiz. Choose a, b or c for each question. Then read your result."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you choose one answer or two?"* (One.)
Pairs compare answers and results. Ask: *"Are you an angel, a realist or a rebel?"*
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the quiz. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Alone or with a partner?"* (With a partner.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Have you found a wallet? Is it real or imaginary?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit the answers. Build the form in the centre of the board: *If + past simple, would / could + base verb*.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis. Draw a timeline with NOW and FUTURE; write *won* under it to show it isn't past time.

**First vs second.** Board *If I pass the exam, I'll celebrate* and *If I won a million rupees, I'd travel the world.* Ask: *"Which one is likely?"* Draw a line from 0% to 100% and place each sentence.
**If I were you.** Board it and ask: *"Is this advice or a story?"* (Advice.)
**Pronunciation.** Drill *I'd* and question intonation: *What would you do if you found a wallet? I'd take it to the police.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form and the contrast accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the sentences. Exercise B: first or second conditional? Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare and justify: *"It's unlikely, so second."*
Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the second conditional fluently in a discussion of dilemmas.
Give each group a set of dilemma cards (Handout 4). Model with one card: *"If my best friend copied my homework, I'd ... because ..."*
Students take turns to read a card. Each person says what they would do and why. The group decides on the best answer (12 minutes).
ICQs: *"Does everyone answer each card?"* (Yes.) *"Do you give a reason?"* (Yes.)
Each group reports the dilemma they disagreed about most (4 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Return to the sentence you boarded in Stage 1. Ask: *"Is it correct now?"* Students correct it if necessary.
Board four sentences from Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a paragraph (120 words): *If I could change one thing about my town, I would ...* Use at least five second conditional sentences.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students sentence starters on the dilemma cards: *If this happened to me, I'd ... · I wouldn't ...* Let them answer with the main clause only at first.
Stronger students ask follow-up questions: *What would you do if your friend got angry?* They use *might* and *could* in the main clause to show different degrees of certainty.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Dilemma Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the discussion, students use the past simple after *if* and *would* in the main clause. 9 out of 11 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. Students correctly choose first or second conditional in 4 of 5 items in Exercise B.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand that the past form doesn't mean past time? Were the dilemmas engaging? Did students give reasons?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Magazine Quiz
text: **ANGEL, REALIST OR REBEL? Do our quiz and find out!**
**1. If you found a wallet with 20,000 rupees in the street, what would you do?** a. I'd take it to the police. b. I'd look for the owner's ID and call them. c. I'd keep the money. Finders keepers!
**2. If your friend gave you a horrible birthday present, what would you say?** a. I'd say, "Thank you! I love it!" b. I'd say thank you, but I wouldn't use it. c. I'd tell them the truth.
**3. If you could be invisible for a day, what would you do?** a. I'd help people secretly. b. I'd go to a concert without a ticket. c. I'd listen to my teachers' conversations!
**4. If a shop assistant gave you too much change, what would you do?** a. I'd give it back immediately. b. I'd give it back if it was a lot of money. c. I wouldn't say anything.
**Results:** Mostly a: You're an angel! · Mostly b: You're a realist. · Mostly c: You're a rebel!

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Third Conditional and Mixed Conditionals, built round the theme "Turning Points".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who are confident with the first and second conditionals. They try to talk about past regrets with the second conditional (If I studied harder, I passed) or with would in both clauses (If I would have known, I would have come).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Pairs" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Third Conditional and Mixed Conditionals
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (magazine article), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (turning point story planner).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of the third conditional for imaginary past situations and mixed conditionals for past causes with present results (and present states with past results).

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell the story of a turning point in their life and imagine how things would be different, e.g. If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met my best friend, and I wouldn't be so happy now.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise the weak forms in would have /ˈwʊdəv/.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in telling a personal story about a turning point.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: would / could / might have + past participle
If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met her.
If I hadn't met her, I wouldn't be so happy now.
If I were braver, I would have applied for the job.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: Contractions in speech: *If I'd known* (= had), *I'd have come* (= would). *I wouldn't have* /aɪ ˈwʊdnt əv/.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: **Third:** an imaginary past. The real past is the opposite: *If I had studied, I would have passed* = I didn't study; I didn't pass.
Used for regrets, criticism, relief and speculation about the past.
**Mixed (past → present):** an unreal past cause with an unreal present result.
**Mixed (present → past):** a present (permanent) state with an unreal past result.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *would have* is weak: /ˈwʊdəv/ or /ˈwʊdə/. *wouldn't have* /ˈwʊdntəv/. *could have* /ˈkʊdəv/.
The contracted *'d* can mean *had* (in the if clause) or *would* (in the main clause): *If I'd known, I'd have come.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***If Amaya hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have met Kavindu.*** Did Amaya miss the bus? (Yes.) · Did she meet Kavindu? (Yes.) · Is this about the past or the present? (The past.)
***If she hadn't met him, she wouldn't be a chef today.*** Is she a chef now? (Yes.) · When did the meeting happen? (In the past.) When is the result? (Now.)

rows: would have in the if clause (If I would have known).
Board the pattern; cross out would in the if clause.
Colour-code: 'd + past participle in the if clause = had; 'd have = would.
Students can't hear or say would have.
Back-chain drill: met her → have met her → wouldn't have met her.
Use timelines with two points: PAST cause → NOW result.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: turning point · by chance · miss the bus · turn down an offer · apply for · regret · relieved · career · scholarship

THIRD: PAST → PAST · If + had + pp, would have + pp · If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met her. (I missed it. I met her.) · MIXED: PAST → NOW · If + had + pp, would + verb · If I hadn't met her, I wouldn't be a chef now. · NOW (state) → PAST: If I were braver, I'd have applied.
would have /ˈwʊdəv/ · wouldn't have /ˈwʊdntəv/ · If I'd (had) known, I'd (would) have come.

blocks.heading: Procedure: Third Conditional and Mixed Conditionals, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the theme of chance and turning points.
Tell a short true or invented story: *"Ten years ago, I nearly became a doctor. But I failed my biology exam, so I studied English instead, and I became a teacher."*
Ask: *"Was failing the exam bad luck or good luck?"* Pairs discuss small moments that changed something in their lives (2 minutes).
Take one or two examples.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the third and mixed conditionals in context and clarify their meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the article. What was the turning point in Amaya's life? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every sentence with if. For each one, decide: is it about the past, the present or both?"* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Third conditional.** Board *If Amaya hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have met Kavindu.* Ask the CCQs. Show the real past next to it: *She missed the bus. She met him.*
Elicit the form: *If + past perfect, would have + past participle.* Cross out *would* in *If she would have ...*
**Mixed conditional.** Board *If she hadn't met him, she wouldn't be a chef today.* Ask the CCQs. Draw a timeline with two points: PAST cause → NOW result.
Show the other mixed type briefly: *If she weren't so brave, she wouldn't have opened a restaurant.*
Point out *'d* = *had* or *would*.
**Pronunciation.** Back-chain drill: *met him → have met him → wouldn't have met him → If she hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have met him.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Do Exercise A: write a conditional sentence for each situation. Then Exercise B: choose the correct form. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check as a class, asking: *"Past result or present result?"*
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then groups
text: **Aim:** To use the forms fluently in a personal story.
Give out Handout 4. Students choose a turning point in their life (or invent one) and make notes in the planner (4 minutes).
ICQs: *"Does it have to be true?"* (No, it can be invented.) *"Do you write full sentences?"* (No, notes.)
**Pairs (6 minutes).** Students tell their story. The listener asks at least two *What would have happened if ...?* questions.

**Groups (6 minutes).** New groups of three. Students retell their partner's story using the third and mixed conditionals: *If Ruwan hadn't broken his leg, he wouldn't have started painting, and he wouldn't be an artist now.*
The class chooses the most surprising turning point (2 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences heard in Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"When do we use the third conditional? When do we use mixed?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write a 180-word blog post about a turning point in your life or in the life of a famous person. Use at least three third conditionals and two mixed conditionals.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the timelines on a card. Provide sentence frames: *If I hadn't ..., I wouldn't have ... · If I hadn't ..., I wouldn't be ... now.*
Stronger students use *could have, might have* and *If it hadn't been for ...*. They use the present → past mixed type: *If I weren't so shy, I'd have spoken to her.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Pairs" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Pairs" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the story task, students use the past perfect after *if* and *would have* + past participle accurately. Students produce at least one mixed conditional with a present result. 5 out of 6 or better on Handout 2, Exercise B.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students hear and produce the weak form of *would have*? Was the mixed conditional clear after the timelines?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Magazine Article
text: **ONE MISSED BUS, ONE NEW LIFE**

Eight years ago, Amaya Wickramasinghe was a shy accounting student in Kandy. One rainy morning, she missed the bus to university by thirty seconds. While she was waiting for the next one, she started talking to a young man at the bus stop. His name was Kavindu, and he was a chef.

"If I hadn't missed that bus, I would never have met Kavindu," Amaya says. "He invited me to his restaurant, and I fell in love with cooking." She left accounting and trained as a chef. If she had stayed at university, she would have become an accountant like her father.

Today, Amaya runs her own restaurant in Galle. "If I hadn't met Kavindu, I wouldn't be a chef today, and I probably wouldn't be so happy," she says. "And if I weren't so stubborn, I wouldn't have opened my own restaurant. Everyone told me it was a bad idea!"
And Kavindu? He's now her husband.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Why did Amaya meet Kavindu? ______________________________
What would Amaya have become if she had stayed at university? ______________________________
According to Amaya, why did she open her own restaurant? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice
text: **Language reference**
**A. Write a conditional sentence for each situation.**
**B. Choose the correct form.**
bullets: I didn't set my alarm. I was late for the exam. → If I ______________________________
She didn't take the job in Dubai. She lives in Colombo now. → If she ______________________________
They didn't bring a map. They got lost. → If they ______________________________
He isn't very patient. He shouted at the waiter. → If he ______________________________
If you **told / had told** me, I would have helped you.
If we hadn't missed the train, we **would be / would have been** at home now.
If she **would have studied / had studied**, she would have passed.
If I hadn't eaten so much, I **wouldn't feel / wouldn't have felt** sick now.
If he **were / had been** taller, he would have joined the basketball team.
I **would have come / would come** to the party if I had known about it.

rows: If + had + pp, would have + pp
If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met him.
If I hadn't met him, I wouldn't be a chef now.
If + past simple, would have + pp
If I weren't so stubborn, I wouldn't have opened a restaurant.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Further Practice
text: **Complete the sentences with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.**
bullets: If I ______________________ (save) more money last year, I ______________________ (be) able to buy a car now.
She ______________________ (not / meet) her husband if she ______________________ (not / go) to that party.
If you ______________________ (listen) to my advice, you ______________________ (not / be) in this situation now.
If I ______________________ (be) better at maths, I ______________________ (study) engineering.
We ______________________ (win) the match if our best player ______________________ (not / get) injured.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: My Turning Point
text: **Make notes about a turning point in your life (true or invented).**
**Questions for your partner**
**Useful language**
bullets: What would have happened if ...?
Would you be ... now if ...?
Do you think you would have ... anyway?
Are you glad it happened?
*If I hadn't ..., I would never have ...*
*If I had ..., I wouldn't be ... now.*
*Looking back, I'm really glad that ...*
*It's funny how one small thing can change everything.*

What would have happened if it hadn't happened?

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Inverted and Alternative Conditionals, built round the theme "Writing a Formal Proposal".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who use all the main conditional types accurately but rely on if in every sentence. Their formal writing sounds repetitive, and they make errors with inversion (Had I knew, Should you will need) and with unless (unless you don't pay).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Inverted and Alternative Conditionals (Had I known, Should you, Were it not for, provided that)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (informal and formal versions), Handout 2 (model proposal for analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (proposal brief and planning sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of inverted conditionals (Had ..., Should ..., Were ... to), conditional linkers (provided / providing that, as long as, on condition that, unless, supposing, otherwise) and but for / were it not for / if it hadn't been for in formal writing and speech.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and present a 150-word formal proposal using at least six inverted or alternative conditional structures accurately.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop awareness of register.
**Subsidiary aim.** To write a formal proposal collaboratively and present it persuasively.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: If you (should) require assistance, ... → Should you require assistance, please contact us.
Were + subject + to + infinitive / Were + subject + complement
If the council approved ... → Were the council to approve the plan, ... · Were I in your position, ...
If we had known ... → Had we known about the problem, we would have acted sooner.
No contraction: Had we not ..., Were it not ..., Should you not ...
blocks.heading: Inverted conditionals (formal; *if* is omitted)

rows: provided / providing (that), as long as, on condition that
only if (a condition must be met)
The project will succeed provided that funding is secured.
Unless action is taken, the problem will worsen. (not unless action isn't taken)
Supposing the plan failed, what would we do?
We must act now; otherwise, costs will rise.
but for + noun / were it not for + noun / if it hadn't been for + noun
But for the volunteers, the event would have failed. Were it not for the grant, the library would close.
Bring an umbrella in case it rains.
blocks.heading: Alternative conditional expressions
Pronunciation
bullets: Inverted auxiliaries are stressed at the start of a sentence: *HAD we known ..., SHOULD you require ...*
A slight pause after the conditional clause in formal speech.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Had we known about the flooding, we would have postponed the event.*** Did we know about the flooding? (No.) · Did we postpone the event? (No.) · Is this formal or informal? (Formal.)

***The library will stay open provided that the council renews the grant.*** Will the library stay open if the council doesn't renew the grant? (No.) · Does *provided that* mean *only if* or *even if*? (Only if.)

rows: Wrong verb form after inversion (Had I knew, Should you will need).
Board the patterns: Had + subject + past participle; Should + subject + base verb.
Show Had we not known; explain that inverted negatives are not contracted.
Double negative with unless (unless you don't pay).
Board unless = if ... not; transformation drill.
Contrast: I'll take an umbrella in case it rains (precaution) vs I'll take an umbrella if it rains (only when it rains).
Discuss balance; one or two inversions per paragraph is enough.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: FORMAL: proposals, reports, official letters, speeches · INFORMAL: conversation, messages (use if)

Should + S + verb · Were + S + to + verb · Were + S + complement · Had + S + pp · Had S not + pp (no contraction) · provided (that) / as long as / on condition that + present · unless + positive verb · But for / Were it not for + noun
Should = less likely future · Were ... to = imaginary future · Had = imaginary past · provided that = only if · unless = if not · but for = without · in case = precaution
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Inverted and Alternative Conditionals, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of formal conditional structures.
Give out Handout 1. Pairs match the five informal sentences with their formal versions (3 minutes).
Check. Ask: *"Which word is missing from the formal versions?"* (*if*.) *"What has happened to the word order?"* Accept ideas; don't explain yet.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present inverted and alternative conditionals in a model text and clarify their form, meaning and register.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the proposal. What does the student council want? What conditions does it offer?"*
Pairs compare answers.
**Part B: Analysis (7 minutes)**
Say: *"In groups, find every conditional structure in the proposal. Rewrite each one with if. Then answer the analysis questions."*
ICQs: *"Do you rewrite with if or without if?"* (With *if*.) *"How many questions?"* (Five.)
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.

**Inversion.** Show the three patterns side by side with their *if* equivalents: *Should you require → If you require; Were the council to approve → If the council approved; Had we known → If we had known.* Ask the CCQs.
**Negatives.** Board *Hadn't we known* ✗ → *Had we not known* ✓.
**Linkers.** Elicit the meaning of *provided that, unless, otherwise, but for*. Board *unless you don't pay* ✗ and ask what's wrong.
**in case.** Contrast *in case* (precaution) with *if* (condition).
**Pronunciation.** Drill with stress on the inverted auxiliary: *HAD we known, we would have acted sooner. SHOULD you require further information, please contact us.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite each sentence using the word in brackets. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class, focusing on word order and verb forms.
**Exercise B:** pairs correct the five errors. Check quickly.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the structures accurately in a formal written proposal and a persuasive presentation.
Give out Handout 4. Say: *"You are a group of residents. Write a formal proposal (about 150 words) to the city council for one of the projects. Use at least six structures from today."*
ICQs: *"Who is the proposal for?"* (The city council.) *"How many structures?"* (At least six.)
Groups choose a project, plan (3 minutes) and write (8 minutes).
Each group presents its proposal in one minute. The "council" (the rest of the class) asks one question each, using a conditional: *"Supposing the funding were cut, what would you do?"* (5 minutes.)
The class votes for the most convincing proposal (2 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board the most effective sentences and two or three with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Would you use Had I known in a text message to a friend?"* (No, *If I'd known*.) Discuss register.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a formal letter (220 words) to a company or official body requesting a change. Use at least three inverted conditionals and three alternative conditional expressions.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a pattern card with each structure and its *if* equivalent. Provide a proposal template with headings: *Purpose · Proposal · Conditions · Benefits · Risks.*

Stronger students use mixed inverted forms: *Had the council invested earlier, the park would be open today.* They use *If it weren't for ... / If it hadn't been for ...* and *Were it not for ...* in the same text and explain the difference in time reference.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The proposal uses at least six inverted or alternative conditional structures accurately. No contracted negatives in inversion and no double negatives with *unless*. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand the time reference of *Should, Were* and *Had*? Was the register appropriate, or did texts become too heavy?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Informal and Formal
text: **Match each informal sentence (1–5) with a formal version (a–e).**
**What happens to the word** ***if*** **in the formal versions? What happens to the word order?**

rows: 1. If you need any help, just ask.
a. Had we known about the delay, we would have informed you.
2. If we'd known about the delay, we'd have told you.
b. Were it not for your support, the project would not exist.
3. Without your help, there'd be no project.
c. Should you require any assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
4. You can borrow the hall, but only if you clean it afterwards.
d. Were the council to reject the plan, we would appeal.
5. If the council said no, we'd appeal.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Model Proposal
text: **PROPOSAL: A STUDY CENTRE FOR THE PUBLIC LIBRARY**
**To:** The Library Committee **From:** The Student Council

**Background:** Each year, hundreds of students use the library to prepare for their exams. Were it not for the library, many students would have nowhere quiet to study. However, the building closes at 5 pm. Had the opening hours been extended last year, more students would have passed their A-level examinations.
**Proposal:** We propose converting the unused ground-floor room into a study centre that is open until 9 pm on weekdays.

**Conditions:** The student council will provide volunteers to supervise the centre, provided that the library provides basic furniture and Wi-Fi. Students will be allowed to use the centre only as long as they register in advance.

**Risks:** Unless additional cleaning is arranged, the room may become untidy. We therefore suggest a small monthly fee of Rs. 200; otherwise, the costs may be too high for the library. Supposing the number of users were lower than expected, the centre could open three evenings a week instead.
**Conclusion:** Were the committee to approve this proposal, the centre could open in January. Should you require any further information, please contact the student council secretary.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Present Simple Passive, built round the theme "Made in Sri Lanka".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** High beginners who know the present simple, am / is / are and common regular and irregular verbs. They want to say where things come from but say Tea is grow in Sri Lanka or Tea grows by farmers.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Quiz" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Present Simple Passive (is made, are grown)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Real objects or pictures (a packet of tea, a coconut, a cricket bat, a mobile phone, a banana), Handout 1 (product labels), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (Where is it from? quiz).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the present simple passive (is / are + past participle) to talk about products and where they are made, grown or sold.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say and write 6 sentences about products, e.g. Tea is grown in Nuwara Eliya. Cars are made in Japan.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To learn eight common past participles (made, grown, sold, eaten, spoken, used, produced, caught).
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a quiz.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Tea is grown in Sri Lanka.
Rice isn't grown in the desert.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **is / are + past participle**.
Past participles: *make → made, grow → grown, sell → sold, eat → eaten, speak → spoken, use → used, produce → produced, catch → caught*.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use the passive when the **thing** is more important than the person who does the action, or when we don't know or care who does it: *Tea is grown in the hills.* (Who grows it? Farmers. Not important.)

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *is* and *are*: *Tea's grown* /tiːz ɡrəʊn/; *are made* /ə meɪd/.
*-ed* participles: *used* /juːzd/, *produced* /prəˈdjuːst/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Tea is grown in Sri Lanka.*** Does tea grow itself? (No, people grow it.) · Who grows it? (Farmers.) Is that important here? (No.) · What is important? (The tea and the place.)

rows: Board is + grown; drill base verb → participle.
Missing is / are (Tea grown in Sri Lanka).
Two-part formula on the board with colours.
Using the active wrongly (Tea grows by farmers).
Show who does the action vs what happens to the thing.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: make → made · grow → grown · sell → sold · eat → eaten · speak → spoken · use → used · produce → produced · catch → caught
Farmers grow tea. (active) → Tea is grown in Sri Lanka. (passive) · is / are + past participle · Phones are made in China. · Where is coffee grown?
Tea's grown /tiːz ɡrəʊn/ · are made /ə meɪd/ · used /juːzd/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Simple Passive, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest and introduce the topic.
Show the objects one by one. Ask: *"What's this? Where is it from?"* Students guess freely.
Hold up the tea. Say: *"Sri Lankan tea is famous!"* Ask: *"Where in Sri Lanka?"* (*Nuwara Eliya, Kandy ...*)

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the labels. Match each label to a product."* (3 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you match or write?"* (Match.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Farmers grow tea.* and *Tea is grown in Sri Lanka.* Ask the CCQs. Point: *"In the second sentence, the tea is more important."*
**Form.** Underline *is grown*. Elicit *is / are + past participle*. Board *Phones are made in China* to show *are* with plurals.
**Participles.** Elicit participles from the labels and complete the list on the left of the board. Drill *grow – grown, make – made*.
**Negatives and questions.** Board *Rice isn't grown in the desert* and *Where is coffee grown?*
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak forms: *Tea's grown in Sri Lanka. Phones are made in China. Where's coffee grown?*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: is or are + past participle. Exercise B: make questions. Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you write the base verb or the past participle?"* (Past participle.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers.
**Quick drill:** say a product and a verb (*rice / grow*); students say the sentence (*Rice is grown in Sri Lanka.*).

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the present simple passive in speaking and writing.

**Quiz (10 minutes).** Give out Handout 3. In teams, students choose the correct country for each product and write a full sentence: *Kiwis are grown in New Zealand.* Then teams ask each other the questions aloud: *"Where are kiwis grown?"*
ICQs: *"Do you write the country or a full sentence?"* (A full sentence.)
Check answers. One point for the correct fact, one for a correct sentence.
**Writing (6 minutes).** Students write 4 sentences about products from their town or country at the bottom of Handout 3: *Coconuts are grown in Kurunegala. Batik is made in Kandy.*
Two students read their sentences (2 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences from the quiz and writing (two with errors). Students correct them.
Quick round: each student says one thing that is made or grown in their country.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Look at 6 things in your kitchen. Write where each one is made or grown: *My rice is grown in Polonnaruwa. My fridge is made in Korea.*
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the participle list on a card. Allow them to complete sentence frames: *___ is grown in ___.*
Stronger students add *by* + agent when it is important: *Batik is made by hand.* They ask and answer *What language is spoken in ...?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Controlled practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Quiz" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Quiz" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students use *is / are* + past participle in their own sentences. Students choose *is* or *are* correctly for singular and plural.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which participles were hardest? Did students understand why we use the passive?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Product Labels
text: **Read the labels. Match each label (1–5) to a product (a–e).**
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What is coconut oil used for? ______________________________

rows: 1. This is grown in the hills of Nuwara Eliya. It is picked by hand and drunk all over the world.
2. These are grown near the coast. Their oil is used for cooking.
3. This is made of wood in Panadura. It is used by top players.
4. These are caught in the sea every morning and sold in the market.
5. This is made in China and sold in shops everywhere.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete with is or are and the past participle.**
**B. Write questions. Then answer them.**
bullets: Rice ______ ______________ (grow) in Polonnaruwa.
These shoes ______ ______________ (make) in Italy.
English ______ ______________ (speak) in many countries.
Bananas ______ ______________ (sell) at the market.
Cheese ______ ______________ (make) from milk.
What language / speak / in Brazil? → ______________________________ (Portuguese)
Where / these phones / make? → ______________________________ (China)

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Where Is It From? Quiz
text: **Choose the correct country. Then write a full sentence.**
**Write 4 sentences about things from your town or country.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Past Simple Passive, built round the theme "Famous Places and Great Inventions".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who know the present simple passive and the past simple. They want to talk about history but say Sigiriya built in the 5th century or The telephone was invent by Bell.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Information gap" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Past Simple Passive (was built, were invented)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Pictures of Sigiriya, a telephone, a light bulb and the Taj Mahal (or descriptions), Handout 1 (fact files), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (quiz cards A and B), Handout 4 (write your own quiz).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the past simple passive (was / were + past participle), with and without by + agent, to talk about famous places and inventions.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and ask quiz questions such as When was the telephone invented? Who was Sigiriya built by? and answer them in full sentences.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review irregular past participles.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read short fact files for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a history quiz.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Sigiriya was built in the 5th century.
The first cars were made in Germany.
It wasn't built by the British.
Where were the first cars made?
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **was / were + past participle**.
**by** + agent when we want to say who did it: *The telephone was invented* ***by*** *Alexander Graham Bell.*
Question about the agent: *Who was it invented by?*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use the passive when the place or object is the topic, and the person is less important, unknown or obvious: *The temple was built in 1592.*
We add *by* + agent only when the person is important or interesting.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *was* /wəz/ and *were* /wə/: *It was built* /ɪt wəz bɪlt/.
*-ed* endings: *invented* /ɪd/, *discovered* /d/, *painted* /ɪd/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Sigiriya was built in the 5th century.*** Is this about the past or now? (The past.) · Did Sigiriya build itself? (No, people built it.) · What is the topic of the sentence: Sigiriya or the builders? (Sigiriya.)
***The telephone was invented by Bell.*** Who invented it? (Bell.) · Why do we say *by Bell*? (Because the person is important.)

rows: Base verb or past simple instead of participle (was invent, was wrote).
Singular / plural contrast in Exercise A.
Overusing by + agent (by people, by someone).
Rule: only when the agent is important.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: build → built · invent → invented · discover → discovered · paint → painted · write → written · make → made · find → found · design → designed
Bell invented the telephone. (active) → The telephone was invented by Bell. (passive) · was / were + past participle · by + agent (only if important) · When was it built? · Who was it invented by?
