blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Simple Passive, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and activate knowledge.
Show the four pictures. Ask: *"What do you know about these? How old are they?"* Pairs discuss (2 minutes).
Take a few ideas. Don't correct yet.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the past simple passive in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the fact files. Find one date and one name in each. Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many fact files?"* (Four.)
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline was or were + another verb."* Pairs compare. Elicit examples and board them.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *King Kashyapa built Sigiriya* and *Sigiriya was built in the 5th century.* Ask the CCQs.
**Form.** Elicit *was / were + past participle*. Highlight *were* with plurals.
**by + agent.** Board *The telephone was invented by Bell.* Ask: *"Why do we say by Bell here?"* Contrast with *The temple was built in 1592* (agent not needed).
**Questions.** Board *When was the telephone invented? Who was it invented by?*
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak forms: *It was built in 1592. When was it invented? They were made in Germany.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: was or were + past participle. Exercise B: rewrite the sentences in the passive. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the past simple passive in a history quiz.

**Information gap (8 minutes).** Give Student A and Student B the quiz cards (Handout 3). Each card has answers the partner needs. Students ask and answer: *"When was the first photograph taken?" "It was taken in 1826."*
ICQs: *"Can you show your card?"* (No.) *"Do you answer in a full sentence?"* (Yes.)
**Write a quiz (10 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Teams write five quiz questions about places and inventions in their own country or the world, then ask another team.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Ask: *"When do we use by?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a fact file (80 words) about a famous place or invention. Use the past simple passive at least four times.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the participle list during the quiz. Provide question frames: *When was ___ built / invented? Who was ___ painted by?*

Stronger students add extra facts with the present simple passive: *It is visited by thousands of tourists every year.* They write negative sentences that correct false facts: *The light bulb wasn't invented by Newton.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Information gap" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Quiz Cards (Information Gap) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Information gap" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students form past passive questions correctly in the quiz. Students use *by* + agent only when the agent is important.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use the past participle, not the past simple form? Did the quiz motivate accurate questions?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Fact Files
text: **Sigiriya** The rock fortress of Sigiriya was built in the 5th century by King Kashyapa. Beautiful paintings were made on the rock walls. Today, it is visited by thousands of tourists every year.
**The Telephone** The telephone was invented in 1876 by Alexander Graham Bell. The first words on the phone were spoken to his assistant: "Come here, I want to see you."
**The Light Bulb** The first electric lights were made in the early 1800s, but the first useful light bulb was designed by Thomas Edison in 1879.
**The Taj Mahal** The Taj Mahal was built in India between 1632 and 1653. It was made of white marble, and it was designed as a tomb for the emperor's wife.

was built · 2. were made · 3. was written · 4. was discovered · 5. were taken
The *Mona Lisa* was painted by Leonardo da Vinci. · 2. My bike was stolen yesterday. · 3. The first plane was built by the Wright brothers.
A: When was the first photograph taken? · Who was the first computer program written by? · When was Galle Fort built?
B: Who was the radio invented by? · When was Pluto discovered? · Where was the first World Cup played?

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Passive in Different Tenses and with Modals, built round the theme "Our Town Is Changing".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use the present and past simple passive accurately but avoid the passive in other tenses. They say The road is repairing or The bridge has built and avoid modal passives.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Spot the changes" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Passive in Different Tenses and with Modals
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (local news report), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (before and after: two town descriptions).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students work out and use the passive in the present continuous, present perfect and future (will, going to), and with modals (can, must, should), to describe changes and rules.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe changes in their town and suggest improvements, e.g. A new park has been opened. The old market is being repaired. More trees should be planted.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read a local news report for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in describing changes and making suggestions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: They clean the streets every day.
The streets are cleaned every day.
They opened the park in May.
The park was opened in May.
They have built a new bridge.
A new bridge has been built.
They will finish the work soon.
The work will be finished soon.
They are going to close the road.
The road is going to be closed.
blocks.heading: Form: be + past participle (the tense is shown by *be*)
Meaning and use
bullets: The passive focuses on the thing or the change, not the person: *A new bridge has been built.*
It is common in news, notices and rules: *Dogs must be kept on a lead.*
Present continuous passive = a change in progress now; present perfect passive = a recent result.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak forms: *has been* /həz bɪn/; *is being* /ɪz ˈbiːɪŋ/; *will be* /wɪl bi/ or *'ll be*.
Stress falls on the participle: *It's being rePAIRED. It's been OPENED.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The road is being repaired.*** Is the work finished? (No, it's happening now.) · Do we know who is repairing it? (No, and it isn't important.)
***A new bridge has been built.*** Is the bridge finished? (Yes.) · Is it new or old news? (New, recent.)

rows: Missing being or been (The road is repaired now; The bridge has built).
Tense table on the board; highlight the form of be in colour.
Active form with passive meaning (The road is repairing).
Board modal + be + pp, no to.
Teach one rule: choose the tense, then change be.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: repair · demolish · build · widen · plant · ban · replace · open · close · renovate
is cleaned · is being repaired · was opened · has been built · will be finished · is going to be closed · must / should / can be + pp · RULE: choose the tense → change be → add pp
has been /həz bɪn/ · is being /ɪz ˈbiːɪŋ/ · It's been OPENED.

blocks.heading: Procedure: Passive in Different Tenses and with Modals, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Ask: *"How has your town changed in the last five years? What's new? What's being built now?"*
Pairs discuss for 2 minutes. Take two or three ideas without correcting.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the passive in different tenses and with modals in context and help students work out the form.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the news report. Which changes are finished? Which are happening now? Which are in the future? Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"How many kinds of change are you looking for?"* (Three: finished, now, future.)
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the report. Complete the table and answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Pairs.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Which word shows the tense?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit answers and build the tense table on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Highlight the rule: *choose the tense → change be → add the past participle.*
Show modal passives: *Dogs must be kept on a lead. More trees should be planted.* No *to* after the modal.
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *The road's being repaired. A new bridge has been built. The work'll be finished in May.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the sentences with the passive. Exercise B: rewrite the signs as passive rules. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the passive in different tenses fluently in describing change and making suggestions.

**Spot the changes (7 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Student A reads the description of Kotagama ten years ago; Student B reads the description of Kotagama today. They describe their town to each other and list as many changes as they can: *"The old cinema has been demolished. A supermarket has been built."*
ICQs: *"Can you show your description?"* (No.) *"Which tense for changes from then to now?"* (Present perfect passive.)

**Our town plan (8 minutes).** Groups discuss their own town and write five sentences: two changes that have been made, one that is being made now and two suggestions (*More bus stops should be built.*).
Groups share their best suggestion (3 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which word changes to show the tense?"* (*be*.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a short news report (120 words) about changes at your school or in your town. Use at least five different passive forms.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the tense table on a card. In the spot-the-changes task, they can use only the present perfect passive.
Stronger students add time expressions and *by* + agent where useful: *The park was opened last month by the mayor.* They use *need to be* + pp and *could be* + pp in suggestions.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Spot the changes" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Spot the changes" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. In the spot-the-changes task, students use the present perfect passive accurately. Students produce at least one modal passive in the group suggestions.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which tense caused the most problems? Did the "change *be*" rule help students?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Local News Report
text: **KOTAGAMA: A TOWN ON THE MOVE**

Kotagama has changed a lot in the last two years. A new bridge has been built over the river, and the main road has been widened. The old cinema was demolished last year, and a modern library has been opened in its place.
At the moment, the bus station is being renovated, and new trees are being planted in the park. Residents say the town looks much greener.

More changes are planned. A sports centre will be built next year, and the old market is going to be replaced by a covered shopping area. The mayor says that cars will be banned from the town centre on weekends.
However, not everyone is happy. "The town is changing too fast," says Mrs Silva, 72. "More benches should be put in the park for older people, and the bus service must be improved."
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What has been built over the river? ______________________________
What is being done at the bus station now? ______________________________
What will happen to the old market? ______________________________
What does Mrs Silva think should be done? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these sentences from the report. Complete the table.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: In every passive sentence, which verb always comes last? ______________________________
Which word changes to show the tense? ______________________________
In sentence 2, is the work finished? ______________________________
In sentence 6, is there *to* after *must*? ______________________________

rows: 1. A new bridge has been built.
2. The bus station is being renovated.
4. A sports centre will be built.
5. The market is going to be replaced.
6. The bus service must be improved.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Complete with the correct passive form of the verb in brackets.**
**B. Rewrite the signs as passive rules.**
bullets: Look! The school gate ______________________ (paint) at the moment.
Three new classrooms ______________________ (build) since January.
The results ______________________ (announce) next Friday.
My phone ______________________ (steal) last week.
The streets ______________________ (clean) every morning.
The old trees ______________________ (cut down) next month. (going to)
Our house ______________________ (not / repair) yet.
YOU MUST WEAR A HELMET. → Helmets ______________________________
YOU CAN'T USE PHONES IN THE EXAM. → Phones ______________________________
YOU SHOULD KEEP DOGS ON A LEAD. → Dogs ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Kotagama: Then and Now
text: **Student A: Kotagama ten years ago**

There was an old cinema on Main Street. The road was very narrow, and there was no bridge over the river; people crossed by boat. The market was in an old building with no roof. There were no trees in the park, and the bus station was small and dirty. There was no library.
**Student B: Kotagama today**

There is a modern library on Main Street. The road is wide, and there is a new bridge over the river. The market has a new roof. There are many trees in the park, and the bus station is clean and modern. There is a big supermarket next to the school.
**List the changes. Use the present perfect passive.**
**Our town plan:** 2 changes that have been made · 1 change that is being made now · 2 suggestions (should / must / could be + pp)

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Causative Have and Get, built round the theme "Services, Favours and Bad Luck".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who use the passive in all tenses. When they talk about services they say I cut my hair yesterday (meaning a hairdresser did it) or I had cut my hair, and they don't know the get passive (get stolen, get fired).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Survey" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Causative Have and Get (have something done) and the Get Passive
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (Kaveesha's busy Saturday: a blog post), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (survey and story cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of the causative (have / get + object + past participle) for services, have something done for bad experiences, and the get passive in informal English.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can talk about services they use and bad things that have happened, e.g. I'm having my phone screen repaired. My cousin had his bag stolen on the train. He got fined for parking.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in describing errands and misfortunes.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise sentence stress in causative sentences.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I had my hair cut yesterday.
I need to get my car serviced.
I'm having my kitchen painted. I've just had my eyes tested. I'll get it fixed tomorrow.
Where did you have your photo taken? I didn't have it delivered.
She had her bag stolen. (Nobody wanted this!)
He got fired. Our flight got cancelled. My phone got broken.
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: Causative: **someone else** does the action for us, usually a service we pay for. *I cut my hair* = I did it myself. *I had my hair cut* = a hairdresser did it.
*have something done* can also describe something bad that happened to us (not arranged): *We had our car broken into.*
*get* passive: informal; often for unexpected or negative events: *get hurt, get lost, get stolen, get caught, get fined, get promoted.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Stress the object and the participle, not *had*: *I had my HAIR CUT. She had her BAG STOLen.*
Weak *had*: /həd/ or /əd/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I had my hair cut yesterday.*** Did I cut my hair myself? (No.) · Who cut it? (A hairdresser.) · Did I pay? (Probably, yes.)
***Malik had his phone stolen.*** Did Malik want this to happen? (No.) · Did he arrange it? (No, it's a bad experience.)

rows: Wrong word order (I had cut my hair).
Board: have + OBJECT + pp; show that I had cut my hair is past perfect (I did it).
Using the active for services (I repaired my phone = a shop did it).
Base verb instead of participle (I had my car wash).
Note: get is informal; use have or the be passive in formal writing.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: hair cut · eyes tested · car serviced · phone screen repaired · photo taken · suit made · house painted · bag stolen · car broken into · flight cancelled

I cut my hair. (myself) · I had my hair cut. (a hairdresser did it) · have / get + OBJECT + pp · not: I had cut my hair ✗ · She had her bag stolen. (bad experience) · get + pp (informal): got fined / lost / hurt / promoted
I had my HAIR CUT. · had /həd/ · She had her BAG STOLen.
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Causative Have and Get, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of services.
Write on the board: *hairdresser · optician · mechanic · photographer · tailor · phone repair shop*.
Ask: *"When did you last visit one of these? Why?"* Pairs discuss (2 minutes).
Take two answers and board one exactly as the student says it (e.g. *I cut my hair last week*).

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the causative and the get passive in context and clarify their form and meaning.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Kaveesha's blog. How many things did she have done? What went wrong? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every example of have or get + another verb. Who did each action: Kaveesha or someone else?"* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
Board *I cut my hair* and *I had my hair cut.* Ask the CCQs. Elicit the form: *have + object + past participle.*
Show that *have* changes tense: *I'm having my phone repaired. I've had my eyes tested. I'll get it fixed.*
Show questions and negatives: *Where did you have it done? I didn't have it delivered.*
**Bad experiences.** Board *She had her bag stolen.* Ask the CCQs.
**get passive.** Elicit examples from the blog: *got broken, got soaked, got cancelled.* Note that they are informal.
Return to the student's sentence from Stage 1. Ask: *"Did you really cut it yourself?"* Correct it together.
**Pronunciation.** Drill with stress on the object and participle: *I had my HAIR CUT. She had her BAG STOLen.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Exercise A: write sentences with have something done. Exercise B: choose the correct form. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use the forms fluently in personalised speaking and storytelling.

**Survey (8 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Students mingle and ask the survey questions: *"Have you ever had your photo taken by a professional photographer?" "When did you last have your eyes tested?"* They ask one follow-up question each time.
ICQs: *"How many follow-up questions?"* (One for each question.)

**Bad luck stories (8 minutes).** In groups, students take a story card and tell a short (true or invented) story of bad luck, using at least one *have something done* and one *get* passive: *"Last year, I had my wallet stolen on the bus, and then I got fined because I didn't have my ticket!"* The group chooses the unluckiest story.
The group tells the unluckiest story to the class (2 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"What's the difference between I painted my house and I had my house painted?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write an email to a friend (150 words) about a busy week of errands that went wrong. Use *have / get something done* at least four times and the *get* passive twice.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the services vocabulary with pictures. Provide frames: *I had my ___ ___ed. I need to get my ___ ___ed.*
Stronger students use the causative with a person: *I had the mechanic check the brakes. I got my brother to fix it.* They use *need* + *-ing* / *need to be* + pp: *My car needs servicing.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Survey" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Survey and Story Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Survey" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 5 out of 6 or better on Handout 2, Exercise B. In the survey, students form causative questions with correct word order. Each story includes at least one causative and one *get* passive used accurately.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students stop confusing *I had my hair cut* and *I had cut my hair*? Was the *get* passive used naturally in the stories?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Kaveesha's Busy Saturday
text: **My Saturday of Errands (and Disasters!)**

Saturday was supposed to be easy. First, I had my hair cut at the salon on Galle Road. It looks great! Then I went to the optician to have my eyes tested, because I've been getting headaches. Good news: I don't need glasses.
Next, I took my laptop to the repair shop. The screen got broken last week when my little brother sat on it. They're going to get it fixed by Wednesday, but it'll cost me Rs. 15,000!

In the afternoon, I wanted to have some photos printed for my grandmother's birthday. But when I got to the bus stop, I realised I'd had my purse stolen. All my money and my bank card! I got soaked in the rain while I was walking to the police station, and then, when I got home, I found out that my evening flight to Jaffna had got cancelled.
Next Saturday, I'm staying in bed.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What did Kaveesha have done at the salon? ______________________________
Why did she have her eyes tested? ______________________________
What happened to her purse? ______________________________
What happened to her flight? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice
text: **Language reference**
**A. Write sentences with have something done in the tense given.**
**B. Choose the correct form.**
bullets: A mechanic is repairing my car. (present continuous) → I ______________________________
A photographer took our wedding photos. (past simple) → We ______________________________
Someone is going to paint our house. (going to) → We ______________________________
Someone broke into my uncle's house last night. (past simple) → My uncle ______________________________
I can't come. I **am cutting my hair / am having my hair cut** at 4 o'clock.
Where did you **have your suit made / have made your suit**?
He **got fined / got fine** for driving too fast.
I **had repaired my phone / had my phone repaired** last week. It works perfectly now.
You should **get checked your teeth / get your teeth checked** every six months.
Last night, my neighbour **stole his car / had his car stolen** from outside his house.

rows: A service (someone does it for you)
I had my hair cut. I'm going to get my car washed.
The flight got cancelled. He got fined.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Further Practice
text: **Complete the sentences using have or get + object + past participle, or the get passive.**
bullets: My watch has stopped. I need to ______________________________ (it / repair).
We ______________________________ (our kitchen / redecorate) at the moment, so we're eating out.
Have you ever ______________________________ (your palm / read)?
She ______________________________ (her passport / steal) when she was on holiday.
Be careful on that ladder! You'll ______________________________ (hurt).
They ______________________________ (lost) on the way to the hotel.
I'm going to ______________________________ (my eyes / test) next week.
He ______________________________ (promote) last month. Now he's the manager.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Survey and Story Cards
text: **Part A: Survey. Ask your classmates. Ask one follow-up question each time.**
**Part B: Bad luck story cards (cut up)**
**Useful language:** *had my ... stolen · had my ... broken into · got soaked · got lost · got fined · got cancelled · got stuck · got hurt*

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Advanced Passive Forms in Academic Writing, built round the theme "Writing Up Research".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students preparing for university study. They use basic passives accurately but their academic writing is too personal (We think that ..., I asked 50 people ...) and they make errors with complex passives (It is believed him to be ..., She hates to be interrupting, The data were looked).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Advanced Passive Forms in Academic Writing (impersonal passives, passive infinitives and gerunds)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (two research summaries for comparison), Handout 2 (language analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (writing task: survey notes).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of impersonal passives (It is thought that ... / X is thought to ...), passive infinitives and gerunds (to be given, being asked), passives of prepositional verbs (was looked into) and passives of verbs with two objects (Participants were given a questionnaire) in academic writing.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can rewrite a personal, informal research summary as a 150-word objective academic paragraph using at least six advanced passive forms.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop awareness of objectivity and hedging in academic style.
**Subsidiary aim.** To edit a student report collaboratively.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: It + is said / thought / believed / reported / claimed / assumed + that-clause
It is widely believed that social media affects sleep.
Subject + is thought / said / believed + to + infinitive
Social media is believed to affect sleep.
Subject + is thought + to have + pp
The decline is thought to have begun in 2015.
Usage is reported to be increasing.
Participants expected to be paid. The results need to be verified.
Many respondents disliked being observed. Without being told the purpose, ...
The issue was looked into. The patients were well cared for.
Participants were given a questionnaire. (also: A questionnaire was given to participants.)
There is thought to be ... / There are said to be ...
There are thought to be over 2,000 species.
blocks.heading: Key forms
Use in academic writing
bullets: Objectivity: the focus is on the research process and findings, not the researcher.
Distance and hedging: reporting passives show that a claim comes from others or is not certain.
Information flow: the passive lets known information (the topic) come first.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak forms in reading aloud: *is thought to have* /ɪz θɔːt tə həv/; *being* /ˈbiːɪŋ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Social media is believed to affect sleep.*** Is this the writer's personal opinion? (Not necessarily; it's a general belief.) · Is it certain? (No, it's believed.)
***Participants disliked being observed.*** Who observed whom? (Researchers observed the participants.) · Did participants like it? (No.)

rows: Mixed patterns (It is believed him to be ...).
Board the two patterns side by side: It is believed that he is ... / He is believed to be ...
Wrong infinitive for earlier time (The decline is thought to begin in 2015).
Timeline: thought = now; to have begun = earlier.
Active gerund with passive meaning (She hates interrupting meaning others interrupt her).
Dropping the preposition (The issue was looked).
Highlight the verb + particle as one unit.
Discuss when the active (This study shows ...) is clearer.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: say · think · believe · report · claim · assume · consider · estimate · expect · know

It is believed that + clause · S + is believed + to + inf · S + is thought + to have + pp (earlier) · S + is said + to be + -ing · to be + pp · being + pp · was looked into · were given a questionnaire · There are thought to be ...
objectivity · distance / hedging · topic first (information flow)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Advanced Passive Forms in Academic Writing, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of academic style.
Write two sentences on the board: *We asked 200 students about their sleep.* / *Two hundred students were asked about their sleep.*
Ask: *"Which sentence sounds more academic? Why?"* Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Elicit: the focus is on the research, not the researchers.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present advanced passive forms in an academic text and clarify their form, meaning and function.
**Part A: Reading and comparison (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the two summaries of the same study. Which one is suitable for a university assignment? List three differences."*
ICQs: *"How many summaries?"* (Two.) *"How many differences?"* (Three.)
Pairs compare. Elicit differences (personal pronouns, informal words, passive structures).
**Part B: Analysis (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"In groups, find the structures in Summary B and complete the table."*
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.
**Impersonal passives.** Board *It is believed that social media affects sleep* → *Social media is believed to affect sleep.* Ask: *"What changes?"* Cross out *It is believed him to be*.
**Time reference.** Draw a timeline for *The decline is thought to have begun in 2015*. Ask the CCQs.
**Passive infinitives and gerunds.** Board *Participants expected to be paid* and *They disliked being observed.* Ask the CCQs.
**Prepositional verbs and two objects.** Board *The issue was looked into* and *Participants were given a questionnaire.*
Discuss function: objectivity, hedging, information flow. Note that the active is still preferred when it is clearer: *This study shows ...*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite each sentence using the word given. Six minutes."*
Pairs check. Feedback as a class.
**Exercise B:** pairs correct the five errors. Check quickly.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use advanced passive forms in an academic paragraph.

Give out Handout 4. Say: *"These are a student's informal notes from a survey. Write an academic paragraph (about 150 words) reporting the method and findings. Use at least six advanced passive forms and hedge any claims."*
ICQs: *"Do you write I and we?"* (No, or very rarely.) *"How many advanced passive forms?"* (At least six.)
Pairs write (11 minutes).
Two pairs join and compare paragraphs. They underline each passive form and choose the clearest sentence from each paragraph (4 minutes).
Two groups read their best sentences aloud (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board strong sentences and two or three with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"When is the active better in academic writing?"* (When the agent matters, or when the passive would be unclear or wordy.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Find a short news article about a scientific study. Rewrite its main findings as a 200-word academic summary using at least eight advanced passive forms and appropriate hedging.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a pattern card with an example of each structure. Provide sentence starters for the writing task: *A total of ... were asked ... · It was found that ... · ... is thought to ...*

Stronger students use *is considered to have been*, *is estimated to have been -ing* and *There is believed to have been ...*. They identify where the active voice would be better and justify their choice.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The paragraph uses at least six advanced passive forms accurately. The paragraph contains no first-person pronouns and uses hedging appropriately. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use the infinitive forms with the correct time reference? Did the writing become more objective without becoming unclear?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Research Summaries
text: **Summary A (informal)**

We asked 200 teenagers in Colombo about how they use their phones at night. We gave them a questionnaire and we also interviewed 20 of them. Lots of people think that social media is bad for sleep, and our results agree. Most teens said they hated it when their parents interrupted them, and they didn't like it when we watched them. We looked at the data carefully. We think the problem started around 2015, when smartphones got cheap. People say it is getting worse.
**Summary B (academic)**

A total of 200 teenagers in Colombo were surveyed about their night-time phone use. Participants were given a questionnaire, and 20 were selected to be interviewed. It is widely believed that social media has a negative effect on sleep, and the findings support this view. Most respondents reported disliking being interrupted by their parents, and many were uncomfortable at being observed. The data were carefully looked into. The problem is thought to have begun around 2015, when smartphones became affordable, and it is reported to be worsening.
**List three differences between the summaries.**

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Analysis
text: **Find an example of each structure in Summary B.**
**Discuss.**
bullets: Why does the writer avoid *we* and *I*? ______________________________
What is the difference in time between *is thought* and *to have begun*? ______________________________
*Most respondents reported disliking being interrupted.* Who interrupted whom? ______________________________

rows: Two objects: indirect object as subject
Subject + is thought + to have + pp

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite each sentence using the word given. Keep the meaning the same.**
**B. Correct the errors.**
bullets: People believe that the new drug is effective. (believed) → The new drug ______________________________
Experts think that the ancient city was destroyed by an earthquake. (thought) → The ancient city ______________________________
Reports say that prices are rising quickly. (reported) → Prices ______________________________
They gave each participant a voucher. (given) → Each participant ______________________________
The committee will look into the complaint. (looked) → The complaint ______________________________
Students don't like it when teachers ignore them. (being) → Students don't like ______________________________
The results must be checked by an independent team. They need this. (need) → The results ______________________________
People say there are over 300 species in the reserve. (said) → There ______________________________
It is believed him to be the best candidate. ______________________________
The study is thought to begin in 2010. (It began in 2010.) ______________________________
The patients were well cared. ______________________________
Most participants hated to be interrupting. ______________________________
A questionnaire was given participants. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **A student's informal notes from a survey. Rewrite them as an academic paragraph (about 150 words).**
**Your paragraph:**
bullets: we surveyed 150 first-year university students in Kandy
we gave everyone an online questionnaire; we chose 15 for interviews
topic: part-time jobs and exam results
lots of people think part-time jobs hurt grades
our results: students who worked more than 15 hours a week got lower marks
many said they hated it when their managers asked them to work extra hours
we think the trend started after fees went up in 2019
people say the number of working students is increasing
the university should look into this

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1 (possible differences)**

Summary B avoids *we / I*; uses the passive to focus on the research; uses formal vocabulary (*respondents, affordable, worsening*); uses reporting passives to distance the writer from claims (*It is widely believed ...*).
**Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B**
**Handout 4 (model paragraph)**

A total of 150 first-year students at a university in Kandy were surveyed about part-time employment and academic performance. All participants were given an online questionnaire, and 15 were selected to be interviewed. It is widely believed that part-time work has a negative effect on grades, and the findings appear to support this view: students who worked more than 15 hours a week were found to have lower marks. Many respondents reported disliking being asked to work extra hours. The trend is thought to have begun after tuition fees were increased in 2019, and the number of working students is reported to be rising. It is recommended that this issue be looked into further.
**Common errors to watch for**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Reporting with Say and Tell in the Present, built round the theme "Passing On Messages".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** High beginners who use the present simple and be confidently. When they pass on a message, they repeat the exact words (Ravi says "I am late") and confuse pronouns (She says I am hungry meaning she is hungry). They mix say and tell (She says me ...).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "The telephone game" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and listening
Grammar: Reporting with Say and Tell in the Present (She says she's ...)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (phone messages), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (message cards for the game), a toy phone or real phone (optional).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise reporting messages in the present with says (that) and tells me (that), changing pronouns and verb forms correctly.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can pass on 5 simple messages, e.g. Kasun says he's at the bus stop. Mum tells me she's busy.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise third person -s.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop listening and speaking through a "telephone" message game.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Kasun says they're at the beach.
Nimmi to me: "I like your bag."
Nimmi tells me (that) she likes my bag.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **say** + (that) + clause: *He says he's hungry.* (no person after *say*)
**tell** + person + (that) + clause: *He tells me he's hungry.* (person after *tell*)
Change the pronoun: *I → he / she*, *we → they*, *my → his / her*.
Change the verb to match the new subject: *I like → she likes*, *I am → he is*.
*that* is optional.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use *says / tells me* + present to pass on a message that someone **is saying now** or has just sent (a text, a phone call).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *says* /sez/ (not /seɪz/). *tells me* /telz mi/.
Contractions: *he's* /hiːz/, *she's* /ʃiːz/, *they're* /ðeə/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Ravi says he's late.*** Who is late: Ravi or me? (Ravi.) · Did Ravi say "he's late"? (No, he said "I'm late".)
***Nimmi tells me she likes my bag.*** Who is Nimmi talking to? (Me.) · Can I say *Nimmi says me*? (No.)

rows: Not changing the pronoun (Ravi says I'm late).
Point to Ravi and to yourself; colour-code I → he.
Drill /sez/ with the sound of Les.
Board: say + what, tell + who + what.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: I → he / she · we → they · my → his / her · our → their · am → is · like → likes
Ravi: "I'm late." → Ravi says (that) he's late. · say + (that) + message · tell + PERSON + (that) + message · She tells me she's busy. · not: She says me ✗
says /sez/ · tells me /telz mi/ · he's /hiːz/ · she's /ʃiːz/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Reporting with Say and Tell in the Present, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the idea of passing on messages.
Pretend to read a message on your phone. Say: *"Oh! It's a message from my sister."* Read it aloud: *"I'm at the hospital. I'm OK."*
Ask: *"Where is my sister? Is she OK?"* Elicit answers: *She's at the hospital. She's OK.*
Say: *"My sister says she's at the hospital. She says she's OK."*

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the phone messages to Dilini. Answer the questions."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Who are the messages to?"* (Dilini.) *"Do you answer the questions?"* (Yes.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
Read Dilini's message to her mother (the second part of the handout). Ask: *"What does Kasun say?"*
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Kasun: "I'm at the bus stop."* and *Kasun says he's at the bus stop.* Ask the CCQs.
**Pronouns.** Underline *I* and *he*. Ask: *"Why he?"* (Because I'm talking about Kasun.) Build the pronoun list on the left.
**Verbs.** Board *Nimmi: "I like your bag."* → *Nimmi says she likes my bag.* Highlight *likes* (-s) and *my*.
**say and tell.** Board *Nimmi tells me she likes my bag.* Ask: *"After tell, who?"* (me.) *"After say?"* (no person.) Board *She says me* ✗.
**Pronunciation.** Drill *says* /sez/ and contractions: *He says he's late. She tells me she's busy.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: report the messages. Exercise B: say or tell? Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you change I?"* (Yes.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers.
**Quick drill:** say a sentence about yourself (*"I'm tired."*); students report it: *"She says she's tired."*

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use reported speech in a fun, communicative game.

**The telephone game (8 minutes).** Groups of four sit in a line. Student 1 takes a message card from Handout 3 and whispers it to Student 2 (*"I'm hungry and I want pizza."*). Student 2 tells Student 3: *"Kasun says he's hungry and he wants pizza."* Student 4 reports the message to the class. Is it the same as the card?
ICQs: *"Do you say I or he when you pass on the message?"* (He / she.)

**My messages (6 minutes).** Each student writes two real or invented short messages on paper (*I love cricket. My cat is black.*) and gives them to a partner. The partner tells a new partner: *"Ayesha says she loves cricket. She says her cat is black."*
**Writing (4 minutes).** Students write 4 reported sentences about their classmates' messages.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two or three students read their sentences.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Ask three people in your family a question (*How are you? What do you like?*). Write what they say: *My father says he's tired. My sister says she likes music.*
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the pronoun list on a card. In the telephone game, use short one-sentence cards.
Stronger students report two-part messages with *and* and *but*: *She says she's tired but she's happy.* They use *asks* for simple questions (preview): *He asks if you're OK.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "The telephone game" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Telephone Game Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "The telephone game" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2. Students change *I* to *he / she* when they pass on messages. Students pronounce *says* as /sez/.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students change pronouns and verb forms? Was the telephone game clear and fun?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Phone Messages
text: **Read the messages to Dilini.**
**Kasun:** I'm at the bus stop. I'm a bit late, sorry!
**Amma:** I'm at the market. I need some rice. Can you help?
**Nimmi:** I like your new bag! It's really nice.
**Ruwan and Sanduni:** We are at the beach. The water is lovely!
**Answer the questions.**
**Now read Dilini's message to her mother.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Reported Statements in the Past, built round the theme "Celebrity Interviews".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who can report messages in the present (She says she's tired). When they report what someone said earlier, they don't change the tense (He said he is tired) and they confuse said and told (He said me).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Report" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Reported Statements in the Past (said that, told me that)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (magazine interview with a young cricketer), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (interview questions and report sheet).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise reported statements with said (that) and told + person (that), with the main tense changes (present → past, will → would, can → could) and pronoun changes.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can report what a classmate said in an interview, e.g. Nimal said he was a good swimmer. He told me he would visit Japan next year.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read an interview for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a "class interview" activity.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: He said he was playing the next day.
blocks.heading: Form: the tense moves back
Form: the tense moves back: notes
bullets: **said** + (that) + clause. **told** + person + (that) + clause.
Pronouns and possessives change: *I → he / she, my → his / her, we → they*.
Time words often change: *today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, now → then*.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use *said / told* + past forms to report what someone said at an earlier time.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *said* /sed/, *told* /təʊld/. *that* is weak /ðət/ or left out.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Interview: "I'm very nervous." → She said she was very nervous.*** When did she speak: now or before? (Before, in the interview.) · Is *was* about the past? (It shows the words were said before; she was nervous at the time of the interview.)
***He told me he could swim.*** Who did he speak to? (Me.) · Can I say *He said me*? (No.)

rows: No tense change (He said he is tired).
Board a "step back" arrow: am → was, like → liked.
Board: say + what; tell + who + what.
Teach only tomorrow → the next day and today → that day.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: am / is → was · are → were · like → liked · 'm playing → was playing · will → would · can → could · I → he / she · my → his / her · tomorrow → the next day
"I'm nervous." → She said (that) she was nervous. · "I can swim." → He told me (that) he could swim. · said + (that) + message · told + PERSON + (that) + message · not: He said me ✗
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Reported Statements in the Past, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest in the topic.
Ask: *"Which famous sports stars do you like? If you met one, what would you ask?"* Pairs list three questions (2 minutes).
Take a few questions and board two.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present reported statements in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the interview with Shenali, a young cricketer. Then read the magazine report. Answer the questions."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many texts?"* (Two: the interview and the report.)
Pairs check. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Find the same information in the interview and in the report. What changes?"* Pairs compare three sentences.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *"I'm very nervous." → She said she was very nervous.* Ask the CCQs.
**Tense changes.** Elicit the changes from the handout and build the list on the left of the board. Draw a "step back" arrow.
**Pronouns and time.** Highlight *I → she, my → her, tomorrow → the next day.*
**said and told.** Board *She told the reporter she could bowl fast.* Ask: *"After told, what comes?"* (A person.) Board *She said me* ✗.
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *She said she was nervous. He told me he could swim.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: report the sentences. Exercise B: said or told? Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then new pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To report what classmates said in a personalised interview.
Give out Handout 3. **Interview (7 minutes).** Students interview a partner with the questions and write the exact answers in the "Answer" column.
ICQs: *"Do you write the exact words or a report?"* (The exact words.)
**Report (7 minutes).** Students change partners and report what their first partner said: *"Nimal said he was a good swimmer. He told me he would visit Japan next year."*
**Writing (4 minutes).** Students write four sentences in the report section of Handout 3.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two students report the most surprising thing their partner said.
Board four sentences from Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Ask a family member five questions about their childhood. Write what they said, using *said* and *told me*.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the "step back" list on a card. Let them report only present simple and *be* sentences.

Stronger students report past simple sentences with the past perfect (preview): *She said she had played for three years.* They use more time changes: *yesterday → the day before, next week → the following week*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Report" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Report" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 6 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. In the report, students change the tense and pronoun correctly in most sentences. Students use *told* + person and *said* without a person.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students remember to change the tense? Was the interview personal and interesting?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Interview with a Young Cricketer
text: **The interview**

**Reporter:** How old are you, Shenali? **Shenali:** I'm 16. **Reporter:** How do you feel about your first big match? **Shenali:** I'm very nervous, but I'm excited too. **Reporter:** What can you do well? **Shenali:** I can bowl very fast. My coach is my father. **Reporter:** What are your plans? **Shenali:** I'm playing in Galle tomorrow. One day I will play for Sri Lanka!
**The magazine report**

Shenali Perera said she was 16. She said she was very nervous about her first big match, but she was excited too. She told our reporter she could bowl very fast, and she said her coach was her father. She said she was playing in Galle the next day, and she told us she would play for Sri Lanka one day.
**Answer the questions.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Reported Questions, Requests and Commands, built round the theme "The Job Interview".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who report statements with tense changes. When they report questions they keep question word order and auxiliaries (She asked me where did I live), and they report commands with said (He said me to sit down).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Reported Questions, Requests and Commands (asked if, told me to)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (job interview dialogue and Ishan's message), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (interview role cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students work out and use reported wh- questions, yes / no questions (if / whether) and reported requests and commands (asked / told + object + (not) to + infinitive).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can report a job interview, e.g. She asked me why I wanted the job. She asked if I could work at weekends. She told me to send my references.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a job interview role-play.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise intonation in direct questions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: She asked me where I lived.
She asked (me) why I wanted the job.
She asked if / whether I could work at weekends.
She asked me to send my references.
She told me to sit down. / She told me not to be late.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: Reported questions use **statement word order** (subject + verb) and **no do / does / did**. No question mark.
*Yes / no* questions use **if** or **whether**.
Requests and commands: **ask / tell + object + (not) to + infinitive**.
Tenses move back as with statements.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: *ask* is used for questions and polite requests; *tell* is used for orders and instructions.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Direct *wh-* questions fall at the end: *Where do you live? ↘*. *Yes / no* questions rise: *Can you work at weekends? ↗*. Reported questions are statements, so they fall: *She asked if I could work at weekends ↘.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***She asked me where I lived.*** Is this a question now? (No, it's a statement about a question.) · Is there a question mark? (No.) Is there *do / did*? (No.)
***She told me not to be late.*** Is this a question or an order? (An order.) · What did she actually say? (Don't be late.)

rows: Question word order (She asked where did I live).
Board: asked + where + SUBJECT + VERB; cross out did.
Missing if (She asked could I work).
Rule: no question word → if / whether.
said for commands (He said me to sit down).
Board: tell / ask + person + to + infinitive.
not in the wrong place (She told me don't be late).
Board: told me not to be late.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: ask · tell · want to know · wonder · order · remind

"Where do you live?" → She asked me where I lived. · asked + wh- + S + V (no do, no ?) · "Can you ...?" → She asked if / whether I could ... · "Please send ..." → She asked me to send ... · "Don't be late." → She told me not to be late. · ask / tell + person + (not) to + infinitive
Where do you live? ↘ · Can you work? ↗ · She asked if I could work ↘
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Reported Questions, Requests and Commands, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic and personalise it.
Ask: *"Have you ever had an interview: for a job, a school or a club? What did they ask you?"*
Pairs list four typical interview questions (2 minutes). Board a few.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present reported questions, requests and commands in context and help students work out the rules.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the job interview. Then read Ishan's message to his friend. Did he get the job?"* (3 minutes.)
Pairs compare. Students answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Compare the interview and Ishan's message. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Alone or with a partner?"* (With a partner.) *"Which two texts do you compare?"* (The interview and the message.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Where is the verb in the reported question? Where is did?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit the answers and build the patterns in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Highlight: statement word order, no *do / did*, no question mark; *if / whether* for *yes / no* questions; *ask / tell + person + (not) to*.
**Pronunciation.** Contrast intonation: *Can you work at weekends? ↗* vs *She asked if I could work at weekends ↘.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: report the questions. Exercise B: report the requests and commands. Seven minutes."*
Pairs compare. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then new pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use reported questions and commands fluently after a role-play.

Give out Handout 4. Student A is an interviewer for a summer job; Student B is the candidate. A asks at least six questions and gives two instructions at the end (*Bring your ID card on Monday. Don't forget ...*). Swap roles with a different job (10 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many questions?"* (At least six.) *"What do you give at the end?"* (Two instructions.)
**Report (6 minutes).** Students change partners and report their interview: *"She asked me why I wanted the job. She asked if I had any experience. She told me to bring my ID card."*
The class decides which candidates got the jobs (2 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"What three things change when we report a question?"* (Word order, no *do / did*, no question mark.)
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a message (120 words) to a friend about an interview, a visit to the doctor or a meeting with a teacher. Report at least four questions and two instructions.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the patterns on a card. In the role-play, provide the interviewer with a list of questions.
Stronger students use *wanted to know, wondered* and *reminded me to*. They report questions politely in the present: *Could you tell me where the station is?* (indirect questions preview).

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Report" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Interview Role Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Report" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In the report, students use statement word order in reported questions. Students use *if / whether* for *yes / no* questions. 9 out of 11 or better on Handout 3.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students stop using *did* in reported questions? Was the role-play realistic enough to produce instructions?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Job Interview
text: **The interview at Ocean View Hotel, Bentota**

**Mrs Jayawardena:** Please sit down. Where do you live, Ishan? **Ishan:** In Kalutara. **Mrs Jayawardena:** Why do you want this job? **Ishan:** I love meeting people, and I want to improve my English. **Mrs Jayawardena:** Have you worked in a hotel before? **Ishan:** No, but I worked in my uncle's shop last summer. **Mrs Jayawardena:** Can you work at weekends? **Ishan:** Yes, I can. **Mrs Jayawardena:** Good. Could you send me two references, please? And don't be late on your first day!
**Ishan's message to his friend**

Hi Dilan! I had my interview today. First, the manager told me to sit down. She asked me where I lived and why I wanted the job. Then she asked if I had worked in a hotel before. I told her about Uncle's shop! She also asked whether I could work at weekends. At the end, she asked me to send two references and told me not to be late on my first day. So I think I've got the job!
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: What did the manager ask him to send? ______________________________

text: **Compare the interview and Ishan's message.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: In the reported questions, does the verb come before or after the subject? ______________________________
Which words do we use when there is no question word? ______________________________
Which verbs report requests and commands? What comes after them? ______________________________
Where does *not* go in a negative command? ______________________________

She asked me why I wanted the job.
"Have you worked in a hotel before?"
She asked if I had worked in a hotel before.

**Useful language for reporting**
