hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Reporting Verbs and Their Patterns, built round the theme "Drama at the Team Meeting".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who report statements, questions and commands accurately with say, tell and ask, but their reports are repetitive. When they try other verbs, they make pattern errors: He suggested me to go, She denied to take it, He apologised to be late.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Reporting Verbs and Their Patterns (advise, refuse, deny, suggest)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (transcript of a team meeting), Handout 2 (reference table and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (role cards for a club meeting).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of a range of reporting verbs and their patterns: verb + infinitive, verb + object + infinitive, verb + -ing, verb + preposition + -ing, and verb + that-clause.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can summarise a meeting using at least eight different reporting verbs, e.g. The coach refused to change the team. Malik apologised for missing training. Ayesha suggested holding extra practice.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in summarising a conversation.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness that reporting verbs show the speaker's purpose and attitude.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten, decide
She refused to change the team.
advise, ask, encourage, invite, persuade, remind, tell, warn
He advised me to rest. He warned us not to be late.
He denied taking the ball. She suggested practising more.
apologise for, insist on, accuse sb of, blame sb for, congratulate sb on
admit, agree, complain, explain, promise, suggest (that sb should)
She suggested (that) we should train on Sundays.
blocks.heading: Patterns
Meaning and use
bullets: Reporting verbs summarise the **function** of what was said (a promise, a refusal, an apology), not the exact words.
*"Sorry I'm late."* → *He apologised for being late.* *"I didn't take it!"* → *He denied taking it.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Stress the reporting verb, which carries the meaning: *She reFUSED to change it. He deNIED taking it.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Malik denied taking the ball.*** Did Malik say he took the ball? (No, he said he didn't.) · Do we know if he took it? (No.)
***The coach advised Ruwan to rest.*** Was it an order or advice? (Advice.) · Who will rest? (Ruwan.)

rows: suggest + object + infinitive (He suggested me to go).
Board: suggest + -ing / suggest (that) + clause; cross out suggested me to.
deny / admit + infinitive (She denied to take).
Group verbs by pattern; card sort.
Preposition + infinitive (apologised for to be late).
not in the wrong place (warned us to not be late).
Board: warned us not to be late.
Learn by pattern groups; students choose 10 to learn.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: promise · refuse · offer · advise · warn · remind · admit · deny · suggest · apologise · insist · accuse

+ to inf: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten · + obj + to inf: advise, persuade, remind, warn · + -ing: admit, deny, suggest, recommend · + prep + -ing: apologise for, insist on, accuse sb of · + that: suggest (that) we should ... · not: suggested me to ✗
She reFUSED to ... · He deNIED ...ing · She sugGESTed ...ing

blocks.heading: Procedure: Reporting Verbs and Their Patterns, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the context and engage students.
Ask: *"Have you ever been in a team or club meeting where people argued? What did people say?"*
Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Take one or two stories.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present reporting verbs in context and clarify their patterns and meanings.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the transcript of the cricket team meeting. What was the problem? How did it end?"* (3 minutes.)
Pairs compare. Then students read the coach's summary email and answer the three questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (5 minutes)**
Say: *"Match each line in the transcript to a sentence in the email. Underline the reporting verb and the word after it."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (9 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2 (reference table). Elicit the five pattern groups and build them in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Focus on the most common errors: *suggest*, *deny / admit*, preposition + *-ing*, the position of *not*.
Point out that the verb summarises the speaker's purpose: *"Sorry I'm late"* = an apology → *apologise for*.
**Pronunciation.** Drill with stress on the reporting verb: *She reFUSED to change the team. He deNIED taking it.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the patterns accurately.
Say: *"Do Exercise A on Handout 2: report each sentence using the verb given. Then Exercise B: correct the mistakes."* (7 minutes.)
Pairs check. Check as a class.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then new groups, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use a range of reporting verbs fluently in summarising a meeting.

Give out Handout 4. Groups of four role-play a meeting of the school drama club about a problem with the end-of-year show. Each student has a role card with things they must say (an apology, a promise, a refusal, a suggestion, a warning, an accusation) (7 minutes).
ICQs: *"Do you read your card aloud?"* (No, use your own words.) *"What must you include?"* (The things on your card.)

**Report (8 minutes).** Students form new groups and summarise their meeting using at least eight reporting verbs: *"Nethmi apologised for losing the script. Kamal refused to play the king. I suggested postponing the show."*
The class votes for the most dramatic meeting (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which pattern does suggest take? Which does deny take?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write the minutes (summary) of a real or imaginary meeting or family discussion (180 words) using at least ten different reporting verbs.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the reference table during the freer practice. Limit them to eight verbs (two from each of four patterns).

Stronger students use *accuse sb of*, *blame sb for*, *congratulate sb on* and *insist that sb (should)*. They use passive and perfect forms: *He denied having been told. She admitted having made a mistake.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Report" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Reference Table and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Club Meeting Role Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Report" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 6 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. The summary uses at least eight different reporting verbs with the correct pattern. No *suggest* + object + infinitive errors in the final summaries.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which patterns caused the most errors? Did students choose verbs that matched the speaker's purpose?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: The Team Meeting
text: **Transcript: Under-17 cricket team meeting**

**Coach:** We lost three matches in a row. Things have to change. **Malik:** Sorry I missed training last week. My grandmother was ill. **Coach:** Ruwan, you look exhausted. You should rest this weekend. **Ayesha:** Why don't we practise on Sunday mornings too? **Coach:** OK, I'll book the ground for Sundays. But I'm not changing the team. **Dinesh:** Someone took my new bat from the changing room. **Malik:** It wasn't me! I didn't take it! **Coach:** If anyone is late on Sunday, they won't play on Saturday. **Kasun:** OK, I'll bring the drinks on Sunday.
**The coach's summary email**

Dear parents, At today's meeting, I explained that we had lost three matches in a row. Malik apologised for missing training. I advised Ruwan to rest this weekend. Ayesha suggested practising on Sunday mornings, so I promised to book the ground. However, I refused to change the team. Dinesh complained that someone had taken his bat; Malik denied taking it. I warned the players not to be late on Sunday, and Kasun offered to bring the drinks.
**Answer the questions.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Reporting in Academic Writing, built round the theme "Writing a Literature Review".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students preparing for university. They report sources mechanically with said and says, always backshift the tense (Silva said that exercise improved memory for a fact still believed), and cannot show their attitude to a source.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Reporting in Academic Writing (stance verbs, tense choice and nominalised reports)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (two versions of a literature review paragraph), Handout 2 (reporting verb analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (source summaries for the writing task).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' ability to report sources in academic writing using stance verbs (argue, claim, acknowledge, contend, refute), appropriate tense choice (present, past, present perfect, no backshift for current truths) and nominalised reports (the claim that ..., Silva's assertion that ...).

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a 150-word literature review paragraph that reports and evaluates three sources using at least six different reporting structures accurately.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of how reporting verbs show agreement, neutrality or doubt.
**Subsidiary aim.** To write a short literature review paragraph that synthesises sources.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: state, report, note, observe, describe, find, explain
Fernando (2019) suggests that screen time may affect sleep.
argue, claim, contend, maintain, assert, insist
Silva (2020) argues that homework should be abolished.
show, demonstrate, establish, confirm, point out
The study demonstrates that ... (the writer accepts it)
Some commentators claim that ... (the writer may not agree)
Silva acknowledges that the data are limited.
blocks.heading: Reporting verbs and stance
Patterns
bullets: verb + *that*-clause: *Silva argues that ...*
verb + noun phrase: *Jayasinghe challenges this view.* / *disputes the findings*.
*as* + subject + verb: *As Perera (2021) notes, ...*
*According to* + source: *According to Silva (2020), ...* (do not combine with *argues*: not *According to Silva, he argues*).
Nominalised reports: *the claim / argument / assertion / finding / suggestion + that*-clause: *Silva's claim that homework is harmful has been widely criticised.*

blocks.heading: Tense choice
bullets: **Present simple**: the most common; the source's view is presented as current: *Silva argues ...*
**Past simple**: a specific study or event: *Perera (2021) found that ...*
**Present perfect**: a research area or several studies: *Several studies have shown ...*
**No backshift** in the reported clause when the content is still considered true: *Perera found that sleep* ***is*** *essential for memory.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Not a focus; when reading aloud, the author's name and date are often said with a slight pause: *Silva, 2020, argues ...*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Silva (2020) claims that homework is harmful.*** Does the writer definitely agree with Silva? (Not necessarily; *claims* can show doubt.) · Would *demonstrates* show more or less agreement? (More.)
***Perera found that sleep is essential for memory.*** Why *is* and not *was*? (Because it is still considered true.)

rows: Contrast found that sleep was essential (in that study only) and is essential (generally true).
Wrong pattern (Silva discusses about, argues that homework to be).
Pattern column in the verb bank.
Choosing a verb with the wrong stance (demonstrates for a weak claim).
Analysis task focusing on writer's attitude.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: NEUTRAL: state, report, note, find · TENTATIVE: suggest, propose · STRONG: argue, claim, contend, maintain · AGREE: show, demonstrate, confirm · CONCEDE: acknowledge, concede · DISAGREE: dispute, challenge, refute
X argues that + clause · X disputes + noun · As X notes, ... · According to X, ... · PRESENT: current view · PAST: one study · PRESENT PERFECT: research area · no backshift for current truths
the claim that ... · X's argument that ... · the finding that ... · this view / this assertion

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Reporting in Academic Writing, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of stance in reporting.
Board three sentences: *Silva says that homework is harmful. / Silva claims that homework is harmful. / Silva demonstrates that homework is harmful.*
Ask: *"Which sentence shows that the writer agrees with Silva? Which shows doubt?"* Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Elicit the differences.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present academic reporting structures in context and clarify their stance, patterns and tense choices.
**Part A: Reading and comparison (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the two versions of the same literature review paragraph. Which is better for a university essay? Why?"*
ICQs: *"How many versions?"* (Two.) *"What do you decide?"* (Which is better and why.)
Pairs compare. Elicit: Version B uses varied verbs, shows the writer's view, connects the sources.
**Part B: Analysis (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"In groups, find the reporting structures in Version B and complete the table."*
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the verb bank by stance on the left of the board.
**Patterns.** Show *argues that, disputes this view, As Perera notes, According to ...* Board *According to Silva, she argues* ✗.
**Tense choice.** Ask: *"Why does the writer use found for Perera but argues for Silva?"* Elicit present for current views, past for specific studies, present perfect for research areas.
**No backshift.** Contrast *Perera found that sleep was essential* (only in her study) and *is essential* (generally accepted). Ask the CCQs.
**Nominalised reports.** Highlight *Silva's claim that ...* and *this view*; show how they connect ideas across sentences.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: choose the most appropriate verb and form. Exercise B: rewrite using the word given. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check and justify their choices (stance and tense). Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To write a literature review paragraph that reports and evaluates sources.

Give out Handout 4. Say: *"Read the three source summaries. Write a literature review paragraph (about 150 words) on whether school should start later. Report all three sources, show your view of each, and connect them. Use at least six different reporting structures."*
ICQs: *"Do you just list the sources?"* (No, connect them and show your view.) *"How many structures?"* (At least six.)
Pairs write (11 minutes).
Pairs swap with another pair and identify the writer's attitude to each source from the verbs alone (4 minutes).
Two pairs read their paragraphs aloud (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board strong sentences and two or three with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which verb would you choose to report a source you disagree with? A source you trust?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Find three short sources (articles, reports or studies) on a topic of your choice. Write a 250-word literature review paragraph that reports, compares and evaluates them, using at least eight different reporting structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the verb bank with patterns on a card. Provide a paragraph frame: *Several studies have ... · X (year) argues that ... · However, Y disputes ... · As Z notes, ... · Overall, ...*

Stronger students use *concede, contend* and *refute* accurately and add evaluative adverbs: *X convincingly argues ..., Y rightly points out ...* They use passive reporting: *It has been argued that ...*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The paragraph uses at least six different reporting structures accurately. Verb choice reflects a clear stance towards each source. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students choose verbs that matched their attitude to each source? Did they avoid automatic backshift?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Literature Review Paragraphs
text: **Version A**

Silva (2020) said that homework was harmful for children. Perera (2021) said that students who slept more did better in exams. Jayasinghe (2022) said that Silva was wrong. Fernando (2019) said that phones affected sleep. All these writers said interesting things about homework and sleep.
**Version B**

The relationship between homework, sleep and academic performance has been widely debated. Silva (2020) argues that homework is harmful for younger children, although she acknowledges that her sample was small. Jayasinghe (2022) disputes this view, contending that moderate homework improves self-discipline. Silva's claim that homework reduces sleep is, however, supported by Perera (2021), who found that students who sleep more than eight hours perform significantly better in examinations. As Fernando (2019) suggests, the effect of homework on sleep may be less important than that of late-night phone use.
**Which version is better for a university essay? Give three reasons.**

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Reporting Verb Analysis
text: **Find these structures in Version B.**
**Discuss.**
bullets: *Perera (2021) found that students who sleep more ... perform better.* Why does the writer use present tenses after *found*? ______________________________
Does the writer seem to agree more with Silva or with Jayasinghe? How do you know? ______________________________
Why is Version B easier to follow than Version A? ______________________________

rows: Present perfect for a research area
Past simple for a specific study

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Choose the most appropriate option.**
**B. Rewrite using the word given.**
bullets: Rodrigo (2018) **argues / demonstrates** that social media is the main cause of teenage anxiety, but she provides little evidence.
In a large study of 5,000 students, Kumar (2020) **found / suggests** that breakfast improves concentration.
Several researchers **have shown / showed** a link between exercise and memory.
Weerasinghe (2017) **acknowledges / insists** that her conclusions are based on a small sample.
**According to Silva, / According to Silva, she argues** homework should be limited.
Perera found that sleep **is / was** essential for memory. (This is now widely accepted.)
Dias (2021) **disputes / disputes about** the findings of earlier studies.
**The claim that / The claiming that** online learning is less effective has been challenged.
Silva says homework is harmful, and I'm not sure she's right. (claims) → ______________________________
Perera's study proved that sleep improves exam results. (demonstrates) → ______________________________
Jayasinghe said Silva was wrong. (disputes) → ______________________________
Silva argues that homework is harmful. This argument has been criticised. (Silva's argument) → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Source Summaries for the Writing Task
text: **Topic: Should schools start later in the morning?**
**Your paragraph (about 150 words):**

rows: A national survey of 3,000 teenagers. Students who started school after 8.30 am slept 45 minutes more and had higher grades. The author admits the survey relied on students' own reports.
An opinion article by a school principal. Strongly believes a later start would cause traffic problems and reduce sports time. Gives no data.
An experiment in Singapore. A 30-minute later start improved attention in class but had no effect on exam results. The author suggests more research is needed.

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1 (possible reasons)**

Version B uses varied reporting verbs; it shows the writer's attitude to each source; it connects sources (*disputes this view, is supported by*); it uses appropriate tenses; it avoids repetition and automatic backshift.
**Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B (examples)**
**Handout 4 (model paragraph)**

Whether schools should start later has attracted growing attention. Gunawardena (2021) found that students who began after 8.30 am slept 45 minutes longer and achieved higher grades, although she acknowledges that the data were self-reported. These findings are partly confirmed by Lim (2022), whose experiment showed improved attention in class; however, Lim found no effect on examination results and suggests that further research is needed. In contrast, Hettiarachchi (2019) argues that a later start would cause traffic problems and reduce time for sport. This claim, however, is not supported by data. Overall, the evidence suggests that a later start benefits sleep and attention, but its effect on academic results remains unclear.
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Present perfect: *has been widely debated* · Strong claim: *argues that homework is harmful*; *contending that ...* · Concession: *acknowledges that her sample was small* · Disagreement: *disputes this view* · Nominalised report: *Silva's claim that homework reduces sleep* · Past simple: *Perera (2021) ... found that* · As + source: *As Fernando (2019) suggests* · Tentative: *suggests ... may be*

Because the finding is presented as still true (no backshift). · 2. With Silva's claim about sleep, partly, because it is *supported by* Perera; the writer reports Jayasinghe neutrally. · 3. Sources are connected and evaluated, not listed.
argues (*demonstrates* would mean the writer accepts it as proven) · 2. found · 3. have shown · 4. acknowledges · 5. According to Silva, · 6. is · 7. disputes · 8. The claim that

Silva claims that homework is harmful. · 2. Perera's study demonstrates that sleep improves exam results. · 3. Jayasinghe disputes Silva's view / conclusion. · 4. Silva's argument that homework is harmful has been criticised.

rows: According to Silva, she argues that ...
According to Silva, ... / Silva argues that ...
Perera found that sleep was essential. (generally true)
Perera found that sleep is essential.
Silva demonstrates that ... (for an unproven opinion)

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Comparative Adjectives, built round the theme "Animals and Cities".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** High beginners who know common adjectives (big, small, tall, fast, cheap, expensive, hot, beautiful) and be. They compare things with very or more + short adjective (An elephant is more big) and forget than.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Comparison cards" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Comparative Adjectives (bigger than, more expensive than)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Pictures of an elephant, a horse, a cheetah, a turtle, Colombo and Nuwara Eliya (or described in words), Handout 1 (Kasun's postcard), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (comparison cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise comparative adjectives with -er, -ier, more, and the irregular forms better and worse, with than.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write and say 6 sentences comparing animals, places and things, e.g. An elephant is bigger than a horse. Colombo is hotter than Nuwara Eliya.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review adjectives for describing animals and places.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise the weak form of than.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a guessing game.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: small → smaller, tall → taller, fast → faster, cheap → cheaper
big → bigger, hot → hotter, thin → thinner
happy → happier, busy → busier, easy → easier
expensive → more expensive, beautiful → more beautiful
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **comparative + than**: *An elephant is bigger* ***than*** *a horse.*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: We use comparatives to compare **two** people, animals or things.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *than* /ðən/: *bigger than* /ˈbɪɡə ðən/.
Weak *-er* /ə/: *taller* /ˈtɔːlə/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***An elephant is bigger than a horse.*** How many animals are we comparing? (Two.) · Which one is big? (Both.) Which one is more big? (The elephant.) · Can I say *more big*? (No, *bigger*.)

rows: Missing than or using that / of (bigger that).
Spelling rules table; quick spelling quiz.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: big · small · tall · fast · slow · hot · cold · cheap · expensive · beautiful · heavy · good · bad
short: + -er → taller · big → bigger · happy → happier · long: more + adj → more expensive · good → better · bad → worse · comparative + than · not: more big ✗
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Comparative Adjectives, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To activate adjectives and introduce the idea of comparing.
Show the elephant and the horse. Ask: *"Is the elephant big? Is the horse big?"* (Yes, both.) *"Which is very, very big?"* (The elephant.)
Show the cheetah and the turtle. Ask: *"Which is fast?"* Elicit adjectives and board them on the left.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present comparatives in context. To clarify form, meaning and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Kasun's postcard from Nuwara Eliya. Is Nuwara Eliya hotter or colder than Colombo?"* (3 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Who is the postcard from?"* (Kasun.)
Students answer the true / false questions. Pairs compare. Check as a class.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *An elephant is bigger than a horse.* Ask the CCQs.

**Form.** Students find comparatives in the postcard. Sort them on the board: *colder, smaller* (-er); *bigger, hotter* (double); *busier* (-ier); *more beautiful, more expensive* (more); *better* (irregular). Elicit the rules.
**Syllables.** Clap the syllables: *cold* (1), *beau-ti-ful* (3). Ask: *"One clap: -er or more?"*
**than.** Highlight *than* after the comparative. Board *bigger that* ✗.
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak *than*: *bigger than, colder than, more expensive than.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: write the comparative. Exercise B: write sentences. Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you write than in Exercise B?"* (Yes.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers. Check spelling on the board.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups, then individual
text: **Aim:** To use comparatives in a game and in writing.

**Comparison cards (8 minutes).** Give each pair a set of cards (Handout 3). Students take two cards and make as many true comparative sentences as they can: *A bicycle is cheaper than a car. A car is faster than a bicycle.* One point for each correct sentence.
ICQs: *"How many cards do you take?"* (Two.)
**Guess what I'm thinking (6 minutes).** In groups, one student thinks of an animal. Others ask: *"Is it bigger than a dog?" "Is it faster than a horse?"* until they guess.
**Writing (4 minutes).** Students write 4 sentences comparing their town with another town they know.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two students read their sentences about their town.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences comparing two members of your family or two of your friends (*My brother is taller than me. My sister is busier than my mother.*).
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the rules table on a card. Let them use only one-syllable adjectives in the card game.
Stronger students add *much* and *a bit*: *An elephant is much bigger than a horse.* They use *less* + long adjective: *A bicycle is less expensive than a car.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Comparison cards" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 1: Kasun's Postcard works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Comparison cards" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. Students use *than* after the comparative in their sentences. Students choose *-er* or *more* correctly.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the syllable clapping help with *-er* or *more*? Which spelling rules caused problems?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Kasun's Postcard
text: Dear Amma,
Nuwara Eliya is great! It's colder than Colombo, so I'm wearing my jumper every day. The town is smaller than Colombo and it's quieter too. There are fewer cars, so the air is better.
The tea plantations are more beautiful than in the photos. Lake Gregory is bigger than our lake at home. The hotel is more expensive than our hotel last year, but the food is better!
Tomorrow we're going to Horton Plains. Dad says the walk is longer and harder than the walk at Sigiriya. I'm happier here than in Colombo. It's not hotter, it's not busier, it's perfect!
Love, Kasun
**True (T) or False (F)?**
bullets: Nuwara Eliya is hotter than Colombo. ______
Nuwara Eliya is smaller than Colombo. ______
The hotel is cheaper than last year's hotel. ______
The walk at Horton Plains is longer than the walk at Sigiriya. ______
Kasun is happier in Nuwara Eliya. ______

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Write the comparative.**
**B. Write sentences with a comparative and than.**
bullets: my homework today / easy / my homework yesterday → ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Comparison Cards (cut up)
text: **Useful adjectives:** big · small · fast · slow · heavy · light · expensive · cheap · hot · cold · sweet · useful · interesting
**Write 4 sentences comparing your town with another town.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Superlative Adjectives, built round the theme "Record Breakers".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who use comparatives with than. They form superlatives without the (It is biggest), use more instead of most, and use of or than instead of in (the tallest of the world).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Record quiz" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Superlative Adjectives (the biggest, the most beautiful)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (world records fact file), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (record quiz), Handout 4 (class superlatives survey).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise superlative adjectives (the + -est / the most + adjective, the best / the worst) with in and of, and to contrast them with comparatives.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can ask and answer quiz questions such as What's the longest river in the world? and describe superlatives in their own lives.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read a short fact text for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a quiz and a class survey (the ... I've ever ... as a fixed phrase).

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

blocks.heading: Form: notes
bullets: **the + -est / the most + adjective**.
**in** + a place or group: *the tallest building* ***in*** *the world, the best student* ***in*** *the class*.
**of** + a period or number: *the hottest day* ***of*** *the year, the best* ***of*** *the three*.
*the ... I've ever ...* (fixed phrase): *It's the best film I've ever seen.*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Superlatives compare **one thing with all the others** in a group (three or more).
Comparatives compare **two** things.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *-est* is weak: /ɪst/: *tallest* /ˈtɔːlɪst/. *the* /ðə/ before consonants, /ði/ before vowels: *the oldest* /ði ˈəʊldɪst/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.*** Are we comparing two mountains or all mountains? (All mountains.) · Is there a higher mountain? (No.)
***K2 is higher than Mont Blanc.*** How many mountains? (Two.) Comparative or superlative? (Comparative.)

rows: more instead of most (the more beautiful).
Table with three columns side by side.
Two vs all the others; controlled practice mixes both.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: high · long · deep · old · heavy · fast · dangerous · popular · crowded · far

tall → taller → the tallest · big → bigger → the biggest · expensive → more expensive → the most expensive · good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · the + -est / the most + adj · in the world / in my class · of the year · the best film I've ever seen
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Superlative Adjectives, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To create interest and review comparatives.
Write *Sigiriya · Adam's Peak · Pidurutalagala* on the board. Ask: *"Which is higher: Sigiriya or Adam's Peak?"* (Adam's Peak.)
Ask: *"Which is the highest of the three?"* (Pidurutalagala.) Let students guess.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present superlatives in context and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the record facts. Which fact is the most surprising? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline all the superlatives. What comes before them? What comes after them?"* Pairs compare. Elicit *the* before; *in / of* after.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.* Ask the CCQs. Contrast with a comparative (two things).
**Form.** Build the three-column table on the board: adjective, comparative, superlative. Elicit the rules from the comparatives they already know.
**in / of.** Board *the highest mountain in the world* and *the hottest day of the year.* Board *of the world* ✗.
**the ... I've ever ...** Board *It's the best film I've ever seen.* Practise with two students.
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *the tallest, the oldest, the most dangerous, the best in the world.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: complete the table. Exercise B: comparative or superlative? Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use superlatives in a quiz and in personalised speaking.
**Record quiz (8 minutes).** Give out Handout 3. Teams complete the questions with superlatives and choose the answers. Then teams take turns to ask another team.
ICQs: *"First you write the question, then you ...?"* (Choose the answer.)

**Class superlatives (8 minutes).** Give out Handout 4. Students mingle and ask: *"What's the best film you've ever seen? What's the most delicious food you've ever eaten?"* They write names and answers.
Students report one interesting answer: *"Ravi says the best film he's ever seen is Spider-Man."* (2 minutes.)
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Ask: *"Two things: comparative or superlative? All the others?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a short paragraph (80 words) about your country's records: the highest mountain, the longest river, the biggest city, the most popular sport, the best food.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the three-column table during the quiz. In the survey, let them answer with short phrases.
Stronger students use *one of the + superlative + plural noun*: *Colombo is one of the busiest cities in Asia.* They use *the least*: *the least expensive restaurant*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Record quiz" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Record quiz" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise B. Students use *the* and *in / of* correctly in quiz questions. Students choose comparative or superlative correctly.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students remember *the*? Was the quiz motivating?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: World Records

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Comparisons with As ... As, built round the theme "Choosing a Phone".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who form comparatives and superlatives correctly but compare only with -er / more. They say very bigger, as big than and don't use not as ... as or less.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: (Not) As ... As, Modifiers and Less / The Least
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (phone comparison chart and reviews), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (product cards for three categories).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students work out and use (not) as + adjective + as, modifiers of comparatives (much, far, a lot, a bit, slightly), and less / the least, to make more precise comparisons.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can compare three products precisely and recommend one, e.g. The Nova is slightly cheaper than the Zeta, but its camera isn't nearly as good. The Lumo is by far the least expensive.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read product reviews for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in comparing and choosing products.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: The Nova is as fast as the Zeta.
not as / not so + adjective + as (= less)
The Lumo isn't as fast as the Zeta.
just as / nearly as / not nearly as / twice as
It's just as good. It isn't nearly as expensive. It's twice as heavy.
much / far / a lot + comparative (big difference)
The Zeta is much more expensive.
a bit / slightly / a little + comparative (small difference)
The Lumo is less expensive than the Nova.
The Lumo is the least expensive.
The Zeta is by far the best camera.
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: *not as ... as* is often more polite than a direct comparative: *My cooking isn't as good as yours* (softer than *Your cooking is better*).
Modifiers make comparisons precise (a big or small difference).
*less / the least* are mostly used with longer adjectives: *less expensive, the least comfortable* (with short adjectives we usually use *not as ... as*: *not as tall as*).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Weak *as* /əz/: *as fast as* /əz ˈfɑːst əz/.
Stress the modifier: *It's MUCH cheaper. It's SLIGHTly bigger.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The Lumo isn't as fast as the Zeta.*** Which phone is faster? (The Zeta.) · Are they the same? (No.)
***The Nova is slightly cheaper than the Zeta.*** Is the price difference big or small? (Small.)

rows: Board: much / far / a lot bigger; cross out very.
as ... than or as -er as (as bigger as).
Prefer not as tall as; note that less tall is possible but less common.
CCQs with a picture of two phones.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: battery · screen · camera · storage · price · weight · fast · light · heavy · reliable

as fast as /əz ˈfɑːst əz/ · It's MUCH cheaper. · SLIGHTly

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Comparisons with As ... As, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Ask: *"What's important when you choose a phone: the price, the camera, the battery?"* Pairs rank five features (2 minutes).
Take ideas and board key words.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target structures in context and help students work out their form and meaning.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Look at the chart and read the review. Which phone does the reviewer recommend for students? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the review and the chart. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Do you use the chart to check?"* (Yes.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Which is faster? Look at the chart."*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit answers and build the patterns in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Draw a scale for modifiers: *slightly / a bit → much / far / a lot*. Board *very bigger* ✗ and *as big than* ✗.
Show politeness: *Your phone isn't as new as mine* vs *My phone is newer than yours.*
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak *as* and stressed modifiers: *It isn't as fast as the Zeta. It's MUCH cheaper. It's SLIGHTly heavier.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite the sentences. Exercise B: correct the mistakes. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of three, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use precise comparisons fluently in a decision-making task.
Give each group a set of product cards (Handout 4). Each group chooses one category (laptops, bicycles or hotels in Kandy).
Groups compare the three products using at least eight structures from today and choose the best one for a given customer (10 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many products do you compare?"* (Three.) *"What do you decide?"* (The best one for the customer.)
Each group presents its recommendation in one minute: *"The Hilltop Inn isn't as cheap as the Lake View, but it's far quieter. The City Lodge is by far the least comfortable."* (6 minutes.)
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"How do you say there's a small difference? A big difference?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a short review (120 words) comparing three things you know well (phones, restaurants, cricket teams, films). Use at least six structures from today.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the patterns on a card. Ask them to compare two products instead of three.
Stronger students use *twice / three times as ... as* and *nowhere near as ... as*. They use *the + comparative + of the two*: *the cheaper of the two*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Product Cards works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The group recommendation uses at least eight different structures accurately. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. No *very* + comparative errors in the presentations.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use modifiers to make their comparisons precise? Did *not as ... as* appear naturally?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Phone Comparison
text: **REVIEW: Which phone should students buy?**

The Zeta X has by far the best camera, but it's the most expensive. The Nova 5 is slightly cheaper than the Zeta, and it's just as fast. Its battery lasts twice as long, but its camera isn't nearly as good. The Lumo A1 is much cheaper than the other two. It's less powerful and it isn't as fast as the Nova, but it's a bit lighter, and its battery is as good as the Nova's.
For most students, I recommend the Lumo. It's the least expensive phone, and it's good enough for messages and homework. If you love taking photos, save your money for the Zeta!
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Which phone has the best camera? ______________________________
Is the Nova faster than the Zeta? ______________________________
Which phone is the least expensive? ______________________________
Which phone does the reviewer recommend for most students? ______________________________

The Nova is **slightly cheaper than** the Zeta.
The Lumo is **much cheaper than** the other two.
The Lumo is **less powerful** and it's **the least expensive**.
The Zeta has **by far the best** camera.

In sentence 2, which phone is faster? ______________________________
What's the difference in price in sentence 3? In sentence 4? Which word shows a small difference? A big difference? ______________________________
What is the opposite of *more* and *the most*? ______________________________
What does *by far* add to a superlative? ______________________________

**B. Correct the mistakes.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Advanced Comparative Structures, built round the theme "Life Then and Now".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who use comparatives, superlatives, as ... as and modifiers accurately. They don't use double comparatives (the more ... the more) or progressive comparatives (more and more), and they compare adverbs inaccurately (He drives more careful).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Advanced Comparative Structures (the more ... the more, -er and -er, nowhere near as)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (interview: three generations), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (discussion cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of double comparatives (the + comparative ..., the + comparative), progressive comparatives (-er and -er, more and more), comparative adverbs, and emphatic structures (nowhere near / nothing like as ... as, considerably, a great deal).

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can discuss how life has changed over three generations, e.g. Life is getting faster and faster. The more technology we have, the less time we seem to have. Our grandparents' lives were nowhere near as stressful.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussing social change.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise the rhythm of double comparatives.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: the + comparative (+ clause), the + comparative (+ clause)
The more you practise, the better you get. The sooner, the better.
Prices are getting higher and higher. Life is becoming more and more stressful.
He drives more carefully than his father. She works harder than anyone.
nowhere near / nothing like + as ... as; considerably / a great deal / way (informal) + comparative
Life was nowhere near as busy. Phones are considerably cheaper now.
Rents are marginally lower this year.
the same as, similar to, different from, like
My life is completely different from my grandmother's.
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: Double comparatives show that two changes are connected: when one increases or decreases, the other changes too.
Progressive comparatives show continuous change over time.
Emphatic structures make comparisons stronger or more precise.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Double comparatives have a balanced rhythm with stress on both comparatives and a slight pause in the middle: *The MORE you practise, | the BETter you get.*
*more and more* /ˌmɔːr ən ˈmɔː/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The more you practise, the better you get.*** Are practising and getting better connected? (Yes.) · If you practise a little, do you get much better? (No.)
***Prices are getting higher and higher.*** Is this a single change or a continuous change? (Continuous.)

rows: Missing the in double comparatives (More you study, better you get).
Wrong word order (The more I study hard).
Contrast careful driver / drives more carefully.
Teach different from as the safest form in British English.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: generation · lifestyle · stressful · convenient · isolated · affordable · traditional · community

the + comparative ..., the + comparative ... · The more you earn, the more you spend. · The sooner, the better. · -er and -er / more and more + adj · He drives more carefully (adverb). · nowhere near / nothing like as ... as · considerably / a great deal + comparative · different from

blocks.heading: Procedure: Advanced Comparative Structures, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of change across generations.
Ask: *"How is your life different from your grandparents' lives when they were your age?"*
Pairs list three differences (2 minutes). Take ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the structures in context and clarify their form, meaning and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the interview with three generations of the same family. Who is the most positive about modern life? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline every comparison. Find a sentence with the ... the, a sentence with -er and -er and a sentence with nowhere near."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Double comparatives.** Board *The more you practise, the better you get.* Ask the CCQs. Elicit the pattern; show the short form *The sooner, the better.*
**Progressive comparatives.** Board *Prices are getting higher and higher.* and *Life is becoming more and more stressful.* Ask the CCQs.
**Adverbs.** Board *He drives more carefully than his father.* Contrast adjective and adverb.
**Emphatic structures.** Draw a scale: *marginally → considerably → nowhere near / nothing like.*
**Pronunciation.** Drill the rhythm: *The MORE you earn, | the MORE you spend. The SOONer, | the BETter.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Exercise A: join the ideas with the ... the. Exercise B: complete the sentences. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the structures fluently in discussion.
Give each group a set of discussion cards (Handout 4). Students take turns to read a card and give their opinion using at least one structure from today; others agree or disagree (10 minutes).
ICQs: *"Do you just answer, or do others respond too?"* (Others agree or disagree.)
**"The more ..., the more ..." chain (4 minutes).** Groups make a chain: *The more you use your phone, the less you sleep. → The less you sleep, the more tired you are. → The more tired you are, ...*
Groups share their longest chain (4 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which structure did you find most useful?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write an article (180 words): *Is life better now than in our grandparents' time?* Use at least two double comparatives, two progressive comparatives and two emphatic structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the patterns on a card. Provide sentence frames: *The more ..., the more ... · ... is getting ... and ...*
Stronger students use double comparatives with nouns: *The more money you have, the more problems you have.* They use *all the more* and *none the wiser*: *It made me all the more determined.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run ""The more ..., the more ..." chain" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Discussion Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for ""The more ..., the more ..." chain" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 5 out of 6 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A. In discussion, students use double and progressive comparatives accurately. Students use comparative adverbs (not adjectives) where needed.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students manage the word order in double comparatives? Did the discussion cards generate real disagreement?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Three Generations
text: **THEN AND NOW: one family, three views**

**Grandmother Sumana, 78:** "When I was young, life was nowhere near as busy as it is now. We didn't have much, but we had time for each other. Nowadays, everyone is getting busier and busier. The more things people buy, the less happy they seem."

**Father Nimal, 48:** "Life is considerably more comfortable now. Travel is easier, and phones are far cheaper than they were. But prices are getting higher and higher, and children spend less time outside. The more time my son spends on his phone, the less he talks to us!"

**Son Kavindu, 17:** "My life is completely different from my grandmother's. I can learn anything online, and the more I learn, the more I want to know. Technology is becoming more and more important. Maybe we're more stressed, but we're nothing like as isolated as people think: my friends are always online!"
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: According to Sumana, how has life changed? ______________________________
What does Nimal say about prices? ______________________________
What happens when Kavindu learns more? ______________________________
Who is the most positive about modern life? ______________________________
