hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Comparison in Formal and Academic Writing, built round the theme "Describing Data".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students preparing for IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 and university assignments. They describe data accurately but repetitively (more than ... more than ...) and make errors with multiples and proportions (two times more bigger, the double of), fewer / less, and comparisons of like with like (Japan's population is older than Sri Lanka).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking and writing
Grammar: Comparison in Formal and Academic Writing (twice as many as, compared with, inversion after than and as)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (chart and model description), Handout 2 (language analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (writing task: a second chart).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' range and accuracy in formal comparison: multiples and fractions (twice as many as, three times higher than, half as much as), compared with / in comparison to / relative to, whereas / while, the same structures with that of / those of, fewer / less, and formal inversion after than and as (than did ..., as does ...).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a 150-word description of a chart using at least eight different comparative structures accurately.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop the skill of selecting and comparing key features in data.
**Subsidiary aim.** To write a 150-word data description collaboratively.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: twice / three times + as + adj / many / much + as
Colombo received twice as many tourists as Kandy.
Prices were three times higher than in 2010.
half / a third / a quarter + as + adj / many / much + as
Galle had half as many visitors as Kandy.
compared with / to, in comparison with / to, relative to
Tourism grew in the south, whereas it fell in the north.
Japan's population is older than that of Sri Lanka.
Women spent more than did men. Tourism grew rapidly, as did hotel construction.
significantly, considerably, marginally, slightly + comparative; by far, by a wide margin
spending was significantly higher; by far the largest share
the highest proportion of, the lowest figure in
blocks.heading: Key structures
Meaning and use
bullets: These structures allow precise, varied and objective comparison of figures in academic and formal writing.
*that of / those of* avoids comparing unlike things (a population with a country).
Inversion after *than* and *as* is optional and formal; it sounds natural with longer subjects.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Not a focus; when presenting data aloud, stress the numbers and the comparative words: *TWICE as many visitors.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Colombo received twice as many tourists as Kandy.*** If Kandy received 100,000, how many did Colombo receive? (200,000.)
***Japan's population is older than that of Sri Lanka.*** What does *that* refer to? (The population.) · Why not *older than Sri Lanka*? (We compare populations, not a population and a country.)

rows: two times more bigger, the double of
Board the two multiple patterns; cross out errors.
Countable / uncountable reminder in the checklist.
Highlight that of / those of with arrows.
Inversion with the wrong auxiliary (than did women spent)
Board than did men (auxiliary + subject only).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: slightly · marginally · considerably · significantly · substantially · by far · by a wide margin

twice / three times as many / much as · three times higher than · half as many as · compared with / relative to · whereas / while · that of / those of · fewer + plural / less + uncountable · than did X / as did X
Like with like? · Countable or uncountable? · Varied structures? · Precise degree? · Data accurate?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Comparison in Formal and Academic Writing, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To activate language of comparison with numbers.
Board: *Kandy: 100 · Colombo: 200 · Galle: 50*. Ask: *"How many ways can you compare these numbers?"*
Pairs write three sentences (2 minutes). Take ideas and board the most varied ones.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present formal comparative structures in a model text and clarify their form and use.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Look at the chart and read the description. Is every statement accurate? Find one key feature."*
Pairs compare.
**Part B: Analysis (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"In groups, find the structures in the model and complete the table. Then answer the questions."*
ICQs: *"Where do you find the examples?"* (In the model description.)
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.
**Multiples and fractions.** Ask the CCQs. Cross out *two times more bigger* and *the double of*.
**Like with like.** Draw an arrow from *that in Kandy* to *spending*, and compare *Japan's population is older than that of Sri Lanka*.
**fewer / less.** Elicit examples from the chart.
**Inversion.** Board *Women spent more than did men* and *Tourism grew, as did hotel construction.* Point out that this is formal and optional.
Build the degree-word list and the checklist.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite each sentence using the word given. Exercise B: correct the errors. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To write an accurate and varied description of data.
Give out Handout 4. Say: *"Write a description of the chart (about 150 words). Select the key features and make comparisons. Use at least eight different structures from today."*
ICQs: *"Do you describe every number?"* (No, the key features.) *"How many structures?"* (At least eight.)
Pairs write (11 minutes).
Two pairs join, swap descriptions and check them with the checklist on the board: accuracy of data, like with like, *fewer / less*, variety (4 minutes).
Two groups read their best sentences aloud (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board strong sentences and two or three with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which structure will you use in your next exam essay?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Find a chart or table in a newspaper or report (or use one provided). Write a 170-word description using at least ten different comparative structures.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a pattern card with examples. Provide an opening sentence for the writing task: *The chart compares ...*
Stronger students use inversion after *than / as* and *by far / by a wide margin*. They add approximate language: *just under half, roughly twice as many, well over a third*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The description uses at least eight different comparative structures accurately. Data are reported accurately, with like compared with like. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students vary their comparisons? Was the *that of / those of* structure used correctly?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Chart and Model Description
text: **International visitors to three Sri Lankan cities (thousands)**
**Model description**
The table compares the number of international visitors to Colombo, Kandy and Galle in 2015 and 2024, together with average spending in 2024.

Colombo attracted the most visitors in both years, and by far the most in 2024, when its figure had doubled. Galle experienced the most dramatic growth: in 2024 it received four times as many visitors as in 2015, whereas Kandy's figure rose only slightly. As a result, Galle and Kandy received the same number of visitors in 2024, although in 2015 Galle had only a third as many as Kandy.

In terms of spending, the average Colombo visitor spent twice as much as the average visitor to Kandy. Spending in Galle was considerably higher than that in Kandy, as was its rate of growth. Overall, fewer visitors went to Kandy than to Colombo, and they spent less money.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Analysis
text: **Find an example of each structure in the model description.**
**Discuss.**
bullets: Why does the writer say *higher than that in Kandy* and not *higher than Kandy*? ______________________________
*as was its rate of growth*: what is the normal word order? ______________________________
Check the data: is *four times as many* accurate for Galle? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite each sentence using the word given. Keep the meaning the same.**
**B. Correct the errors.**
bullets: Kandy had 200 visitors. Colombo had 400. (twice) → Colombo had ______________________________
Prices in 2024 were 300% of prices in 2014. (times) → Prices in 2024 were ______________________________
Galle had 50 hotels. Kandy had 100. (half) → Galle had ______________________________
Men spent less than women. (did) → Women spent more ______________________________
Japan's population is older than Sri Lanka's population. (that) → Japan's population is older ______________________________
Exports rose in 2023. Imports also rose. (as) → Exports rose in 2023, ______________________________
Spending in 2024 was much higher than in 2015. (compared) → ______________________________, spending in 2024 was much higher.
The north received 10% of visitors. The south received 60%. (whereas) → ______________________________
Colombo had two times more bigger number of visitors. ______________________________
The salaries of doctors are higher than teachers. ______________________________
Women spent more than did women spend. ______________________________
Galle received the double of visitors. ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Writing Task
text: **Write a description of the chart (about 150 words). Select and compare the key features.**
**How students travel to school in two districts (% of students)**
**Your description:**

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B**
**Handout 4 (model description)**

The table compares how students in Colombo and Kurunegala travelled to school in 2014 and 2024. In both years, walking was by far the most common method in Kurunegala, whereas in Colombo the bus was the most popular. However, the proportion of Colombo students who walked halved over the decade, falling from 30% to 15%. Over the same period, the use of private cars in Colombo doubled, and school vans became considerably more popular, rising from 20% to 30%. In Kurunegala, changes were far less dramatic: the figure for walking fell by only ten percentage points, bus use remained unchanged, and van and car use each rose marginally to 15%. In 2024, the proportion of Colombo students travelling by van was twice that in Kurunegala. Overall, fewer students walked to school in both districts, and car use grew more quickly in Colombo than it did in Kurunegala.
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: by far the most (in 2024) · four times as many visitors as in 2015; twice as much as · a third as many as Kandy · whereas Kandy's figure rose only slightly · higher than that in Kandy · as was its rate of growth · fewer visitors · less money
To compare spending with spending (like with like), not spending with a city. · 2. *as its rate of growth was* · 3. Yes: 100,000 → 400,000.

twice as many visitors as Kandy. · 2. three times higher than in 2014 / three times as high as in 2014. · 3. half as many hotels as Kandy. · 4. than did men. · 5. than that of Sri Lanka. · 6. as did imports. · 7. Compared with / to 2015 · 8. The north received 10% of visitors, whereas the south received 60%. / Whereas the north received 10% of visitors, the south received 60%.

Colombo had twice as many visitors. / Colombo's number of visitors was twice as high. · 2. There were fewer tourists in 2020. · 3. The salaries of doctors are higher than those of teachers. · 4. Women spent more than men did. / Women spent more than did men. · 5. Galle received twice as many visitors.

than did men / than men did

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A1 lesson on Who, That and Which, built round the theme "What's the Word? Jobs and Objects".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** High beginners who know jobs and everyday objects and use the present simple. When they don't know a word, they can't describe it, or they use two sentences (He is a person. He helps sick people.). They use which for people.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Guessing game" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Who and That / Which for Describing People and Things
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Picture cards of jobs and objects, Handout 1 (picture dictionary definitions), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (guessing game cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise simple defining relative clauses with who (people) and that / which (things) to describe and define jobs and objects.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can define 6 jobs or objects, e.g. A pilot is a person who flies planes. A fridge is a thing that keeps food cold.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To review jobs and objects vocabulary.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop a useful communication strategy (describing a word you don't know).
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking through a guessing game.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: A doctor is a person who helps sick people.
A fridge is a thing that keeps food cold.
A library is a place where you can read books.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
bullets: **who** for people; **that** or **which** for things and animals.
The verb after *who / that* agrees with the noun: *a person who helps, people who help*.
Don't repeat the pronoun: *a person who* ***he*** *helps* ✗.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Relative clauses tell us **which** person or thing, or define a word: *A chef is a person who cooks in a restaurant.*
Useful when you don't know a word: *I need the thing that opens bottles!*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *who* /huː/ is weak and quick; *that* is weak /ðət/: *a thing that keeps* /ə θɪŋ ðət kiːps/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***A pilot is a person who flies planes.*** Is a pilot a person or a thing? (A person.) So *who* or *which*? (*Who*.) · What does a pilot do? (Flies planes.)
***A fridge is a thing that keeps food cold.*** Is a fridge a person? (No, a thing.) So *who* or *that*? (*That*.)

rows: Two columns on the board: people → who; things → that / which.
Repeating the pronoun (a person who he cooks).
Board the error and cross out he.
Model short definitions: noun + who / that + one verb phrase.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: doctor · pilot · farmer · chef · teacher · police officer · fridge · umbrella · key · bottle opener · clock · knife

PEOPLE: a person who + verb-s: A pilot is a person who flies planes. · THINGS: a thing that / which + verb-s: A fridge is a thing that keeps food cold. · not: a person which ✗ · not: a person who he ... ✗
who /huː/ · that /ðət/ · a thing that keeps /ə θɪŋ ðət kiːps/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Who, That and Which, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To activate vocabulary and introduce the idea of describing words.
Say: *"I'm thinking of a person. This person works in a hospital and helps sick people. Who is it?"* (A doctor / a nurse.)
Say: *"I'm thinking of a thing. It tells the time."* (A clock / a watch.)
Show the picture cards; students name them quickly.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context. To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**Part A: Context (8 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the definitions from a picture dictionary. Match each definition to a word."* (4 minutes.)
ICQs: *"Do you write the word or draw it?"* (Write the word.)
Pairs compare. Check as a class.
**Part B: Language clarification (12 minutes)**
**Meaning.** Board *A pilot is a person who flies planes.* Ask the CCQs. Underline *who flies planes*: *"This part tells us what a pilot does."*
**who / that / which.** Sort the definitions from the handout into two columns: people (*who*) and things (*that / which*). Board *a person which* ✗.
**Form.** Highlight the verb + -s after *who / that*. Board *a person who he cooks* ✗ and cross out *he*.
**A useful strategy.** Say: *"You don't know the word? Say: It's a thing that ... / It's a person who ..."* Model: *"I need the thing that opens bottles!"* (A bottle opener.)
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *a person who flies planes, a thing that keeps food cold.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: who or that? Exercise B: join the sentences. Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"People: who or that?"* (Who.)
Pairs check. Nominate students to read answers.

stages.name: Freer practice
text: **Aim:** To use relative clauses to describe words in a game.

**Guessing game (10 minutes).** Groups of four. Each student takes a card from Handout 3 and describes the word without saying it: *"It's a person who works in a school."* The group guesses. One point for the guesser and one for the describer.
ICQs: *"Can you say the word on the card?"* (No.)
**My own definitions (5 minutes).** Pairs write definitions for three new words (people or things in the classroom or at home) and read them to another pair to guess.
**Writing (3 minutes).** Students write their best three definitions at the bottom of Handout 3.
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Two pairs read their definitions; the class guesses.
Board four sentences from your notes (two with errors). Students correct them.
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write definitions for 6 words: 3 people (jobs or family members) and 3 things in your house.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students sentence frames: *It's a person who ... · It's a thing that ...* Give them cards with easier words (teacher, chair, phone).
Stronger students use *where* for places: *It's a place where you buy medicine.* They add a second clause: *It's a person who works in a hospital and who helps doctors.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Guessing game" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 3: Guessing Game Cards (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 3 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Guessing game" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 2. Students use *who* for people and *that / which* for things in the game. Students' definitions are clear enough for others to guess.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students use *who* and *that* correctly? Did they use the "It's a thing that ..." strategy naturally?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Picture Dictionary
text: **Match the definitions (1–6) to the words (a–f).**
**Which definitions are about people? Which are about things?**

rows: 2. a thing that keeps food cold
3. a person who grows rice and vegetables
4. a thing that tells the time
5. a person who cooks in a restaurant
6. a thing which keeps you dry in the rain

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Write who or that.**
**B. Join the sentences with who or that.**
bullets: A teacher is a person ______ helps students learn.
A key is a thing ______ opens a door.
A dentist is a person ______ looks after your teeth.
A phone is a thing ______ you use to call people.

A knife is a thing ______ cuts food.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Guessing Game Cards (cut up)
text: **Useful language:** *It's a person who ... · It's a thing that ... · You use it to ... · It's a job.*
**Write your best three definitions.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute A2 lesson on Defining Relative Clauses, built round the theme "My Favourite People and Places".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Elementary students who can define words with a person who and a thing that. They don't use where for places, they repeat the object (the book that I read it), and they don't know that the pronoun can be left out.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only "Pairs" of the two tasks in "Freer practice" and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Speaking
Grammar: Defining Relative Clauses (who, which, that, where; leaving out the pronoun)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (blog: My Favourite Things), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (personal survey), Handout 4 (sentence-joining cards).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise defining relative clauses with who, which, that (subject and object) and where, and leaving out the pronoun when it is the object.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe their favourite people, places and things, e.g. Kandy is the city where I was born. Amma is the person who makes the best curry. This is the song (that) I listen to every morning.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read a personal blog for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking about favourite people, places and things.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: She's the teacher who helped me.
It's the book which changed my life.
This is the café where we first met.
blocks.heading: Form

columns: Can we leave out the pronoun?
rows: the girl who lives next door
No: the girl lives next door ✗
blocks.heading: Subject or object?
Subject or object?: notes
bullets: Don't repeat the object: *the book that I read it* ✗.
*where* = *in which / at which*: *the town where I live*.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Defining relative clauses tell us **which** person, thing or place we mean. Without them, the sentence is incomplete or unclear: *That's the girl.* (Which girl?) *That's the girl who won the race.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *who, that, which* are weak in connected speech: *the girl who lives next door* /ðə ɡɜːl hu lɪvz/.
When the pronoun is left out, the clause follows the noun without a pause: *the film I watched*.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***This is the café where we first met.*** Is the café a person, a thing or a place? (A place.) So which word? (*where*.)
***That's the film I watched yesterday.*** Who watched the film? (I did.) Is *I* the subject of *watched*? (Yes.) · Can we add *that*? (Yes: *the film that I watched*.)

rows: Repeating the object (the book that I read it).
Board the error; cross out it.
Leaving out a subject pronoun (the girl lives next door is ...).
Test: Is there a new subject after the pronoun? If not, keep it.
which for places (the town which I live).
Board where for places + subject + verb.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: favourite · born · grow up · cheer me up · remind me of · relax · special
PEOPLE: who / that · THINGS: which / that · PLACES: where · SUBJECT: the girl who lives next door (keep who) · OBJECT: the film (that) I watched (leave out that) · not: the book that I read it ✗
the girl who lives /ðə ɡɜːl hu lɪvz/ · the film I watched (no pause)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Defining Relative Clauses, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To personalise the topic.
Show a photo (real or described) of your favourite place. Say: *"This is the beach where I go every weekend."*
Ask: *"What's your favourite place? Your favourite food?"* Pairs share (2 minutes).

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present defining relative clauses in context and clarify form, meaning and pronunciation.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Nethmi's blog. What is her favourite place? Who is her favourite person? Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Underline who, which, that and where. Circle the noun before each one: is it a person, a thing or a place?"* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**who / which / that / where.** Build the three columns on the board from the blog examples.
**Subject or object.** Board *the teacher who helped me* and *the song (that) I listen to*. Ask the CCQs. Show the test: if there is a new subject after the pronoun (*I*), you can leave it out.
Find a sentence in the blog without a pronoun (*the curry my grandmother makes*). Ask: *"Where's the pronoun? Can we add one?"*
**No repeated object.** Board *the book that I read it* ✗.
**Pronunciation.** Drill: *the girl who lives next door, the town where I was born, the film I watched.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Exercise A: choose the pronoun. Exercise B: can you leave it out? Exercise C: join the sentences. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then groups
text: **Aim:** To use defining relative clauses in personalised speaking and writing.
Give out Handout 3. Students complete the sentences about their own lives (5 minutes): *The place where I feel happiest is ... · The person who makes me laugh most is ...*
ICQs: *"Do you write about you or your partner?"* (About me.)
**Pairs (6 minutes).** Students share their answers and ask a follow-up question each time: *"Why is the beach the place where you feel happiest?"*
**Groups (5 minutes).** Students use the cards (Handout 4) to make a chain of definitions about their town: *Kandy is the city where ... The Temple of the Tooth is the place that ...*
Two students share their most interesting sentence (2 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences heard in Stage 4 (two with errors). Students correct them.
Ask: *"When can we leave out who or that?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a blog post (100 words): *My favourite things*. Use at least six relative clauses with *who, which, that* and *where*, and leave out the pronoun at least once.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the three-column table on a card. In Handout 3, let them complete only the first four sentences.
Stronger students use *whose* (preview): *She's the friend whose mother is a doctor.* They use prepositions at the end: *the friend I go to school with*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Pairs" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. Handout 4: Our Town (cut up) works read out from the front: learners note what they need rather than holding a card. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Pairs" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With young learners, cut the writing at the end and give that time to the speaking task; keep the drilling short, and let them draw or mime where the plan allows it. With adults, keep the writing and ask for a short spoken summary in place of anything drawn or mimed.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: 10 out of 12 or better on Handout 2. Students use *where* for places and leave out object pronouns correctly. No repeated objects in the written sentences.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students understand when the pronoun can be left out? Was the personal survey motivating?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: My Favourite Things
text: **Nethmi's Blog: My Favourite Things**
My favourite place is Unawatuna. It's the beach where my family goes every holiday. There's a small café there which sells the best mango juice in the world!
My favourite person is my grandmother. She's the person who taught me to cook. The curry my grandmother makes is better than any restaurant curry.
My favourite teacher is Mr Perera. He's the teacher who helped me with English when I was in Grade 6. He gave me a book that I still read every year: *Charlotte's Web*.
My favourite song is one that my brother wrote for me on my birthday. It's the song I listen to every morning!
**Answer the questions.**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B1 lesson on Non-defining Relative Clauses, built round the theme "Famous Sri Lankans".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Intermediate students who use defining relative clauses accurately. Their writing is choppy (many short sentences), and when they add extra information they use that after a comma (Kandy, that is ...), leave out commas, or don't know whose.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Non-defining Relative Clauses (commas, which, who, whose)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (two short biographies), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (fact files for the writing task).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students work out and use non-defining relative clauses (with commas, who, which, whose, where; not that; pronoun never omitted) and contrast them with defining clauses.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a short biography of a famous person using at least three non-defining relative clauses, e.g. Muttiah Muralitharan, who was born in Kandy, is the highest wicket-taker in Test cricket.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To read short biographies for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop writing by combining sentences into a fluent biography.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Yes: before and after (or before and full stop)
The player who took the most wickets is Muralitharan.
Muralitharan, who was born in Kandy, took 800 Test wickets.
blocks.heading: Defining vs non-defining
Pronouns in non-defining clauses
bullets: **who** (people), **which** (things), **where** (places), **whose** (possession: people or things).
*whose* + noun: *Kumar Sangakkara,* ***whose*** *father was a lawyer, studied law.*

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: Non-defining clauses are common in writing (biographies, news, descriptions) to add information smoothly.
The sentence still makes sense without the clause: *Muralitharan took 800 Test wickets.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: In speech, non-defining clauses are marked by pauses and a lower, faster voice: *Muralitharan, | who was born in Kandy, | took 800 wickets.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Muralitharan, who was born in Kandy, took 800 Test wickets.*** Do we know who Muralitharan is without the clause? (Yes.) · Is the information about Kandy essential or extra? (Extra.) · Can we use *that*? (No.)
***Sangakkara, whose father was a lawyer, studied law.*** Whose father was a lawyer? (Sangakkara's.)

rows: that in non-defining clauses (Kandy, that is ...).
Board the rule; cross out that after a comma.
"Remove it" test: if the sentence works without it, use commas.
Contrast who's = who is; whose = possession.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: was born · grew up · studied · became famous · won · retired · record · achievement

DEFINING (which one?): no commas, that OK, can omit object · NON-DEFINING (extra info): , who / which / where / whose ..., · no that · never omit · Remove test: sentence still OK → commas · whose + noun = possession
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Non-defining Relative Clauses, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To engage students and activate knowledge.
Board the names: *Muttiah Muralitharan, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, Kumar Sangakkara, Susanthika Jayasinghe*.
Ask: *"What do you know about these people?"* Pairs share facts (2 minutes). Take ideas.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present non-defining relative clauses in context and help students work out the rules.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the two biographies. Find one surprising fact in each. Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Finding the rules (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences. Answer the questions with your partner."*
ICQs: *"Alone or with a partner?"* (With a partner.)
Monitor. Ask stuck pairs: *"Cover the part between the commas. Does the sentence still make sense?"*
**Part C: Clarification (7 minutes)**
Elicit answers. Build the defining / non-defining contrast in the centre of the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis. Demonstrate the "remove it" test.
Highlight *whose*. Board *who's* vs *whose*.
**Pronunciation.** Read a sentence aloud with pauses and a lower voice for the extra information. Students repeat.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: add commas where necessary. Exercise B: join the sentences. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use non-defining relative clauses in writing a biography.
Give out Handout 4. Each pair chooses one fact file and writes a biography (about 100 words) using at least three non-defining relative clauses (10 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many non-defining clauses?"* (At least three.) *"Do you copy the notes?"* (No, write full sentences.)
**Read and guess (6 minutes).** Pairs read their biography to another pair without saying the name; the other pair guesses who it is.
Two pairs read their biographies to the class (2 minutes).
Monitor and note errors.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors (commas, *that*, *whose*).
Ask: *"How do you know when to use commas?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a biography (150 words) of a person you admire (famous or in your family). Use at least four non-defining relative clauses, including one with *whose*.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the rules on a card. Give them the first sentence of their biography.
Stronger students use *which* to refer to a whole clause: *He took 800 wickets, which is a world record.* They use *when* in non-defining clauses: *in 1996, when Sri Lanka won the World Cup*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Run "Read and guess" once, with two pairs reporting, rather than hearing every pair. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for "Read and guess" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The biography includes at least three accurate non-defining clauses with commas. No *that* in non-defining clauses. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the "remove it" test help students decide on commas? Was *whose* used correctly?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Biographies
text: **Muttiah Muralitharan** Muttiah Muralitharan, who was born in Kandy in 1972, is one of the greatest bowlers in the history of cricket. He went to St. Anthony's College, where he started bowling spin when he was 14. In 1996, he was part of the team that won the Cricket World Cup. Muralitharan, whose bowling action was very unusual, took 800 Test wickets, which is still a world record.

**Sirimavo Bandaranaike** Sirimavo Bandaranaike, whose husband was also prime minister, became the world's first female prime minister in 1960. She was born in Balangoda, which is in the Sabaragamuwa Province. She served three terms as prime minister. Her daughter, Chandrika, who later became president, continued her political work.
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Where did Muralitharan start bowling spin? ______________________________
What is still a world record? ______________________________
Why is Sirimavo Bandaranaike famous? ______________________________
Who later became president? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Focus
text: **Look at these sentences.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: Muttiah Muralitharan, **who was born in Kandy in 1972**, is one of the greatest bowlers.
He went to St. Anthony's College, **where he started bowling spin**.
He was part of the team **that won the Cricket World Cup**.
Muralitharan, **whose bowling action was very unusual**, took 800 Test wickets.
She was born in Balangoda, **which is in the Sabaragamuwa Province**.
Cover the bold part in sentence 1. Does the sentence still make sense? Do we know who Muralitharan is? ______________________________
Now cover the bold part in sentence 3. Do we know which team? Is the clause essential? ______________________________
Which sentences have commas? Which one doesn't? Why? ______________________________
Which sentence uses *that*? Do any of the sentences with commas use *that*? ______________________________
In sentence 4, what does *whose* mean? ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Add commas where necessary. Two sentences don't need commas.**
**B. Join the sentences with who, which, where or whose.**
bullets: My brother who lives in Dubai is an engineer. (I have only one brother.)
The students who passed the exam can go to the next level.
Galle which is on the south coast is famous for its fort.
The book that you lent me was fantastic.
My grandmother whose house is near the sea makes the best fish curry.
Kumar Sangakkara is a former captain. He studied law. → Kumar Sangakkara, ______________________________
Sigiriya is visited by thousands of tourists. It was built in the 5th century. → Sigiriya, ______________________________
I visited Jaffna. My father grew up there. → I visited Jaffna, ______________________________
My friend Ayesha is a singer. Her mother is a famous actress. → My friend Ayesha, ______________________________
The test was very difficult. It lasted three hours. → The test, ______________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Fact Files
text: **Fact file 1: Susanthika Jayasinghe**
**Fact file 2: Kumar Sangakkara**
**Fact file 3: Your choice**
A famous person from your country or town:
**Your biography (about 100 words):**

athlete; ran the 200 m
won a silver medal at the 2000 Sydney Olympics (later upgraded from bronze)
first Sri Lankan woman to win an Olympic medal
her family was poor; she trained without good equipment

went to Trinity College, Kandy; studied law

hero.text: A complete 60-minute B2 lesson on Prepositions in Relative Clauses, built round the theme "Writing a Travel Guide".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Upper-intermediate students who use defining and non-defining clauses accurately. They avoid prepositions in relative clauses or use them wrongly (the hotel which we stayed, the man to who I spoke), use what instead of which for whole clauses (He was late, what annoyed me), and their writing is wordy.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Prepositions in Relative Clauses, Sentence Relatives and Reduced Relative Clauses
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (travel guide extract), Handout 2 (language reference and practice), Handout 3 (further practice), Handout 4 (place notes for the writing task).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of prepositions in relative clauses (informal: the hotel we stayed in; formal: the hotel in which we stayed, to whom), sentence relatives with which, and reduced relative clauses with -ing and past participles (the road leading to the fort, a temple built in 1592).

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a 150-word travel guide entry using all three structures, e.g. The Fort, built by the Portuguese in 1588, is a place in which history comes alive. Visitors arriving early can enjoy the sunrise, which is unforgettable.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop concise, descriptive writing.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of register (formal / informal).

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: preposition at the end; pronoun often left out
the hotel (that) we stayed in · the friend (who) I went with
the hotel in which we stayed · the man to whom I spoke
the hotel in that ✗ · the man to who ✗
some / many / most / all / none of whom / which
200 people came, most of whom were tourists.
blocks.heading: Prepositions in relative clauses
Sentence relatives
bullets: *which* can refer to a **whole clause**, often to comment on it: *The train was late,* ***which*** *meant we missed the boat.* (not *what*)

blocks.heading: Reduced relative clauses
bullets: **Active** → *-ing*: *the road* ***that leads*** *to the fort* → *the road* ***leading*** *to the fort*.
**Passive** → past participle: *a temple* ***which was built*** *in 1592* → *a temple* ***built*** *in 1592*.
Common in guides, news and academic writing because they are concise.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Sentence relatives have a pause before *which* and a falling intonation: *We missed the boat, | which was a shame ↘.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The hotel in which we stayed was by the sea.*** Did we stay in the hotel? (Yes.) · Is this formal or informal? (Formal.) What's the informal version? (*the hotel we stayed in*.)
***The train was late, which meant we missed the boat.*** What does *which* refer to: the train or the fact that it was late? (The fact that it was late.)
***a temple built in 1592*** Did the temple build something? (No, it was built.) Active or passive meaning? (Passive.)

rows: Missing preposition (the hotel which we stayed).
Ask: "stay ___ a hotel?" Put the preposition back.
Board: after a preposition → whom / which only.
what for sentence relatives (..., what annoyed me).
Board which in colour; cross out what.
Active or passive? Test with which was / which is.
Discuss register: use end prepositions when speaking.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: ramparts · colonial · lighthouse · vibrant · spice · stroll · panoramic · bustling · overlooking

the hotel (that) we stayed in → the hotel in which we stayed · the man to whom I spoke · most of whom / some of which · ..., which meant ... (whole clause) · not: ..., what ... ✗ · the road that leads → the road leading · a temple which was built → a temple built
INFORMAL: end preposition · FORMAL: preposition + which / whom · NEVER: in that / to who

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Prepositions in Relative Clauses, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic and engage students.
Ask: *"Imagine a tourist asks you for the best place to visit in your town. What would you recommend? Why?"*
Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Take two or three recommendations.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present the structures in context and clarify their form, meaning and register.
**Part A: Reading (6 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the travel guide entry about Galle Fort. Would you like to visit? Find three things to do. Three minutes."*
Pairs compare. Students answer the four questions. Check as a class.
**Part B: Noticing (4 minutes)**
Say: *"Find: two relative clauses with a preposition, one sentence where which refers to a whole idea, and three -ing or -ed phrases that describe a noun."* Pairs compare.
**Part C: Clarification (10 minutes)**
**Prepositions.** Board *the hotel in which we stayed* and *the hotel we stayed in.* Ask the CCQs. Discuss register. Board *in that* ✗ and *to who* ✗.
**Quantity.** Board *most of whom were tourists*.
**Sentence relatives.** Board *The train was late, which meant we missed the boat.* Ask the CCQs. Board *what* ✗.
**Reduced clauses.** Expand *the road leading to the fort* → *the road that leads* and *a temple built in 1592* → *which was built*. Ask the CCQs.
**Pronunciation.** Drill the pause and fall: *We missed the boat, | which was a shame.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the reference box. Exercise A: rewrite in a formal style. Exercise B: reduce the relative clauses. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.
Fast finishers do Handout 3 (further practice); otherwise set it for homework.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the structures accurately in a piece of descriptive writing.

Give out Handout 4. Pairs choose one place and write a travel guide entry (about 150 words). They must use at least two prepositions in relative clauses, one sentence relative and three reduced relative clauses (11 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many reduced clauses?"* (At least three.) *"Formal or informal style?"* (Quite formal: it's a guide.)
Pairs swap with another pair and underline each structure. They suggest one improvement (4 minutes).
Two pairs read their entries aloud. The class votes for the place they most want to visit (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board sentences from Stage 4 (correct and incorrect). Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"How would you say 'the hotel in which we stayed' to a friend?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Complete Handout 3. Then write a travel guide entry (180 words) for a place in your town, using all the structures from today.
blocks.caption: PPP (presentation, practice, production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the reference table during the writing. Reduce the requirement to one of each structure.
Stronger students use *whereby*, *during which* and *by which time*. They use reduced clauses with *having + pp*: *Visitors, having explored the ramparts, can relax in a café.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 2: Language Focus and Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.
With teenagers, shorten the analysis and get to the task sooner. With adults in a work context, keep the forms exactly as they are and swap the lesson's theme for one from their own field.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The travel guide entry includes all three structures used accurately. No *in that / to who* or *..., what ...* errors. 6 out of 8 or better on Handout 2, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did students choose the right register for prepositions? Did the reduced clauses make the writing more concise?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Travel Guide Extract
text: **GALLE FORT: Where History Meets the Sea**

Galle Fort, built by the Portuguese in 1588 and later strengthened by the Dutch, is the town in which most visitors to the south coast spend at least a day. The narrow streets, lined with colonial houses, are full of cafés, boutiques and galleries.

Start your visit on the ramparts, from which you can see the whole bay. Visitors arriving early in the morning will see local fishermen at work, which is an unforgettable sight. The lighthouse, standing at the southern tip of the fort, is the most photographed building in Galle.
The Fort is home to around 400 families, most of whom have lived there for generations. Ask any of the shopkeepers you talk to, and they'll tell you stories about the history of their houses.
In the evening, walk along the walls as the sun goes down, which is the best time of day to be there.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute C1 lesson on Advanced Relative Structures, built round the theme "Pioneers and Innovations".

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: **Who it is for.** Advanced students who use all standard relative clauses accurately. In formal essays they rely on that / which / who, and they make errors with more complex structures (the thing what I need, the first woman who climb, a system which by people pay, how far that it works).

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis, the timed stages with the teacher's own words and instruction-checking questions, the differentiation, the printable handouts and the answer key.

items.definition: CEFR C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run "Freer practice" once through without the second round and cut "Feedback and wrap-up" to board-based error correction.
Writing
Grammar: Advanced Relative Structures (nominal relatives, relative infinitives, whereby, the extent to which)
PPP (presentation, practice, production)
Handout 1 (article: pioneers and innovations), Handout 2 (language analysis), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (essay task and planning notes).
About 10 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4, one per learner, and read the language analysis. The answer key is for you, not the class.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' use of advanced relative structures: nominal relative clauses (what, whatever, whoever), relative infinitive clauses (the first to ..., a place to stay, someone on whom to rely), connective relatives (whereby, in which case, by which time, at which point) and the extent / degree / way to which / in which.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can write a 150-word essay paragraph about an innovation using at least six advanced relative structures, e.g. What makes mobile banking revolutionary is the system whereby payments are made instantly. The extent to which it has changed rural life is remarkable.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop cohesion and concision in formal writing.
**Subsidiary aim.** To discuss innovation and its impact.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: What surprised me was the price.
Whoever designed this was a genius. Take whatever you need.
Relative infinitive (after superlatives, ordinals, only, next, last)
the first / last / only + noun + to-infinitive
She was the first woman to climb Everest from Sri Lanka.
noun + to-infinitive; noun + preposition + whom / which + to-infinitive (formal)
a place to stay; someone on whom to rely; a reason for which to fight
whereby (= by which); in which case; by which time; at which point
a system whereby users pay by phone; The bank may refuse, in which case ...
the extent / degree to which; the way in which
The extent to which this helped is unclear.
blocks.heading: Key structures
Accuracy notes
bullets: *what* is not used after a noun: *the thing* ***what*** *I need* ✗ → *the thing (that) I need* or *what I need*.
After *the first / the only*, use the infinitive, not a full clause with the wrong tense: *the first person to land* (or *who landed*).
*whereby* is formal and refers to a system, method or arrangement.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Nominal relatives used as subjects are often followed by a pause in speech: *What surprised me | was the price.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***What surprised me was the price.*** What does *what* mean here? (The thing that.) · What was surprising? (The price.)
***a system whereby users pay by phone*** What does *whereby* mean? (By which / through which.) · Is it formal or informal? (Formal.)
***She was the first Sri Lankan woman to climb Everest.*** Did she climb Everest? (Yes.) · Had any Sri Lankan woman done it before? (No.)

rows: Board: noun + that / which; OR what alone.
Tense errors with the first who
Teach the first + noun + to-infinitive as a chunk.
whereby overused or misused for places
Clumsy the extent to which sentences
Model: The extent to which X ... is unclear.
Students select four to master in their writing.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: pioneer · breakthrough · transform · access · revolutionise · widespread · rural · affordable

What + clause + is / was ... · whatever / whoever / wherever · the first / only / last + noun + to-inf · a place to stay · someone on whom to rely · whereby (= by which) · in which case · by which time · at which point · the extent to which / the way in which · not: the thing what ✗
emphasis (what ... was) · concision (to-inf) · cohesion (whereby, in which case) · precision (the extent to which)

blocks.heading: Procedure: Advanced Relative Structures, step by step

stages.name: Warm-up
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic and engage students.
Ask: *"Which invention of the last 30 years has changed life most in your country? Why?"*
Pairs discuss (2 minutes). Take two or three ideas and board one sentence exactly as a student says it.

stages.name: Presentation
text: **Aim:** To present advanced relative structures in an article and clarify their form, meaning and function.
**Part A: Reading (5 minutes)**
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read the article. Which pioneer do you find most inspiring? Why?"*
Pairs compare.
**Part B: Analysis (7 minutes)**
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"In groups, find the structures in the article and complete the table. Then answer the questions."*
ICQs: *"How many structures do you find?"* (Eight.) *"Where?"* (In the article.)
Monitor and help.
**Part C: Clarification (8 minutes)**
Feedback. Build the patterns in the centre of the board.
**Nominal relatives.** Board *What surprised me was the price.* Ask the CCQs. Board *the thing what* ✗. Show how *what ... was* gives emphasis.
**Relative infinitives.** Board *the first Sri Lankan woman to climb Everest* and *someone on whom to rely.* Ask the CCQs.
**Connective relatives.** Board *a system whereby users pay by phone* and *The bank may refuse, in which case ...* Ask the CCQs.
**Degree.** Board *The extent to which mobile banking has helped farmers is remarkable.*
Return to the student's sentence from Stage 1 and improve it with one structure.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.time: 10 minutes · Individual, then pairs, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Say: *"Exercise A: rewrite each sentence using the word given. Exercise B: correct the errors. Seven minutes."*
Pairs check. Check as a class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 18 minutes · Pairs, then groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To use the structures in a formal essay paragraph.

Give out Handout 4. Pairs choose one innovation from the notes (or their own) and write a 150-word essay paragraph evaluating its impact. They must use at least six structures from today (11 minutes).
ICQs: *"How many structures?"* (At least six.) *"Do you describe or evaluate?"* (Evaluate the impact.)
Two pairs join, read each other's paragraphs and underline the structures. They choose one sentence that could be more concise and rewrite it (4 minutes).
Two groups read their best sentences aloud (3 minutes).
Monitor and note language use.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board strong sentences and two or three with errors. Students correct the errors.
Ask: *"Which structure adds emphasis? Which makes writing more concise?"*
Set the homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 250-word essay: *Which innovation has had the greatest impact on your country?* Use at least eight advanced relative structures.

items.definition: Give weaker students a pattern card with examples. Provide sentence starters: *What makes ... important is ... · ... was the first ... to ... · ... is a system whereby ...*
Stronger students use *all of which, none of whom, the result of which* and *in the course of which*. They combine structures: *What remains unclear is the extent to which ...*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the pairwork in "Freer practice" in fixed pairs rather than a mingle, and take feedback from four or five pairs instead of the whole room. Monitor one half of the room during "Controlled practice" and the other half during "Freer practice".

Put the exercises from Handout 3: Practice on the board for learners to copy into their notebooks, and read any text aloud twice instead of printing it. The board plan above is this lesson's minimum - with that on the board, it runs on no paper at all.

Send Handouts 1 to 4 in the chat before the lesson and put the board plan on a shared slide. Use breakout rooms for the pairwork in "Freer practice" and visit each room once. Have learners type the controlled answers in the chat, so you see every answer at once instead of nominating.

With teenagers at this level, cut the academic framing and keep the examples in their own world; the forms do not change. With adults in a work context, swap the lesson's texts for ones from their own field and keep the analysis as it stands.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The paragraph uses at least six advanced relative structures accurately. No *the thing what* or incorrect *whereby* errors. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which structures did students use most naturally? Did the writing become more concise and cohesive?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Pioneers and Innovations
text: **SMALL IDEAS, BIG CHANGES**

What makes an innovation truly important is not its complexity but the extent to which it changes ordinary lives. Consider mobile money, a system whereby people send and receive payments using a basic phone. In rural areas, where banks are often hours away, it has become a lifeline. Whoever has a phone can now pay school fees, receive wages and save, which was unimaginable twenty years ago.

Another example is solar lanterns. For families with no electricity, there was often no safe way in which children could study after dark. Today, a lantern costing less than a pair of shoes gives them light to read by.

Pioneers matter too. In 2016, Jayanthi Kuru-Utumpala became the first Sri Lankan to climb Mount Everest. It was a climb on which there was no one on whom to rely but her team. She spent weeks acclimatising, by which time several climbers had already turned back.

What these stories show is that innovation is about access: giving people whatever they need to take control of their own lives. If the technology is too expensive, it will fail, in which case even the best idea changes nothing.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Language Analysis
text: **Find an example of each structure in the article.**
**Discuss.**
bullets: Rewrite *What makes an innovation truly important is ...* without *what*. Which version is more emphatic? ______________________________
What does *whereby* mean? Could you use *where* instead? ______________________________
*light to read by*: what is the full relative clause? ______________________________

rows: by which time / in which case

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite each sentence using the word given. Keep the meaning the same.**
**B. Correct the errors.**

Anyone who finds the keys should take them to reception. (Whoever) → ______________________________

I need someone I can rely on. (whom) → I need someone ______________________________
The thing what I need is more time. ______________________________
He was the only player who score twice. ______________________________
This is a hotel whereby you can see the sea. ______________________________
Whatever told you that was wrong. ______________________________
The extent which it worked is unclear. ______________________________

*... is a system whereby ...*
*The extent to which ... is ...*
*... was the first ... to ...*

text: **Handout 2**

**Common errors to watch for**

*The thing that makes an innovation truly important is ...*; the *what* version is more emphatic and concise. · 2. *by which / through which*; no, *where* refers to a place. · 3. *light which they can read by / by which they can read*.

blocks.heading: Task 1. First conditional
text: Complete with the present simple or will / won't.
Example: If it **rains** (rain), we **will stay** (stay) at home.
numbered: If you ________ (not hurry), you ________ (miss) the bus.
If she ________ (pass) the test, her parents ________ (be) very happy.
We ________ (not go) to the beach if the weather ________ (be) bad.

blocks.heading: Task 2. Second conditional
text: Complete with the past simple or would / wouldn't.
Example: If I **had** (have) more time, I **would learn** (learn) the guitar.
numbered: If I ________ (be) you, I ________ (talk) to the teacher.
She ________ (travel) more if she ________ (not have) a small child.
If we ________ (live) near the sea, we ________ (swim) every day.
They ________ (not complain) if the food ________ (be) better.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Which one?
text: Choose the first or the second conditional, and write the sentence. Ask yourself: is this a real possibility?
Example: (my bus is late most days) If the bus ________ late again, I ________ walk. → If the bus is late again, I will walk.
numbered: (I have no money for a trip) If I ________ (have) the money, I ________ (go) to Japan.
(there is a test next week) If I ________ (study) every evening, I ________ (pass) it.
(I am not the head teacher) If I ________ (be) the head teacher, I ________ (change) the timetable.
(rain is forecast for tomorrow) If it ________ (rain), the match ________ (be) cancelled.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Commas
text: Write each sentence the other way round, and punctuate it correctly.
Example: If I see her, I'll tell her. → I'll tell her if I see her.
numbered: If you need help, ask me. → ________________________
I would buy a bicycle if I lived closer. → ________________________
If we left now, we would arrive before dark. → ________________________
She'll be angry if you forget again. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn: give advice
text: Write advice for each problem using If I were you, I'd ... Then write one first conditional sentence about your own week.
bullets: A friend is always late for class. → ________________________
Your cousin wants to learn English quickly. → ________________________
Someone has lost their phone at school. → ________________________

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 don't hurry / will miss  2 will call / finish  3 passes / will be  4 won't go / is  5 will ... do / say
1 were / would talk  2 would travel / didn't have  3 lived / would swim  4 would ... say / asked  5 wouldn't complain / were

1 If I had the money, I would go to Japan. (unreal)  2 If I study every evening, I will pass it. (real)  3 If I were the head teacher, I would change the timetable. (unreal)  4 If it rains, the match will be cancelled. (real)

1 Ask me if you need help.  2 If I lived closer, I would buy a bicycle.  3 We would arrive before dark if we left now.  4 If you forget again, she'll be angry. (Comma only when the if-clause comes first.)
Answers will vary. Check: *If I were you, I'd* + base verb; and the first conditional sentence has a present tense after if, never will.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**The one to watch:** *will* after *if*. It is the most persistent mistake in the whole B1 syllabus, and it appears in Tasks 1, 3 and 5. One rule on the board beats twenty corrections.
**If I were or if I was:** *were* is the form expected in exams and in writing, and *was* is very common in speech. Teach *were*, and do not mark *was* wrong when a learner says it aloud.
**Task 3 is the thinking task.** Learners who can do Tasks 1 and 2 but not Task 3 have the forms without the meaning, which is exactly what to spend the next lesson on.
**Extension:** learners write three dilemmas of their own and swap them with a partner, who answers each with one conditional sentence.

blocks.title: Passive Voice · Level B1 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. The third form
text: Write the past participle of each verb.
Example: build → built

blocks.heading: Task 2. Complete the passive
text: Use the present or past simple passive of the verb in brackets.
Example: The bridge **was built** (build) in 1908.
numbered: Rice ________ (grow) in many parts of Asia.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Active to passive
text: Rewrite each sentence in the passive. Leave out the doer if it adds nothing.
Example: Somebody cleans the office every evening. → The office is cleaned every evening.
numbered: Farmers grow tea on these hills. → ________________________
Someone stole my phone at the station. → ________________________
The council checks the water twice a year. → ________________________
Millions of people watch this programme. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. With by, or without?
text: Decide whether the doer is worth keeping. Write the sentence with by ... or without it.
Example: The window was broken (by somebody). → The window was broken.
numbered: This novel was written (by a teenager). → ________________________
The room is cleaned (by a cleaner). → ________________________
The bridge is used (by thousands of drivers). → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Describe a process you know in six sentences: how something is made, grown, cooked or organised. Use the passive where the doer is not important.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: made, written, taken, grown, sent, repaired, spoken, found.
1 is grown  2 were sent  3 is cleaned  4 was stolen  5 are made  6 have not been published (or: were not published)  7 Were ... repaired

1 The school was built in 1975.  2 Tea is grown on these hills.  3 My phone was stolen at the station.  4 The water is checked twice a year.  5 This programme is watched by millions of people. (Here the doer is worth keeping.)

1 This novel was written by a teenager. (Keep: it is the surprise.)  2 The room is cleaned. (Drop: obvious.)  3 The bridge is used by thousands of drivers. (Keep: it is information.)  4 My car was repaired. (Drop: says nothing.)
Answers will vary. Check: be is present in every passive sentence, the participle is the third form, and by is used only where the doer matters.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**The one to watch:** the missing *be* (*the school built in 1975*) and the past simple used instead of the participle (*was build*). Both come from the same place - the passive needs two parts, and learners produce one.

**Task 2, item 6** accepts two answers. *Have not been published* is the present perfect passive and is what a fluent speaker would say with *yet*; *were not published* is acceptable at B1. Praise the first if it appears.
**Task 4 is the thinking task.** Learners who keep every *by* have the form but not the purpose, and that is what makes passive writing sound wrong.
**Extension:** learners rewrite a short paragraph from their coursebook in the passive and decide whether it is improved. Often it is not, and noticing that is the point.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Regular or irregular?
text: These verbs are from the story about Lina. Write R (regular) or I (irregular) next to each one. The first one is done for you.
Example: visited → R
bullets: got ____
caught ____
took ____
listened ____
read ____
arrived ____
cooked ____
walked ____
left ____
found ____
enjoyed ____

blocks.heading: Task 2. Write the past simple form
text: Write the past simple of each verb. Be careful with spelling.
Example: play → played

blocks.heading: Task 3. Complete the sentences
text: Use the past simple of the verb in brackets. Some sentences are negative or questions.
Example: I **watched** (watch) a film last night.
numbered: We ________ (not go) to school on Monday.
They ________ (not like) the food at the new café.
Kenji ________ (study) for his test all evening.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Three sounds
text: Say the verbs aloud. Write each one under the sound of its -ed ending.
bullets: Verbs to sort: watched, called, needed, cooked, listened, visited

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write five sentences about what you did yesterday. Use at least one negative. Then write two questions to ask a partner about their day.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: Regular: listened, arrived, cooked, walked, enjoyed. Irregular: got, caught, took, read, left, found.
watched, studied, stopped, arrived, went, had, saw, bought, made, wrote.
1 didn't go  2 Did ... see  3 bought  4 didn't like  5 did ... go  6 studied  7 stopped  8 didn't have
/t/: worked, watched, cooked. /d/: played, called, listened. /ɪd/: wanted, needed, visited.
Answers will vary. Check: past forms correct, didn't + base verb in negatives, did + subject + base verb in questions.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**Common mistakes:** *didn't went*, *did you saw*, *goed*, and saying walked as two syllables. Task 3 items 1, 4 and 8 and Task 4 target exactly these.
**Using it:** learners check Tasks 1 to 3 in pairs before you give the answers, so every learner explains at least one answer aloud.

hero.text: A printable present perfect worksheet for B1 learners: past participles, have and has, the contrast with the past simple, questions with ever, and a writing task about their own experiences. Full answer key and teacher's notes.
